It equals one minus one divided by the pressure ratio raised to the power gamma minus one over gamma, where gamma is the ratio of specific heats, about 1.4 for air. Increasing the pressure ratio therefore increases the ideal efficiency. For a pressure ratio of ten, the ideal efficiency is about 48 percent, and for a ratio of twenty it rises to about 58 percent.

However, efficiency is not the only consideration. The net work output per unit mass of air, which determines the size of the engine for a given power, depends on both the pressure ratio and the turbine inlet temperature, the highest temperature in the cycle. For a fixed turbine inlet temperature, the net work first increases as the pressure ratio rises and then decreases, because at very high pressure ratios the compressor work grows while the heat that can be added before reaching the temperature limit becomes small. The maximum net work occurs at an intermediate pressure ratio. Raising the turbine inlet temperature increases both efficiency and specific work, but it is limited by the ability of turbine blade materials to withstand high temperatures and stresses. Modern gas turbines use nickel-based superalloys, thermal barrier coatings, and internal air cooling of blades to allow turbine inlet temperatures well above the melting point of the blade material itself.

Real gas turbines differ from the ideal cycle because of irreversibilities. Compressors and turbines are not isentropic; friction, turbulence, and leakage cause losses, which are represented by isentropic efficiencies, typically around 80 to 90 percent. The compressor requires more work than the ideal value, and the turbine produces less. Pressure losses occur in the combustion chamber and ducts. A significant feature of gas turbines is the large back work ratio, the fraction of turbine work used to drive the compressor, which often ranges from forty to more than fifty percent. As a result, component inefficiencies have a strong effect on net output, and the development of practical gas turbines depended on achieving high compressor and turbine efficiencies.

Several modifications improve performance. Regeneration uses a heat exchanger, called a regenerator or recuperator, to transfer heat from the hot turbine exhaust to the compressed air before it enters the combustion chamber, reducing the fuel required. Regeneration is effective only when the exhaust temperature is higher than the compressor outlet temperature, which is typically the case at low pressure ratios. Intercooling cools the air between stages of compression, reducing compressor work, while reheating adds heat between turbine stages, increasing turbine work. These techniques increase net work and, when combined with regeneration, can improve efficiency.

The most important method of improving overall efficiency in power generation is the combined cycle. The exhaust gases of a gas turbine typically leave at temperatures of around 500 to 600 degrees Celsius, carrying substantial energy. In a combined cycle power plant, this exhaust passes through a heat recovery steam generator, where it produces steam to drive a steam turbine operating on the Rankine cycle. The combination of a high-temperature gas cycle and a lower-temperature steam cycle allows overall efficiencies of about 60 percent, higher than either cycle alone. Combined cycle plants fuelled by natural gas are widely used because of their high efficiency, relatively low emissions per unit of electricity, and flexibility.

In aircraft jet engines, the gas turbine is used to produce thrust. In a turbojet, the turbine extracts only enough work to drive the compressor, and the remaining energy accelerates the exhaust through a nozzle. Most modern airliners use turbofan engines, in which part of the energy drives a large fan that accelerates a large mass of air around the core, producing thrust more efficiently and quietly at subsonic speeds.
summary:
Gas turbines, used in aircraft, power stations, pipelines, and ships, offer high power-to-weight ratios, fast starts, and fuel flexibility, and are modelled by the Brayton cycle. A compressor raises air pressure, a combustion chamber burns fuel at nearly constant pressure, and a turbine expands the hot gas, driving the compressor and producing net work or jet thrust; the open cycle is analysed as an idealized closed cycle. The ideal air-standard cycle consists of isentropic compression, constant-pressure heat addition, isentropic expansion, and constant-pressure heat rejection.

Ideal efficiency, 1 − 1/r_p^((γ−1)/γ), depends only on pressure ratio, about 48% at 10 and 58% at 20, while specific net work peaks at an intermediate pressure ratio for a given turbine inlet temperature. Higher inlet temperatures raise efficiency and work but are limited by blade materials, addressed with superalloys, thermal barrier coatings, and blade cooling. Real engines have compressor and turbine isentropic efficiencies of about 80–90%, duct pressure losses, and large back work ratios of 40–50% or more, making component efficiency critical. Regeneration recovers exhaust heat when exhaust is hotter than compressed air, while intercooling and reheating increase net work. Combined cycle plants use 500–600 °C exhaust in a heat recovery steam generator for a Rankine steam cycle, reaching about 60% efficiency. Turbojets use leftover energy for nozzle thrust, while turbofans use a large fan for more efficient, quieter subsonic propulsion.

source_text:
Nonwoven fabrics are sheet or web structures made by bonding or interlocking fibres or filaments directly, without first converting them into yarns and then weaving or knitting them. This direct route from fibre to fabric makes nonwoven production fast and economical, and it allows properties to be engineered for specific uses. Nonwovens are used in an enormous range of products, including disposable hygiene items such as diapers and sanitary pads, medical gowns, surgical masks and drapes, wipes, filtration media, geotextiles for civil engineering, automotive insulation and carpets, roofing materials, agricultural covers, and interlinings in garments.

Nonwoven manufacturing generally involves three stages: forming a web of fibres, bonding the web to give it strength and integrity, and finishing. The choice of methods at each stage determines the structure and properties of the final fabric.

Web formation can be carried out by dry-laid, wet-laid, or polymer-laid methods. In dry-laid processes, staple fibres are first opened and blended and then formed into a web. Carding, using machinery similar to that used in spinning preparation, produces a thin web in which fibres are largely oriented in the machine direction; several webs may be layered by cross-lapping to increase thickness and improve strength in the cross direction. Air-laying disperses fibres in an air stream and collects them on a moving screen, producing a web with more random fibre orientation and greater bulk; it is used for absorbent products and for short fibres such as wood pulp. Wet-laid processes, derived from papermaking, disperse short fibres in water and deposit them on a moving screen, where the water drains away. Wet-laid nonwovens can be very uniform and are used for filters, tea bags, and specialty papers.

Polymer-laid processes, also called spun-laid processes, produce webs directly from polymer chips, combining fibre production and web formation in one continuous operation. In spunbonding, molten polymer, commonly polypropylene or polyester, is extruded through spinnerets to form continuous filaments, which are drawn by air to orient the molecules and increase strength, and then laid randomly on a moving conveyor. Spunbonded fabrics are strong and are used in hygiene products, geotextiles, and agricultural covers. In meltblowing, molten polymer is extruded through fine nozzles into a stream of high-velocity hot air, which attenuates it into very fine microfibres, often only a few micrometres in diameter, that are collected as a web. Meltblown webs have small pores and large surface areas, giving excellent filtration properties, though they are relatively weak. They form the critical filtration layer in many face masks and respirators. Composite structures such as spunbond-meltblown-spunbond, SMS, combine the strength of spunbond layers with the barrier properties of a meltblown core and are widely used in medical gowns and drapes.

Once formed, a web of loose fibres has little strength and must be bonded. Mechanical bonding entangles the fibres physically. In needle punching, barbed needles repeatedly penetrate the web, carrying fibres through its thickness and interlocking them. Needle-punched fabrics are relatively thick and dense and are used for geotextiles, carpets, felts, and automotive applications. In hydroentanglement, or spunlacing, fine high-pressure water jets entangle the fibres, producing soft, drapeable, cloth-like fabrics used for wipes and medical products. Stitch bonding uses stitches of yarn or the fibres themselves to reinforce the web.

Thermal bonding uses heat to fuse thermoplastic fibres. In calender bonding, the web passes between heated rollers, one of which is often engraved with a pattern so that bonding occurs at discrete points, maintaining flexibility. Through-air bonding passes hot air through the web, partially melting bicomponent or low-melt binder fibres to bond the structure while preserving loft, which suits hygiene product layers and insulation. Ultrasonic bonding uses high-frequency vibrations to generate localized heat. Chemical bonding applies a liquid binder, such as an acrylic or latex emulsion, by spraying, saturating, foaming, or printing, after which the web is dried and the binder cured. Chemical bonding allows a wide range of properties but requires handling and drying of chemicals.

Finishing processes adapt nonwovens to their end uses. They may include treatments to make fabrics hydrophilic, so that they absorb liquids, as required for diaper topsheets, or hydrophobic, so that they repel fluids, as required for barrier gowns. Other finishes provide antimicrobial properties, flame retardancy, antistatic behaviour, softness, or colour. Mechanical finishes such as embossing, laminating, coating, and cutting to size are also common. Electrostatic charging, called electret treatment, is applied to meltblown filter media to improve the capture of fine particles without increasing resistance to airflow.

Nonwovens are characterized by properties such as basis weight, measured in grams per square metre, thickness, tensile strength in the machine and cross directions, elongation, tear strength, air permeability, pore size, liquid absorption, and barrier performance. Because fibre orientation in many webs is not uniform, strength often differs between directions.

The nonwoven industry faces sustainability challenges because many products are disposable and made from petroleum-based polymers such as polypropylene. Efforts to reduce environmental impact include using biodegradable or bio-based fibres such as viscose, lyocell, cotton, and polylactic acid, increasing recycled content, reducing material weight, and designing products that can be recycled. Regulations on single-use plastics have increased interest in plastic-free wipes and other alternatives.
summary:
Nonwovens are fabrics made by bonding or interlocking fibres or filaments directly without yarn formation, enabling fast, economical, engineered production for hygiene products, medical gowns and masks, wipes, filters, geotextiles, automotive and roofing materials, agricultural covers, and interlinings. Production involves web formation, bonding, and finishing.

Dry-laid webs are carded and often cross-lapped or air-laid for random, bulky structures; wet-laid webs, derived from papermaking, give uniform filters and tea bags; and polymer-laid processes form webs directly from polymer. Spunbonding produces strong continuous-filament webs, meltblowing produces fine microfibre webs with excellent filtration for masks, and SMS composites combine strength and barrier properties for medical uses. Mechanical bonding includes needle punching for dense geotextiles and felts, hydroentanglement or spunlacing for soft wipes, and stitch bonding. Thermal bonding uses patterned calender rollers, through-air bonding of bicomponent fibres preserving loft, or ultrasonic heating, while chemical bonding applies and cures binders. Finishes provide hydrophilic or hydrophobic behaviour, antimicrobial, flame-retardant, antistatic, and softness properties, embossing, lamination, coating, and electret charging for filtration. Key properties include basis weight, thickness, directional tensile strength, elongation, tear, permeability, pore size, absorption, and barrier performance. Sustainability concerns about disposable polypropylene products drive use of bio-based fibres, recycled content, lighter weights, recyclable designs, and plastic-free alternatives.

topic: Phase I and Phase II Drug Metabolism
source_text:
Drug metabolism, also called biotransformation, is the chemical modification of drugs and other foreign compounds by enzymes in the body. Many drugs are lipophilic, which allows them to cross cell membranes and reach their sites of action, but the same property means that they are readily reabsorbed from the kidney tubules and would remain in the body for long periods if they were not modified. Metabolism generally converts lipophilic compounds into more polar, water-soluble metabolites that can be excreted in urine or bile. Although metabolism usually inactivates drugs, it can also produce active or even toxic metabolites. The liver is the main site of drug metabolism, but significant metabolism also occurs in the intestinal wall, kidneys, lungs, and other tissues.

Drug metabolism reactions are traditionally divided into two phases. Phase I reactions, often called functionalization reactions, introduce or expose a polar functional group, such as a hydroxyl, amino, or carboxyl group, on the drug molecule. Phase II reactions, called conjugation reactions, attach a large polar endogenous molecule to the drug or to its phase I metabolite. Many drugs undergo phase I followed by phase II metabolism, but some undergo only one phase, and the sequence is not always fixed.

The most important phase I reactions are oxidations, catalysed mainly by the cytochrome P450 enzymes, commonly abbreviated CYP. These are haem-containing enzymes located in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum of liver cells, in membrane fractions known as microsomes. CYP enzymes use molecular oxygen and electrons supplied by NADPH-cytochrome P450 reductase to insert one oxygen atom into the substrate, producing reactions such as aromatic and aliphatic hydroxylation, N- and O-dealkylation, and N-oxidation. The CYP enzymes form a large superfamily classified into families and subfamilies. A small number of isoforms are responsible for metabolizing most clinically used drugs. CYP3A4 is the most abundant in the liver and intestine and metabolizes roughly half of all drugs, including many calcium channel blockers, statins, and immunosuppressants. Other important isoforms include CYP2D6, which metabolizes many antidepressants, antipsychotics, and beta blockers and converts the prodrug codeine into morphine; CYP2C9, which metabolizes warfarin and several nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs; CYP2C19, which activates the antiplatelet drug clopidogrel; and CYP1A2, which metabolizes caffeine and theophylline. Other phase I reactions include reductions, such as reduction of nitro and azo groups, and hydrolysis of esters and amides by esterases and amidases, which is important for drugs such as aspirin and many local anaesthetics.

Phase II conjugation reactions are catalysed by transferase enzymes that combine the drug with an endogenous molecule. Glucuronidation, catalysed by UDP-glucuronosyltransferases, attaches glucuronic acid and is the most common conjugation pathway; it is important for drugs such as morphine and paracetamol. Sulfation, catalysed by sulfotransferases, adds a sulfate group. Acetylation, catalysed by N-acetyltransferases, adds an acetyl group to amines and hydrazines; drugs metabolized this way include isoniazid and some sulfonamides. Glutathione conjugation, catalysed by glutathione S-transferases, detoxifies reactive electrophilic compounds. Methylation and conjugation with amino acids such as glycine are also important for certain compounds. Most phase II products are more water-soluble and pharmacologically inactive, although there are exceptions; morphine-6-glucuronide, for example, is an active metabolite.

Metabolism can produce clinically important active and toxic metabolites. Prodrugs are administered in an inactive form and activated by metabolism; examples include enalapril, which is hydrolysed to the active enalaprilat, and clopidogrel. Paracetamol illustrates the formation of toxic metabolites. At therapeutic doses, most paracetamol is conjugated by glucuronidation and sulfation, and a small fraction is oxidized by CYP enzymes to a reactive metabolite, N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine, NAPQI, which is detoxified by conjugation with glutathione. In overdose, the conjugation pathways become saturated, more NAPQI is produced, glutathione is depleted, and the reactive metabolite damages liver cells. The antidote, acetylcysteine, works by replenishing glutathione.

Drugs that are extensively metabolized as they pass from the intestine through the liver before reaching the systemic circulation undergo first-pass metabolism, which reduces their oral bioavailability. Glyceryl trinitrate, for instance, is subject to such extensive first-pass metabolism that it is given sublingually to bypass the liver.

The activity of metabolizing enzymes varies considerably between individuals, causing differences in drug response. Genetic polymorphisms produce poor, intermediate, extensive or normal, and ultrarapid metabolizer phenotypes for enzymes such as CYP2D6 and CYP2C19. Poor metabolizers may accumulate drugs and experience toxicity, while ultrarapid metabolizers of CYP2D6 may convert codeine to morphine so quickly that they are at risk of opioid toxicity. Similarly, people classified as slow acetylators are more susceptible to certain adverse effects of isoniazid. Age also matters: neonates have immature metabolizing enzymes, and older people may have reduced hepatic blood flow and enzyme activity. Liver disease can impair metabolism, requiring dose adjustment.

Drug interactions frequently involve metabolism. Enzyme inducers, such as rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, and the herbal product St John's wort, increase the synthesis of CYP enzymes over days to weeks, accelerating the metabolism of other drugs and potentially causing therapeutic failure, as with oral contraceptives. Enzyme inhibitors, such as ketoconazole, clarithromycin, and grapefruit juice, which inhibits intestinal CYP3A4, reduce the metabolism of other drugs, increasing their concentrations and risk of toxicity. Understanding these pathways is essential for safe prescribing and for drug development.
summary:
Drug metabolism (biotransformation) enzymatically converts lipophilic drugs, which would otherwise be reabsorbed by the kidney, into polar, excretable metabolites, usually inactivating them but sometimes producing active or toxic products; the liver is the main site, with contributions from the intestine, kidneys, and lungs. Phase I functionalization introduces polar groups, and phase II conjugation attaches large endogenous molecules, often in sequence but not always.

Phase I is dominated by cytochrome P450 oxidations in liver microsomes using oxygen and NADPH-cytochrome P450 reductase, including hydroxylation, dealkylation, and N-oxidation. CYP3A4 metabolizes about half of drugs, CYP2D6 handles antidepressants, antipsychotics, beta blockers, and codeine activation, CYP2C9 warfarin and NSAIDs, CYP2C19 clopidogrel activation, and CYP1A2 caffeine and theophylline; reductions and ester or amide hydrolysis also occur. Phase II includes glucuronidation (morphine, paracetamol), sulfation, acetylation (isoniazid), glutathione conjugation of reactive compounds, methylation, and amino acid conjugation, with exceptions such as active morphine-6-glucuronide. Prodrugs such as enalapril and clopidogrel require activation, and paracetamol overdose saturates conjugation, producing NAPQI that depletes glutathione and damages the liver, treated with acetylcysteine. First-pass metabolism lowers oral bioavailability, so glyceryl trinitrate is given sublingually. Genetic polymorphisms create poor to ultrarapid metabolizers, such as CYP2D6 codeine risks and slow isoniazid acetylators, while age and liver disease alter metabolism. Inducers such as rifampicin and St John's wort cause therapeutic failure, and inhibitors such as ketoconazole, clarithromycin, and grapefruit juice increase toxicity.

source_text:
Growing microorganisms in the laboratory is fundamental to microbiology. Culturing allows microbiologists to isolate pathogens from clinical specimens, identify bacteria and fungi, test their susceptibility to antimicrobial drugs, study their physiology, monitor food and water quality, and produce microbial products. Successful cultivation requires two things: a medium that provides the nutrients and conditions the organism needs, and techniques that prevent contamination by unwanted microorganisms, known as aseptic technique.

A culture medium is a preparation of nutrients designed to support the growth of microorganisms. Media must supply a source of carbon and energy, nitrogen, minerals, water, and, for some organisms, growth factors such as vitamins and amino acids. The pH, osmotic conditions, and oxygen availability must also suit the organism. Media can be described by their physical state. Liquid media, called broths, are used to grow large numbers of cells and to study growth characteristics. Solid media are made by adding agar, a polysaccharide derived from red seaweed, usually at about 1.5 percent. Agar is ideal because few microorganisms can degrade it, it melts at around 85 to 100 degrees Celsius but solidifies only at about 32 to 40 degrees Celsius, so heat-sensitive supplements can be added and the medium poured before it sets, and it remains solid at incubation temperatures. Solid media allow microorganisms to grow as visible colonies, each typically derived from a single cell, which makes them essential for isolating pure cultures. Semisolid media containing lower agar concentrations are used to test motility.

Media are also classified by their chemical composition. Chemically defined, or synthetic, media have an exactly known composition and are used in research where precise nutrient control is required. Complex media contain ingredients of incompletely defined composition, such as peptones, which are protein digests, meat or yeast extracts, and blood, and they support the growth of a wide variety of organisms. Nutrient agar and tryptic soy agar are common general-purpose complex media.

Several functional types of media help in the isolation and identification of microorganisms. Enriched media contain additional nutrients, such as blood or serum, to support fastidious organisms with demanding growth requirements; chocolate agar, which contains blood heated to release nutrients, is used to grow organisms such as Haemophilus influenzae and Neisseria species. Selective media contain substances that inhibit the growth of some organisms while allowing others to grow. MacConkey agar contains bile salts and crystal violet, which inhibit most Gram-positive bacteria, allowing selective growth of Gram-negative enteric bacteria. Mannitol salt agar contains a high concentration of sodium chloride, which selects for salt-tolerant staphylococci. Differential media contain indicators that allow different organisms to be distinguished by the appearance of their colonies. MacConkey agar is also differential, because it contains lactose and a pH indicator: lactose-fermenting bacteria such as Escherichia coli produce acid and form pink colonies, while non-fermenters such as Salmonella form colourless colonies. Blood agar is differential for haemolysis, distinguishing beta-haemolytic organisms that completely lyse red cells, producing clear zones, from alpha-haemolytic organisms that produce partial greenish haemolysis and gamma or non-haemolytic organisms. Enrichment broths, such as selenite broth for Salmonella, increase the proportion of a target organism in a mixed sample before plating.

Aseptic technique comprises the practices used to prevent contamination of cultures, media, and sterile materials, and to protect laboratory workers and the environment. All media and equipment must first be sterilized. Media are commonly sterilized in an autoclave, using saturated steam under pressure at 121 degrees Celsius for about fifteen minutes or longer, depending on volume. Heat-sensitive solutions, such as some antibiotics and vitamins, are sterilized by membrane filtration and added to the cooled medium. Glassware may be sterilized by dry heat. Working surfaces are disinfected before and after use.

During handling, microbiologists minimize exposure of sterile items to the environment. Inoculating loops and needles made of metal wire are sterilized by heating them to redness in a Bunsen burner flame or by using an electric loop sterilizer, and allowed to cool before touching cultures. The mouths of tubes and bottles may be briefly passed through a flame after opening and before closing. Containers are opened for as short a time as possible and held at an angle to reduce airborne contamination, and lids of Petri dishes are lifted only partially. Work is often performed near a flame, which creates an upward air current, or in a biological safety cabinet, which uses filtered airflow to protect the sample, the worker, or both, depending on its class. Personal protective equipment such as laboratory coats and gloves, and practices such as not eating or drinking in the laboratory, protect workers.

Obtaining a pure culture, containing a single species, is a central goal. The streak plate method spreads an inoculum over the surface of an agar plate in successive sections, diluting the cells so that isolated colonies appear in the later sections. A well-isolated colony can then be picked and subcultured. The spread plate and pour plate methods distribute diluted samples over or within agar and are also used to count viable microorganisms, expressed as colony-forming units per millilitre, because each colony is assumed to arise from a single cell or cluster.

Incubation conditions must match the organism's requirements. Most human pathogens grow well at about 35 to 37 degrees Celsius. Aerobes require oxygen, while obligate anaerobes are killed by oxygen and must be grown in anaerobic jars or chambers that remove oxygen. Capnophilic organisms grow best with increased carbon dioxide, provided in candle jars or CO2 incubators. Not all microorganisms can be cultured using standard methods, and many environmental species remain uncultured, which has encouraged the development of culture-independent molecular techniques.
summary:
Culturing microorganisms is fundamental for isolating pathogens, identification, antimicrobial susceptibility testing, physiological study, food and water monitoring, and production, and requires suitable media and aseptic technique. Media supply carbon, energy, nitrogen, minerals, water, and growth factors under appropriate pH, osmotic, and oxygen conditions. Broths grow large populations, solid media use about 1.5% agar, which few microbes degrade and which melts at 85–100 °C but sets at 32–40 °C, enabling isolated colonies, and semisolid media test motility. Defined media have exact composition, while complex media such as nutrient and tryptic soy agar contain peptones and extracts.

Enriched media such as chocolate agar support fastidious organisms like Haemophilus and Neisseria; selective media such as MacConkey and mannitol salt agar inhibit unwanted organisms; differential media distinguish lactose fermenters (pink E. coli versus colourless Salmonella) and haemolysis types on blood agar; and enrichment broths such as selenite favour targets. Aseptic technique sterilizes media by autoclaving at 121 °C for about 15 minutes, filters heat-sensitive solutions, dry-heats glassware, and disinfects surfaces. Workers flame-sterilize and cool loops, flame tube mouths, minimize exposure, work near flames or in biological safety cabinets, and use protective equipment. Pure cultures are obtained by streak plating, while spread and pour plates count viable cells as CFU/mL. Incubation matches organism needs: about 35–37 °C for pathogens, anaerobic jars for obligate anaerobes, and CO2 for capnophiles, and many environmental species remain uncultured, motivating molecular methods.

source_text:
Antibodies are proteins produced by B lymphocytes that recognize and bind specific molecular structures, called antigens, with high precision. A single antigen, such as a bacterial protein, usually contains several distinct regions, called epitopes, that different antibodies can recognize. When an animal is immunized with an antigen, many different B-cell clones respond, and the resulting serum contains a mixture of antibodies that bind different epitopes with different affinities. Such polyclonal antibodies are useful, but their composition varies from one animal or batch to another. Monoclonal antibodies, by contrast, are identical antibodies produced by a single clone of cells, all recognizing the same epitope with the same affinity. Their uniformity, specificity, and potentially unlimited supply have made them among the most important tools in biomedical research, diagnostics, and therapy.

The difficulty in producing monoclonal antibodies was that normal antibody-producing B cells do not survive for long in culture. In 1975, Georges Köhler and César Milstein solved this problem by developing hybridoma technology, for which they shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1984. Their method fused antibody-producing B cells with myeloma cells, cancerous plasma cells that can divide indefinitely in culture. The resulting hybrid cells, called hybridomas, combined the antibody-producing capacity of the B cell with the immortality of the myeloma cell.

The classic procedure begins with immunizing a mouse with the antigen of interest, often with repeated booster doses to increase the number of B cells producing high-affinity antibodies. The animal's spleen, which is rich in B cells, is then removed, and the spleen cells are mixed with myeloma cells in the presence of a fusing agent, typically polyethylene glycol, which promotes the merging of cell membranes. Only a small fraction of cells fuse to form hybridomas, and the mixture also contains unfused spleen cells, unfused myeloma cells, and fused cells of the same type.

A selective medium is used to isolate the hybridomas. The myeloma cells used for fusion are chosen to lack the enzyme hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase, HGPRT. The cells are cultured in HAT medium, which contains hypoxanthine, aminopterin, and thymidine. Aminopterin blocks the main pathway for nucleotide synthesis, forcing cells to rely on an alternative salvage pathway that uses hypoxanthine and thymidine and requires HGPRT. Unfused myeloma cells, lacking HGPRT, cannot use the salvage pathway and die. Unfused spleen cells have HGPRT but cannot divide indefinitely and die naturally after a short time. Only hybridomas, which inherit HGPRT from the spleen cell and immortality from the myeloma cell, survive and multiply.

The surviving hybridomas are then screened to identify those producing antibodies against the desired antigen, commonly using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays, ELISA. Because a culture well may initially contain more than one hybridoma clone, positive cultures are cloned by limiting dilution, in which cells are diluted so that each well receives on average less than one cell, ensuring that the resulting population derives from a single cell. Selected clones are expanded and characterized for antibody specificity, affinity, and isotype. They can be grown in large-scale cell culture bioreactors to produce antibodies in quantity, and they can be frozen and stored for future use, providing a permanent source of the same antibody.

Monoclonal antibodies have many applications. In research, they are used to detect and localize proteins in cells and tissues through techniques such as Western blotting, immunohistochemistry, and immunofluorescence, and to separate cell types using flow cytometry. In diagnostics, they form the basis of many immunoassays, including pregnancy tests that detect human chorionic gonadotropin, rapid tests for infectious diseases, blood typing, and laboratory assays for hormones, drugs, and tumour markers. In therapy, monoclonal antibodies have become a major class of medicines used to treat cancers, autoimmune diseases, infectious diseases, and other conditions. They act through mechanisms such as blocking growth factor receptors, neutralizing inflammatory signalling molecules like tumour necrosis factor, marking cancer cells for destruction by the immune system, and inhibiting immune checkpoints that tumours use to evade immune attack.

The first therapeutic monoclonal antibodies were derived entirely from mice, but they had significant limitations when given to patients. The human immune system recognized the mouse proteins as foreign and produced human anti-mouse antibodies, which neutralized the therapy and could cause allergic reactions. Mouse antibodies also interacted poorly with human immune effector functions and were cleared rapidly. Genetic engineering has addressed these problems. Chimeric antibodies combine the antigen-binding variable regions of a mouse antibody with human constant regions. Humanized antibodies retain only the small complementarity-determining regions, the loops that directly contact the antigen, from the mouse antibody, grafted onto a human antibody framework. Fully human antibodies can be produced using transgenic mice whose antibody genes have been replaced by human genes, or by phage display, a technique in which libraries of antibody fragments are displayed on bacteriophages and selected for binding to the target. The international naming convention reflects these origins: therapeutic antibody names end in -mab, and earlier conventions used infixes such as -xi- for chimeric, -zu- for humanized, and -u- for fully human antibodies, as in rituximab, trastuzumab, and adalimumab.

Antibody engineering has produced further innovations. Antibody-drug conjugates link a monoclonal antibody to a potent cytotoxic drug, allowing targeted delivery to cells expressing a particular antigen. Bispecific antibodies are engineered to bind two different antigens simultaneously, for example linking cancer cells to T cells. Antibody fragments, which are smaller than complete antibodies, can penetrate tissues more readily.

Despite their success, monoclonal antibody therapies face challenges. They are large proteins that must usually be administered by injection or infusion. Their production in mammalian cell cultures is complex and expensive, contributing to high prices and limited access in many countries. Biosimilars, highly similar versions of approved biological medicines produced after patents expire, are helping to reduce costs. Monoclonal antibodies can also cause adverse effects, including infusion reactions and increased susceptibility to infections when they suppress immune functions.
summary:
Antibodies from B lymphocytes bind specific epitopes on antigens; immunization yields variable polyclonal mixtures, whereas monoclonal antibodies are identical products of a single clone with uniform specificity and affinity, making them vital for research, diagnostics, and therapy. Because normal B cells do not survive in culture, Köhler and Milstein (1975, Nobel Prize 1984) developed hybridoma technology, fusing antibody-producing B cells with immortal myeloma cells. A mouse is immunized, spleen cells are fused with myeloma cells using polyethylene glycol, and HAT medium selects hybridomas: HGPRT-deficient myeloma cells die because aminopterin forces use of the salvage pathway, unfused spleen cells die naturally, and hybridomas survive.

Hybridomas are screened by ELISA, cloned by limiting dilution, characterized, expanded in bioreactors, and frozen as permanent sources. Monoclonal antibodies are used in Western blotting, immunohistochemistry, immunofluorescence, and flow cytometry; in pregnancy tests, rapid infectious disease tests, blood typing, and immunoassays; and as therapies for cancer, autoimmune and infectious diseases by blocking receptors, neutralizing TNF, marking cells for destruction, and inhibiting immune checkpoints. Mouse antibodies provoked anti-mouse responses and poor effector function, so chimeric, humanized (CDR grafting), and fully human antibodies from transgenic mice or phage display were developed, reflected in names such as rituximab, trastuzumab, and adalimumab. Innovations include antibody-drug conjugates, bispecific antibodies, and fragments. Challenges include injection-only administration, expensive production and limited access, partly addressed by biosimilars, and adverse effects such as infusion reactions and infections.

A prosthesis is an artificial device that replaces a missing body part. Lower-limb prostheses replace part or all of a leg lost through amputation, which may result from vascular disease, often associated with diabetes, from trauma such as road accidents or industrial injuries, from cancer, or from congenital limb differences. Prosthetic technology aims to restore mobility, independence, and participation in daily activities, while ensuring comfort, safety, and acceptable appearance. Designing and fitting a lower-limb prosthesis is a multidisciplinary process involving surgeons, prosthetists, physiotherapists, engineers, and, most importantly, the user.

Lower-limb amputations are classified by level. Transtibial amputation, below the knee, preserves the knee joint, which greatly improves walking ability and reduces the energy required for walking. Transfemoral amputation, above the knee, removes the knee joint, so the prosthesis must replace both knee and ankle functions, and walking typically requires considerably more energy. Other levels include partial foot amputations, ankle disarticulation, knee disarticulation, and hip disarticulation. Generally, the more of the limb that is preserved, the more functional the outcome, because longer residual limbs provide better leverage and more surface area for load bearing and control.

A lower-limb prosthesis has several main components. The socket is the interface between the residual limb and the prosthesis and is often considered the most critical component. It must transmit body weight and forces during walking without causing pain, skin breakdown, or excessive movement. Sockets are custom-made for each individual, traditionally by taking a plaster cast of the residual limb and modifying the resulting model to load pressure-tolerant areas and relieve pressure-sensitive areas. Computer-aided design and manufacturing, using digital scanning and three-dimensional printing or carving, increasingly supports this process. In transtibial sockets, the patellar tendon-bearing design concentrates load on the tendon below the kneecap and other tolerant regions, while total surface-bearing designs distribute load more evenly over the whole residual limb. Transfemoral sockets include quadrilateral designs and ischial containment designs that capture part of the pelvis to improve stability.

Suspension systems hold the prosthesis securely on the residual limb. Options include straps and belts, suction systems that create a seal between the socket and the skin, silicone or gel liners with a pin that locks into the socket, and vacuum-assisted systems that actively remove air to maintain close contact. Liners also cushion the limb and reduce shear forces on the skin. Poor suspension causes the prosthesis to move relative to the limb, a problem called pistoning, which can lead to discomfort and skin injury.

Below the socket, a pylon, or shank, connects the socket to the foot and, in transfemoral prostheses, to the knee. Modular designs use standardized components that can be adjusted or replaced as the user's needs change. Alignment, the spatial relationship among the socket, knee, and foot, strongly affects stability, energy use, and gait quality, and it is adjusted by the prosthetist during fitting and gait training.

Prosthetic feet range from simple to highly sophisticated. The solid ankle cushion heel, or SACH, foot is inexpensive and durable and is widely used in low-resource settings, but it offers limited motion. Single-axis and multiaxial feet allow movement at the ankle, improving adaptation to uneven ground. Energy-storing and energy-returning feet, typically made from carbon fibre composites, deform under load during stance and release stored energy at push-off, improving walking efficiency for active users and enabling running in specialized designs. Microprocessor-controlled and powered ankles can adjust stiffness or actively generate push-off power, more closely replicating the function of the natural ankle.

Prosthetic knees for transfemoral users must provide stability during stance, when the limb bears weight, while allowing smooth flexion during swing. Simple single-axis knees may include manual locks for users who require maximum stability. Polycentric knees use multiple linkages to move the centre of rotation, increasing stability early in stance. Fluid-controlled knees use hydraulic or pneumatic cylinders to adjust resistance according to walking speed. Microprocessor-controlled knees use sensors to monitor knee angle, loading, and timing many times per second and automatically adjust resistance, improving stability on slopes and stairs and reducing the risk of falls.

Rehabilitation is as important as the device. After amputation, the residual limb must heal and its swelling must be controlled, often using compression bandages or shrinker socks. Users then receive training in donning the prosthesis, balance, walking, managing stairs and slopes, and caring for the skin. The energy cost of walking with a prosthesis is higher than normal, particularly for transfemoral users and for those with vascular disease, so cardiovascular fitness and strength are important. Psychological adjustment, including coping with changes in body image and phantom limb sensations or pain, requires support.

Several challenges affect access to prosthetic care. Advanced components are expensive, and many people in low- and middle-income countries lack access to trained prosthetists and appropriate devices. The residual limb changes in volume over time, requiring socket adjustments and replacements. Skin problems, discomfort, and poor socket fit are the most common reasons for prosthesis abandonment. Research directions include osseointegration, in which a metal implant is anchored directly into the bone and attached to the prosthesis without a socket; targeted muscle reinnervation and neural interfaces to provide intuitive control; sensory feedback systems; and low-cost, locally manufactured components designed for resource-limited settings.
summary:
Lower-limb prostheses replace legs lost through vascular disease (often diabetes), trauma, cancer, or congenital differences, aiming to restore mobility and independence through multidisciplinary care centred on the user. Transtibial amputation preserves the knee and reduces walking energy, whereas transfemoral amputation requires replacing knee and ankle function and demands more energy; preserving more limb generally improves function.

The custom socket is the critical interface, made from casts or digital scans and shaped to load tolerant areas, using patellar tendon-bearing or total surface-bearing transtibial designs and quadrilateral or ischial containment transfemoral designs. Suspension uses straps, suction, pin-locking silicone or gel liners, or vacuum systems to prevent pistoning. Modular pylons and careful alignment affect stability and gait. Feet range from durable SACH feet to single-axis and multiaxial feet, carbon-fibre energy-storing feet, and microprocessor or powered ankles. Knees include locking single-axis, polycentric, hydraulic or pneumatic fluid-controlled, and microprocessor-controlled designs that adjust resistance and reduce falls. Rehabilitation involves healing, swelling control, gait and skin-care training, fitness, and psychological support for body image and phantom pain. Barriers include cost, scarce prosthetists in low-resource settings, limb volume changes, and poor fit causing abandonment, while research explores osseointegration, targeted muscle reinnervation, neural interfaces, sensory feedback, and low-cost local manufacturing.

Tobacco use is the leading preventable cause of death worldwide. Smoking and other forms of tobacco use cause lung cancer and many other cancers, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, heart disease, stroke, and adverse pregnancy outcomes, and second-hand smoke harms non-smokers, including children. The World Health Organization estimates that tobacco kills more than eight million people each year, including over one million deaths from exposure to second-hand smoke. In South Asia, including Bangladesh, the burden includes not only cigarettes but also bidi, a cheap hand-rolled cigarette, and widespread use of smokeless tobacco products such as zarda, gul, and betel quid with tobacco, which cause oral cancers and other diseases.

Because tobacco is addictive and heavily marketed, individual education alone has limited effect. Public health experts emphasise comprehensive policy approaches that change the environment in which people decide whether to use tobacco. The WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control, FCTC, adopted in 2003 and entering into force in 2005, was the first international treaty negotiated under the auspices of WHO and has been ratified by most countries, including Bangladesh. It commits parties to evidence-based measures to reduce both the demand for and the supply of tobacco. To help countries implement the treaty, WHO introduced the MPOWER package, which summarizes six key measures.

The first measure, Monitor, involves tracking tobacco use and the effectiveness of prevention policies. Surveys such as the Global Adult Tobacco Survey and the Global Youth Tobacco Survey provide comparable data on prevalence, exposure to second-hand smoke, quit attempts, and exposure to marketing, allowing governments to set targets and evaluate progress.

The second measure, Protect, refers to protecting people from tobacco smoke through smoke-free laws covering indoor workplaces, public places, and public transport. There is no safe level of exposure to second-hand smoke, and designated smoking rooms and ventilation systems do not provide adequate protection, so comprehensive bans are recommended. Smoke-free laws reduce exposure among non-smokers, encourage smokers to cut down or quit, and contribute to changing social norms. Studies in several countries have found reductions in hospital admissions for heart attacks after the introduction of comprehensive smoke-free legislation.

The third measure, Offer, involves offering help to quit tobacco use. Most smokers want to stop, but nicotine dependence makes quitting difficult. Effective cessation support includes brief advice from health professionals, telephone quit lines, behavioural counselling, and pharmacotherapy such as nicotine replacement therapy, varenicline, and bupropion. Integrating cessation advice into primary health care allows large numbers of tobacco users to be reached.

The fourth measure, Warn, involves warning about the dangers of tobacco through health warnings on packages and mass media campaigns. Large graphic pictorial warnings, showing the health consequences of tobacco use, are more noticeable and effective than text-only warnings, particularly for people with low literacy. The FCTC guidelines recommend that warnings cover at least half of the principal display areas of packs. Plain or standardized packaging, which removes logos, colours, and promotional design and requires a uniform plain colour, has been introduced in a growing number of countries to reduce the appeal of packs and increase the effectiveness of warnings. Mass media campaigns can increase knowledge of risks and motivate quitting.

The fifth measure, Enforce, involves enforcing bans on tobacco advertising, promotion, and sponsorship. Tobacco marketing attracts new users, especially young people, and normalizes tobacco use. Partial bans are relatively ineffective because the industry shifts spending to permitted channels, so comprehensive bans covering direct and indirect advertising, point-of-sale displays, sponsorship of events, and online and social media promotion are recommended.

The sixth measure, Raise, refers to raising taxes on tobacco. Tobacco taxation is considered the single most effective and cost-effective tobacco control measure. Higher taxes increase prices, which reduces consumption, prevents initiation, and encourages quitting. Young people and low-income groups are particularly responsive to price increases, so taxes can reduce health inequalities. Evidence from many countries indicates that a ten percent increase in price reduces tobacco consumption by around four percent in high-income countries and by a larger amount in low- and middle-income countries. Taxes also generate revenue that can be used for health programmes. For maximum effectiveness, tax increases should exceed inflation and income growth so that tobacco becomes less affordable, and tax structures should minimize the price gap between cheap and expensive products, which otherwise allows users to switch to cheaper brands.

Additional supply-side measures include combating illicit trade through tracking and tracing systems, licensing retailers, prohibiting sales to minors, and supporting tobacco farmers in shifting to alternative livelihoods. The FCTC also requires parties to protect public health policies from the commercial interests of the tobacco industry, recognizing that the industry has historically opposed and delayed effective control measures.

Tobacco control faces continuing challenges. The industry adapts to regulations through new products and marketing strategies. Electronic nicotine delivery systems, including e-cigarettes, and heated tobacco products raise complex regulatory questions about their potential role in helping smokers quit versus the risk of attracting young people to nicotine use. In countries with large informal markets, enforcing regulations on loose cigarettes, bidi, and smokeless products is difficult. Nevertheless, comprehensive implementation of MPOWER measures has contributed to substantial declines in smoking prevalence in many countries, demonstrating that policy can significantly reduce the burden of tobacco-related disease.
summary:
Tobacco use is the leading preventable cause of death, causing cancers, COPD, heart disease, stroke, and pregnancy harm, with second-hand smoke also harming non-smokers; WHO estimates over eight million deaths yearly, and South Asia, including Bangladesh, also bears burdens from bidi and smokeless products such as zarda and gul. Because tobacco is addictive and heavily marketed, comprehensive policy is emphasised under the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (adopted 2003, in force 2005), implemented through the MPOWER package.

Monitor tracks use and policy impact through surveys such as GATS and GYTS. Protect requires comprehensive smoke-free laws, since no exposure level is safe and ventilation is inadequate, reducing exposure, encouraging quitting, and lowering heart attack admissions. Offer provides cessation support through brief advice, quit lines, counselling, and pharmacotherapy such as nicotine replacement, varenicline, and bupropion. Warn uses large pictorial warnings covering at least half of pack display areas, plain packaging, and mass media campaigns. Enforce requires comprehensive bans on advertising, promotion, sponsorship, point-of-sale displays, and online marketing. Raise taxes is the most effective measure: a 10% price rise cuts consumption by about 4% in high-income countries and more in low- and middle-income countries, especially among youth and the poor, and taxes should outpace inflation and income while narrowing price gaps. Supply measures address illicit trade, retail licensing, sales to minors, farmer livelihoods, and industry interference. Challenges include industry adaptation, e-cigarettes and heated products, and enforcement in informal markets, yet MPOWER has substantially reduced smoking prevalence.

Food additives are substances that are not normally consumed as foods themselves but are intentionally added to food for technological purposes during manufacturing, processing, preparation, packaging, transport, or storage. They have been used for centuries; salt, sugar, vinegar, and smoke have long been used to preserve foods, and natural colours such as turmeric and saffron have been used to enhance appearance. In modern food processing, a wide range of additives helps to keep foods safe, maintain their quality over longer periods, improve texture and appearance, and make it possible to produce the variety of convenient foods that consumers expect.

Food additives are classified according to their functions. Preservatives prevent or slow spoilage caused by microorganisms; examples include benzoates in acidic beverages, sorbates in cheese and baked goods, nitrites in cured meats, which also inhibit the dangerous bacterium Clostridium botulinum, and sulphites in dried fruits and wine. Antioxidants, such as ascorbic acid, tocopherols, butylated hydroxyanisole, and butylated hydroxytoluene, prevent oxidative deterioration of fats and oils, which would otherwise cause rancidity and off-flavours. Colours restore colour lost during processing or make foods more attractive; they include natural colours such as carotenoids, chlorophyll, and beetroot red, and synthetic dyes such as tartrazine and sunset yellow. Flavour enhancers, such as monosodium glutamate, intensify existing flavours, while flavourings add specific tastes or aromas. Sweeteners include high-intensity non-nutritive sweeteners such as aspartame, sucralose, and saccharin, which provide sweetness with few or no calories, and bulk sweeteners such as sorbitol.

Other categories modify texture and physical properties. Emulsifiers, such as lecithin and mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids, allow oil and water to mix and remain stable, as in mayonnaise, margarine, and ice cream. Stabilizers and thickeners, such as pectin, starches, gelatin, carrageenan, guar gum, and xanthan gum, increase viscosity, create gels, and prevent separation. Acidity regulators, such as citric acid and sodium bicarbonate, control the pH of foods, affecting flavour, safety, and stability. Raising agents release carbon dioxide to make baked goods rise. Anti-caking agents keep powdered products such as salt and milk powder free-flowing, humectants retain moisture, and flour treatment agents improve baking quality. Processing aids, such as certain enzymes and filtration agents, are used during processing but may not be present in significant amounts in the final product.

Because additives are consumed regularly over a lifetime, their safety must be evaluated scientifically before they are approved. At the international level, the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives, JECFA, evaluates the safety of additives based on toxicological data, including studies of absorption, metabolism, acute and chronic toxicity, reproductive and developmental toxicity, genotoxicity, and carcinogenicity, mainly from animal studies and, where available, human data. A key output of this assessment is the acceptable daily intake, ADI, defined as the amount of a substance, expressed in milligrams per kilogram of body weight, that can be consumed every day over a lifetime without appreciable health risk. The ADI is typically derived by identifying the highest dose at which no adverse effect was observed in the most sensitive relevant animal study, the no-observed-adverse-effect level, and dividing it by a safety factor, commonly 100, to account for differences between animals and humans and for variability among people. For some additives of very low toxicity, an ADI may be described as not specified.

Approval also requires that an additive have a demonstrated technological need, that it not mislead consumers, for example by disguising poor-quality ingredients, and that it be used at the lowest level necessary to achieve its function, a principle known as good manufacturing practice. The Codex Alimentarius Commission, established by FAO and WHO, sets international food standards, including the General Standard for Food Additives, which specifies which additives may be used in which food categories and at what maximum levels. National authorities establish their own regulations, often harmonized with Codex. In Bangladesh, food safety regulation is the responsibility of the Bangladesh Food Safety Authority, established under the Food Safety Act of 2013. In the European Union, approved additives are assigned E numbers, such as E330 for citric acid, and their use is listed in regulations.

Labelling is an important part of regulation, enabling consumers to make informed choices. Ingredient lists typically identify additives by their functional class and either name or code number, for example preservative followed by the specific substance. Certain additives must carry specific warnings; products containing aspartame, for instance, must indicate that they contain a source of phenylalanine, which is important for people with the inherited condition phenylketonuria.

Monitoring continues after approval. Authorities conduct dietary exposure assessments to ensure that intake, including by high consumers and vulnerable groups such as children, remains below the ADI. Additives may be re-evaluated when new scientific evidence emerges, and approvals may be revised or withdrawn. For example, some synthetic food colours have been subject to warning labels in Europe following studies suggesting possible effects on hyperactivity in some children, and some additives have been banned in certain countries.

Public concern about food additives is widespread, and many consumers prefer foods described as natural or free from additives. Scientific assessment, however, considers safety according to the substance and the dose rather than its origin; some natural substances can be harmful, and many synthetic additives have been extensively tested. A significant food safety problem in many low- and middle-income countries is not the regulated use of approved additives but the illegal adulteration of foods with unapproved substances, such as formalin used to preserve fish, calcium carbide used to ripen fruits artificially, and industrial dyes added to sweets and spices. Combating such adulteration requires effective inspection, laboratory testing, enforcement, and public awareness.
summary:
Food additives are substances intentionally added for technological purposes during manufacturing, processing, packaging, transport, or storage, ranging from traditional salt, sugar, vinegar, smoke, turmeric, and saffron to modern additives that ensure safety, extend shelf life, and improve texture, appearance, and convenience. Functional classes include preservatives such as benzoates, sorbates, nitrites that inhibit Clostridium botulinum, and sulphites; antioxidants such as ascorbic acid, tocopherols, BHA, and BHT; natural and synthetic colours; flavour enhancers such as MSG and flavourings; intense and bulk sweeteners; emulsifiers; stabilizers and thickeners; acidity regulators; raising, anti-caking, humectant, and flour treatment agents; and processing aids.

JECFA evaluates safety using toxicological data and sets an acceptable daily intake (ADI), usually the no-observed-adverse-effect level divided by a safety factor of 100, sometimes "not specified" for very low toxicity. Approval also requires technological need, no consumer deception, and use at the lowest effective level. Codex Alimentarius sets the General Standard for Food Additives, national authorities such as the Bangladesh Food Safety Authority (Food Safety Act 2013) regulate use, and the EU assigns E numbers. Labels list additives by function and name or code, with warnings such as phenylalanine for aspartame. Exposure assessments, re-evaluations, warnings for some colours, and bans maintain safety. Safety depends on substance and dose rather than natural or synthetic origin, and in many low- and middle-income countries the greater problem is illegal adulteration with formalin, calcium carbide, and industrial dyes, requiring inspection, testing, enforcement, and awareness.
