Islamic architecture refers to the architectural traditions that developed in regions where Islam became a major religion, from the seventh century onwards, extending across a vast area from Spain and North Africa through the Middle East and Central Asia to South Asia and Southeast Asia. It encompasses religious buildings, such as mosques, madrasas, mausoleums, and Sufi shrines, as well as palaces, fortresses, caravanserais, bazaars, bathhouses, gardens, and urban housing. Rather than being a single uniform style, Islamic architecture combines shared principles and building types with great regional diversity, as Muslim builders adapted local materials, climates, and earlier traditions such as Roman, Byzantine, Sasanian Persian, and Indian architecture.

The mosque is the central building type of Islamic architecture. Its essential requirements are relatively simple: a space for congregational prayer oriented towards Mecca. The direction of prayer, called the qibla, is marked by the qibla wall, in the centre of which is usually a niche called the mihrab. Next to the mihrab, larger mosques contain a minbar, a raised pulpit from which the imam delivers the Friday sermon. Many mosques include a courtyard, often with a fountain or basin for ritual ablutions performed before prayer, and one or more minarets, towers from which the call to prayer was traditionally made. The earliest mosques, including the house of the Prophet Muhammad in Medina, were simple courtyard enclosures with shaded prayer areas supported by palm trunks.

Several regional mosque plans developed. The hypostyle mosque, common in the early centuries, consists of a large prayer hall with a forest of columns supporting a flat roof, combined with a courtyard. The Great Mosque of Córdoba in Spain, begun in the eighth century, is a famous example, with its repeated double-tiered arches of alternating red brick and white stone. In Iran and Central Asia, the four-iwan plan became characteristic, in which a central courtyard is surrounded by four iwans, large vaulted halls open on one side, as in the Friday Mosque of Isfahan. Ottoman architects, most famously Mimar Sinan in the sixteenth century, developed central-domed mosques inspired partly by the Byzantine church of Hagia Sophia, creating vast, unified interior spaces under large domes supported by semi-domes and buttresses, as in the Süleymaniye Mosque in Istanbul. In South Asia, Mughal mosques combined large courtyards with prayer halls crowned by bulbous domes, flanked by minarets, as in the Jama Masjid in Delhi.

Islamic architecture made distinctive contributions in structural and decorative forms. The pointed arch, which distributes loads efficiently and allows greater flexibility in design, was widely used and later influenced Gothic architecture in Europe. Other arch types include the horseshoe arch, characteristic of the Islamic architecture of Spain and North Africa, and multifoil or lobed arches. Domes were constructed in many forms and sizes, and builders developed techniques for transitioning from a square base to a circular dome using squinches and pendentives. Muqarnas, a three-dimensional decorative system of small niche-like elements arranged in tiers, often described as honeycomb or stalactite vaulting, was used to decorate domes, portals, and transitional zones, creating complex effects of light and shadow.

Decoration is one of the most recognizable features of Islamic architecture. In religious contexts, Islamic tradition generally avoided figurative images of humans and animals, partly to prevent idolatry, which encouraged the development of non-figurative ornament. Three main types of decoration are prominent. Calligraphy, the art of beautiful writing, is used to inscribe verses from the Quran and other texts on buildings, in scripts such as the angular Kufic and the more flowing Thuluth, and it serves both decorative and spiritual purposes. Geometric patterns, based on complex interlocking polygons and star shapes generated from circles and grids, reflect a sophisticated understanding of geometry and are often interpreted as expressing the order and infinity of creation. Arabesque, or vegetal ornament, uses stylized, endlessly repeating plant forms such as scrolling vines and leaves. These patterns are executed in materials such as carved stucco, stone, wood, brick, and glazed ceramic tiles. The tilework of Iranian and Central Asian buildings, with brilliant blue, turquoise, and other colours, is particularly renowned.

Islamic architecture also includes notable traditions of secular buildings and landscapes. The Alhambra in Granada, a palace complex built mainly in the fourteenth century under the Nasrid dynasty, is celebrated for its courtyards, water channels, intricate stucco decoration, and muqarnas ceilings. Gardens were important elements of palaces and tombs. The chahar bagh, a quadripartite garden divided into four parts by water channels or paths, was associated with the Quranic imagery of paradise and was developed extensively in Persian and Mughal architecture. The Taj Mahal in Agra, built in the seventeenth century by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan as a mausoleum for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, places a white marble tomb at the end of a vast chahar bagh garden and is often regarded as one of the finest achievements of Mughal architecture, combining Persian, Indian, and Islamic elements.

Bengal developed a distinctive regional tradition of Islamic architecture. Because stone was scarce and the climate wet, mosques in the Bengal sultanate period, from the fourteenth to the sixteenth centuries, were often built of brick and decorated with terracotta panels of floral and geometric designs. Many adopted the curved cornice and roof forms derived from local thatched bamboo huts, as well as multiple small domes. The Sixty Dome Mosque in Bagerhat, built in the fifteenth century and now a UNESCO World Heritage Site in Bangladesh, has a large prayer hall covered by many domes supported on stone columns. Later Mughal buildings in Dhaka, such as Lalbagh Fort and the Star Mosque, with its later decoration of mosaic tiles, illustrate continuing development.

Islamic architecture was also strongly shaped by climate. Thick walls, inward-facing courtyards, shaded arcades, water features, and wind catchers, tall towers that capture breezes and direct them into buildings, as in Iran and the Gulf, helped moderate hot climates. Screens called mashrabiya or jali, made of carved wood or stone, allowed ventilation and light while providing privacy and shade. These climatic strategies have attracted renewed interest from contemporary architects seeking sustainable, regionally appropriate design.
summary:
Islamic architecture, developing from the seventh century across Spain, North Africa, the Middle East, Central Asia, South Asia, and Southeast Asia, includes mosques, madrasas, mausoleums, shrines, palaces, forts, caravanserais, bazaars, baths, gardens, and housing, combining shared types with regional adaptation of Roman, Byzantine, Sasanian, and Indian traditions. Mosques require a prayer space oriented to Mecca via the qibla wall and mihrab, with a minbar, courtyards with ablution fountains, and minarets, beginning with the Prophet's simple Medina house. Plans include hypostyle halls such as the Great Mosque of Córdoba, Iranian four-iwan courtyards as at Isfahan, Ottoman central domes by Mimar Sinan such as the Süleymaniye, and Mughal courtyard mosques like Delhi's Jama Masjid.

Structural innovations include pointed arches that influenced Gothic architecture, horseshoe and multifoil arches, domes with squinch and pendentive transitions, and honeycomb muqarnas. Religious avoidance of figurative imagery fostered Kufic and Thuluth Quranic calligraphy, geometric star patterns expressing order and infinity, and arabesque vegetal ornament in stucco, stone, wood, brick, and brilliant Iranian tilework. The Alhambra exemplifies palace courtyards and water, while chahar bagh paradise gardens frame the Taj Mahal. Bengal's sultanate mosques used brick, terracotta, curved hut-derived roofs, and many domes, as at the Sixty Dome Mosque in Bagerhat, followed by Mughal Lalbagh Fort and the Star Mosque in Dhaka. Climate strategies—thick walls, courtyards, arcades, water, wind catchers, and mashrabiya or jali screens—inspire contemporary sustainable design.

Systems of linear equations arise throughout science and engineering. Structural engineers solve them to find forces in trusses and frames, electrical engineers to determine currents and voltages in circuits, economists in input-output models, and computer programs in simulations, optimization, and data analysis. Such systems can be written in matrix form as A x equals b, where A is a square matrix of coefficients, x is the vector of unknowns, and b is the vector of constants. For small systems, methods such as substitution or Cramer's rule may be used, but these become impractical or inefficient for larger systems. Gaussian elimination is the standard direct method, and LU decomposition is an efficient way of organizing it, particularly when the same coefficient matrix must be used with many different right-hand sides.

Gaussian elimination transforms the system into an equivalent upper triangular system, in which all entries below the main diagonal are zero. It does so by subtracting suitable multiples of one row from rows below it, eliminating the unknowns one column at a time. The multiples used are called multipliers, and the diagonal element used to eliminate entries below it is called the pivot. Once the matrix is upper triangular, the unknowns can be found by back substitution, starting with the last equation, which contains only one unknown, and working upwards.

LU decomposition, also called LU factorization, expresses the matrix A as the product of two triangular matrices: a lower triangular matrix L, with zeros above the diagonal, and an upper triangular matrix U, with zeros below the diagonal. The matrix U is the upper triangular matrix produced by Gaussian elimination, and L records the multipliers used during elimination, placed below its diagonal. In the Doolittle form of the decomposition, the diagonal entries of L are all one; in the Crout form, the diagonal entries of U are all one instead.

For example, consider the matrix A with first row 2 and 1, and second row 4 and 3. To eliminate the entry 4 in the second row, the first row is multiplied by 2 and subtracted from the second row, giving a new second row of 0 and 1. The resulting upper triangular matrix U has rows 2 and 1, and 0 and 1. The multiplier 2 is placed in L, which has rows 1 and 0, and 2 and 1. Multiplying L by U reproduces the original matrix A.

Once A has been factorized, solving A x equals b involves two simple steps. Since A equals L U, the system becomes L U x equals b. Introducing an intermediate vector y equal to U x, one first solves L y equals b by forward substitution, starting from the first equation and working downwards, because L is lower triangular. One then solves U x equals y by back substitution. Each triangular solve requires a number of operations proportional to n squared for an n by n system, whereas the factorization itself requires about two thirds of n cubed operations.

The main advantage of LU decomposition appears when a system must be solved repeatedly with the same matrix but different right-hand sides, a common situation in engineering. In structural analysis, for example, the stiffness matrix of a building depends on its geometry and materials, while the load vector changes for different load cases such as dead load, wind, and earthquake loading. With LU decomposition, the expensive factorization is performed once, and each new load case requires only the inexpensive forward and back substitutions. The same idea is used in iterative methods and time-stepping simulations where the matrix stays constant. LU decomposition also provides a convenient way to compute the determinant of A, which equals the product of the diagonal entries of U when L has ones on its diagonal, and it can be used to compute the inverse of A by solving for each column of the identity matrix, although explicitly computing inverses is usually unnecessary and less efficient than solving systems directly.

Not every matrix can be factorized in this simple way. If a zero appears in a pivot position during elimination, the process fails, even though the system may have a unique solution. Small pivots also cause problems in computer arithmetic, because dividing by a very small number can magnify rounding errors and lead to inaccurate results. These issues are addressed by pivoting. In partial pivoting, before eliminating each column, the rows are rearranged so that the entry with the largest absolute value in the current column, among the remaining rows, becomes the pivot. The row interchanges are recorded in a permutation matrix P, and the decomposition becomes P A equals L U. Partial pivoting is used in almost all practical implementations because it greatly improves numerical stability. Complete pivoting, which also interchanges columns, offers further stability but is more costly and rarely necessary.

The accuracy of solutions also depends on the condition of the matrix. A matrix is ill-conditioned if small changes in its entries or in the right-hand side produce large changes in the solution. The condition number of a matrix measures this sensitivity; large condition numbers indicate that even a stable algorithm may produce solutions with significant errors when data contain small uncertainties. Recognizing ill-conditioning is important in interpreting numerical results.

Special forms of LU decomposition exist for particular classes of matrices. For symmetric positive definite matrices, which arise frequently in engineering and statistics, the Cholesky decomposition expresses A as L multiplied by the transpose of L. It requires about half the computation of general LU decomposition, needs no pivoting for stability, and is widely used in finite element analysis and in fitting statistical models. Tridiagonal systems, in which non-zero entries occur only on the main diagonal and the diagonals immediately above and below it, arise in discretized differential equations and can be solved very efficiently with a specialized version of LU decomposition known as the Thomas algorithm, which requires only a number of operations proportional to n. For large sparse matrices, in which most entries are zero, sparse LU methods reorder equations to limit the creation of new non-zero entries, called fill-in, during factorization.

LU decomposition is implemented in standard numerical libraries, such as LAPACK, and in software environments including MATLAB and Python's scientific libraries, where solving a linear system typically calls an LU-based routine internally. Understanding the method helps users interpret numerical results, choose efficient approaches for repeated solutions, and recognize when special structure in a matrix can be exploited.
summary:
Linear systems Ax = b arise in structural analysis, circuits, input-output economics, simulation, optimization, and data analysis, and Gaussian elimination is the standard direct method, reducing A to upper triangular form using multipliers and pivots before back substitution. LU decomposition factorizes A into a lower triangular L holding the multipliers and an upper triangular U from elimination, with Doolittle (unit diagonal L) and Crout (unit diagonal U) forms; in the example, A = [[2,1],[4,3]] gives U = [[2,1],[0,1]] and L = [[1,0],[2,1]].

Solving then uses forward substitution for Ly = b and back substitution for Ux = y, each about n² operations, after a factorization of about (2/3)n³, so it is efficient for repeated right-hand sides such as multiple structural load cases and constant-matrix simulations; it also gives the determinant as the product of U's diagonal and can produce inverses, though these are rarely needed. Zero or small pivots cause failure or error amplification, addressed by partial pivoting (PA = LU) and, rarely, complete pivoting, while ill-conditioning, measured by the condition number, limits accuracy even with stable algorithms. Cholesky decomposition (A = LLᵀ) halves the work for symmetric positive definite matrices without pivoting, the Thomas algorithm solves tridiagonal systems in O(n), and sparse LU reduces fill-in. LU methods underlie LAPACK, MATLAB, and Python solvers.

Many research questions concern relationships between categorical variables, variables whose values fall into distinct categories rather than being measured on a numerical scale. A public health researcher may ask whether smoking status is related to the presence of a respiratory disease, a marketer may ask whether product preference differs among age groups, and an educator may ask whether pass rates differ between teaching methods. Data on two categorical variables are commonly summarized in a contingency table, also called a cross-tabulation, in which rows represent categories of one variable, columns represent categories of the other, and each cell contains the number of observations, or frequency, with that combination of categories. The chi-square test of independence, developed from the work of Karl Pearson around 1900, is the most widely used method for testing whether two categorical variables are associated.

The test begins with a null hypothesis that the two variables are independent in the population, meaning that the distribution of one variable is the same across all categories of the other. The alternative hypothesis states that the variables are associated, that is, not independent. For example, if smoking status and respiratory disease are independent, the proportion of people with the disease should be the same among smokers and non-smokers, apart from random sampling variation.

The key idea of the test is to compare the observed frequencies in each cell with the frequencies that would be expected if the null hypothesis of independence were true. The expected frequency for each cell is calculated by multiplying the total for its row by the total for its column and dividing by the overall total number of observations. This formula follows from the definition of independence: if the variables are independent, the probability of an observation falling into a particular cell equals the product of the probabilities of falling into its row and its column.

Consider a study of 200 adults in which 80 are smokers and 120 are non-smokers, and 50 people in total have a respiratory disease. Suppose 30 smokers and 20 non-smokers have the disease. Under independence, the expected number of smokers with the disease is 80 multiplied by 50 divided by 200, which equals 20, while the expected number of non-smokers with the disease is 120 multiplied by 50 divided by 200, which equals 30. The observed numbers, 30 and 20, differ from these expected values, suggesting a possible association.

The chi-square statistic measures the overall discrepancy between observed and expected frequencies. For each cell, the difference between the observed and expected frequency is squared and divided by the expected frequency, and these values are summed over all cells. Squaring ensures that positive and negative differences do not cancel, and dividing by the expected frequency scales each difference relative to the size of the cell. If the observed frequencies are close to those expected under independence, the statistic will be small; large values indicate substantial departures from independence. In the smoking example, the four cells contribute values that sum to a chi-square statistic of about 8.33.

To determine whether the statistic is large enough to reject the null hypothesis, it is compared with the chi-square distribution. The relevant distribution depends on the degrees of freedom, which for a contingency table equal the number of rows minus one multiplied by the number of columns minus one. A table with two rows and two columns has one degree of freedom. The critical value for one degree of freedom at the 0.05 significance level is about 3.84. Because the calculated statistic of 8.33 exceeds this value, with a p-value of about 0.004, the null hypothesis of independence would be rejected, suggesting an association between smoking and respiratory disease in this sample.

The chi-square test relies on several assumptions. Observations must be independent, so each individual should contribute to only one cell, and the data should come from a random sample or random assignment. The data must be frequencies, not percentages or means. The test is based on a large-sample approximation, so expected frequencies must not be too small. A widely used guideline states that no expected frequency should be less than one and no more than twenty percent of expected frequencies should be less than five. When expected frequencies are small, particularly in two-by-two tables, Fisher's exact test, which calculates exact probabilities rather than relying on the chi-square approximation, is preferred. For two-by-two tables, Yates's continuity correction, which reduces each absolute difference by 0.5 before squaring, has sometimes been used to improve the approximation, although it is considered overly conservative by many statisticians. For paired or matched categorical data, such as measurements on the same individuals before and after an intervention, McNemar's test is appropriate instead.

A significant chi-square test indicates that an association exists but does not show its strength or direction, and with very large samples, even weak associations can be statistically significant. Measures of association are therefore reported alongside the test. For two-by-two tables, the phi coefficient measures the strength of association, and in epidemiology the relative risk and odds ratio describe the direction and size of the relationship. For larger tables, Cramér's V, which ranges from zero to one, provides a standardized measure of association. Examining standardized residuals, the differences between observed and expected frequencies scaled by their standard errors, identifies which cells contribute most to the overall association.

As with other statistical methods, association does not imply causation. An observed relationship between two categorical variables in observational data may be explained by a confounding variable related to both, and causal conclusions require careful study design and analysis. A related procedure, the chi-square goodness-of-fit test, compares the observed distribution of a single categorical variable with a hypothesized distribution, such as testing whether a die is fair or whether observed proportions of genotypes match those predicted by Mendelian genetics.
summary:
The chi-square test of independence, developed from Karl Pearson's work around 1900, assesses whether two categorical variables summarized in a contingency table are associated. The null hypothesis states that the variables are independent, so one variable's distribution is the same across the other's categories. Expected cell frequencies under independence equal row total × column total ÷ grand total; in the example of 200 adults (80 smokers, 50 with disease), expected diseased smokers and non-smokers are 20 and 30, compared with observed 30 and 20.

The statistic sums (observed − expected)²/expected across cells, giving about 8.33 in the example. It is compared with the chi-square distribution with (rows − 1)(columns − 1) degrees of freedom; for a 2×2 table, the 0.05 critical value is 3.84, so 8.33 (p ≈ 0.004) rejects independence. Assumptions include independent observations, frequency data, and adequate expected counts (none below 1 and no more than 20% below 5), with Fisher's exact test for small counts, Yates's correction sometimes used for 2×2 tables though often too conservative, and McNemar's test for paired data. Significance does not show strength or direction, so phi, relative risk, odds ratios, Cramér's V, and standardized residuals are reported. Association does not imply causation because of confounding, and the related goodness-of-fit test compares one variable's distribution with a hypothesis, such as die fairness or Mendelian ratios.

Theories of chemical bonding seek to explain why atoms combine, how strongly they are held together, and what properties the resulting molecules have. Simple models, such as Lewis structures and valence bond theory, describe bonds as pairs of electrons localized between two atoms. These models are useful but cannot explain certain observations. A notable example is oxygen. The Lewis structure of the oxygen molecule shows a double bond with all electrons paired, which predicts that oxygen should be diamagnetic, weakly repelled by a magnetic field. In fact, liquid oxygen is paramagnetic and is attracted to the poles of a strong magnet, indicating that it contains unpaired electrons. Molecular orbital theory, developed in the late 1920s and 1930s by Friedrich Hund, Robert Mulliken, and others, explains such observations by treating electrons as belonging to the molecule as a whole rather than to individual bonds.

In molecular orbital theory, atomic orbitals of the bonding atoms combine to form molecular orbitals, which extend over the entire molecule. A common approximation, called the linear combination of atomic orbitals, describes each molecular orbital as a sum or difference of atomic orbitals. When two atomic orbitals combine, they form two molecular orbitals. Constructive combination, in which the wave functions add in phase, produces a bonding molecular orbital with increased electron density between the nuclei. Electrons in this orbital attract both nuclei and hold them together, so the bonding orbital is lower in energy than the original atomic orbitals. Destructive combination, in which the wave functions are out of phase, produces an antibonding molecular orbital, usually marked with an asterisk, which has a node, a region of zero electron density, between the nuclei. Electrons in antibonding orbitals destabilize the molecule, and the antibonding orbital is higher in energy than the original atomic orbitals. The number of molecular orbitals formed always equals the number of atomic orbitals combined.

Molecular orbitals are classified by their symmetry. Sigma orbitals are symmetrical around the axis joining the two nuclei, and they are formed by head-on overlap of s orbitals or of p orbitals pointing along the bond axis. Pi orbitals are formed by side-by-side overlap of p orbitals perpendicular to the bond axis, and they have electron density above and below the axis, with a nodal plane containing the axis. Electrons fill molecular orbitals according to the same rules that govern atomic orbitals: the Aufbau principle, filling the lowest energy orbitals first; the Pauli exclusion principle, allowing at most two electrons with opposite spins in each orbital; and Hund's rule, placing electrons singly in orbitals of equal energy before pairing them.

The stability of a molecule can be assessed using bond order, defined as one half of the difference between the number of electrons in bonding orbitals and the number in antibonding orbitals. A bond order of one corresponds to a single bond, two to a double bond, and three to a triple bond. A higher bond order generally indicates a stronger and shorter bond, and a bond order of zero suggests that the molecule is not stable. The hydrogen molecule provides the simplest example. Two hydrogen 1s orbitals combine to form a sigma bonding orbital and a sigma antibonding orbital. The two electrons occupy the bonding orbital, giving a bond order of one, consistent with a stable single bond. For a hypothetical helium molecule, He2, four electrons would fill both the bonding and antibonding orbitals, giving a bond order of zero, which explains why helium exists as separate atoms. The helium ion He2+, with three electrons, would have a bond order of one half and is observed in the gas phase as a weakly bound species.

For diatomic molecules of second-period elements, the 2s and 2p atomic orbitals combine to form a set of molecular orbitals: sigma 2s and sigma star 2s; a sigma 2p orbital formed from p orbitals along the bond axis; two degenerate pi 2p orbitals; and their corresponding antibonding orbitals, two pi star 2p orbitals and a sigma star 2p orbital. The relative order of the sigma 2p and pi 2p orbitals depends on the element. For oxygen, fluorine, and neon, the sigma 2p orbital lies below the pi 2p orbitals. For lithium through nitrogen, interaction between 2s and 2p orbitals raises the energy of the sigma 2p orbital above that of the pi 2p orbitals.

Applying this diagram to oxygen explains its paramagnetism. The oxygen molecule has twelve valence electrons. After filling the sigma 2s, sigma star 2s, sigma 2p, and the two pi 2p orbitals, two electrons remain. These occupy the two degenerate pi star 2p orbitals, one in each, with parallel spins according to Hund's rule. The presence of two unpaired electrons accounts for the paramagnetism of oxygen. The bond order is one half of eight bonding electrons minus four antibonding electrons, which equals two, consistent with the double bond length and strength observed experimentally. The theory also explains trends among related species. Removing an electron from an antibonding orbital to form the dioxygenyl cation, O2+, increases the bond order to 2.5, producing a shorter and stronger bond, while adding electrons to form superoxide and peroxide ions lowers the bond order. Nitrogen, with ten valence electrons, has all its electrons paired and a bond order of three, explaining the exceptional strength and stability of the nitrogen triple bond.

Molecular orbital theory extends to more complex molecules. In molecules such as benzene, the pi electrons occupy molecular orbitals delocalized over the entire ring rather than in alternating single and double bonds, which explains benzene's equal carbon-carbon bond lengths and unusual stability, often described as aromaticity. In heteronuclear diatomic molecules, such as carbon monoxide and hydrogen fluoride, atomic orbitals of different energies combine unequally, and the bonding orbitals have greater contributions from the more electronegative atom, reflecting bond polarity. The highest occupied molecular orbital, HOMO, and the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital, LUMO, are central to understanding chemical reactivity and the absorption of light, because many reactions involve interactions between the HOMO of one molecule and the LUMO of another, and the energy gap between them influences the colours of compounds. In solids, the combination of very large numbers of atomic orbitals produces bands of closely spaced energy levels, forming the basis of band theory, which explains the electrical properties of metals, semiconductors, and insulators.

Molecular orbital theory is more mathematically complex than localized bonding models, and for many purposes chemists continue to use Lewis structures, VSEPR theory, and hybridization because they are simpler and give useful predictions. Molecular orbital calculations, however, form the basis of modern computational chemistry, which allows the structures, energies, and properties of molecules to be predicted with considerable accuracy.
summary:
Molecular orbital (MO) theory, developed by Hund, Mulliken, and others in the late 1920s–1930s, treats electrons as belonging to the whole molecule and explains observations that localized Lewis and valence bond models cannot, such as the paramagnetism of liquid oxygen. Using linear combinations of atomic orbitals, in-phase combination forms lower-energy bonding orbitals that concentrate density between nuclei, while out-of-phase combination forms higher-energy antibonding orbitals with nodes; the number of molecular orbitals equals the atomic orbitals combined. Sigma orbitals are symmetric about the bond axis, pi orbitals arise from side-by-side p overlap, and filling follows the Aufbau principle, Pauli exclusion, and Hund's rule.

Bond order, half the difference between bonding and antibonding electrons, indicates strength: H2 has bond order 1, He2 has 0 and does not exist, and He2⁺ has ½. Second-period diatomics use σ2s, σ*2s, σ2p, two π2p, two π*2p, and σ*2p orbitals, with σ2p below π2p for O, F, and Ne but above for Li through N. In O2, two unpaired electrons in degenerate π* orbitals explain paramagnetism with bond order 2; O2⁺ has bond order 2.5 while superoxide and peroxide have lower orders, and N2's bond order of 3 explains its stability. Delocalized pi orbitals explain benzene's aromaticity, unequal contributions explain polarity in CO and HF, HOMO-LUMO interactions explain reactivity and colour, and orbital bands explain conductivity in solids. MO theory is more complex than Lewis, VSEPR, and hybridization models but underpins modern computational chemistry.

Gases are composed of enormous numbers of molecules moving rapidly in all directions. The macroscopic properties of a gas that we can measure, such as its pressure, temperature, and volume, arise from the combined behaviour of these molecules. The kinetic theory of gases connects these macroscopic properties with the microscopic motion of molecules. Developed in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries by scientists including Daniel Bernoulli, Rudolf Clausius, James Clerk Maxwell, and Ludwig Boltzmann, kinetic theory was one of the first successful applications of statistical reasoning in physics, and it provided strong support for the existence of atoms and molecules before they could be observed directly.

The simplest version of kinetic theory describes an ideal gas and rests on several assumptions. A gas consists of a very large number of identical molecules in continuous, random motion. The molecules are very small compared with the average distances between them, so their own volume is negligible compared with the volume of the container. The molecules exert no forces on one another except during collisions, which are brief. Collisions between molecules and with the walls of the container are perfectly elastic, meaning that total kinetic energy is conserved. Between collisions, molecules move in straight lines at constant speed, and the motion obeys Newton's laws.

Pressure arises from the collisions of molecules with the walls of the container. When a molecule strikes a wall and rebounds, its momentum perpendicular to the wall reverses direction, and the wall exerts a force on it; by Newton's third law, the molecule exerts an equal and opposite force on the wall. Because there are vast numbers of molecules striking the walls every second, these individual impulses combine to produce a steady average force per unit area, which we measure as pressure. Analysing the momentum transfer for molecules moving in random directions leads to an important result: the pressure equals one third of the number of molecules per unit volume multiplied by the mass of each molecule and the mean of the squared speeds of the molecules. In other words, pressure is proportional to the density of the gas and to the average of the square of molecular speeds.

Comparing this result with the ideal gas law, which states that pressure multiplied by volume equals the number of moles multiplied by the gas constant and the absolute temperature, reveals the microscopic meaning of temperature. The average translational kinetic energy of a gas molecule equals three halves of the Boltzmann constant multiplied by the absolute temperature. The Boltzmann constant, about 1.38 times ten to the power minus twenty-three joules per kelvin, links the energy of individual molecules to temperature and equals the gas constant divided by Avogadro's number. Temperature is therefore a measure of the average kinetic energy of random molecular motion. At absolute zero, the classical theory would predict that molecular motion ceases, although quantum mechanics shows that some zero-point energy remains.

This relationship has several consequences. At the same temperature, molecules of all gases have the same average translational kinetic energy, regardless of their mass. Because kinetic energy equals one half of mass multiplied by speed squared, lighter molecules must move faster on average than heavier ones at the same temperature. The root-mean-square speed, the square root of the mean of the squared speeds, equals the square root of three times the Boltzmann constant times temperature divided by the molecular mass, or equivalently three times the gas constant times temperature divided by the molar mass. At room temperature, the root-mean-square speed of nitrogen molecules is about 500 metres per second, while hydrogen molecules move about four times faster. This explains Graham's law of effusion, which states that the rate at which a gas escapes through a tiny hole is inversely proportional to the square root of its molar mass, a principle historically used to separate isotopes of uranium. It also helps explain why light gases such as hydrogen and helium escape from planetary atmospheres more readily.

The molecules of a gas do not all move at the same speed. Collisions constantly exchange energy, so at any instant some molecules move slowly and others very fast. Maxwell and Boltzmann derived the distribution of molecular speeds in a gas at equilibrium, known as the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution. The distribution curve rises from zero at zero speed to a maximum at the most probable speed and then falls off gradually, with a long tail towards high speeds. Three characteristic speeds can be distinguished: the most probable speed, the mean speed, and the root-mean-square speed, which increase in that order. As temperature rises, the distribution broadens and shifts to higher speeds, and the fraction of molecules with very high speeds increases sharply. This explains why the rates of chemical reactions and evaporation increase rapidly with temperature, because only molecules with energies above a certain threshold can react or escape from a liquid surface.

Kinetic theory also explains the heat capacities of gases. According to the equipartition theorem, each independent way in which a molecule can store energy, called a degree of freedom, contributes on average one half of the Boltzmann constant times temperature to the molecule's energy. Monatomic gases such as helium and argon have three translational degrees of freedom, giving a molar heat capacity at constant volume of three halves of the gas constant. Diatomic molecules such as nitrogen and oxygen also have two rotational degrees of freedom at ordinary temperatures, giving five halves of the gas constant. At high temperatures, vibrational modes also become active. The failure of classical theory to explain why some degrees of freedom are frozen out at low temperatures was one of the puzzles resolved by quantum mechanics.

Other properties of gases can also be understood using kinetic theory. The mean free path, the average distance a molecule travels between collisions, depends on the size of the molecules and the number density of the gas; at atmospheric pressure it is on the order of tens of nanometres for air. Diffusion, viscosity, and thermal conductivity of gases arise from the transport of mass, momentum, and energy by moving molecules, and kinetic theory predicts how these properties depend on temperature and pressure.

Real gases deviate from ideal behaviour, especially at high pressures and low temperatures, when molecules are close together. Their finite size and the attractive forces between them become significant. The van der Waals equation modifies the ideal gas law by adding correction terms for molecular volume and intermolecular attraction, explaining phenomena such as liquefaction. Nevertheless, the ideal gas model and kinetic theory provide an excellent description of most gases under ordinary conditions and remain fundamental to thermodynamics, atmospheric science, and chemical engineering.
summary:
The kinetic theory of gases, developed by Bernoulli, Clausius, Maxwell, and Boltzmann, explains pressure, temperature, and volume through molecular motion and supported the reality of atoms. Its ideal-gas assumptions are many identical molecules in random motion, negligible molecular volume, no forces except brief elastic collisions, and straight-line Newtonian motion between collisions. Pressure arises from momentum changes as molecules strike walls, giving p = ⅓(N/V)m⟨v²⟩, proportional to density and mean squared speed.

Combining this with the ideal gas law shows that average translational kinetic energy equals (3/2)kT, where the Boltzmann constant k ≈ 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K equals R divided by Avogadro's number, so temperature measures random molecular kinetic energy, with zero-point energy persisting at absolute zero. All gases share the same average energy at a given temperature, so lighter molecules move faster; v_rms = √(3kT/m) = √(3RT/M), about 500 m/s for nitrogen at room temperature and four times faster for hydrogen, explaining Graham's law, uranium isotope separation, and atmospheric escape of light gases. The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution gives the most probable, mean, and rms speeds in increasing order and shifts and broadens with temperature, increasing high-energy molecules and thus reaction and evaporation rates. Equipartition assigns ½kT per degree of freedom, giving molar heat capacities of (3/2)R for monatomic and (5/2)R for diatomic gases, with frozen modes explained by quantum mechanics. Kinetic theory also explains mean free path, diffusion, viscosity, and thermal conductivity, while real gases at high pressure and low temperature require the van der Waals equation.

Many practical problems require connecting a set of locations as cheaply as possible. A telecommunications company may want to connect cities with fibre-optic cable using the minimum total length of cable, an electricity utility may want to link substations, and a town planner may want to connect villages with roads at the lowest construction cost. Such problems can be modelled using a connected, undirected graph in which vertices represent locations and weighted edges represent possible connections and their costs. A spanning tree of the graph is a subset of edges that connects all the vertices without forming any cycles. A graph with V vertices has spanning trees containing exactly V minus one edges. The minimum spanning tree, MST, is the spanning tree whose total edge weight is as small as possible. If all edge weights are distinct, the minimum spanning tree is unique; otherwise, there may be several with the same total weight.

Minimum spanning tree algorithms rely on two fundamental properties. The cut property states that for any partition of the vertices into two non-empty sets, called a cut, the lightest edge crossing the cut belongs to some minimum spanning tree. Intuitively, any spanning tree must cross the cut somewhere, and choosing the cheapest crossing edge can never be a mistake. The cycle property states that for any cycle in the graph, the heaviest edge in the cycle does not belong to any minimum spanning tree when edge weights are distinct, because removing it and keeping the rest of the cycle still connects the same vertices at lower cost. These properties justify greedy algorithms, which build the tree by repeatedly making locally optimal choices.

Kruskal's algorithm, published by Joseph Kruskal in 1956, considers edges in order of increasing weight. It begins with each vertex as a separate component, forming a forest of single-vertex trees. It then examines the edges one by one, from lightest to heaviest. If an edge connects two vertices in different components, it is added to the tree, merging the two components into one. If the edge connects two vertices already in the same component, adding it would create a cycle, so it is skipped. The algorithm stops when V minus one edges have been added and all vertices belong to a single tree. Kruskal's algorithm can be described as growing a forest that gradually merges into one tree.

An efficient implementation of Kruskal's algorithm requires a way to determine quickly whether two vertices belong to the same component. This is achieved with a disjoint-set data structure, also called union-find. The structure supports two operations: find, which identifies the representative of the set containing a vertex, and union, which merges two sets. With optimizations known as union by rank, which attaches the smaller tree under the root of the larger, and path compression, which makes every vertex on a search path point directly to the root, these operations take nearly constant time on average. The overall running time of Kruskal's algorithm is dominated by sorting the edges, giving a time proportional to E multiplied by the logarithm of E, where E is the number of edges.

Prim's algorithm, first discovered by Vojtěch Jarník in 1930 and later independently by Robert Prim and Edsger Dijkstra, grows a single tree from a starting vertex. At each step, it adds the lightest edge that connects a vertex in the tree to a vertex outside it, thereby adding a new vertex to the tree. This is a direct application of the cut property, with the cut separating the vertices already in the tree from the rest. The algorithm continues until all vertices are included. Prim's algorithm is efficiently implemented using a priority queue that stores, for each vertex not yet in the tree, the weight of the lightest edge connecting it to the tree. When a vertex is added, the priority values of its neighbours are updated if the new edges are lighter. Using a binary heap, the running time is proportional to E multiplied by the logarithm of V, and with a Fibonacci heap it can be reduced to E plus V log V. For dense graphs, a simple array-based implementation runs in time proportional to V squared, which can be faster than heap-based versions.

The two algorithms suit different situations. Kruskal's algorithm works well for sparse graphs, in which the number of edges is close to the number of vertices, and when edges are already sorted or can be sorted efficiently. Its forest-merging approach also extends naturally to finding minimum spanning forests in graphs that are not connected. Prim's algorithm is often preferred for dense graphs, especially with the array implementation, and is convenient when the graph is represented by adjacency lists or matrices. A third classical method, Borůvka's algorithm, developed in 1926 for designing an electrical network in Moravia, repeatedly adds the cheapest edge leaving each component simultaneously; it is well suited to parallel computation.

A simple example illustrates Kruskal's algorithm. Suppose four towns, A, B, C, and D, can be connected by roads with costs AB 1, BC 2, AC 3, CD 4, and BD 5. Sorting the edges by weight gives AB, BC, AC, CD, and BD. Kruskal's algorithm adds AB and BC, then skips AC because A and C are already connected through B, adds CD to connect D, and stops, having added three edges. The minimum spanning tree has total cost 1 plus 2 plus 4, which equals 7. Prim's algorithm starting from A would add AB, then BC, then CD, producing the same tree.

Minimum spanning trees have applications beyond network design. In cluster analysis, removing the heaviest edges from a minimum spanning tree divides data points into groups, a technique called single-linkage clustering. Minimum spanning trees provide approximation algorithms for harder problems, such as the travelling salesman problem, where a tour based on the MST can be shown to be no more than twice the length of the optimal tour when distances satisfy the triangle inequality. They are also used in image segmentation, in analysing networks in biology and social science, and in designing circuits.

It is important to distinguish the minimum spanning tree from the shortest path tree produced by algorithms such as Dijkstra's. A minimum spanning tree minimizes the total weight of all edges needed to connect every vertex, whereas a shortest path tree minimizes the distance from a particular source to each vertex. The path between two vertices in a minimum spanning tree is not necessarily the shortest path between them in the original graph.
summary:
Minimum spanning tree (MST) problems connect locations at minimum total cost, such as fibre networks, power substations, and village roads, modelled as weighted undirected graphs. A spanning tree connects all V vertices with V − 1 edges and no cycles, and the MST minimizes total weight, unique when weights are distinct. The cut property (the lightest edge across any cut belongs to an MST) and cycle property (the heaviest edge in a cycle is excluded with distinct weights) justify greedy algorithms.

Kruskal's algorithm (1956) sorts edges by weight and adds each edge joining different components, skipping cycle-forming edges, using a union-find structure with union by rank and path compression for near-constant operations, giving O(E log E) time. Prim's algorithm, discovered by Jarník (1930) and later by Prim and Dijkstra, grows one tree by repeatedly adding the lightest edge leaving it, using a priority queue for O(E log V) with a binary heap, E + V log V with a Fibonacci heap, or O(V²) with arrays for dense graphs. Kruskal suits sparse graphs and minimum spanning forests, Prim suits dense graphs, and Borůvka's 1926 algorithm adds the cheapest edge from every component at once and parallelizes well. In the four-town example, Kruskal selects AB, BC, and CD for a total cost of 7, the same tree Prim finds from A. MSTs support single-linkage clustering, a 2-approximation for the metric travelling salesman problem, image segmentation, biological and social network analysis, and circuit design, but differ from Dijkstra's shortest path trees, since MST paths need not be shortest paths.

source_text:
Most physical quantities, such as temperature, pressure, sound, light intensity, and voltage from biomedical electrodes, vary continuously, while computers, microcontrollers, and digital signal processors work with discrete numbers. An analog-to-digital converter, ADC, bridges these domains by converting a continuous input voltage into a digital code. ADCs are found in smartphones, digital audio equipment, medical monitors, industrial control systems, communication receivers, and scientific instruments. Different applications place very different demands on conversion speed, resolution, accuracy, power consumption, and cost, so several distinct ADC architectures have been developed, each suited to particular requirements.

Several performance parameters describe an ADC. Resolution is the number of bits in the output code. An n-bit converter divides its input range into two to the power n levels, so a 12-bit ADC has 4,096 levels. The voltage corresponding to one step, the least significant bit, equals the full-scale range divided by two to the power n; for a 12-bit converter with a 3.3-volt range, it is about 0.8 millivolts. Because a continuous input is mapped to a finite number of levels, every ADC introduces quantization error of up to half a least significant bit. The sampling rate is the number of conversions per second. Accuracy is affected by offset and gain errors and by nonlinearity, described by differential nonlinearity, the deviation of step widths from the ideal, and integral nonlinearity, the deviation of the transfer characteristic from a straight line. Because real converters also add noise and distortion, the effective number of bits, ENOB, derived from the measured signal-to-noise-and-distortion ratio, is often lower than the nominal resolution. The ideal signal-to-noise ratio of an n-bit converter is approximately 6.02 times n plus 1.76 decibels.

Most ADCs include a sample-and-hold circuit at the input. It captures the input voltage at a precise instant and holds it constant while the conversion takes place, because many architectures require the input to remain stable during conversion. An anti-aliasing low-pass filter is usually placed before the ADC to remove frequency components above half the sampling rate, which would otherwise appear as false lower-frequency components in the digitized signal.

The flash ADC, also called a parallel converter, is the fastest architecture. It uses a resistor ladder to generate a set of reference voltages, one for each possible threshold, and a bank of comparators, each comparing the input with one reference voltage. For an n-bit converter, two to the power n minus one comparators are required. All comparators operate simultaneously, producing a thermometer code in which all comparators below the input level output one and those above output zero, and an encoder converts this into a binary output. Because the conversion occurs in a single step, flash ADCs can operate at sampling rates of billions of samples per second, making them suitable for high-speed applications such as oscilloscopes, radar, and high-frequency communication receivers. Their disadvantage is that the number of comparators doubles with each additional bit, so power consumption, chip area, and input capacitance grow rapidly, limiting practical resolution to around eight bits.

The successive approximation register ADC, SAR, offers a balance between speed, resolution, and power and is one of the most widely used architectures, commonly built into microcontrollers. It performs a binary search over the possible codes. The converter contains a comparator, a digital-to-analog converter, and a successive approximation register. In the first step, the most significant bit is set to one, and the DAC produces the corresponding voltage, half of full scale. The comparator determines whether the input is above or below this voltage, and the bit is kept or cleared accordingly. The process is repeated for each successive bit, from most significant to least significant, each time narrowing the range in which the input lies. An n-bit SAR ADC therefore requires n comparison cycles to complete a conversion. SAR converters typically provide resolutions of eight to eighteen bits at sampling rates from thousands to several million samples per second, with low power consumption, making them suitable for data acquisition, battery-powered devices, and industrial sensing.

The pipelined ADC achieves high speed with moderate to high resolution by dividing the conversion into several stages connected in series. Each stage resolves a few bits using a small flash converter, subtracts the corresponding analog value from its input, amplifies the remaining difference, called the residue, and passes it to the next stage. While one stage processes a new sample, later stages work on earlier samples, so a new output is produced on every clock cycle, although each result appears after a latency of several cycles. Digital error correction compensates for small inaccuracies in the stages. Pipelined ADCs commonly provide ten to sixteen bits at rates of tens to hundreds of millions of samples per second and are used in video processing, medical ultrasound, and wireless base stations.

The sigma-delta ADC, also called delta-sigma, achieves very high resolution at lower bandwidths. It uses a technique called oversampling, sampling the input at a rate many times higher than required, together with a simple low-resolution quantizer, often a single comparator, inside a feedback loop. The loop includes an integrator and a one-bit DAC, and the output is a high-speed stream of bits whose average density represents the input value. A key feature is noise shaping: the feedback loop pushes quantization noise towards higher frequencies, outside the signal band of interest. A digital decimation filter then removes the high-frequency noise and reduces the data rate, producing high-resolution output samples. Sigma-delta converters can achieve sixteen to twenty-four bits of resolution and are widely used in digital audio, precision measurement, weighing scales, and sensors such as thermocouples and strain gauges. Their limitations include restricted bandwidth and the latency introduced by the digital filter, which makes them less suitable for fast multiplexing between channels.

The dual-slope or integrating ADC is another precision architecture. It integrates the input voltage for a fixed time and then measures the time required to discharge the integrator with a known reference voltage; this time is proportional to the input. Integrating converters are slow but highly accurate and inherently reject noise at frequencies such as the power line frequency when the integration time is chosen appropriately, so they are used in digital multimeters.

Choosing an ADC involves balancing these characteristics against application requirements. Flash and pipelined converters serve high-speed applications, SAR converters cover a broad middle ground with low power, and sigma-delta and integrating converters serve high-precision, low-bandwidth applications. Designers must also consider input range, reference voltage stability, interface type, power supply, and cost, as well as the analog front end, including amplification and filtering, which strongly influences overall system performance.
summary:
Analog-to-digital converters (ADCs) convert continuous voltages into digital codes for phones, audio, medical monitors, control systems, receivers, and instruments, and different architectures balance speed, resolution, accuracy, power, and cost. An n-bit ADC has 2ⁿ levels with an LSB of full scale ÷ 2ⁿ (about 0.8 mV for 12 bits over 3.3 V), and quantization error of up to ½ LSB; other parameters include sampling rate, offset and gain errors, differential and integral nonlinearity, and effective number of bits, with ideal SNR ≈ 6.02n + 1.76 dB. Sample-and-hold circuits stabilize inputs, and anti-aliasing filters remove components above half the sampling rate.

Flash ADCs use a resistor ladder and 2ⁿ − 1 parallel comparators producing a thermometer code for gigasample speeds in oscilloscopes and radar, but rapidly growing power and area limit them to about 8 bits. SAR ADCs, common in microcontrollers, perform an n-step binary search with a comparator and DAC, offering 8–18 bits at thousands to millions of samples per second with low power. Pipelined ADCs pass amplified residues through stages resolving a few bits each, producing one output per clock after latency with digital error correction, giving 10–16 bits at tens to hundreds of megasamples per second for video, ultrasound, and base stations. Sigma-delta ADCs use oversampling, a one-bit quantizer, integrator feedback, noise shaping, and decimation filtering for 16–24 bits in audio, precision sensing, and scales, but have limited bandwidth and latency. Dual-slope integrating ADCs are slow but accurate and reject power-line noise in multimeters. Selection weighs speed, precision, power, input range, reference stability, interface, cost, and analog front-end design.

Steel structures, such as industrial buildings, multi-storey frames, bridges, transmission towers, and warehouses, are assembled from individual members, including beams, columns, braces, and truss elements, which are fabricated in workshops and joined together either in the shop or on site. The connections between these members are critical parts of the structure. They must transfer forces safely from one member to another, provide the intended structural behaviour, such as allowing rotation or resisting moments, and be practical and economical to fabricate and erect. Many structural failures have originated in connections rather than in the members themselves, which makes their careful design and inspection essential. The two principal methods of connecting structural steel are bolting and welding.

Connections are classified according to the forces they transmit and their rotational behaviour. Simple or shear connections are designed mainly to transfer shear force and allow relatively free rotation between connected members, behaving approximately as pinned joints. Examples include beam-to-column connections using web angles, fin plates, or end plates attached only to the beam web. Moment connections, also called rigid connections, transfer both shear and bending moment and maintain the angle between members, enabling frames to resist lateral loads from wind and earthquakes through frame action. Semi-rigid connections fall between these extremes, providing partial moment resistance. The choice of connection type affects the analysis of the entire structure, because assumptions about joint stiffness determine how forces are distributed.

Bolted connections are widely used, particularly for site connections, because bolting requires relatively simple equipment and can be performed in a range of weather conditions with fewer skilled personnel than welding. Structural bolts are classified by strength grade; common grades include ordinary bolts, such as grade 4.6, and high-strength bolts, such as grades 8.8 and 10.9, where the first number indicates the ultimate tensile strength in hundreds of megapascals and the second, multiplied by the first and by ten, indicates the yield strength. Bolted connections may be designed as bearing-type or slip-critical connections.

In bearing-type connections, bolts are tightened enough to bring the connected parts into firm contact, and loads are transferred through the bolts bearing against the sides of the holes and through shear in the bolt shanks. Several failure modes must be checked. Bolt shear failure occurs when the bolt is cut across its shear planes; a bolt connecting two plates in a lap joint is in single shear, while a bolt connecting a central plate between two cover plates is in double shear, giving twice the shear capacity. Bearing failure occurs when the bolt crushes or tears the plate material around the hole. Tension failure of the plate can occur across the net section, the cross-section reduced by bolt holes, so the effective area available to resist tension must be calculated by deducting hole areas. Block shear is a failure mode in which a block of material tears out along a combination of shear and tension planes around a bolt group, particularly at the ends of members such as angles and gusset plates. Minimum edge distances, end distances, and spacing between bolts are specified to prevent tearing and to allow access for tightening.

Slip-critical, or friction-grip, connections use high-strength bolts tightened to a high specified preload, so that the clamping force between the plates creates friction that resists slip under service loads. Load is transferred through friction between the contact surfaces rather than through bearing, so the connection remains rigid without movement. Slip-critical connections are used where slip would be undesirable, such as under fatigue or reversing loads in bridges and crane girders, or where connection movement would affect structural behaviour. Their capacity depends on the bolt preload, the number of friction surfaces, and the slip coefficient of the contact surfaces, which is influenced by surface preparation, such as blast cleaning. Bolt preload is achieved using methods such as the turn-of-nut method, calibrated torque wrenches, or direct tension indicators.

Bolts may also be subjected to tension, as in hanger connections and end-plate moment connections, where the bolts in the tension region resist forces pulling the plates apart. In such connections, flexible plates can bend and produce additional tension in the bolts, an effect known as prying action, which must be considered in design. Bolts subjected to combined shear and tension must satisfy interaction requirements.

Welded connections join steel by melting and fusing the base metal with filler metal to form a continuous joint. The most common processes in structural fabrication include shielded metal arc welding, often called stick welding, gas metal arc welding, flux-cored arc welding, and submerged arc welding, which is used for long, heavy welds in fabrication shops. Welding offers several advantages. It can produce compact, rigid, and continuous connections without the need for holes, which avoids reducing the cross-section; it allows a clean appearance; and it is often efficient for shop fabrication. However, welding requires skilled welders, careful control of quality, and suitable conditions, and site welding can be more difficult and expensive than bolting.

The two principal types of structural welds are fillet welds and groove welds, also called butt welds. Fillet welds have a roughly triangular cross-section and join members at right angles or in lap joints; they are the most common welds because they require little edge preparation. Their strength is calculated using the effective throat, the shortest distance from the root of the weld to its face, multiplied by the effective length, with the weld generally assumed to fail in shear through the throat. Groove welds are placed in a gap between members, often with bevelled edges, and complete joint penetration groove welds can develop the full strength of the connected parts. Weld symbols on drawings specify the type, size, length, and location of welds.

Quality and inspection are crucial for welded connections. Defects such as porosity, lack of fusion, incomplete penetration, slag inclusions, undercut, and cracking can reduce strength and serve as starting points for fatigue cracks. Welding also introduces residual stresses and distortion because of uneven heating and cooling, which must be controlled through welding procedures, preheating of thick sections, and proper sequencing. Inspection methods include visual inspection, magnetic particle testing, dye penetrant testing, ultrasonic testing, and radiographic testing. The brittle fractures observed in some welded steel moment frames after the 1994 Northridge earthquake in California led to major research and revisions to the design and detailing of welded moment connections for seismic resistance.

In practice, many connections combine both methods. Brackets, plates, and stiffeners are often welded to members in the fabrication shop, while the final connections between members on site are bolted, combining the quality control advantages of shop welding with the speed and simplicity of site bolting. Design codes, such as those of the American Institute of Steel Construction, the Eurocodes, and the Bangladesh National Building Code, specify methods for calculating connection capacities, minimum dimensions, and detailing requirements.
summary:
Steel structures such as buildings, bridges, towers, and warehouses depend on connections between beams, columns, braces, and truss members that must transfer forces, provide intended behaviour, and be practical to fabricate and erect, and many failures start at connections. Simple shear connections such as web angles and fin plates behave like pins, moment connections transfer shear and bending to resist wind and earthquakes, and semi-rigid connections lie between, affecting structural analysis.

Bolting suits site work; grades such as 4.6, 8.8, and 10.9 encode ultimate and yield strengths. Bearing-type connections transfer load by bolt shear and bearing and must be checked for single or double shear, plate bearing, net-section tension failure, and block shear, with minimum edge distances and spacing. Slip-critical connections use preloaded high-strength bolts so friction resists slip under fatigue or reversing loads, depending on preload, friction surfaces, and slip coefficient, achieved by turn-of-nut, calibrated torque, or direct tension indicators; tension connections must consider prying action and combined shear-tension interaction. Welding by shielded metal arc, gas metal arc, flux-cored, and submerged arc processes gives compact, rigid, hole-free joints but needs skill and quality control. Fillet welds, the most common, are designed on effective throat and length, while complete joint penetration groove welds develop full member strength, specified by weld symbols. Defects such as porosity, lack of fusion, slag, undercut, and cracks, plus residual stress and distortion, require procedures, preheating, sequencing, and visual, magnetic particle, dye penetrant, ultrasonic, and radiographic inspection; Northridge 1994 brittle fractures prompted seismic redesign. Practice often combines shop welding with site bolting under codes such as AISC, Eurocodes, and the Bangladesh National Building Code.

Additive manufacturing, commonly known as three-dimensional printing, refers to processes that build objects by adding material layer by layer according to a digital model. It contrasts with traditional subtractive manufacturing, such as milling and turning, in which material is removed from a solid block, and with formative processes, such as casting, forging, and injection moulding, in which material is shaped using moulds or dies. Since the first commercial systems appeared in the late 1980s, additive manufacturing has grown from a tool for producing prototypes into a technology used to manufacture functional parts in aerospace, medical devices, automotive engineering, tooling, consumer products, and construction.

All additive manufacturing processes follow a similar digital workflow. A three-dimensional model of the part is created using computer-aided design software or obtained by scanning a physical object. The model is converted into a standard file format, traditionally the STL format, which approximates the surfaces as a mesh of triangles, or newer formats that can include colour and material information. Slicing software divides the model into thin horizontal layers and generates the instructions, or toolpaths, that the machine follows to build each layer. The software also plans support structures where needed to hold overhanging features during building. After printing, parts usually require post-processing, which may include removing supports, cleaning, curing, heat treatment, machining critical surfaces, and finishing to improve surface quality.

The ISO/ASTM 52900 standard classifies additive manufacturing processes into seven categories. Material extrusion, best known as fused filament fabrication or fused deposition modelling, melts a thermoplastic filament, such as polylactic acid or acrylonitrile butadiene styrene, and extrudes it through a heated nozzle that moves to deposit material layer by layer. It is the most widely used process for low-cost desktop printers and is valued for its simplicity and affordability, but parts have visible layer lines, limited resolution, and weaker properties between layers than within them, a characteristic known as anisotropy.

Vat photopolymerization uses light to cure liquid photosensitive resin selectively. In stereolithography, the first commercial additive process, an ultraviolet laser traces each layer on the surface of a resin bath, solidifying the resin, while digital light processing projects an entire layer image at once. These processes produce parts with fine detail and smooth surfaces, used for dental models, jewellery patterns, and prototypes, although many resins are brittle and require post-curing.

Powder bed fusion processes use thermal energy to fuse regions of a powder bed. Selective laser sintering uses a laser to fuse polymer powders, such as nylon, and the surrounding unfused powder supports the part, eliminating the need for separate supports. For metals, laser powder bed fusion, also called selective laser melting, and electron beam melting fully melt metal powders, such as titanium alloys, stainless steels, nickel superalloys, and aluminium alloys, to produce dense functional parts. These processes are used to manufacture aerospace components, medical implants, and high-performance parts, but they require expensive equipment, controlled atmospheres, careful handling of powders, and attention to residual stresses that can cause distortion or cracking.

Material jetting deposits droplets of photopolymer material, which are cured by ultraviolet light, and can combine multiple materials and colours in a single part. Binder jetting deposits a liquid binding agent onto a powder bed to bond particles; parts are then typically sintered or infiltrated to increase strength, and the process is relatively fast and can be used for metals, ceramics, and sand moulds for casting. Directed energy deposition uses a focused heat source, such as a laser, electron beam, or electric arc, to melt material as it is deposited, often from a nozzle feeding powder or wire, and it is used to repair worn components and build large metal structures. Sheet lamination bonds sheets of material, such as paper or metal foil, and cuts them to shape layer by layer.

Additive manufacturing offers important advantages over conventional methods. It provides great design freedom, allowing complex geometries that would be difficult or impossible to machine or mould, such as internal cooling channels, lattice structures, and organic shapes. Combined with topology optimization, a computational method that removes material from regions that carry little load, it can produce lightweight parts with high stiffness, valuable in aerospace, where reducing mass saves fuel. Several components that would traditionally be assembled can be consolidated into a single printed part, reducing assembly work and potential failure points; a well-known example is a fuel nozzle for jet engines that combined about twenty parts into one. Because no moulds or dedicated tooling are required, additive manufacturing is economical for small production quantities, prototypes, and customized products. Medical applications exploit this capability through patient-specific implants, surgical guides, dental aligners, and prosthetics designed from medical scans. Additive manufacturing can also reduce material waste compared with machining from solid blocks and supports distributed production of spare parts close to where they are needed.

The technology also has limitations. Build speeds are relatively slow, and costs per part are often higher than conventional mass production methods for large quantities, so additive manufacturing is generally not economical for high-volume production of simple parts. Build volumes are limited by machine size. Surface finish and dimensional accuracy may require post-processing. Material choices, although expanding, remain narrower than in conventional manufacturing, and the mechanical properties of printed parts can vary with build orientation, process parameters, and internal defects such as porosity and lack of fusion. Ensuring consistent quality, particularly for safety-critical components, requires process monitoring, qualification, inspection methods such as computed tomography, and certification standards. Design rules differ from those of conventional processes, so engineers must learn design for additive manufacturing, considering factors such as minimum wall thickness, overhang angles, support removal, and residual stress.

Research and industrial development continue to expand the capabilities of additive manufacturing, including faster processes, larger machines, new materials such as high-temperature polymers and composites, multi-material printing, bioprinting of tissues using cell-laden materials, and the use of large-scale printers to construct buildings from concrete. As these technologies mature, additive manufacturing is increasingly integrated with conventional processes rather than replacing them, forming part of digital manufacturing systems.
summary:
Additive manufacturing (3D printing) builds parts layer by layer from digital models, unlike subtractive machining or formative casting, forging, and moulding, and has grown since the late 1980s from prototyping to functional parts in aerospace, medicine, automotive, tooling, consumer goods, and construction. The workflow converts CAD or scanned models to STL or newer formats, slices them into layers and toolpaths with supports, prints, and post-processes by removing supports, cleaning, curing, heat treating, machining, and finishing.

ISO/ASTM 52900 defines seven categories. Material extrusion (fused filament fabrication) deposits melted PLA or ABS cheaply but with layer lines, low resolution, and anisotropy. Vat photopolymerization (stereolithography, DLP) gives fine, smooth dental and jewellery parts from often brittle resins. Powder bed fusion includes support-free polymer laser sintering and metal laser powder bed fusion or electron beam melting for dense titanium, steel, superalloy, and aluminium aerospace and implant parts, requiring costly equipment, controlled atmospheres, powder safety, and residual stress control. Material jetting prints multi-material, coloured photopolymers; binder jetting bonds powders for sintered metals, ceramics, and sand moulds; directed energy deposition melts fed powder or wire for repairs and large structures; and sheet lamination bonds cut sheets. Advantages include design freedom, internal channels, lattices, topology-optimized lightweight parts, part consolidation such as a twenty-part jet fuel nozzle, toolless economical small runs, patient-specific medical devices, less waste, and distributed spare parts. Limitations include slow builds, high per-part cost at volume, limited build size, finishing needs, narrower materials, orientation-dependent properties and porosity, qualification and CT inspection, and new design rules. Development targets speed, size, new materials, multi-material and bioprinting, and concrete building printing, integrated with conventional manufacturing.

source_text:
Colour is one of the most important quality attributes of textile products. Consumers often decide whether to buy a garment based on its colour, and brands require that colours match their specifications precisely and consistently across production lots, different suppliers, and different materials, such as a shirt fabric, its buttons, and its sewing thread. Traditionally, colour matching was performed visually by experienced colourists who compared samples with standards. Visual assessment remains important, but it is subjective, influenced by lighting, the observer's colour vision, fatigue, and surrounding colours, and it is difficult to communicate precisely between suppliers in different countries. Instrumental colour measurement provides objective, numerical descriptions of colour that support recipe formulation, quality control, and communication throughout global textile supply chains.

The perception of colour involves three components: a light source, an object, and an observer. The light source emits radiation across the visible spectrum, approximately 400 to 700 nanometres in wavelength. The object reflects, absorbs, or transmits different wavelengths to different degrees; a red fabric reflects mainly long wavelengths and absorbs much of the shorter ones. The reflected light enters the eye, where three types of cone cells, sensitive to long, medium, and short wavelengths, respond in different proportions, and the brain interprets these signals as colour. Because all three components influence colour perception, instrumental systems must take each into account.
