The representation affects the time and memory cost of traversal, especially for large sparse networks. Breadth-first search uses a queue to explore the graph in layers. Starting from a source vertex, it marks the source as visited, adds it to the queue and repeatedly removes a vertex to examine its unvisited neighbours. Each newly discovered neighbour is marked before being enqueued so that it is not added multiple times. In an unweighted graph, BFS finds shortest paths measured by number of edges from the source to every reachable vertex. A parent or predecessor array can reconstruct a shortest path. BFS can also determine distances by level, test whether a graph is bipartite and identify connected components when restarted from each unvisited vertex. Depth-first search explores one branch as far as possible before backtracking. It can be implemented recursively or with an explicit stack. The algorithm marks a vertex when it is first discovered, explores each unvisited neighbour and then returns to earlier vertices when no further neighbour is available. DFS supports cycle detection, topological sorting in directed acyclic graphs, connected-component analysis and strongly connected component algorithms. In directed graphs, edge classifications such as tree, back, forward and cross edges can help identify cycles and understand reachability. Recursion depth can become a problem for very large graphs, so an iterative implementation may be preferable in environments with limited call-stack capacity. With an adjacency-list representation, BFS and DFS each run in O(V+E) time because every vertex is processed a limited number of times and every edge is examined a bounded number of times. With an adjacency matrix, examining neighbours may require scanning an entire row for each vertex, producing O(V squared) time. Space use includes the graph representation, visited structure, queue or stack and any parent or distance arrays. Traversal order can vary depending on the order in which neighbours are stored. This can change the exact BFS tree or DFS tree but not the set of vertices reachable from a given start vertex. For disconnected graphs, a traversal from one start vertex reaches only its connected component. To visit every vertex, the algorithm iterates over all vertices and starts a new traversal whenever it finds an unvisited vertex. In directed graphs, reachability depends on edge direction, and strongly connected components are maximal sets in which every vertex can reach every other vertex. Algorithms such as Kosaraju's and Tarjan's use DFS structure to identify these components efficiently. Topological sorting uses DFS finishing order or Kahn's algorithm and is defined only for directed acyclic graphs; if a directed cycle exists, no topological ordering can satisfy all edge directions. Graph traversal is used in route exploration, web crawling, dependency analysis, social-network analysis, garbage collection, maze solving, network broadcast and program analysis. Ordinary BFS is not sufficient for weighted shortest paths when edge weights differ; Dijkstra's algorithm is suitable for nonnegative weights, while Bellman-Ford can handle negative edge weights provided there is no reachable negative cycle affecting the result. Traversal code should handle empty graphs, isolated vertices, self-loops, parallel edges and invalid vertex identifiers according to the chosen graph model. Correctness depends on marking vertices consistently, respecting direction and using an appropriate data structure. BFS and DFS are foundational because many more advanced graph algorithms build on their exploration order and parent relationships. A useful implementation invariant is that a vertex is marked visited when it is first discovered, not only after it is removed from the queue or stack. This prevents the same vertex from being inserted many times when several neighbours connect to it. In BFS, recording the parent at discovery time preserves a shortest-path tree in an unweighted graph. In DFS, discovery and finishing times can support interval-based reasoning about ancestor relationships and help identify back edges. When a graph is stored in an adjacency list, the traversal should iterate over each vertex's neighbour collection and should handle vertices that have no neighbours. The algorithm should also define how invalid start vertices are reported.
summary: Graph traversal algorithms systematically visit vertices in a graph while managing which vertices have already been explored. Breadth-first search (BFS) uses a queue and explores vertices in layers according to distance in number of edges from a starting vertex. BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs and can identify connected components, levels and bipartite structure. Both algorithms typically run in O(V+E) time with adjacency-list representation, where V is the number of vertices and E is the number of edges. Traversal results depend on the starting vertex and the order in which neighbors are considered, although core reachability properties remain the same. Weighted shortest-path problems require algorithms such as Dijkstra's or Bellman-Ford rather than ordinary BFS unless all edge weights are equal.

source_text:
Every business must decide how much to produce, and this decision depends heavily on how its costs change with the level of output. Economists analyse cost behaviour using cost curves, which show the relationship between output and different measures of cost. A crucial distinction in this analysis is between the short run and the long run. The short run is a period in which at least one factor of production, usually capital such as buildings and machinery, is fixed, while other factors, such as labour and raw materials, can be varied. The long run is a period long enough for all factors to be varied, allowing a firm to change the size of its plant, adopt new technology, or enter or leave an industry. These periods are defined by flexibility of inputs, not by a specific length of calendar time; the long run may be a few months for a small bakery but many years for a steel plant or power station.

In the short run, total cost consists of fixed costs and variable costs. Fixed costs do not change with output, at least within the relevant range; they include rent, insurance, interest on loans, depreciation, and the salaries of permanent managerial staff. Fixed costs must be paid even if output is zero. Variable costs change with output; they include raw materials, energy used in production, and wages of workers paid according to hours or output. Total cost equals total fixed cost plus total variable cost.

Average and marginal cost measures are derived from these totals. Average fixed cost is total fixed cost divided by output, and it declines continuously as output increases, because the same fixed cost is spread over more units. Average variable cost is total variable cost divided by output, and average total cost is total cost divided by output, equal to the sum of average fixed and average variable cost. Marginal cost is the additional cost of producing one more unit of output, equal to the change in total cost divided by the change in output. Because fixed costs do not change with output, marginal cost depends only on changes in variable cost.

The shapes of short-run cost curves are explained by the law of diminishing marginal returns. When additional units of a variable input, such as labour, are added to a fixed amount of capital, output may at first increase rapidly, because workers can specialize and use the fixed equipment more fully. Beyond some point, however, each additional worker adds less to output than the previous one, because workers increasingly crowd the fixed equipment and space. When marginal product falls, the cost of producing each additional unit rises. As a result, the marginal cost curve typically falls at low levels of output and then rises, forming a U shape or a curve that rises steeply after a minimum.

The average variable cost and average total cost curves are also typically U-shaped. Their relationship to marginal cost follows a general mathematical rule: when the marginal value is below the average, it pulls the average down, and when the marginal value is above the average, it pulls the average up. Consequently, the marginal cost curve intersects both the average variable cost curve and the average total cost curve at their minimum points. The minimum point of average total cost occurs at a higher output than the minimum of average variable cost, because average fixed cost continues to fall as output rises, offsetting the increase in average variable cost for a while. The vertical distance between average total cost and average variable cost equals average fixed cost and narrows as output increases.

These curves are important for business decisions. A firm maximizes profit by producing the output at which marginal cost equals marginal revenue. In a perfectly competitive market, where marginal revenue equals the market price, the portion of the marginal cost curve above the minimum of average variable cost forms the firm's short-run supply curve. If the price falls below the minimum average variable cost, the firm minimizes losses by shutting down temporarily, because it cannot even cover its variable costs, while still paying fixed costs. If the price is between minimum average variable cost and minimum average total cost, the firm continues producing in the short run, covering its variable costs and part of its fixed costs, even though it makes a loss.

In the long run, all costs are variable, and a firm can choose the plant size that minimizes the cost of producing any given level of output. For each possible plant size, there is a corresponding short-run average total cost curve. The long-run average cost curve is formed by the lowest points of cost achievable at each output level when the firm can choose among all plant sizes; geometrically, it is the envelope of the short-run average cost curves, touching each of them at one point. For this reason, it is sometimes called the planning curve, because it guides decisions about the scale of production.

The shape of the long-run average cost curve is determined by returns to scale and by economies and diseconomies of scale. When a firm expands all of its inputs and output increases more than proportionally, average costs fall, and the firm enjoys economies of scale. Sources of economies of scale include technical economies, such as the ability to use larger, more efficient machinery and to benefit from specialization of labour; purchasing economies, through bulk buying discounts; financial economies, as large firms can often borrow at lower interest rates; marketing economies, as advertising costs are spread over more units; and managerial economies, through specialized managers. Over some range of output, average costs may be roughly constant, a situation called constant returns to scale. Beyond a certain size, firms may experience diseconomies of scale, in which average costs rise as the firm grows. These may result from difficulties of coordinating and controlling a large organization, communication problems, slower decision-making, and reduced employee motivation.

The output level at which long-run average cost reaches its minimum is called the minimum efficient scale. It has important implications for market structure. In industries where the minimum efficient scale is large relative to market demand, such as electricity transmission, aircraft manufacturing, or railways, only a few firms can operate efficiently, and the industry may become an oligopoly or a natural monopoly. In industries where minimum efficient scale is small, such as hairdressing or small retail shops, many firms can coexist. External economies of scale, which arise when an entire industry grows in a particular area, for example through shared suppliers, skilled labour pools, and infrastructure, can lower costs for all firms in the industry, as seen in industrial clusters.
summary:
Cost curves show how costs vary with output, distinguishing the short run, in which at least one input such as capital is fixed, from the long run, in which all inputs vary, defined by input flexibility rather than calendar time. Short-run total cost equals fixed costs (rent, insurance, interest, depreciation, permanent salaries), paid even at zero output, plus variable costs (materials, energy, hourly wages). Average fixed cost falls continuously, average total cost equals average fixed plus average variable cost, and marginal cost, the extra cost of one more unit, depends only on variable cost.

Diminishing marginal returns from adding labour to fixed capital make marginal cost fall then rise, producing U-shaped average variable and average total cost curves; marginal cost intersects both at their minima, and average total cost reaches its minimum at higher output because average fixed cost keeps falling. Profit is maximized where marginal cost equals marginal revenue; in perfect competition, marginal cost above minimum average variable cost is the supply curve, firms shut down below minimum average variable cost, and they operate at a loss between average variable and average total cost minima. The long-run average cost curve is the envelope of short-run curves, a planning curve for scale. Economies of scale—technical, purchasing, financial, marketing, and managerial—lower costs, constant returns follow, and diseconomies from coordination, communication, slow decisions, and motivation raise costs. Minimum efficient scale shapes market structure, with large scale relative to demand leading to oligopoly or natural monopoly and small scale permitting many firms, while external economies benefit industrial clusters.

Fixed costs must be paid even if output is zero. Variable costs change with output; they include raw materials, energy used in production, and wages of workers paid according to hours or output. Total cost equals total fixed cost plus total variable cost.

Average and marginal cost measures are derived from these totals. Average fixed cost is total fixed cost divided by output, and it declines continuously as output increases, because the same fixed cost is spread over more units. Average variable cost is total variable cost divided by output, and average total cost is total cost divided by output, equal to the sum of average fixed and average variable cost. Marginal cost is the additional cost of producing one more unit of output, equal to the change in total cost divided by the change in output. Because fixed costs do not change with output, marginal cost depends only on changes in variable cost.

The shapes of short-run cost curves are explained by the law of diminishing marginal returns. When additional units of a variable input, such as labour, are added to a fixed amount of capital, output may at first increase rapidly, because workers can specialize and use the fixed equipment more fully. Beyond some point, however, each additional worker adds less to output than the previous one, because workers increasingly crowd the fixed equipment and space. When marginal product falls, the cost of producing each additional unit rises. As a result, the marginal cost curve typically falls at low levels of output and then rises, forming a U shape or a curve that rises steeply after a minimum.

The average variable cost and average total cost curves are also typically U-shaped. Their relationship to marginal cost follows a general mathematical rule: when the marginal value is below the average, it pulls the average down, and when the marginal value is above the average, it pulls the average up. Consequently, the marginal cost curve intersects both the average variable cost curve and the average total cost curve at their minimum points. The minimum point of average total cost occurs at a higher output than the minimum of average variable cost, because average fixed cost continues to fall as output rises, offsetting the increase in average variable cost for a while. The vertical distance between average total cost and average variable cost equals average fixed cost and narrows as output increases.

These curves are important for business decisions. A firm maximizes profit by producing the output at which marginal cost equals marginal revenue. In a perfectly competitive market, where marginal revenue equals the market price, the portion of the marginal cost curve above the minimum of average variable cost forms the firm's short-run supply curve. If the price falls below the minimum average variable cost, the firm minimizes losses by shutting down temporarily, because it cannot even cover its variable costs, while still paying fixed costs. If the price is between minimum average variable cost and minimum average total cost, the firm continues producing in the short run, covering its variable costs and part of its fixed costs, even though it makes a loss.

In the long run, all costs are variable, and a firm can choose the plant size that minimizes the cost of producing any given level of output. For each possible plant size, there is a corresponding short-run average total cost curve. The long-run average cost curve is formed by the lowest points of cost achievable at each output level when the firm can choose among all plant sizes; geometrically, it is the envelope of the short-run average cost curves, touching each of them at one point. For this reason, it is sometimes called the planning curve, because it guides decisions about the scale of production.

The shape of the long-run average cost curve is determined by returns to scale and by economies and diseconomies of scale. When a firm expands all of its inputs and output increases more than proportionally, average costs fall, and the firm enjoys economies of scale. Sources of economies of scale include technical economies, such as the ability to use larger, more efficient machinery and to benefit from specialization of labour; purchasing economies, through bulk buying discounts; financial economies, as large firms can often borrow at lower interest rates; marketing economies, as advertising costs are spread over more units; and managerial economies, through specialized managers. Over some range of output, average costs may be roughly constant, a situation called constant returns to scale. Beyond a certain size, firms may experience diseconomies of scale, in which average costs rise as the firm grows. These may result from difficulties of coordinating and controlling a large organization, communication problems, slower decision-making, and reduced employee motivation.

In industries where minimum efficient scale is small, such as hairdressing or small retail shops, many firms can coexist. External economies of scale, which arise when an entire industry grows in a particular area, for example through shared suppliers, skilled labour pools, and infrastructure, can lower costs for all firms in the industry, as seen in industrial clusters.

source_text:
Managers need ways to plan costs in advance and to evaluate whether actual performance matches expectations. Standard costing provides such a framework. A standard cost is a predetermined estimate of what a unit of product or service should cost under efficient operating conditions. By comparing actual costs with standard costs and analysing the differences, known as variances, managers can identify areas where performance is better or worse than expected, investigate causes, and take corrective action. Standard costing is widely used in manufacturing and has also been applied in service organizations such as hospitals, banks, and fast-food restaurants.

Standards are set separately for the quantity and the price of each input. A standard cost card for a product lists the standard quantity of each direct material, such as kilograms of raw material per unit, and its standard price per kilogram; the standard direct labour hours per unit and the standard wage rate per hour; and the standard overhead rate applied per unit of an allocation base, such as labour or machine hours. Standards may be set at different levels of difficulty. Ideal standards assume perfect efficiency, with no waste, breakdowns, or idle time; they are rarely achieved and may discourage employees. Practical or attainable standards allow for normal waste, machine downtime, and rest periods, and are challenging but achievable with reasonable effort, so they are generally preferred for motivation and planning. Standards are developed from engineering studies, time and motion analysis, historical data, supplier price information, and discussions with managers and employees.

Variance analysis compares actual results with standards. A favourable variance occurs when actual costs are lower than standard, increasing profit, while an unfavourable or adverse variance occurs when actual costs exceed standard. A central principle is to separate each total cost variance into a price component and a quantity component, because different managers are usually responsible for them and they have different causes. This analysis is commonly based on a flexible budget, which adjusts budgeted costs to the actual level of output achieved. Comparing actual costs with a static budget prepared for the originally planned output would mix the effects of volume differences with those of efficiency and prices.

For direct materials, the materials price variance equals the actual quantity purchased multiplied by the difference between the actual price and the standard price. It is usually the responsibility of the purchasing manager. An unfavourable price variance may result from rising market prices, buying in small quantities, urgent orders, or purchasing higher-quality materials than specified, while a favourable variance may arise from discounts or lower-quality materials. The materials quantity or usage variance equals the standard price multiplied by the difference between the actual quantity used and the standard quantity allowed for the actual output. It is usually the responsibility of the production manager. Unfavourable usage variances may result from waste, spoilage, poorly maintained machines, inexperienced workers, or low-quality materials.

Consider a garment factory with a standard of two metres of fabric per shirt at 150 taka per metre. During a month, it produces 1,000 shirts and uses 2,100 metres of fabric purchased at 145 taka per metre. The standard quantity allowed is 2,000 metres. The price variance is 2,100 metres multiplied by 5 taka, or 10,500 taka favourable, because the fabric cost less than standard. The quantity variance is 150 taka multiplied by 100 metres, or 15,000 taka unfavourable, because more fabric was used than allowed. The total materials variance is therefore 4,500 taka unfavourable. The analysis reveals an important possibility: the cheaper fabric might have been of lower quality, causing more waste, so the favourable price variance may be linked to the unfavourable quantity variance. Variances should therefore be interpreted together, not in isolation.

For direct labour, the labour rate variance equals the actual hours worked multiplied by the difference between the actual and standard wage rates. It may result from overtime premiums, wage changes, or using workers with higher or lower skill levels than planned. The labour efficiency variance equals the standard rate multiplied by the difference between actual hours worked and the standard hours allowed for actual output. Unfavourable efficiency variances may result from inexperienced workers, poor supervision, machine breakdowns, poor-quality materials, or production scheduling problems, while favourable variances may reflect improved methods or motivation. Some organizations also calculate an idle time variance for hours paid but not worked.

Overhead variances are more complex. Variable overhead can be analysed into a spending variance, comparing actual variable overhead with the budget for actual hours, and an efficiency variance, which arises because variable overhead is applied according to an activity base such as labour hours, so inefficient use of labour also causes more variable overhead to be incurred. Fixed overhead is analysed into a budget or spending variance, the difference between actual and budgeted fixed overhead, and a volume variance, which arises when actual production differs from the planned level used to calculate the fixed overhead rate. The volume variance reflects the utilization of capacity rather than cost control, because fixed costs do not change with output in the short term.

Sales variances complete the picture of performance. The sales price variance measures the effect of selling at prices different from standard, and the sales volume variance measures the effect on profit of selling more or fewer units than budgeted, sometimes further divided into sales mix and quantity variances when several products are sold.

Variance analysis supports management by exception, in which managers focus their attention on significant variances rather than reviewing every detail. Organizations often set thresholds, such as variances greater than a certain percentage or amount, or patterns of repeated variances, that trigger investigation. Investigation should consider the costs and benefits of further analysis and should seek causes rather than simply assigning blame.

Standard costing has been criticized in modern business environments. Rapidly changing technologies and products can make standards quickly outdated. In highly automated factories, direct labour may be a small proportion of costs, reducing the usefulness of labour variances. An emphasis on favourable price and efficiency variances may encourage behaviour that conflicts with broader goals, such as buying cheap but poor-quality materials, producing excess inventory to absorb fixed overhead and avoid adverse volume variances, or neglecting quality and customer service. Philosophies such as total quality management and just-in-time production emphasise continuous improvement rather than meeting fixed standards. As a result, many organizations supplement standard costing with non-financial performance measures, such as quality, delivery time, and customer satisfaction, and update standards regularly to reflect current conditions.
summary:
Standard costing sets predetermined costs of products or services under efficient conditions, and variance analysis compares actual results with these standards to identify, investigate, and correct deviations, in manufacturing and services such as hospitals and banks. Standard cost cards specify quantity and price standards for materials, labour hours and rates, and overhead rates; ideal standards assume perfect efficiency, while attainable standards allowing normal waste and downtime are preferred, derived from engineering studies, time and motion analysis, history, and supplier data.

Favourable variances lower costs and unfavourable ones raise them; total variances are split into price and quantity components using flexible budgets adjusted to actual output rather than static budgets. The materials price variance (actual quantity × price difference) is usually purchasing's responsibility, and the usage variance (standard price × quantity difference) production's; in the shirt example, cheaper fabric gave a 10,500-taka favourable price variance but extra usage a 15,000-taka unfavourable variance, netting 4,500 taka unfavourable and suggesting linked quality problems. Labour rate and efficiency variances reflect wages, overtime, skills, supervision, breakdowns, and materials, with optional idle time variances. Variable overhead splits into spending and efficiency variances, and fixed overhead into budget and volume variances reflecting capacity use; sales price and volume (mix and quantity) variances complete the picture. Variance analysis supports management by exception with investigation thresholds focused on causes. Critics note outdated standards, small labour shares in automated plants, and incentives for cheap materials, excess inventory, and neglect of quality, so firms add non-financial measures, continuous improvement, and frequently updated standards.

By comparing actual costs with standard costs and analysing the differences, known as variances, managers can identify areas where performance is better or worse than expected, investigate causes, and take corrective action. Standard costing is widely used in manufacturing and has also been applied in service organizations such as hospitals, banks, and fast-food restaurants.

Standards are set separately for the quantity and the price of each input. A standard cost card for a product lists the standard quantity of each direct material, such as kilograms of raw material per unit, and its standard price per kilogram; the standard direct labour hours per unit and the standard wage rate per hour; and the standard overhead rate applied per unit of an allocation base, such as labour or machine hours. Standards may be set at different levels of difficulty. Ideal standards assume perfect efficiency, with no waste, breakdowns, or idle time; they are rarely achieved and may discourage employees. Practical or attainable standards allow for normal waste, machine downtime, and rest periods, and are challenging but achievable with reasonable effort, so they are generally preferred for motivation and planning. Standards are developed from engineering studies, time and motion analysis, historical data, supplier price information, and discussions with managers and employees.

Variance analysis compares actual results with standards. A favourable variance occurs when actual costs are lower than standard, increasing profit, while an unfavourable or adverse variance occurs when actual costs exceed standard. A central principle is to separate each total cost variance into a price component and a quantity component, because different managers are usually responsible for them and they have different causes. This analysis is commonly based on a flexible budget, which adjusts budgeted costs to the actual level of output achieved. Comparing actual costs with a static budget prepared for the originally planned output would mix the effects of volume differences with those of efficiency and prices.

For direct materials, the materials price variance equals the actual quantity purchased multiplied by the difference between the actual price and the standard price. It is usually the responsibility of the purchasing manager. An unfavourable price variance may result from rising market prices, buying in small quantities, urgent orders, or purchasing higher-quality materials than specified, while a favourable variance may arise from discounts or lower-quality materials. The materials quantity or usage variance equals the standard price multiplied by the difference between the actual quantity used and the standard quantity allowed for the actual output. It is usually the responsibility of the production manager. Unfavourable usage variances may result from waste, spoilage, poorly maintained machines, inexperienced workers, or low-quality materials.

Consider a garment factory with a standard of two metres of fabric per shirt at 150 taka per metre. During a month, it produces 1,000 shirts and uses 2,100 metres of fabric purchased at 145 taka per metre. The standard quantity allowed is 2,000 metres. The price variance is 2,100 metres multiplied by 5 taka, or 10,500 taka favourable, because the fabric cost less than standard. The quantity variance is 150 taka multiplied by 100 metres, or 15,000 taka unfavourable, because more fabric was used than allowed. The total materials variance is therefore 4,500 taka unfavourable. The analysis reveals an important possibility: the cheaper fabric might have been of lower quality, causing more waste, so the favourable price variance may be linked to the unfavourable quantity variance. Variances should therefore be interpreted together, not in isolation.

For direct labour, the labour rate variance equals the actual hours worked multiplied by the difference between the actual and standard wage rates. It may result from overtime premiums, wage changes, or using workers with higher or lower skill levels than planned. The labour efficiency variance equals the standard rate multiplied by the difference between actual hours worked and the standard hours allowed for actual output. Unfavourable efficiency variances may result from inexperienced workers, poor supervision, machine breakdowns, poor-quality materials, or production scheduling problems, while favourable variances may reflect improved methods or motivation. Some organizations also calculate an idle time variance for hours paid but not worked.

Overhead variances are more complex. Variable overhead can be analysed into a spending variance, comparing actual variable overhead with the budget for actual hours, and an efficiency variance, which arises because variable overhead is applied according to an activity base such as labour hours, so inefficient use of labour also causes more variable overhead to be incurred. Fixed overhead is analysed into a budget or spending variance, the difference between actual and budgeted fixed overhead, and a volume variance, which arises when actual production differs from the planned level used to calculate the fixed overhead rate. The volume variance reflects the utilization of capacity rather than cost control, because fixed costs do not change with output in the short term.

Sales variances complete the picture of performance. The sales price variance measures the effect of selling at prices different from standard, and the sales volume variance measures the effect on profit of selling more or fewer units than budgeted, sometimes further divided into sales mix and quantity variances when several products are sold.

Variance analysis supports management by exception, in which managers focus their attention on significant variances rather than reviewing every detail. Organizations often set thresholds, such as variances greater than a certain percentage or amount, or patterns of repeated variances, that trigger investigation. Investigation should consider the costs and benefits of further analysis and should seek causes rather than simply assigning blame.

Standard costing has been criticized in modern business environments. Rapidly changing technologies and products can make standards quickly outdated. In highly automated factories, direct labour may be a small proportion of costs, reducing the usefulness of labour variances. An emphasis on favourable price and efficiency variances may encourage behaviour that conflicts with broader goals, such as buying cheap but poor-quality materials, producing excess inventory to absorb fixed overhead and avoid adverse volume variances, or neglecting quality and customer service. Philosophies such as total quality management and just-in-time production emphasise continuous improvement rather than meeting fixed standards. As a result, many organizations supplement standard costing with non-financial performance measures, such as quality, delivery time, and customer satisfaction, and update standards regularly to reflect current conditions.

source_text:
Gases are composed of enormous numbers of molecules moving rapidly in all directions. The macroscopic properties of a gas that we can measure, such as its pressure, temperature, and volume, arise from the combined behaviour of these molecules. The kinetic theory of gases connects these macroscopic properties with the microscopic motion of molecules. Developed in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries by scientists including Daniel Bernoulli, Rudolf Clausius, James Clerk Maxwell, and Ludwig Boltzmann, kinetic theory was one of the first successful applications of statistical reasoning in physics, and it provided strong support for the existence of atoms and molecules before they could be observed directly.

The simplest version of kinetic theory describes an ideal gas and rests on several assumptions. A gas consists of a very large number of identical molecules in continuous, random motion. The molecules are very small compared with the average distances between them, so their own volume is negligible compared with the volume of the container. The molecules exert no forces on one another except during collisions, which are brief. Collisions between molecules and with the walls of the container are perfectly elastic, meaning that total kinetic energy is conserved. Between collisions, molecules move in straight lines at constant speed, and the motion obeys Newton's laws.

Pressure arises from the collisions of molecules with the walls of the container. When a molecule strikes a wall and rebounds, its momentum perpendicular to the wall reverses direction, and the wall exerts a force on it; by Newton's third law, the molecule exerts an equal and opposite force on the wall. Because there are vast numbers of molecules striking the walls every second, these individual impulses combine to produce a steady average force per unit area, which we measure as pressure. Analysing the momentum transfer for molecules moving in random directions leads to an important result: the pressure equals one third of the number of molecules per unit volume multiplied by the mass of each molecule and the mean of the squared speeds of the molecules. In other words, pressure is proportional to the density of the gas and to the average of the square of molecular speeds.

Comparing this result with the ideal gas law, which states that pressure multiplied by volume equals the number of moles multiplied by the gas constant and the absolute temperature, reveals the microscopic meaning of temperature. The average translational kinetic energy of a gas molecule equals three halves of the Boltzmann constant multiplied by the absolute temperature. The Boltzmann constant, about 1.38 times ten to the power minus twenty-three joules per kelvin, links the energy of individual molecules to temperature and equals the gas constant divided by Avogadro's number. Temperature is therefore a measure of the average kinetic energy of random molecular motion. At absolute zero, the classical theory would predict that molecular motion ceases, although quantum mechanics shows that some zero-point energy remains.

This relationship has several consequences. At the same temperature, molecules of all gases have the same average translational kinetic energy, regardless of their mass. Because kinetic energy equals one half of mass multiplied by speed squared, lighter molecules must move faster on average than heavier ones at the same temperature. The root-mean-square speed, the square root of the mean of the squared speeds, equals the square root of three times the Boltzmann constant times temperature divided by the molecular mass, or equivalently three times the gas constant times temperature divided by the molar mass. At room temperature, the root-mean-square speed of nitrogen molecules is about 500 metres per second, while hydrogen molecules move about four times faster. This explains Graham's law of effusion, which states that the rate at which a gas escapes through a tiny hole is inversely proportional to the square root of its molar mass, a principle historically used to separate isotopes of uranium. It also helps explain why light gases such as hydrogen and helium escape from planetary atmospheres more readily.

The molecules of a gas do not all move at the same speed. Collisions constantly exchange energy, so at any instant some molecules move slowly and others very fast. Maxwell and Boltzmann derived the distribution of molecular speeds in a gas at equilibrium, known as the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution. The distribution curve rises from zero at zero speed to a maximum at the most probable speed and then falls off gradually, with a long tail towards high speeds. Three characteristic speeds can be distinguished: the most probable speed, the mean speed, and the root-mean-square speed, which increase in that order. As temperature rises, the distribution broadens and shifts to higher speeds, and the fraction of molecules with very high speeds increases sharply. This explains why the rates of chemical reactions and evaporation increase rapidly with temperature, because only molecules with energies above a certain threshold can react or escape from a liquid surface.

Kinetic theory also explains the heat capacities of gases. According to the equipartition theorem, each independent way in which a molecule can store energy, called a degree of freedom, contributes on average one half of the Boltzmann constant times temperature to the molecule's energy. Monatomic gases such as helium and argon have three translational degrees of freedom, giving a molar heat capacity at constant volume of three halves of the gas constant. Diatomic molecules such as nitrogen and oxygen also have two rotational degrees of freedom at ordinary temperatures, giving five halves of the gas constant. At high temperatures, vibrational modes also become active. The failure of classical theory to explain why some degrees of freedom are frozen out at low temperatures was one of the puzzles resolved by quantum mechanics.

Other properties of gases can also be understood using kinetic theory. The mean free path, the average distance a molecule travels between collisions, depends on the size of the molecules and the number density of the gas; at atmospheric pressure it is on the order of tens of nanometres for air. Diffusion, viscosity, and thermal conductivity of gases arise from the transport of mass, momentum, and energy by moving molecules, and kinetic theory predicts how these properties depend on temperature and pressure.

Real gases deviate from ideal behaviour, especially at high pressures and low temperatures, when molecules are close together. Their finite size and the attractive forces between them become significant. The van der Waals equation modifies the ideal gas law by adding correction terms for molecular volume and intermolecular attraction, explaining phenomena such as liquefaction. Nevertheless, the ideal gas model and kinetic theory provide an excellent description of most gases under ordinary conditions and remain fundamental to thermodynamics, atmospheric science, and chemical engineering.
summary:
The kinetic theory of gases, developed by Bernoulli, Clausius, Maxwell, and Boltzmann, explains pressure, temperature, and volume through molecular motion and supported the reality of atoms. Its ideal-gas assumptions are many identical molecules in random motion, negligible molecular volume, no forces except brief elastic collisions, and straight-line Newtonian motion between collisions. Gases are composed of enormous numbers of molecules moving rapidly in all directions. The macroscopic properties of a gas that we can measure, such as its pressure, temperature, and volume, arise from the combined behaviour of these molecules. The kinetic theory of gases connects these macroscopic properties with the microscopic motion of molecules. Developed in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries by scientists including Daniel Bernoulli, Rudolf Clausius, James Clerk Maxwell, and Ludwig Boltzmann, kinetic theory was one of the first successful applications of statistical reasoning in physics, and it provided strong support for the existence of atoms and molecules before they could be observed directly.

The simplest version of kinetic theory describes an ideal gas and rests on several assumptions. A gas consists of a very large number of identical molecules in continuous, random motion. The molecules are very small compared with the average distances between them, so their own volume is negligible compared with the volume of the container. The molecules exert no forces on one another except during collisions, which are brief. Collisions between molecules and with the walls of the container are perfectly elastic, meaning that total kinetic energy is conserved. Between collisions, molecules move in straight lines at constant speed, and the motion obeys Newton's laws.

Pressure arises from the collisions of molecules with the walls of the container. When a molecule strikes a wall and rebounds, its momentum perpendicular to the wall reverses direction, and the wall exerts a force on it; by Newton's third law, the molecule exerts an equal and opposite force on the wall. Because there are vast numbers of molecules striking the walls every second, these individual impulses combine to produce a steady average force per unit area, which we measure as pressure. Analysing the momentum transfer for molecules moving in random directions leads to an important result: the pressure equals one third of the number of molecules per unit volume multiplied by the mass of each molecule and the mean of the squared speeds of the molecules. In other words, pressure is proportional to the density of the gas and to the average of the square of molecular speeds.

Comparing this result with the ideal gas law, which states that pressure multiplied by volume equals the number of moles multiplied by the gas constant and the absolute temperature, reveals the microscopic meaning of temperature. The average translational kinetic energy of a gas molecule equals three halves of the Boltzmann constant multiplied by the absolute temperature. The Boltzmann constant, about 1.38 times ten to the power minus twenty-three joules per kelvin, links the energy of individual molecules to temperature and equals the gas constant divided by Avogadro's number. Temperature is therefore a measure of the average kinetic energy of random molecular motion. At absolute zero, the classical theory would predict that molecular motion ceases, although quantum mechanics shows that some zero-point energy remains.

This relationship has several consequences. At the same temperature, molecules of all gases have the same average translational kinetic energy, regardless of their mass. Because kinetic energy equals one half of mass multiplied by speed squared, lighter molecules must move faster on average than heavier ones at the same temperature. The root-mean-square speed, the square root of the mean of the squared speeds, equals the square root of three times the Boltzmann constant times temperature divided by the molecular mass, or equivalently three times the gas constant times temperature divided by the molar mass. At room temperature, the root-mean-square speed of nitrogen molecules is about 500 metres per second, while hydrogen molecules move about four times faster. This explains Graham's law of effusion, which states that the rate at which a gas escapes through a tiny hole is inversely proportional to the square root of its molar mass, a principle historically used to separate isotopes of uranium. It also helps explain why light gases such as hydrogen and helium escape from planetary atmospheres more readily.

The molecules of a gas do not all move at the same speed. Collisions constantly exchange energy, so at any instant some molecules move slowly and others very fast. Maxwell and Boltzmann derived the distribution of molecular speeds in a gas at equilibrium, known as the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution. The distribution curve rises from zero at zero speed to a maximum at the most probable speed and then falls off gradually, with a long tail towards high speeds. Three characteristic speeds can be distinguished: the most probable speed, the mean speed, and the root-mean-square speed, which increase in that order. As temperature rises, the distribution broadens and shifts to higher speeds, and the fraction of molecules with very high speeds increases sharply. This explains why the rates of chemical reactions and evaporation increase rapidly with temperature, because only molecules with energies above a certain threshold can react or escape from a liquid surface.

Kinetic theory also explains the heat capacities of gases. According to the equipartition theorem, each independent way in which a molecule can store energy, called a degree of freedom, contributes on average one half of the Boltzmann constant times temperature to the molecule's energy. Monatomic gases such as helium and argon have three translational degrees of freedom, giving a molar heat capacity at constant volume of three halves of the gas constant. Diatomic molecules such as nitrogen and oxygen also have two rotational degrees of freedom at ordinary temperatures, giving five halves of the gas constant. At high temperatures, vibrational modes also become active. The failure of classical theory to explain why some degrees of freedom are frozen out at low temperatures was one of the puzzles resolved by quantum mechanics.

Other properties of gases can also be understood using kinetic theory. The mean free path, the average distance a molecule travels between collisions, depends on the size of the molecules and the number density of the gas; at atmospheric pressure it is on the order of tens of nanometres for air. Diffusion, viscosity, and thermal conductivity of gases arise from the transport of mass, momentum, and energy by moving molecules, and kinetic theory predicts how these properties depend on temperature and pressure.

Real gases deviate from ideal behaviour, especially at high pressures and low temperatures, when molecules are close together. Their finite size and the attractive forces between them become significant. The van der Waals equation modifies the ideal gas law by adding correction terms for molecular volume and intermolecular attraction, explaining phenomena such as liquefaction. Nevertheless, the ideal gas model and kinetic theory provide an excellent description of most gases under ordinary conditions and remain fundamental to thermodynamics, atmospheric science, and chemical engineering.

source_text:
Theories of chemical bonding seek to explain why atoms combine, how strongly they are held together, and what properties the resulting molecules have. Simple models, such as Lewis structures and valence bond theory, describe bonds as pairs of electrons localized between two atoms. These models are useful but cannot explain certain observations. A notable example is oxygen. The Lewis structure of the oxygen molecule shows a double bond with all electrons paired, which predicts that oxygen should be diamagnetic, weakly repelled by a magnetic field. In fact, liquid oxygen is paramagnetic and is attracted to the poles of a strong magnet, indicating that it contains unpaired electrons. Molecular orbital theory, developed in the late 1920s and 1930s by Friedrich Hund, Robert Mulliken, and others, explains such observations by treating electrons as belonging to the molecule as a whole rather than to individual bonds.

In molecular orbital theory, atomic orbitals of the bonding atoms combine to form molecular orbitals, which extend over the entire molecule. A common approximation, called the linear combination of atomic orbitals, describes each molecular orbital as a sum or difference of atomic orbitals. When two atomic orbitals combine, they form two molecular orbitals. Constructive combination, in which the wave functions add in phase, produces a bonding molecular orbital with increased electron density between the nuclei. Electrons in this orbital attract both nuclei and hold them together, so the bonding orbital is lower in energy than the original atomic orbitals. Destructive combination, in which the wave functions are out of phase, produces an antibonding molecular orbital, usually marked with an asterisk, which has a node, a region of zero electron density, between the nuclei. Electrons in antibonding orbitals destabilize the molecule, and the antibonding orbital is higher in energy than the original atomic orbitals. The number of molecular orbitals formed always equals the number of atomic orbitals combined.

Molecular orbitals are classified by their symmetry. Sigma orbitals are symmetrical around the axis joining the two nuclei, and they are formed by head-on overlap of s orbitals or of p orbitals pointing along the bond axis. Pi orbitals are formed by side-by-side overlap of p orbitals perpendicular to the bond axis, and they have electron density above and below the axis, with a nodal plane containing the axis. Electrons fill molecular orbitals according to the same rules that govern atomic orbitals: the Aufbau principle, filling the lowest energy orbitals first; the Pauli exclusion principle, allowing at most two electrons with opposite spins in each orbital; and Hund's rule, placing electrons singly in orbitals of equal energy before pairing them.

The stability of a molecule can be assessed using bond order, defined as one half of the difference between the number of electrons in bonding orbitals and the number in antibonding orbitals. A bond order of one corresponds to a single bond, two to a double bond, and three to a triple bond. A higher bond order generally indicates a stronger and shorter bond, and a bond order of zero suggests that the molecule is not stable. The hydrogen molecule provides the simplest example. Two hydrogen 1s orbitals combine to form a sigma bonding orbital and a sigma antibonding orbital. The two electrons occupy the bonding orbital, giving a bond order of one, consistent with a stable single bond. For a hypothetical helium molecule, He2, four electrons would fill both the bonding and antibonding orbitals, giving a bond order of zero, which explains why helium exists as separate atoms. The helium ion He2+, with three electrons, would have a bond order of one half and is observed in the gas phase as a weakly bound species.

For diatomic molecules of second-period elements, the 2s and 2p atomic orbitals combine to form a set of molecular orbitals: sigma 2s and sigma star 2s; a sigma 2p orbital formed from p orbitals along the bond axis; two degenerate pi 2p orbitals; and their corresponding antibonding orbitals, two pi star 2p orbitals and a sigma star 2p orbital. The relative order of the sigma 2p and pi 2p orbitals depends on the element. For oxygen, fluorine, and neon, the sigma 2p orbital lies below the pi 2p orbitals. For lithium through nitrogen, interaction between 2s and 2p orbitals raises the energy of the sigma 2p orbital above that of the pi 2p orbitals.

Applying this diagram to oxygen explains its paramagnetism. The oxygen molecule has twelve valence electrons. After filling the sigma 2s, sigma star 2s, sigma 2p, and the two pi 2p orbitals, two electrons remain. These occupy the two degenerate pi star 2p orbitals, one in each, with parallel spins according to Hund's rule. The presence of two unpaired electrons accounts for the paramagnetism of oxygen. The bond order is one half of eight bonding electrons minus four antibonding electrons, which equals two, consistent with the double bond length and strength observed experimentally. The theory also explains trends among related species. Removing an electron from an antibonding orbital to form the dioxygenyl cation, O2+, increases the bond order to 2.5, producing a shorter and stronger bond, while adding electrons to form superoxide and peroxide ions lowers the bond order. source_text:
Air conditioning involves controlling the temperature, humidity, cleanliness, and movement of air in an enclosed space to provide comfort for people or suitable conditions for industrial processes, data centres, hospitals, and storage of products. Atmospheric air is a mixture of dry air, mainly nitrogen and oxygen, and water vapour. Although water vapour usually makes up only a small percentage of the mixture, it has a large effect on human comfort and on the energy required for conditioning, because adding or removing moisture involves significant amounts of latent heat. Psychrometrics is the study of the thermodynamic properties of moist air, and it provides the tools needed to design and analyse air-conditioning systems.

Several properties describe the state of moist air. The dry-bulb temperature is the ordinary air temperature measured by a thermometer shielded from radiation and moisture. The humidity ratio, also called specific humidity or moisture content, is the mass of water vapour per unit mass of dry air, typically expressed in grams of water per kilogram of dry air. Relative humidity is the ratio of the partial pressure of water vapour in the air to the saturation pressure of water vapour at the same temperature, usually expressed as a percentage. Air at one hundred percent relative humidity is saturated and cannot hold additional water vapour at that temperature. Because the saturation pressure rises rapidly with temperature, warm air can hold much more moisture than cold air, so the same moisture content corresponds to a lower relative humidity at higher temperatures.

The dew point temperature is the temperature at which air becomes saturated when cooled at constant pressure and constant moisture content. If air is cooled below its dew point, water vapour condenses, which is why water droplets form on cold drink glasses and why cooling coils in air conditioners remove moisture from the air. The wet-bulb temperature is measured by a thermometer whose bulb is covered with a wet wick over which air flows; evaporation from the wick cools the thermometer to a temperature that depends on how dry the air is. The difference between dry-bulb and wet-bulb temperatures, called the wet-bulb depression, indicates the humidity of the air, and for saturated air the two temperatures are equal. A sling psychrometer, which contains both thermometers and is swung through the air, provides a simple method of measuring humidity. Many practical problems require connecting a set of locations as cheaply as possible. A telecommunications company may want to connect cities with fibre-optic cable using the minimum total length of cable, an electricity utility may want to link substations, and a town planner may want to connect villages with roads at the lowest construction cost. Such problems can be modelled using a connected, undirected graph in which vertices represent locations and weighted edges represent possible connections and their costs. A spanning tree of the graph is a subset of edges that connects all the vertices without forming any cycles. A graph with V vertices has spanning trees containing exactly V minus one edges. The minimum spanning tree, MST, is the spanning tree whose total edge weight is as small as possible. If all edge weights are distinct, the minimum spanning tree is unique; otherwise, there may be several with the same total weight.

Minimum spanning tree algorithms rely on two fundamental properties. The cut property states that for any partition of the vertices into two non-empty sets, called a cut, the lightest edge crossing the cut belongs to some minimum spanning tree. Intuitively, any spanning tree must cross the cut somewhere, and choosing the cheapest crossing edge can never be a mistake. The cycle property states that for any cycle in the graph, the heaviest edge in the cycle does not belong to any minimum spanning tree when edge weights are distinct, because removing it and keeping the rest of the cycle still connects the same vertices at lower cost. These properties justify greedy algorithms, which build the tree by repeatedly making locally optimal choices.

Kruskal's algorithm, published by Joseph Kruskal in 1956, considers edges in order of increasing weight. It begins with each vertex as a separate component, forming a forest of single-vertex trees. It then examines the edges one by one, from lightest to heaviest. If an edge connects two vertices in different components, it is added to the tree, merging the two components into one. If the edge connects two vertices already in the same component, adding it would create a cycle, so it is skipped. The algorithm stops when V minus one edges have been added and all vertices belong to a single tree. Kruskal's algorithm can be described as growing a forest that gradually merges into one tree.

An efficient implementation of Kruskal's algorithm requires a way to determine quickly whether two vertices belong to the same component. This is achieved with a disjoint-set data structure, also called union-find. The structure supports two operations: find, which identifies the representative of the set containing a vertex, and union, which merges two sets. With optimizations known as union by rank, which attaches the smaller tree under the root of the larger, and path compression, which makes every vertex on a search path point directly to the root, these operations take nearly constant time on average. The overall running time of Kruskal's algorithm is dominated by sorting the edges, giving a time proportional to E multiplied by the logarithm of E, where E is the number of edges.

Prim's algorithm, first discovered by Vojtěch Jarník in 1930 and later independently by Robert Prim and Edsger Dijkstra, grows a single tree from a starting vertex. At each step, it adds the lightest edge that connects a vertex in the tree to a vertex outside it, thereby adding a new vertex to the tree. This is a direct application of the cut property, with the cut separating the vertices already in the tree from the rest. The algorithm continues until all vertices are included. Prim's algorithm is efficiently implemented using a priority queue that stores, for each vertex not yet in the tree, the weight of the lightest edge connecting it to the tree. When a vertex is added, the priority values of its neighbours are updated if the new edges are lighter. Using a binary heap, the running time is proportional to E multiplied by the logarithm of V, and with a Fibonacci heap it can be reduced to E plus V log V. For dense graphs, a simple array-based implementation runs in time proportional to V squared, which can be faster than heap-based versions.

The two algorithms suit different situations. Kruskal's algorithm works well for sparse graphs, in which the number of edges is close to the number of vertices, and when edges are already sorted or can be sorted efficiently. Its forest-merging approach also extends naturally to finding minimum spanning forests in graphs that are not connected. Prim's algorithm is often preferred for dense graphs, especially with the array implementation, and is convenient when the graph is represented by adjacency lists or matrices. A third classical method, Borůvka's algorithm, developed in 1926 for designing an electrical network in Moravia, repeatedly adds the cheapest edge leaving each component simultaneously; it is well suited to parallel computation.

A simple example illustrates Kruskal's algorithm. Suppose four towns, A, B, C, and D, can be connected by roads with costs AB 1, BC 2, AC 3, CD 4, and BD 5. A minimum spanning tree minimizes the total weight of all edges needed to connect every vertex, whereas a shortest path tree minimizes the distance from a particular source to each vertex. The path between two vertices in a minimum spanning tree is not necessarily the shortest path between them in the original graph.

source_text:
Copyright is a form of intellectual property that protects original works of authorship. It gives creators exclusive rights to control certain uses of their works for a limited period, allowing them to benefit financially and to be recognized for their creative efforts. The underlying policy rationale is to encourage the creation and dissemination of knowledge and culture by rewarding authors, while ultimately enriching the public domain when protection expires. Copyright is relevant to writers, musicians, filmmakers, photographers, software developers, publishers, broadcasters, educators, and anyone who creates or uses creative content, and it has become increasingly important and contested in the digital age, when works can be copied and distributed instantly worldwide.

Copyright protects a wide range of works. These include literary works, such as books, articles, and computer programs; dramatic works, such as plays and screenplays; musical works and sound recordings; artistic works, such as paintings, drawings, photographs, sculptures, and architectural works; cinematographic films and other audiovisual works; and, in many jurisdictions, broadcasts and the typographical arrangement of published editions. Computer software is protected as a literary work under international agreements, and databases may be protected if their selection or arrangement is original.

Two fundamental requirements determine whether a work is protected. First, the work must be original. Originality does not require novelty or artistic merit; it generally means that the work originates from the author and involves at least a minimal degree of independent creative effort or skill, rather than being copied. The level of creativity required varies between jurisdictions, but mere facts and purely mechanical compilations may not qualify. Second, copyright protects the expression of ideas, not the ideas themselves, a principle known as the idea-expression dichotomy. A novelist cannot prevent others from writing a story about a detective solving a murder, but can prevent others from copying the specific text, characters, and detailed plot developed in the novel. Similarly, copyright does not protect facts, methods of operation, procedures, or mathematical concepts. In many countries, copyright arises automatically when an original work is fixed in a tangible form, such as written down or recorded, without any requirement for registration, although registration may provide evidentiary advantages.

The copyright owner has a bundle of exclusive economic rights. These typically include the rights to reproduce the work, to distribute copies to the public, to perform or display the work publicly, to communicate it to the public, including through broadcasting and making it available online, to translate it, and to make adaptations or derivative works, such as turning a novel into a film. These rights can be licensed or assigned to others, and much of the creative economy depends on such transactions, for example when authors license publishers to print their books or musicians assign rights to record labels. In addition to economic rights, many legal systems recognize moral rights, which protect the personal connection between authors and their works. These include the right of attribution, to be identified as the author, and the right of integrity, to object to distortion, mutilation, or modification of the work that would harm the author's honour or reputation. Moral rights often cannot be transferred, though they may sometimes be waived.

Copyright protection lasts for a limited period. Under the Berne Convention, the minimum term for most works is the life of the author plus fifty years, and many countries, including those of the European Union and the United States, provide life plus seventy years. Different terms may apply to sound recordings, films, works created by companies, and anonymous works. When copyright expires, works enter the public domain and can be freely used by anyone, which allows classic literature, music, and art to be republished, adapted, and studied without permission.

The international framework for copyright is based largely on treaties. The Berne Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works, first adopted in 1886, established the principle of national treatment, under which each member country must give works from other member countries the same protection it gives to its own nationals, and it prohibited formalities as a condition of protection. The Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights, TRIPS, administered by the World Trade Organization, incorporated Berne standards and added enforcement obligations. The World Intellectual Property Organization Copyright Treaty and Performances and Phonograms Treaty of 1996 addressed digital issues, including the right of making works available online and legal protection for technological protection measures. In Bangladesh, copyright is governed by the Copyright Act of 2000, which was amended and later replaced by the Copyright Act of 2023, and is administered by the Copyright Office.

Copyright is not absolute; laws provide limitations and exceptions that permit certain uses without permission, balancing the interests of rights holders with those of the public. In the United States, the fair use doctrine considers four factors: the purpose and character of the use, including whether it is commercial or transformative; the nature of the copyrighted work; the amount and substantiality of the portion used; and the effect of the use on the potential market for the work. Many Commonwealth countries, including Bangladesh and India, use a fair dealing approach, which allows specified purposes such as research, private study, criticism, review, and reporting current events, subject to fairness. Other exceptions commonly cover education, libraries and archives, quotation, parody, and access for people with visual impairments, as encouraged by the Marrakesh Treaty of 2013.

Infringement occurs when someone exercises one of the exclusive rights without authorization and without the benefit of an exception. To establish infringement, a copyright owner typically must show ownership of a valid copyright and copying of a substantial part of the protected expression, which may be inferred from access to the work and substantial similarity. Remedies include injunctions, damages or an account of profits, and the seizure of infringing copies, and serious commercial piracy may be a criminal offence. Online infringement has led to systems under which internet service providers and platforms may avoid liability if they remove infringing content after receiving notice from rights holders, as well as debates about the responsibilities of platforms.

Copyright continues to face new challenges. Digital technologies make copying and sharing easy, raising difficult questions about piracy, enforcement across borders, and the appropriate scope of exceptions. Open licensing models, such as Creative Commons licences and open-source software licences, allow creators to grant permissions in advance while retaining some rights. The rise of artificial intelligence raises questions about whether works generated by machines can be protected and whether training AI systems on copyrighted material is permitted, issues that courts and legislatures are actively considering.

source_text:
A bioreactor is a vessel in which a biological process is carried out under controlled conditions. Bioreactors are used to grow microorganisms, animal cells, or plant cells in order to produce useful products, such as antibiotics, enzymes, vaccines, therapeutic proteins, monoclonal antibodies, organic acids, biofuels, and fermented foods. They are also used in environmental engineering, for example in wastewater treatment. The purpose of a bioreactor is to provide an environment in which cells can grow and produce the desired product efficiently, consistently, and safely, by controlling factors such as temperature, pH, dissolved oxygen, nutrient supply, mixing, and sterility. Bioreactor design and operation form a central part of bioprocess engineering, which links laboratory discoveries to industrial production.

The most widely used industrial bioreactor is the stirred-tank bioreactor. It consists of a cylindrical vessel, typically made of stainless steel for large-scale microbial processes, fitted with a motor-driven agitator that has one or more impellers mounted on a central shaft. Baffles, vertical strips attached to the vessel wall, prevent the liquid from simply rotating as a vortex and improve mixing. Air or oxygen is introduced at the bottom through a sparger, a perforated ring or pipe that releases gas bubbles, and the impellers break the bubbles into smaller ones and distribute them throughout the liquid. Temperature is controlled using a jacket around the vessel or internal coils through which cooling or heating water circulates. The bioreactor is equipped with ports for adding nutrients, acids, bases, and antifoam agents, for taking samples, and for inoculation, and with sensors for temperature, pH, dissolved oxygen, pressure, and foam.

Other designs are used for particular purposes. Airlift bioreactors have no mechanical agitator; instead, gas introduced at the bottom of one section, the riser, reduces the density of the liquid there, causing circulation between the riser and a downcomer. They provide gentler mixing with lower shear and lower energy consumption and are used for some shear-sensitive cells and large-scale processes. Bubble column bioreactors are simple tall vessels in which mixing is provided only by rising gas bubbles. Packed-bed and fluidized-bed bioreactors contain immobilized cells or enzymes attached to solid supports, which allow continuous processing. Photobioreactors provide light for the cultivation of algae and other photosynthetic organisms. In the biopharmaceutical industry, single-use bioreactors made from pre-sterilized plastic bags supported in rigid containers have become widely used for mammalian cell cultures, because they reduce cleaning and sterilization requirements and allow flexible, rapid changeover between products.

Several key factors must be controlled for successful operation. Oxygen supply is often the most critical requirement for aerobic cultures. Oxygen is only sparingly soluble in water, so it must be transferred continuously from gas bubbles to the liquid at a rate that matches the cells' consumption. The rate of oxygen transfer is commonly described by the volumetric mass transfer coefficient, kLa, multiplied by the difference between the saturation concentration of dissolved oxygen and its actual concentration. Engineers increase oxygen transfer by increasing agitation speed, which creates smaller bubbles and more interfacial area, by increasing the gas flow rate, by using oxygen-enriched air, or by increasing pressure. If oxygen supply is insufficient, dissolved oxygen falls and growth or product formation may be limited.

Mixing ensures uniform distribution of nutrients, oxygen, and temperature and prevents the settling of cells. In large vessels, achieving homogeneity is challenging, and gradients in substrate concentration, pH, or dissolved oxygen can develop, exposing cells to fluctuating conditions. However, mixing generates shear forces, which can damage cells. Microorganisms such as bacteria and yeasts are generally robust, but mammalian cells, which lack cell walls, are much more sensitive to shear, so animal cell cultures use gentler agitation, specially designed impellers, and careful gas sparging.

Temperature must be maintained within a narrow range suited to the organism, often around 30 to 37 degrees Celsius, and cooling systems must remove the considerable heat generated by microbial metabolism and agitation in large vessels. The pH is controlled by automatic addition of acid or base, because metabolic products such as organic acids or ammonia can shift pH. Foaming, caused by proteins and gas sparging, can block exhaust filters and lead to contamination, so antifoam agents are added or mechanical foam breakers are used.

Sterility is essential, because contaminating microorganisms can consume nutrients, produce unwanted products, or destroy the culture. Stainless steel bioreactors are sterilized in place using steam, and media are sterilized by heat or filtration. Air entering and leaving the bioreactor passes through sterile filters, and aseptic techniques are used for inoculation and sampling.

Bioreactors can be operated in different modes. In batch operation, the vessel is filled with medium and inoculated, and the culture grows without further addition of nutrients, apart from acid, base, and antifoam, until the process is complete, after which the product is harvested. Batch cultures pass through characteristic growth phases, including lag, exponential, stationary, and death phases. Fed-batch operation adds nutrients gradually during the process, which allows high cell densities to be reached while avoiding the inhibitory effects of high initial nutrient concentrations; it is the most common mode for producing recombinant proteins and antibiotics. In continuous operation, fresh medium is added continuously while culture broth is removed at the same rate, maintaining a steady state; in a chemostat, the growth rate is controlled by the dilution rate. Continuous operation can be highly productive but is more vulnerable to contamination and genetic instability over long periods. Perfusion cultures, used for some mammalian cell processes, continuously replace medium while retaining cells in the bioreactor.

Scale-up, the process of moving from laboratory bioreactors of a few litres to production vessels of thousands or even hundreds of thousands of litres, is one of the major challenges of bioprocess engineering. As vessel size increases, it becomes impossible to keep all parameters identical, because surface-to-volume ratios, mixing times, and heat removal capacity change. Engineers therefore choose scale-up criteria, such as maintaining constant power input per unit volume, constant kLa, constant impeller tip speed, or constant mixing time, depending on which factor is most critical for the process. Pilot-scale studies and computational fluid dynamics help predict performance at large scale.

Modern bioreactors are increasingly controlled by computer systems that monitor process variables in real time and adjust conditions automatically. Process analytical technology aims to monitor critical quality attributes during production, and good manufacturing practice requirements apply to bioreactors used for pharmaceutical products, ensuring consistent quality and regulatory compliance.
