topic: Good Manufacturing Practice in the Pharmaceutical Industry
source_text:
Patients cannot usually tell whether a tablet contains the correct amount of active ingredient, whether an injection is sterile, or whether a medicine has been contaminated or mixed up with another product. They must rely on manufacturers to produce medicines that are consistently safe, effective, and of the stated quality. Testing samples of finished products alone cannot guarantee this, because only a small fraction of each batch is tested, and many quality problems, such as contamination or mix-ups, may affect only some units. Good Manufacturing Practice, GMP, is the part of quality assurance that ensures medicines are consistently produced and controlled according to quality standards appropriate to their intended use and as required by their marketing authorization. Its central principle is that quality must be built into the product throughout manufacturing rather than tested into it at the end.

GMP requirements developed largely in response to serious incidents. In 1937, more than one hundred people in the United States died after taking a liquid formulation of the antibiotic sulfanilamide dissolved in diethylene glycol, a toxic solvent that had not been tested for safety. The thalidomide disaster of the late 1950s and early 1960s, in which a drug used during pregnancy caused severe birth defects in thousands of children, led to stricter regulation of drug development and manufacturing worldwide. More recently, contamination of medicines with toxic substances has caused deaths in several countries, demonstrating the continuing importance of strict controls. Today, GMP guidelines are issued by the World Health Organization, regional authorities such as the European Medicines Agency, national regulators such as the United States Food and Drug Administration, whose regulations are known as current Good Manufacturing Practice, cGMP, and the Pharmaceutical Inspection Co-operation Scheme. In Bangladesh, the Directorate General of Drug Administration inspects manufacturers against GMP requirements, and compliance with international GMP standards has been essential for the growth of the country's pharmaceutical exports.

GMP covers all aspects of production and quality control, often summarized as the five Ps: people, premises, processes, products, and procedures. A pharmaceutical quality system provides the overall framework, defining responsibilities and ensuring that quality is managed systematically. Senior management is responsible for establishing this system and providing adequate resources.

Personnel must be qualified, trained, and aware of their responsibilities. Manufacturers must have sufficient staff with appropriate education and experience, clear job descriptions, and ongoing training in GMP and in the specific operations they perform. Key positions include the head of production, the head of quality control, and, in many systems, an authorized or qualified person responsible for certifying that each batch meets requirements before release. Personal hygiene requirements, including appropriate protective clothing, handwashing, and health monitoring, prevent workers from contaminating products.

Premises and equipment must be designed, constructed, and maintained to suit the operations performed and to minimize the risk of errors, contamination, and cross-contamination. The flow of materials and personnel is arranged to avoid mix-ups, and separate areas are provided for different operations, such as receiving, storage, weighing, production, packaging, and quality control laboratories. Production of sterile products requires cleanrooms classified according to the permitted concentration of airborne particles and microorganisms, with filtered air supplied through high-efficiency particulate air filters, pressure differentials between rooms, and gowning procedures. Highly potent products, such as certain hormones and cytotoxic drugs, may require dedicated facilities. Equipment must be suitable for its purpose, easy to clean, and regularly calibrated and maintained, and utilities such as purified water and compressed air must meet specified quality standards.

Documentation is often described as the backbone of GMP. The principle is that if it is not documented, it was not done. Written procedures, known as standard operating procedures, describe how operations are performed. Specifications define the quality requirements for starting materials, packaging materials, intermediate products, and finished products. Manufacturing formulae and processing instructions specify the ingredients and steps for each product. Batch manufacturing records document each step of production for every batch as it is carried out, including the materials used, equipment, process parameters, in-process checks, and the signatures of the people who performed and checked each step. These records allow the history of each batch to be traced and investigated if problems arise. Data integrity, ensuring that records are complete, consistent, accurate, attributable, and protected from alteration, has become a major focus of regulatory inspections, often summarized by the acronym ALCOA, meaning attributable, legible, contemporaneous, original, and accurate.

Production must follow approved procedures. Starting materials are purchased from approved suppliers, sampled, and tested before use. Steps are taken to prevent mix-ups and cross-contamination, such as line clearance, verifying that the production area and equipment have been cleared of materials from previous products before starting a new batch, and labelling of containers and equipment. In-process controls monitor critical parameters during manufacturing, such as tablet weight, hardness, and disintegration time.

Validation is a key GMP concept. It provides documented evidence that a process, procedure, method, or system consistently produces results meeting predetermined acceptance criteria. Process validation demonstrates that the manufacturing process consistently produces products of the required quality. Cleaning validation demonstrates that cleaning procedures remove residues of previous products and cleaning agents to acceptable levels. Analytical method validation confirms that testing methods are accurate, precise, specific, and reliable. Equipment qualification includes design, installation, operational, and performance qualification. Computerized systems used in manufacturing and laboratories must also be validated.

Quality control involves sampling and testing starting materials, intermediates, and finished products against specifications, and ensuring that materials are not released until their quality has been judged satisfactory. Retained samples of each batch are stored for future reference. Stability testing provides data to support shelf life and storage conditions.

GMP also requires systems to handle problems and continuous improvement. Deviations from procedures must be recorded and investigated. Corrective and preventive actions, CAPA, address the root causes of problems to prevent recurrence. Change control ensures that changes to materials, equipment, processes, or facilities are evaluated and approved before implementation. Complaints are investigated, and recall procedures allow defective products to be withdrawn from the market quickly. Self-inspections and audits of suppliers help identify weaknesses. Quality risk management, described in international guidelines, encourages manufacturers to focus resources on the aspects of production that pose the greatest risk to patients.

Documentation—SOPs, specifications, manufacturing instructions, and batch records—ensures traceability, guided by ALCOA data integrity principles. Production uses approved suppliers, tested materials, line clearance, labelling, and in-process controls such as tablet weight and hardness. Quality control tests materials and products, retains samples, and supports shelf life through stability studies. Deviation investigation, CAPA, change control, complaint handling, recalls, self-inspections, supplier audits, and quality risk management support continual improvement and patient safety.

source_text:
Walking is one of the most common human activities, yet it is a complex motor task that requires coordinated action of the nervous system, muscles, bones, and joints. Gait analysis is the systematic study of human locomotion. It provides quantitative information about how people walk, which is used to diagnose movement disorders, plan surgical and therapeutic interventions, design and evaluate orthotic and prosthetic devices, assess rehabilitation progress, and improve athletic performance. Biomechanics, the application of mechanical principles to living systems, provides the framework for describing and explaining gait.

The basic unit of walking is the gait cycle, defined as the sequence of events from the initial contact of one foot with the ground to the next initial contact of the same foot. The cycle is divided into two main phases for each limb. The stance phase is the period when the foot is in contact with the ground and accounts for about sixty percent of the cycle at normal walking speed. The swing phase is the period when the foot is off the ground and moving forward, accounting for about forty percent. Because the stance phases of the two legs overlap, there are two periods of double support, when both feet are on the ground, each lasting about ten percent of the cycle. Walking is distinguished from running by the presence of double support; in running, there are periods when neither foot touches the ground.

The stance and swing phases are further divided into subphases. Stance begins with initial contact, usually with the heel in normal walking, followed by loading response, during which body weight is transferred onto the limb and the knee flexes slightly to absorb shock. Mid-stance follows, as the body moves over the supporting foot, and then terminal stance, when the heel rises and the body moves ahead of the foot. Pre-swing, the final part of stance, occurs as the opposite limb makes contact and weight shifts to it. Swing consists of initial swing, when the foot lifts off and the knee flexes to provide clearance, mid-swing, when the limb advances beneath the body, and terminal swing, when the knee extends and the limb decelerates in preparation for the next initial contact.

Spatiotemporal parameters describe the overall pattern of walking. Step length is the distance between successive contacts of opposite feet, while stride length is the distance between successive contacts of the same foot, equal to two step lengths in symmetrical walking. Cadence is the number of steps per minute, typically around 100 to 120 steps per minute for adults. Walking speed equals stride length multiplied by stride frequency, and comfortable walking speed for healthy adults is typically around 1.2 to 1.4 metres per second. Step width is the side-to-side distance between the feet. Changes in these parameters, such as shorter steps, slower speed, increased step width, and longer double support, are common in older adults and in people with neurological or musculoskeletal conditions, and they may indicate an increased risk of falls.

Kinematics describes the motion of body segments and joints without reference to the forces that cause it. In a typical gait cycle, the hip flexes at initial contact and extends during stance, reaching maximum extension near the end of stance, before flexing again during swing. The knee is nearly extended at initial contact, flexes slightly during loading response, extends in mid-stance, and then flexes substantially during pre-swing and initial swing, reaching about sixty degrees, which is essential for foot clearance. At the ankle, the foot moves into plantarflexion after heel contact as it is lowered to the ground, then the tibia rotates forward over the foot in dorsiflexion during mid-stance, followed by rapid plantarflexion at push-off, and dorsiflexion during swing to keep the toes from dragging.

Kinetics examines the forces and moments that produce motion. Ground reaction forces, measured using force plates embedded in a walkway, typically show a characteristic double-peaked vertical force pattern during stance: a first peak during loading response and a second peak during push-off, each exceeding body weight, separated by a trough in mid-stance. Horizontal ground reaction forces show an initial braking force followed by a propulsive force. Using these forces together with kinematic data and the mass properties of body segments, inverse dynamics calculations estimate the net moments and powers at each joint. Such analysis shows, for example, that the ankle plantarflexor muscles generate a large burst of positive power at push-off, providing much of the energy for forward progression, while the knee extensors absorb energy during loading response.

Muscle activity during gait is studied using electromyography, EMG, which records the electrical signals produced by contracting muscles. EMG shows that many muscles are active in short bursts at specific times in the cycle. The tibialis anterior controls the lowering of the foot after heel contact and lifts the foot during swing, the quadriceps control knee flexion during loading response, the calf muscles provide push-off, and the hip abductors stabilize the pelvis during single-limb support.

Walking is often described as energy efficient. The body's centre of mass rises and falls with each step, reaching its highest point in mid-stance and lowest during double support, and it also moves from side to side. In the inverted pendulum model, the stance leg acts like a rigid pendulum over which the body vaults, exchanging gravitational potential and kinetic energy, which reduces the muscular work required. Determinants of gait, such as pelvic rotation and knee flexion during stance, have traditionally been proposed to smooth the motion of the centre of mass, although their exact contributions have been debated.

Clinical gait analysis is performed in specialized laboratories using motion capture systems, in which infrared cameras track reflective markers placed on anatomical landmarks, together with force plates and EMG. Wearable inertial sensors containing accelerometers and gyroscopes allow gait to be measured outside laboratories. Gait analysis is particularly valuable in planning treatment for children with cerebral palsy, where it helps surgeons decide which muscles or bones to operate on, and it is used in assessing patients after stroke, people with Parkinson's disease, osteoarthritis, and amputations, and in evaluating footwear, orthoses, and prostheses.

topic: Uniform Flow in Open Channels and Manning's Equation
source_text:
Open channel flow is the flow of a liquid with a free surface exposed to the atmosphere. It occurs in rivers, streams, irrigation canals, drainage ditches, sewers flowing partly full, and road gutters. Unlike flow in closed pipes, which is driven mainly by pressure differences, open channel flow is driven by gravity, and the position of the free surface is free to adjust to changes in discharge, slope, and channel shape. The design of irrigation and drainage systems, flood channels, culverts, and stormwater networks depends on understanding how water depth and velocity are related to channel properties.

Open channel flows are classified in several ways. Steady flow does not change with time at a given location, while unsteady flow does, as during a flood wave. Uniform flow occurs when depth, velocity, and flow area remain constant along the length of the channel, whereas in non-uniform, or varied, flow these quantities change with distance. Varied flow may be gradually varied, as in the backwater upstream of a weir, or rapidly varied, as in a hydraulic jump. Flow is also classified by the Froude number, the ratio of the flow velocity to the speed of a small surface wave, which equals the square root of gravitational acceleration times hydraulic depth. When the Froude number is less than one, the flow is subcritical, deep and relatively slow, and disturbances can travel upstream. When it is greater than one, the flow is supercritical, shallow and fast, and disturbances are swept downstream. Critical flow, with a Froude number of one, separates these regimes.

Uniform flow is the reference condition for channel design. It develops in long, straight channels of constant cross-section, slope, and roughness, when the component of the water's weight acting down the slope is exactly balanced by the resistance of the channel boundary. Because the forces are in balance, the water surface, the channel bed, and the energy grade line are all parallel, and their slopes are equal. The depth at which uniform flow occurs for a given discharge is called the normal depth. Although perfectly uniform flow rarely exists in natural streams, many artificial channels are designed on the assumption of uniform flow, and the normal depth provides a basis for analysing more complex conditions.

Several geometric properties of the channel cross-section are used in flow calculations. The flow area, A, is the cross-sectional area of the water. The wetted perimeter, P, is the length of the channel boundary in contact with the water, excluding the free surface. The hydraulic radius, R, is the flow area divided by the wetted perimeter, and it describes how efficiently a section conveys water: a larger hydraulic radius means less boundary contact per unit of flow area and therefore less resistance. The top width is the width of the free surface, and the hydraulic depth is the flow area divided by the top width.

Several empirical equations relate velocity in uniform flow to these properties. The Chézy equation, developed in the eighteenth century, states that the mean velocity equals a coefficient C multiplied by the square root of the hydraulic radius times the channel slope. The most widely used equation in practice, however, is the Manning equation, proposed by the Irish engineer Robert Manning in 1889. In SI units, it states that the mean velocity, V, equals one divided by n, multiplied by the hydraulic radius raised to the power two thirds, multiplied by the square root of the channel bed slope, S. The discharge, Q, is obtained by multiplying the velocity by the flow area. In US customary units, a constant of 1.49 replaces the value one in the numerator.

The Manning roughness coefficient, n, represents the resistance of the channel boundary and is one of the most important and uncertain parameters in open channel hydraulics. Smooth surfaces have low values; for example, finished concrete is commonly assigned values around 0.012 to 0.015, while clean earth channels may have values near 0.022, gravel-bed streams around 0.030, and natural channels with vegetation, stones, and irregularities may have values of 0.035 to 0.1 or more. The value of n depends on surface material, vegetation, channel irregularity, obstructions, meandering, and even the depth of flow and season. Engineers select n from published tables, photographs of reference channels, or calibration against measured flows, and errors in n directly affect predicted depths and capacities.

The Manning equation can be used for three main types of problem. If the channel geometry, slope, roughness, and depth are known, the velocity and discharge can be calculated directly. If the discharge is known, the normal depth can be found, but because the area and hydraulic radius both depend on depth, the equation usually must be solved by trial and error, graphical methods, or numerical techniques. Finally, for design, the equation can be used to determine the channel dimensions or slope required to carry a given discharge.

Channel design also considers the most efficient hydraulic section, the shape that conveys the maximum discharge for a given flow area, or equivalently requires the minimum area for a given discharge. Since discharge increases with hydraulic radius, the most efficient section minimizes the wetted perimeter for a given area. For rectangular channels, the most efficient shape has a width equal to twice the depth. For trapezoidal channels, the most efficient section is half of a regular hexagon, with side slopes of sixty degrees to the horizontal. In practice, side slopes are often chosen according to soil stability rather than hydraulic efficiency, because steep earth banks may collapse.

Practical design must also ensure that velocities fall within acceptable limits. Velocities that are too low allow sediment to deposit and vegetation to grow, reducing capacity, while velocities that are too high can erode unlined earth channels or damage linings. Minimum non-silting and maximum permissible velocities depend on the sediment load and the channel material. Channels are designed with freeboard, an additional height above the design water level, to accommodate waves, surges, and uncertainty in flow estimates. For conditions that differ from uniform flow, such as flow approaching structures or changes in slope, gradually varied flow analysis is used to compute water surface profiles, building on the concepts of normal and critical depth.
summary:
Open channel flow has a free surface and is driven by gravity, occurring in rivers, canals, ditches, partly full sewers, and gutters, and its analysis underpins irrigation, drainage, flood channel, culvert, and stormwater design. Flows are steady or unsteady, uniform or varied (gradually or rapidly), and subcritical, critical, or supercritical according to the Froude number, the ratio of velocity to surface wave speed.

Uniform flow, in which gravity down the slope balances boundary resistance so that bed, water surface, and energy line are parallel, defines the normal depth and is the basis for channel design. Key geometry includes flow area A, wetted perimeter P, hydraulic radius R = A/P, top width, and hydraulic depth. The Chézy equation relates velocity to √(RS), while the widely used Manning equation gives V = (1/n)R^(2/3)S^(1/2) in SI units (1.49 in US units) and Q = VA. The roughness coefficient n, about 0.012–0.015 for concrete, 0.022 for clean earth, 0.030 for gravel beds, and 0.035–0.1 or more for vegetated natural channels, is uncertain and strongly affects results. Manning's equation computes discharge, finds normal depth iteratively, or sizes channels. Efficient sections minimize wetted perimeter—width twice depth for rectangles and half-hexagon trapezoids—but side slopes often follow soil stability. Designs keep velocities between non-silting and erosive limits, include freeboard, and use gradually varied flow analysis where flow is not uniform.

The hydraulic radius, R, is the flow area divided by the wetted perimeter, and it describes how efficiently a section conveys water: a larger hydraulic radius means less boundary contact per unit of flow area and therefore less resistance. The top width is the width of the free surface, and the hydraulic depth is the flow area divided by the top width.

Several empirical equations relate velocity in uniform flow to these properties. The Chézy equation, developed in the eighteenth century, states that the mean velocity equals a coefficient C multiplied by the square root of the hydraulic radius times the channel slope. The most widely used equation in practice, however, is the Manning equation, proposed by the Irish engineer Robert Manning in 1889. In SI units, it states that the mean velocity, V, equals one divided by n, multiplied by the hydraulic radius raised to the power two thirds, multiplied by the square root of the channel bed slope, S. The discharge, Q, is obtained by multiplying the velocity by the flow area. In US customary units, a constant of 1.49 replaces the value one in the numerator.

The Manning roughness coefficient, n, represents the resistance of the channel boundary and is one of the most important and uncertain parameters in open channel hydraulics. Smooth surfaces have low values; for example, finished concrete is commonly assigned values around 0.012 to 0.015, while clean earth channels may have values near 0.022, gravel-bed streams around 0.030, and natural channels with vegetation, stones, and irregularities may have values of 0.035 to 0.1 or more. The value of n depends on surface material, vegetation, channel irregularity, obstructions, meandering, and even the depth of flow and season. Engineers select n from published tables, photographs of reference channels, or calibration against measured flows, and errors in n directly affect predicted depths and capacities.

The Manning equation can be used for three main types of problem. If the channel geometry, slope, roughness, and depth are known, the velocity and discharge can be calculated directly. If the discharge is known, the normal depth can be found, but because the area and hydraulic radius both depend on depth, the equation usually must be solved by trial and error, graphical methods, or numerical techniques. Finally, for design, the equation can be used to determine the channel dimensions or slope required to carry a given discharge.

Channel design also considers the most efficient hydraulic section, the shape that conveys the maximum discharge for a given flow area, or equivalently requires the minimum area for a given discharge. Since discharge increases with hydraulic radius, the most efficient section minimizes the wetted perimeter for a given area. For rectangular channels, the most efficient shape has a width equal to twice the depth. For trapezoidal channels, the most efficient section is half of a regular hexagon, with side slopes of sixty degrees to the horizontal. In practice, side slopes are often chosen according to soil stability rather than hydraulic efficiency, because steep earth banks may collapse.

Practical design must also ensure that velocities fall within acceptable limits. Velocities that are too low allow sediment to deposit and vegetation to grow, reducing capacity, while velocities that are too high can erode unlined earth channels or damage linings. Minimum non-silting and maximum permissible velocities depend on the sediment load and the channel material. Channels are designed with freeboard, an additional height above the design water level, to accommodate waves, surges, and uncertainty in flow estimates. For conditions that differ from uniform flow, such as flow approaching structures or changes in slope, gradually varied flow analysis is used to compute water surface profiles, building on the concepts of normal and critical depth.

topic: Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points
source_text:
Ensuring that food is safe to eat is a fundamental responsibility of food producers, processors, and regulators. Foodborne illnesses caused by bacteria, viruses, parasites, toxins, and chemical contaminants affect hundreds of millions of people each year and can cause serious illness and death, particularly among young children, older people, pregnant women, and people with weakened immune systems. Traditional food safety control relied heavily on inspecting final products and testing samples at the end of production. This approach has important weaknesses: testing only a small sample may fail to detect contamination, results may arrive after products have been distributed, and the approach identifies problems after they occur rather than preventing them. Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points, HACCP, is a systematic, preventive approach to food safety that identifies hazards and controls them at specific points during production.

HACCP originated in the 1960s, when the Pillsbury Company worked with the United States National Aeronautics and Space Administration and the US Army laboratories to develop food for astronauts that would be completely safe, since foodborne illness in space could be catastrophic. The developers recognized that testing finished products could not provide sufficient assurance and instead focused on controlling the process. HACCP was later adopted widely in the food industry and became the basis of food safety regulations in many countries. The Codex Alimentarius Commission, the international food standards body established by the Food and Agriculture Organization and the World Health Organization, published guidelines on HACCP principles that are recognized internationally.

HACCP addresses three main categories of hazards. Biological hazards include pathogenic bacteria such as Salmonella, Listeria monocytogenes, Escherichia coli O157:H7, Campylobacter, and Clostridium botulinum, as well as viruses such as norovirus and hepatitis A, and parasites. Chemical hazards include pesticide residues, veterinary drug residues, natural toxins such as aflatoxins produced by moulds, allergens, cleaning chemicals, and unapproved additives. Physical hazards are foreign objects such as glass, metal fragments, stones, and hard plastic that may cause injury.

Before applying the HACCP principles, preliminary steps are carried out. A multidisciplinary HACCP team is assembled, including people with expertise in production, quality assurance, microbiology, and engineering. The team describes the product, including its ingredients, processing methods, packaging, storage conditions, and shelf life, and identifies its intended use and consumers, particularly whether vulnerable groups will consume it. The team then constructs a flow diagram showing every step of the process from receipt of raw materials to distribution and verifies the diagram on site to ensure that it accurately reflects actual operations.

HACCP is built on seven principles. The first principle is to conduct a hazard analysis. The team identifies potential hazards at each step of the process and evaluates them according to their likelihood of occurrence and the severity of their effects. It then identifies control measures that can prevent, eliminate, or reduce each significant hazard to an acceptable level.

The second principle is to determine the critical control points, CCPs. A CCP is a step at which control can be applied and is essential to prevent or eliminate a food safety hazard or reduce it to an acceptable level. Typical CCPs include cooking, pasteurization, chilling, acidification, and metal detection. A decision tree, a series of structured questions, is often used to help determine whether a step is a CCP. Not every step that affects safety is a CCP; many hazards are controlled by general hygiene measures.

The third principle is to establish critical limits for each CCP. A critical limit is a measurable criterion that separates acceptable from unacceptable conditions, such as a minimum cooking temperature and time, a maximum pH, a maximum water activity, or the detection of metal particles above a specified size. For example, a critical limit for cooking poultry might require reaching a core temperature of at least 75 degrees Celsius.

The fourth principle is to establish a monitoring system for each CCP. Monitoring involves planned observations or measurements, such as continuous temperature recording during pasteurization or regular checks of a metal detector, to assess whether a CCP is under control. Monitoring procedures specify what is measured, how, how often, and by whom.

The fifth principle is to establish corrective actions to be taken when monitoring indicates that a CCP is not under control. Corrective actions specify how to bring the process back under control and how to handle products produced during the deviation, such as holding, reprocessing, or destroying them.

The sixth principle is to establish verification procedures to confirm that the HACCP system is working effectively. Verification includes reviewing monitoring records, calibrating instruments, conducting microbiological testing of products and the environment, and auditing the system. Validation, a related activity, provides evidence that the control measures and critical limits are capable of controlling the hazards, for example through scientific studies showing that a particular heat treatment destroys target pathogens.

The seventh principle is to establish documentation and record keeping. Records of hazard analyses, CCP determinations, critical limits, monitoring results, deviations, corrective actions, and verification activities demonstrate that the system is being implemented and allow problems to be traced.

HACCP is not a stand-alone system. It depends on prerequisite programmes, sometimes called good hygiene practices or good manufacturing practices, which provide the basic environmental and operating conditions for safe food production. These include sanitation and cleaning procedures, pest control, personal hygiene and training of staff, maintenance of equipment, control of water quality, supplier approval, allergen management, and appropriate facility design that separates raw and cooked products. Without strong prerequisite programmes, a HACCP plan would have to control too many hazards and would be unmanageable.

HACCP has been incorporated into international food safety management standards, such as ISO 22000, and is required by regulations in many countries for sectors such as meat, seafood, and juice processing. Its benefits include a preventive focus, more efficient use of resources, improved consumer confidence, and easier access to international markets, which is important for exporters, including seafood processors in Bangladesh. Challenges include the need for training and expertise, documentation demands that can burden small businesses, and the need to keep plans updated when products, processes, or scientific knowledge change.

Before applying the HACCP principles, preliminary steps are carried out. A multidisciplinary HACCP team is assembled, including people with expertise in production, quality assurance, microbiology, and engineering. The team describes the product, including its ingredients, processing methods, packaging, storage conditions, and shelf life, and identifies its intended use and consumers, particularly whether vulnerable groups will consume it. The team then constructs a flow diagram showing every step of the process from receipt of raw materials to distribution and verifies the diagram on site to ensure that it accurately reflects actual operations.

The team identifies potential hazards at each step of the process and evaluates them according to their likelihood of occurrence and the severity of their effects. It then identifies control measures that can prevent, eliminate, or reduce each significant hazard to an acceptable level.

The second principle is to determine the critical control points, CCPs. The third principle is to establish critical limits for each CCP. A critical limit is a measurable criterion that separates acceptable from unacceptable conditions, such as a minimum cooking temperature and time, a maximum pH, a maximum water activity, or the detection of metal particles above a specified size. For example, a critical limit for cooking poultry might require reaching a core temperature of at least 75 degrees Celsius.

The fourth principle is to establish a monitoring system for each CCP. Monitoring involves planned observations or measurements, such as continuous temperature recording during pasteurization or regular checks of a metal detector, to assess whether a CCP is under control. Monitoring procedures specify what is measured, how, how often, and by whom.

The fifth principle is to establish corrective actions to be taken when monitoring indicates that a CCP is not under control. Corrective actions specify how to bring the process back under control and how to handle products produced during the deviation, such as holding, reprocessing, or destroying them.

The sixth principle is to establish verification procedures to confirm that the HACCP system is working effectively. Verification includes reviewing monitoring records, calibrating instruments, conducting microbiological testing of products and the environment, and auditing the system. Its benefits include a preventive focus, more efficient use of resources, improved consumer confidence, and easier access to international markets, which is important for exporters, including seafood processors in Bangladesh. Challenges include the need for training and expertise, documentation demands that can burden small businesses, and the need to keep plans updated when products, processes, or scientific knowledge change.

Integration is used throughout science and engineering to calculate areas, volumes, work done by forces, total quantities from rates, probabilities, and averages. In many practical situations, however, a definite integral cannot be evaluated exactly. The integrand may have no antiderivative expressible in terms of elementary functions, as with the integral of e to the power minus x squared, which is central to probability theory. The function may be known only through measured data at discrete points, such as velocities recorded at intervals or flow rates measured across a river. Even when an exact antiderivative exists, it may be too complicated to use conveniently. Numerical integration, also called numerical quadrature, provides methods for approximating definite integrals using a finite number of function values.

Most elementary numerical integration methods are based on the idea of replacing the integrand over small subintervals with a simpler function, usually a polynomial, whose integral can be computed exactly. The interval of integration, from a to b, is divided into n subintervals, often of equal width h, equal to b minus a divided by n. The function values at the endpoints of the subintervals, called nodes, are combined with weights to approximate the integral. Methods that use equally spaced nodes are known as Newton-Cotes formulas.

The simplest approaches are rectangle rules, which approximate the area under the curve in each subinterval by a rectangle whose height is the function value at the left endpoint, right endpoint, or midpoint. The midpoint rule is generally more accurate than the left and right endpoint rules, because errors on either side of the midpoint tend to cancel.

The trapezoidal rule approximates the function on each subinterval by a straight line joining the function values at its endpoints, so the area of each strip is a trapezium. For a single interval, the area is the width multiplied by the average of the two endpoint values. For the composite trapezoidal rule over n subintervals, the integral is approximated by h divided by two, multiplied by the sum of the first and last function values plus twice the sum of all interior function values. The trapezoidal rule is exact for linear functions. Its error is proportional to h squared and to the second derivative of the function, so halving the step size reduces the error by a factor of about four. When the function is concave up, the trapezoidal rule overestimates the integral, and when it is concave down, it underestimates it. The rule is particularly effective for periodic functions integrated over a full period, where errors cancel to a remarkable extent.

Simpson's rule improves accuracy by approximating the function on each pair of subintervals by a quadratic polynomial, a parabola, passing through three points. It requires an even number of subintervals. For a single pair of subintervals of width h, the integral is approximated by h divided by three, multiplied by the first value plus four times the middle value plus the last value. The composite Simpson's one-third rule applies this pattern across the whole interval, giving weights in the repeating pattern one, four, two, four, two, and so on, ending with four and one, all multiplied by h over three. Although it is based on quadratic interpolation, Simpson's rule is exact for polynomials up to degree three, because of a symmetry that cancels the cubic error term. Its error is proportional to h to the fourth power and to the fourth derivative of the function, so halving the step size reduces the error by a factor of about sixteen. Simpson's three-eighths rule uses cubic polynomials over groups of three subintervals and can be combined with the one-third rule when the number of subintervals is odd.

As an example, consider approximating the integral of e to the power x from zero to one, whose exact value is about 1.71828. Using the trapezoidal rule with four subintervals gives approximately 1.7272, an error of about 0.009. Simpson's rule with the same four subintervals gives approximately 1.71832, an error of less than 0.0001. This illustrates the substantial improvement that higher-order methods can provide for smooth functions.

The accuracy of numerical integration can be estimated and improved in several ways. Comparing results with different step sizes gives an indication of the error. Richardson extrapolation combines results obtained with different step sizes to eliminate the leading error term and produce a more accurate estimate. Applying Richardson extrapolation repeatedly to the trapezoidal rule leads to Romberg integration, which can achieve very high accuracy efficiently for smooth functions. Adaptive quadrature methods automatically use smaller subintervals where the function changes rapidly and larger ones where it is smooth, concentrating computational effort where it is needed and stopping when a specified error tolerance is reached.

Gaussian quadrature takes a different approach. Instead of using equally spaced points, it chooses both the locations of the nodes and the weights to achieve the highest possible accuracy. An n-point Gaussian quadrature rule can integrate polynomials of degree up to two n minus one exactly, roughly twice the degree achievable by Newton-Cotes rules with the same number of points. The nodes for the standard Gauss-Legendre rule are the roots of Legendre polynomials, transformed to the interval of integration. Gaussian quadrature is highly efficient for smooth functions that can be evaluated at arbitrary points, and it is widely used in the finite element method. It is not suitable, however, when the function is known only at fixed, equally spaced data points.

Numerical integration faces challenges when integrands have singularities, discontinuities, or infinite intervals. Such cases require special techniques, such as variable transformations, splitting the interval at discontinuities, or specialized quadrature rules. In multiple dimensions, the cost of grid-based methods grows rapidly with the number of dimensions, and Monte Carlo integration, which estimates integrals using random sampling, becomes attractive because its error decreases at a rate that does not depend on dimensionality.
summary:
Numerical integration approximates definite integrals when integrands lack elementary antiderivatives, such as e^(−x²), when functions are known only from data, or when exact antiderivatives are impractical. Most methods replace the integrand on subintervals of width h = (b − a)/n with polynomials, and equally spaced Newton-Cotes formulas combine weighted function values. Rectangle rules use left, right, or midpoint heights, with the midpoint rule more accurate. The composite trapezoidal rule, (h/2)[f0 + 2(interior values) + fn], is exact for linear functions, has error proportional to h² and the second derivative (halving h cuts error about fourfold), overestimates concave-up functions, and excels for periodic functions over full periods.

Simpson's one-third rule fits parabolas over pairs of subintervals, needs an even number of intervals, uses weights 1, 4, 2, 4, …, 4, 1 times h/3, is exact up to cubics, and has error proportional to h⁴ (halving h cuts error about sixteenfold); the three-eighths rule handles odd counts. For ∫₀¹ eˣ dx ≈ 1.71828, four-interval trapezoidal and Simpson estimates give about 1.7272 and 1.71832. Accuracy improves through step-size comparison, Richardson extrapolation, Romberg integration, and adaptive quadrature that refines where functions change rapidly. Gaussian quadrature chooses optimal nodes and weights, exactly integrating polynomials up to degree 2n − 1 using Legendre roots, and is used in finite elements but not with fixed data. Singularities, discontinuities, and infinite intervals require transformations or special rules, and high-dimensional integrals favour Monte Carlo methods whose error rate is independent of dimension.

The midpoint rule is generally more accurate than the left and right endpoint rules, because errors on either side of the midpoint tend to cancel.

For a single interval, the area is the width multiplied by the average of the two endpoint values. For the composite trapezoidal rule over n subintervals, the integral is approximated by h divided by two, multiplied by the sum of the first and last function values plus twice the sum of all interior function values. Adaptive quadrature methods automatically use smaller subintervals where the function changes rapidly and larger ones where it is smooth, concentrating computational effort where it is needed and stopping when a specified error tolerance is reached.

Numerical integration faces challenges when integrands have singularities, discontinuities, or infinite intervals. Such cases require special techniques, such as variable transformations, splitting the interval at discontinuities, or specialized quadrature rules. In multiple dimensions, the cost of grid-based methods grows rapidly with the number of dimensions, and Monte Carlo integration, which estimates integrals using random sampling, becomes attractive because its error decreases at a rate that does not depend on dimensionality.

source_text:
Many research questions involve outcomes that take only two values. A patient either develops a disease or does not, a customer either buys a product or does not, a loan is either repaid or defaults, and a student either passes or fails an examination. Ordinary linear regression is not appropriate for such binary outcomes, because it can predict probabilities below zero or above one, and its assumptions of normally distributed errors with constant variance are violated. Logistic regression is the standard method for modelling the relationship between one or more explanatory variables and a binary response.

Logistic regression models the probability that the outcome equals one, often called the probability of success, as a function of the predictors. Instead of modelling this probability directly as a straight line, it models the log odds, also called the logit. The odds of an event are the probability that it occurs divided by the probability that it does not occur. If the probability of passing an examination is 0.8, the odds of passing are 0.8 divided by 0.2, or 4, meaning that passing is four times as likely as failing. The log odds is the natural logarithm of the odds. The logistic regression model states that the log odds is a linear function of the predictors: the logit of p equals beta zero plus beta one times x one plus beta two times x two, and so on. Solving for p gives the logistic function, p equals one divided by one plus e to the power minus the linear predictor. This S-shaped curve always produces values between zero and one, approaching zero for very negative values of the linear predictor and one for very positive values.

The coefficients are estimated by maximum likelihood rather than least squares. The method finds the coefficient values that make the observed pattern of successes and failures most probable under the model. Because there is no closed-form solution, the estimates are found using iterative numerical algorithms, such as Newton-Raphson or iteratively reweighted least squares, which statistical software performs automatically.

Interpreting the coefficients requires care. A coefficient in logistic regression represents the change in the log odds of the outcome associated with a one-unit increase in the predictor, holding other predictors constant. Because log odds are difficult to interpret directly, coefficients are usually exponentiated to give odds ratios. The odds ratio, e to the power beta, indicates the multiplicative change in the odds for a one-unit increase in the predictor. An odds ratio of 1 indicates no association, an odds ratio greater than 1 indicates that higher values of the predictor are associated with higher odds of the outcome, and an odds ratio less than 1 indicates lower odds. For example, if a model of heart disease includes smoking as a binary predictor and the estimated odds ratio is 2.5, smokers have 2.5 times the odds of heart disease compared with non-smokers, after adjustment for the other variables in the model. For a continuous predictor such as age, an odds ratio of 1.05 means that each additional year of age multiplies the odds by 1.05, an increase of about five percent. It is important to remember that odds ratios describe changes in odds, not in probabilities; when the outcome is common, the odds ratio can be considerably larger than the corresponding ratio of probabilities, known as the relative risk.

Statistical inference in logistic regression uses several tests. The Wald test examines whether an individual coefficient differs significantly from zero, by dividing the estimate by its standard error. Confidence intervals for odds ratios are obtained by exponentiating the confidence limits for the coefficients. The likelihood ratio test compares the fit of nested models, for example a model with and without a particular group of predictors, by examining the change in the deviance, a measure of lack of fit based on the log-likelihood. Because there is no exact equivalent of R squared in logistic regression, various pseudo R squared measures have been proposed, but they should be interpreted cautiously.

Assessing model performance involves evaluating both calibration and discrimination. Calibration refers to how well predicted probabilities agree with observed outcomes; the Hosmer-Lemeshow test, which groups observations by predicted probability and compares observed and expected numbers of events, is one common approach, although it has limitations. Discrimination refers to how well the model distinguishes between cases with and without the outcome. A popular measure is the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, AUC, which plots the true positive rate against the false positive rate across different classification thresholds. An AUC of 0.5 indicates no discrimination, equivalent to chance, while an AUC of 1.0 indicates perfect discrimination. When predicted probabilities are converted into classifications using a threshold, often 0.5, performance can also be summarized by sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy, but the choice of threshold should reflect the costs of different types of error.

Logistic regression relies on several assumptions. Observations should be independent. The relationship between continuous predictors and the log odds should be linear, which can be checked by adding transformed terms or using flexible functions. There should be no severe multicollinearity among predictors. The sample should contain enough events relative to the number of predictors; a frequently cited guideline suggests at least about ten events per predictor, although requirements depend on the context. When one predictor perfectly separates the outcomes, a situation called complete separation, maximum likelihood estimates fail to converge, and penalized methods may be needed.

Logistic regression has many extensions and applications. Multinomial logistic regression handles outcomes with more than two unordered categories, and ordinal logistic regression handles ordered categories such as disease severity. In epidemiology, logistic regression is widely used to analyse case-control studies and to estimate adjusted associations between exposures and diseases. In machine learning, it serves as a fundamental classification algorithm and a baseline against which more complex models are compared, valued for its interpretability. As with all regression methods, associations estimated from observational data do not necessarily indicate causation, and confounding must be considered carefully.
summary:
Logistic regression models binary outcomes, such as disease or loan default, for which linear regression is unsuitable because it can predict impossible probabilities and violates its assumptions. It models the log odds (logit) of success as a linear function of predictors; odds are p/(1 − p), so a probability of 0.8 gives odds of 4. The resulting logistic function keeps predicted probabilities between 0 and 1 in an S-shaped curve. Coefficients are estimated by maximum likelihood using iterative algorithms.

Each coefficient is the change in log odds per unit increase in a predictor, and exponentiating gives an odds ratio: 1 means no association, above 1 higher odds, and below 1 lower odds; for example, an odds ratio of 2.5 for smoking and 1.05 per year of age. Odds ratios differ from relative risks when outcomes are common. Inference uses Wald tests, confidence intervals for odds ratios, likelihood ratio tests on deviance for nested models, and cautious pseudo R² measures. Performance is assessed by calibration, such as the Hosmer-Lemeshow test, and discrimination, such as the ROC curve's AUC (0.5 chance, 1.0 perfect), with thresholds reflecting error costs. Assumptions include independence, linearity in the logit, limited multicollinearity, and enough events per predictor (about ten), while complete separation requires penalized methods. Extensions include multinomial and ordinal logistic regression, and the method is central to case-control epidemiology and interpretable machine learning, though observational associations do not prove causation.

Because log odds are difficult to interpret directly, coefficients are usually exponentiated to give odds ratios. The odds ratio, e to the power beta, indicates the multiplicative change in the odds for a one-unit increase in the predictor. An odds ratio of 1 indicates no association, an odds ratio greater than 1 indicates that higher values of the predictor are associated with higher odds of the outcome, and an odds ratio less than 1 indicates lower odds. The Wald test examines whether an individual coefficient differs significantly from zero, by dividing the estimate by its standard error. Confidence intervals for odds ratios are obtained by exponentiating the confidence limits for the coefficients. The likelihood ratio test compares the fit of nested models, for example a model with and without a particular group of predictors, by examining the change in the deviance, a measure of lack of fit based on the log-likelihood. Because there is no exact equivalent of R squared in logistic regression, various pseudo R squared measures have been proposed, but they should be interpreted cautiously.

topic: Behavioural Risk Factors for Non-Communicable Diseases
source_text:
Non-communicable diseases, NCDs, are chronic conditions that are not transmitted from person to person. The four main groups are cardiovascular diseases, including heart attacks and strokes; cancers; chronic respiratory diseases, such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and asthma; and diabetes. Together, NCDs cause the majority of deaths worldwide, around seventy percent, and a large proportion of these deaths occur before the age of seventy in low- and middle-income countries. Countries such as Bangladesh are experiencing an epidemiological transition, in which the burden of disease is shifting from infectious diseases and maternal and child conditions towards NCDs, as populations age, urbanize, and adopt new lifestyles, even while infectious diseases remain important.

NCDs develop over many years through the interaction of genetic, physiological, environmental, and behavioural factors. Public health places particular emphasis on modifiable behavioural risk factors, because they can be changed through individual action and public policy. The World Health Organization identifies four major behavioural risk factors shared by the main NCDs: tobacco use, unhealthy diet, physical inactivity, and harmful use of alcohol. Because these factors contribute to several diseases simultaneously, interventions targeting them can prevent multiple conditions at once.

Tobacco use, including smoking cigarettes and bidis and using smokeless tobacco, is the leading preventable risk factor. It causes many cancers, especially lung, mouth, throat, and bladder cancers; cardiovascular disease, by damaging blood vessels, promoting atherosclerosis, and increasing blood clotting; and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Exposure to second-hand smoke also increases disease risk among non-smokers. The risk of disease falls substantially after quitting, which makes cessation beneficial at any age.

Unhealthy diet contributes to cardiovascular disease, diabetes, some cancers, and obesity. Key concerns include high intake of salt, which raises blood pressure; high intake of saturated fats and industrially produced trans fats, which raise harmful cholesterol levels; high intake of free sugars, particularly from sugar-sweetened beverages, which contributes to weight gain and dental caries; and low intake of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, legumes, and nuts. In many South Asian countries, diets high in refined rice, salt, and fried foods, combined with increasing consumption of processed and fast foods, contribute to rising rates of hypertension and diabetes. The World Health Organization recommends limiting salt intake to less than five grams per day and free sugars to less than ten percent of total energy intake.

Physical inactivity increases the risk of cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, some cancers, depression, and premature death. Regular physical activity improves cardiovascular fitness, helps control body weight, improves insulin sensitivity, lowers blood pressure, and benefits mental health. Global recommendations advise adults to undertake at least 150 to 300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity, such as brisk walking, or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous activity each week, along with muscle-strengthening activities, and to reduce sedentary time. Urbanization, motorized transport, sedentary occupations, and screen-based leisure have reduced activity levels in many populations, and safe spaces for walking and recreation are often limited in densely populated cities.

Harmful use of alcohol contributes to liver cirrhosis, several cancers, cardiovascular disease, injuries, and violence. Its prevalence varies greatly between countries and cultures, and in some predominantly Muslim countries, including Bangladesh, reported alcohol consumption is low, although it remains a concern in particular groups.

These behavioural risk factors act partly through metabolic or physiological risk factors, sometimes called intermediate risk factors. Raised blood pressure, or hypertension, is the leading metabolic risk factor for death globally, contributing to strokes, heart attacks, and kidney disease. Overweight and obesity, often measured by body mass index and waist circumference, increase the risk of diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and several cancers. Raised blood glucose and abnormal blood lipids, such as high levels of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, also increase cardiovascular risk. South Asian populations tend to develop diabetes and cardiovascular disease at lower levels of body mass index than European populations, partly because of a tendency towards central fat accumulation, which has led to lower BMI cut-offs being suggested for defining overweight in these populations.

Risk factors frequently cluster in the same individuals and interact with one another, so that a person who smokes, has high blood pressure, and has diabetes faces a much greater risk than the sum of the separate risks might suggest. Risk is also strongly shaped by social and environmental conditions, sometimes called the social determinants of health. Income, education, occupation, urban design, food prices, marketing, and the availability of tobacco and processed foods influence behaviours. For example, cheap and heavily marketed sugary drinks and processed snacks make unhealthy choices easier, while lack of safe places for exercise discourages activity. In low- and middle-income countries, poorer groups may face high exposure to tobacco and indoor air pollution and limited access to diagnosis and treatment.

Prevention and control strategies operate at both population and individual levels. Population-wide approaches aim to shift the distribution of risk factors in the whole population and are often highly cost-effective. Examples include tobacco taxes, smoke-free laws, and advertising bans; reducing salt in processed foods through reformulation and labelling; eliminating industrial trans fats; taxes on sugar-sweetened beverages; and urban planning that encourages walking and cycling. The World Health Organization has identified a set of highly cost-effective measures, often called best buys, for NCD prevention. Individual-level approaches include screening for hypertension, diabetes, and certain cancers; counselling on diet, activity, and smoking cessation; and treatment with medications such as antihypertensives, statins, and glucose-lowering drugs for people at high risk. Integrating NCD services into primary health care, using approaches such as the WHO package of essential NCD interventions, helps detect and manage conditions early. Global targets, including the Sustainable Development Goal to reduce premature NCD mortality by one third by 2030, encourage countries to strengthen monitoring, prevention, and treatment.
summary:
Non-communicable diseases—cardiovascular disease, cancers, chronic respiratory diseases, and diabetes—cause about 70% of global deaths, many premature in low- and middle-income countries, and countries such as Bangladesh face an epidemiological transition towards NCDs. WHO identifies four modifiable behavioural risk factors shared across NCDs: tobacco use, unhealthy diet, physical inactivity, and harmful alcohol use. Tobacco, including bidis and smokeless products, causes many cancers, cardiovascular disease, and COPD, harms non-smokers, and quitting reduces risk at any age. Unhealthy diets high in salt, saturated and trans fats, and free sugars and low in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, legumes, and nuts drive hypertension, diabetes, and obesity; WHO recommends under 5 g of salt daily and free sugars under 10% of energy.

Inactivity raises cardiovascular, diabetes, cancer, depression, and mortality risks, and adults are advised to do 150–300 minutes of moderate or 75–150 minutes of vigorous activity weekly plus strengthening, though urban life limits activity. Alcohol harms vary by culture and are low in Bangladesh overall. Behaviours act through hypertension, the leading metabolic risk, obesity, raised glucose, and abnormal lipids, and South Asians develop disease at lower BMI, prompting lower cut-offs. Risks cluster and are shaped by social determinants such as income, education, marketing, food prices, and urban design. Population measures—tobacco controls, salt reformulation, trans fat elimination, sugary drink taxes, and walkable cities—are WHO "best buys," complemented by screening, counselling, medications, and primary care integration toward the SDG target of a one-third reduction in premature NCD mortality by 2030.

source_text:
Plants require at least seventeen essential elements for growth, of which carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen are obtained from air and water. The remaining mineral nutrients come mainly from the soil. Nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium, often abbreviated NPK, are the primary macronutrients, required in the largest quantities and most often limiting crop yields. Secondary macronutrients include calcium, magnesium, and sulphur, and micronutrients such as zinc, iron, boron, manganese, copper, molybdenum, chlorine, and nickel are needed in smaller amounts. Fertilizers supply nutrients that the soil cannot provide in sufficient quantity to meet crop demand. Effective nutrient management aims to supply the right amounts at the right time and place to maximize yield and profit while minimizing environmental harm.

Nitrogen is a component of amino acids, proteins, nucleic acids, and chlorophyll, and it strongly influences vegetative growth, leaf area, and yield. Plants absorb nitrogen mainly as nitrate and ammonium ions. Deficiency causes stunted growth and yellowing, or chlorosis, that typically begins in older leaves because nitrogen is mobile within the plant and is moved to younger tissues. Excess nitrogen can produce lush vegetative growth, delayed maturity, lodging of cereal crops, and increased susceptibility to some pests and diseases. Common nitrogen fertilizers include urea, which contains forty-six percent nitrogen and is the most widely used fertilizer in Bangladesh and many other countries, ammonium sulphate, ammonium nitrate, and diammonium phosphate, which also supplies phosphorus. Nitrogen is highly dynamic in soils and can be lost through several pathways. Urea applied to the soil surface can be lost as ammonia gas through volatilization, nitrate can be washed below the root zone by leaching, and in waterlogged soils such as flooded rice fields, nitrate can be converted to nitrogen gases by denitrification. As a result, nitrogen use efficiency, the proportion of applied nitrogen taken up by the crop, is often only thirty to fifty percent.

Phosphorus is essential for energy transfer through adenosine triphosphate, for nucleic acids and membranes, and for root development, flowering, and seed formation. Deficiency causes stunted growth, poor root development, delayed maturity, and sometimes a dark green or purplish colour in older leaves. Unlike nitrogen, phosphorus is relatively immobile in soils. It reacts with calcium in alkaline soils and with iron and aluminium in acidic soils to form compounds of low solubility, a process called phosphorus fixation, which reduces its availability to plants. Consequently, only a small fraction of applied phosphorus is used by the crop in the year of application, although residual phosphorus may become available later. Common phosphorus fertilizers include triple superphosphate, single superphosphate, and diammonium phosphate. Because phosphorus moves little in soil, it is usually applied at or before planting and placed near the root zone, for example by banding.

Potassium is involved in enzyme activation, osmotic regulation, the opening and closing of stomata, photosynthesis, and the transport of sugars. It improves drought tolerance, disease resistance, grain quality, and the strength of plant stems. Deficiency typically causes scorching or browning along the margins of older leaves and weak stems. Potassium is held on soil clay and organic matter particles as an exchangeable cation and can be lost by leaching in sandy soils. The most common potassium fertilizer is muriate of potash, potassium chloride, while sulphate of potash is preferred for chloride-sensitive crops such as tobacco and some fruits.

Determining the appropriate fertilizer rate requires knowledge of both crop requirements and soil nutrient supply. Soil testing measures the available nutrients in soil samples and is the foundation of rational fertilizer recommendations. Plant tissue analysis and visual symptoms can also indicate nutrient status during the growing season. Fertilizer recommendation guides, such as those published by agricultural research institutes, combine soil test results with crop yield targets to suggest rates for different crops and regions. Balanced fertilization, which supplies all limiting nutrients in appropriate proportions, is important. In many areas, farmers apply large amounts of urea but little phosphorus, potassium, or sulphur, leading to nutrient imbalances, declining soil fertility, and reduced efficiency, since yield is limited by the most deficient nutrient according to Liebig's law of the minimum.

The 4R nutrient stewardship framework summarizes good practice: applying the right source, at the right rate, at the right time, in the right place. The right source means choosing fertilizers that supply the nutrients the crop needs in available forms and suit soil conditions. The right rate matches application to crop demand and soil supply. The right time synchronizes nutrient availability with periods of crop uptake; for nitrogen, this often means splitting applications into several doses rather than applying everything at planting. The right place ensures that nutrients are positioned where roots can access them, for example by banding or incorporating fertilizer rather than broadcasting it on the surface. In rice, deep placement of urea briquettes, small compressed pellets inserted into the soil, has been shown in Bangladesh to reduce nitrogen losses and increase efficiency compared with broadcasting prilled urea. Tools such as the leaf colour chart help farmers judge when rice plants need additional nitrogen.

Integrated nutrient management combines mineral fertilizers with organic sources such as farmyard manure, compost, crop residues, green manures, and biofertilizers, including nitrogen-fixing bacteria and legumes in crop rotations. Organic sources supply nutrients and improve soil organic matter, structure, water-holding capacity, and biological activity, while mineral fertilizers supply nutrients in concentrated, readily available forms. Combining them can sustain productivity while maintaining soil health.

Poor nutrient management has environmental consequences. Nitrate leaching can contaminate groundwater, runoff of nitrogen and phosphorus can cause eutrophication of rivers and lakes, and nitrous oxide emitted from fertilized soils is a potent greenhouse gas. Improving nutrient use efficiency therefore benefits both farmers, by reducing input costs, and the environment.

source_text:
Many of the most important determinants of health are related to behaviour, such as whether people get vaccinated, attend screening tests, use condoms, wash their hands, take medications as prescribed, or stop smoking. Public health programmes therefore need to understand why people do or do not adopt health-promoting behaviours. Theories of health behaviour provide frameworks for explaining and predicting behaviour and for designing interventions. The Health Belief Model, one of the earliest and most widely used of these theories, was developed in the 1950s by social psychologists working in the United States Public Health Service, including Godfrey Hochbaum, Irwin Rosenstock, and Stephen Kegels. They were trying to understand why so few people participated in free tuberculosis screening programmes using mobile X-ray units, even when the service was convenient and free of charge.

The Health Belief Model proposes that people's willingness to take action to prevent, detect, or control illness depends on their beliefs about the health threat and about the behaviour that could reduce it. In its original form, the model included four main constructs, to which two others were later added.

Perceived susceptibility refers to an individual's belief about the likelihood of experiencing a health problem. A person who believes that they are unlikely to develop lung cancer or contract a sexually transmitted infection is less likely to take preventive action, even if their actual risk is high. Perceptions of susceptibility are influenced by personal experience, knowledge, and comparison with others, and people often display optimistic bias, believing that they are less at risk than others.

Perceived severity, or seriousness, refers to beliefs about how serious the consequences of a health problem would be, including medical consequences such as pain, disability, and death, and social consequences such as effects on work, family life, and relationships. Perceived susceptibility and perceived severity together form the perceived threat. People who believe that a disease is both likely and serious are more motivated to act.

Perceived benefits refer to beliefs about the effectiveness of the recommended action in reducing the threat. Even if a person feels threatened by a disease, they are unlikely to act unless they believe that the action, such as vaccination or screening, will actually reduce their risk or improve outcomes. Perceived benefits may also include non-health benefits, such as saving money or pleasing family members.

Perceived barriers refer to beliefs about the potential negative aspects of taking the action, including cost, inconvenience, time, pain, side effects, embarrassment, fear, and difficulty in accessing services. Research using the model has often found perceived barriers to be among the strongest predictors of behaviour. The model suggests that individuals weigh perceived benefits against perceived barriers in a kind of informal cost-benefit analysis. A woman may believe that a mammogram could detect breast cancer early, a benefit, but may also fear pain, worry about cost, or find it difficult to travel to a clinic, barriers that may prevent her from attending.

Cues to action are triggers that prompt a person to take action. They may be internal, such as noticing symptoms, or external, such as reminder letters, advice from a health worker, media campaigns, illness of a friend or family member, or community events. Cues to action are thought to be particularly important when perceived threat and readiness to act are present but the person has not yet acted.

Self-efficacy, added to the model in 1988 by Rosenstock, Victor Strecher, and Marshall Becker, refers to a person's confidence in their ability to successfully perform the behaviour. The concept was borrowed from Albert Bandura's social cognitive theory. Self-efficacy is especially important for complex behaviours that require sustained effort, such as quitting smoking, changing diet, or managing chronic diseases like diabetes, because a person who believes that change is beneficial may still fail to act if they doubt their ability to succeed.

The model also recognizes modifying factors, such as age, sex, ethnicity, education, socioeconomic status, personality, and knowledge, which influence perceptions and therefore indirectly influence behaviour.

The Health Belief Model has been used to explain and design interventions for a wide range of health behaviours, including vaccination, cancer screening, HIV prevention, adherence to medication, use of insecticide-treated bed nets to prevent malaria, and preventive practices during disease outbreaks. Its constructs translate readily into intervention strategies. To increase perceived susceptibility, programmes may provide personalized risk information. To increase perceived severity, they may communicate the consequences of the disease, although using excessive fear can backfire. To strengthen perceived benefits, they explain clearly how and how much the action reduces risk. To reduce barriers, they may provide free or low-cost services, convenient locations and hours, transport, reassurance about procedures, and correction of misconceptions. To provide cues to action, they use reminders, text messages, and community health workers. To build self-efficacy, they offer training, demonstrations, step-by-step guidance, and support. In Bangladesh and other countries, community health workers who visit households, explain the benefits of immunization or family planning, address concerns, and remind families about appointments implement many of these strategies in practice.

The model also has limitations. It focuses on individual beliefs and assumes that people make relatively rational decisions about health, whereas behaviour is also shaped by habits, emotions, social norms, culture, and environmental and economic conditions that individuals may not control. It does not specify precisely how the constructs combine or which are most important in particular situations, and research has found varying predictive power for different constructs. It gives limited attention to social influences, such as the expectations of family and peers, which other theories, such as the theory of planned behaviour, address more directly. For these reasons, the Health Belief Model is often combined with other theories and with structural interventions that change the environment in which people make health decisions.
