Lecture material:
Knitting is a method of fabric formation in which yarn is formed into loops that are interlinked with one another. It differs fundamentally from weaving, in which two sets of yarns, warp and weft, interlace at right angles. Because a knitted fabric is made of loops that can open, close, and change shape when the fabric is stretched, knitted fabrics are generally more extensible, softer, and more conforming to the body than woven fabrics. These properties make knitting the dominant technology for T-shirts, underwear, sportswear, socks, sweaters, and many medical and technical products. Knitting is broadly divided into two categories, weft knitting and warp knitting, which differ in the direction in which loops are formed and in the way yarn is supplied.

The basic unit of any knitted fabric is the loop, or stitch. The vertical columns of loops running along the length of the fabric are called wales, and the horizontal rows of loops running across the fabric are called courses. The number of wales per centimetre and courses per centimetre describe the density of the fabric, and together they determine the stitch density. Loop length, the length of yarn in one loop, is one of the most important parameters in knitting, because it strongly influences fabric dimensions, weight per unit area, tightness, and dimensional stability. The tightness factor relates loop length to yarn fineness and indicates whether a fabric is tightly or loosely knitted.

Knitting machines form loops using needles. The most common needle type is the latch needle, which has a hook at its top and a pivoting latch below the hook. As the needle rises, the existing loop slides down below the latch and opens it; the needle then receives new yarn in its hook. As the needle descends, the old loop closes the latch over the hook, and the new yarn is drawn through the old loop, which is cast off over the needle head. This sequence of clearing, yarn feeding, latch closing, knocking over, and loop formation is repeated at every needle. Bearded needles and compound needles are also used, particularly on warp knitting machines, because they can operate at high speeds. The gauge of a machine, the number of needles per inch, determines the fineness of fabric that can be produced.

In weft knitting, loops are formed across the width of the fabric, and each course can be produced from a single yarn feeding successive needles in turn, much as in hand knitting. Weft knitting machines may be circular, with needles arranged around a rotating cylinder producing tubular fabric, or flat, with needles in straight beds. Circular machines with many yarn feeders are highly productive and produce most jersey fabrics, while flat machines, often computer controlled, are used for sweaters and shaped garment pieces.

Four basic weft-knitted structures are widely recognized. Single jersey, also called plain knit, is produced on a single set of needles and shows V-shaped face loops on the technical face and semicircular loops on the back. It is lightweight and extensible but tends to curl at the edges and can ladder, or run, if a loop is broken. Rib fabrics are produced on two sets of needles, with face and back loops alternating along the courses, for example in a one-by-one or two-by-two arrangement; they have high widthwise elasticity and are used for cuffs, collars, and waistbands. Interlock is a double-knit structure made from two interlocked rib fabrics, giving a smooth appearance on both sides, greater stability, and resistance to curling and laddering. Purl fabrics contain both face and back loops within the same wale, producing a similar appearance on both sides and high lengthwise extensibility. Variations are created with knit, tuck, and miss stitches. A tuck stitch occurs when a needle receives new yarn without casting off the old loop, while a miss or float stitch occurs when a needle does not receive yarn, leaving the yarn floating behind. These stitches create textures, patterns, and fabrics such as pique.

Warp knitting forms loops in a fundamentally different way. Instead of one yarn running across the width, a large number of parallel yarns are supplied from warp beams, and each needle is usually fed by its own yarn or yarns. Guide bars move the yarns sideways between needles in a coordinated pattern called lapping, so that loops in each course are formed simultaneously across the whole width of the fabric and each yarn zigzags along the length, connecting adjacent wales. The two main types of warp knitting machines are tricot machines, which typically use compound needles and produce fine, smooth fabrics for lingerie, linings, and sportswear, and raschel machines, which are often equipped with several guide bars and are used for laces, nets, power-net fabrics, curtains, and technical textiles.

Warp-knitted fabrics have distinct properties. Because loops are formed from yarns running lengthwise and interlocked across wales, they are generally more stable and less extensible than weft-knitted fabrics, and they do not ladder or unravel easily. Production speeds are very high, since an entire course is formed at once, making warp knitting economical for large volumes of standard fabrics. The need to prepare warp beams with many yarns, however, makes warp knitting less flexible for small orders and frequent pattern changes than weft knitting.

Knitted fabrics require careful attention to dimensional stability. During knitting, yarns are stretched, and after the fabric is relaxed, washed, or finished, loops tend to return to a more stable shape, causing shrinkage. Spirality, the twisting of wales in single jersey fabrics, can result from yarn twist liveliness. Manufacturers control these problems through yarn selection, loop length, machine settings, and finishing processes such as compacting and heat setting for synthetic fibres. Fabric quality is assessed by measuring areal weight, wales and courses, shrinkage, spirality, bursting strength, and defects such as holes, drop stitches, and barre, which are horizontal bars caused by variations in yarn or tension.<|im_end|>

source_text:
Systems of linear equations arise throughout science and engineering. Structural engineers solve them to find forces in trusses and frames, electrical engineers to determine currents and voltages in circuits, economists in input-output models, and computer programs in simulations, optimization, and data analysis. Such systems can be written in matrix form as A x equals b, where A is a square matrix of coefficients, x is the vector of unknowns, and b is the vector of constants. For small systems, methods such as substitution or Cramer's rule may be used, but these become impractical or inefficient for larger systems. Gaussian elimination is the standard direct method, and LU decomposition is an efficient way of organizing it, particularly when the same coefficient matrix must be used with many different right-hand sides.

Gaussian elimination transforms the system into an equivalent upper triangular system, in which all entries below the main diagonal are zero. It does so by subtracting suitable multiples of one row from rows below it, eliminating the unknowns one column at a time. The multiples used are called multipliers, and the diagonal element used to eliminate entries below it is called the pivot. Once the matrix is upper triangular, the unknowns can be found by back substitution, starting with the last equation, which contains only one unknown, and working upwards.

LU decomposition, also called LU factorization, expresses the matrix A as the product of two triangular matrices: a lower triangular matrix L, with zeros above the diagonal, and an upper triangular matrix U, with zeros below the diagonal. The matrix U is the upper triangular matrix produced by Gaussian elimination, and L records the multipliers used during elimination, placed below its diagonal. In the Doolittle form of the decomposition, the diagonal entries of L are all one; in the Crout form, the diagonal entries of U are all one instead.

For example, consider the matrix A with first row 2 and 1, and second row 4 and 3. To eliminate the entry 4 in the second row, the first row is multiplied by 2 and subtracted from the second row, giving a new second row of 0 and 1. The resulting upper triangular matrix U has rows 2 and 1, and 0 and 1. The multiplier 2 is placed in L, which has rows 1 and 0, and 2 and 1. Multiplying L by U reproduces the original matrix A.

Once A has been factorized, solving A x equals b involves two simple steps. Since A equals L U, the system becomes L U x equals b. Introducing an intermediate vector y equal to U x, one first solves L y equals b by forward substitution, starting from the first equation and working downwards, because L is lower triangular. One then solves U x equals y by back substitution. Each triangular solve requires a number of operations proportional to n squared for an n by n system, whereas the factorization itself requires about two thirds of n cubed operations.

The main advantage of LU decomposition appears when a system must be solved repeatedly with the same matrix but different right-hand sides, a common situation in engineering. In structural analysis, for example, the stiffness matrix of a building depends on its geometry and materials, while the load vector changes for different load cases such as dead load, wind, and earthquake loading. With LU decomposition, the expensive factorization is performed once, and each new load case requires only the inexpensive forward and back substitutions. The same idea is used in iterative methods and time-stepping simulations where the matrix stays constant. LU decomposition also provides a convenient way to compute the determinant of A, which equals the product of the diagonal entries of U when L has ones on its diagonal, and it can be used to compute the inverse of A by solving for each column of the identity matrix, although explicitly computing inverses is usually unnecessary and less efficient than solving systems directly.

Not every matrix can be factorized in this simple way. If a zero appears in a pivot position during elimination, the process fails, even though the system may have a unique solution. Small pivots also cause problems in computer arithmetic, because dividing by a very small number can magnify rounding errors and lead to inaccurate results. These issues are addressed by pivoting. In partial pivoting, before eliminating each column, the rows are rearranged so that the entry with the largest absolute value in the current column, among the remaining rows, becomes the pivot. The row interchanges are recorded in a permutation matrix P, and the decomposition becomes P A equals L U. Partial pivoting is used in almost all practical implementations because it greatly improves numerical stability. Complete pivoting, which also interchanges columns, offers further stability but is more costly and rarely necessary.

The accuracy of solutions also depends on the condition of the matrix. A matrix is ill-conditioned if small changes in its entries or in the right-hand side produce large changes in the solution. The condition number of a matrix measures this sensitivity; large condition numbers indicate that even a stable algorithm may produce solutions with significant errors when data contain small uncertainties. Recognizing ill-conditioning is important in interpreting numerical results.

Special forms of LU decomposition exist for particular classes of matrices. For symmetric positive definite matrices, which arise frequently in engineering and statistics, the Cholesky decomposition expresses A as L multiplied by the transpose of L. It requires about half the computation of general LU decomposition, needs no pivoting for stability, and is widely used in finite element analysis and in fitting statistical models. Tridiagonal systems, in which non-zero entries occur only on the main diagonal and the diagonals immediately above and below it, arise in discretized differential equations and can be solved very efficiently with a specialized version of LU decomposition known as the Thomas algorithm, which requires only a number of operations proportional to n. For large sparse matrices, in which most entries are zero, sparse LU methods reorder equations to limit the creation of new non-zero entries, called fill-in, during factorization.

LU decomposition is implemented in standard numerical libraries, such as LAPACK, and in software environments including MATLAB and Python's scientific libraries, where solving a linear system typically calls an LU-based routine internally. Understanding the method helps users interpret numerical results, choose efficient approaches for repeated solutions, and recognize when special structure in a matrix can be exploited.

Solving then uses forward substitution for Ly = b and back substitution for Ux = y, each about n² operations, after a factorization of about (2/3)n³, so it is efficient for repeated right-hand sides such as multiple structural load cases and constant-matrix simulations; it also gives the determinant as the product of U's diagonal and can produce inverses, though these are rarely needed. Lecture material:
Systems of linear equations arise throughout science and engineering. Structural engineers solve them to find forces in trusses and frames, electrical engineers to determine currents and voltages in circuits, economists in input-output models, and computer programs in simulations, optimization, and data analysis. Such systems can be written in matrix form as A x equals b, where A is a square matrix of coefficients, x is the vector of unknowns, and b is the vector of constants. For small systems, methods such as substitution or Cramer's rule may be used, but these become impractical or inefficient for larger systems. Gaussian elimination is the standard direct method, and LU decomposition is an efficient way of organizing it, particularly when the same coefficient matrix must be used with many different right-hand sides.

Gaussian elimination transforms the system into an equivalent upper triangular system, in which all entries below the main diagonal are zero. It does so by subtracting suitable multiples of one row from rows below it, eliminating the unknowns one column at a time. The multiples used are called multipliers, and the diagonal element used to eliminate entries below it is called the pivot. Once the matrix is upper triangular, the unknowns can be found by back substitution, starting with the last equation, which contains only one unknown, and working upwards.

LU decomposition, also called LU factorization, expresses the matrix A as the product of two triangular matrices: a lower triangular matrix L, with zeros above the diagonal, and an upper triangular matrix U, with zeros below the diagonal. The matrix U is the upper triangular matrix produced by Gaussian elimination, and L records the multipliers used during elimination, placed below its diagonal. In the Doolittle form of the decomposition, the diagonal entries of L are all one; in the Crout form, the diagonal entries of U are all one instead.

For example, consider the matrix A with first row 2 and 1, and second row 4 and 3. To eliminate the entry 4 in the second row, the first row is multiplied by 2 and subtracted from the second row, giving a new second row of 0 and 1. The resulting upper triangular matrix U has rows 2 and 1, and 0 and 1. The multiplier 2 is placed in L, which has rows 1 and 0, and 2 and 1. Multiplying L by U reproduces the original matrix A.

Once A has been factorized, solving A x equals b involves two simple steps. Since A equals L U, the system becomes L U x equals b. Introducing an intermediate vector y equal to U x, one first solves L y equals b by forward substitution, starting from the first equation and working downwards, because L is lower triangular. One then solves U x equals y by back substitution. Each triangular solve requires a number of operations proportional to n squared for an n by n system, whereas the factorization itself requires about two thirds of n cubed operations.

The main advantage of LU decomposition appears when a system must be solved repeatedly with the same matrix but different right-hand sides, a common situation in engineering. In structural analysis, for example, the stiffness matrix of a building depends on its geometry and materials, while the load vector changes for different load cases such as dead load, wind, and earthquake loading. With LU decomposition, the expensive factorization is performed once, and each new load case requires only the inexpensive forward and back substitutions. The same idea is used in iterative methods and time-stepping simulations where the matrix stays constant. LU decomposition also provides a convenient way to compute the determinant of A, which equals the product of the diagonal entries of U when L has ones on its diagonal, and it can be used to compute the inverse of A by solving for each column of the identity matrix, although explicitly computing inverses is usually unnecessary and less efficient than solving systems directly.

Not every matrix can be factorized in this simple way. If a zero appears in a pivot position during elimination, the process fails, even though the system may have a unique solution. Small pivots also cause problems in computer arithmetic, because dividing by a very small number can magnify rounding errors and lead to inaccurate results. These issues are addressed by pivoting. In partial pivoting, before eliminating each column, the rows are rearranged so that the entry with the largest absolute value in the current column, among the remaining rows, becomes the pivot. The row interchanges are recorded in a permutation matrix P, and the decomposition becomes P A equals L U. Partial pivoting is used in almost all practical implementations because it greatly improves numerical stability. Complete pivoting, which also interchanges columns, offers further stability but is more costly and rarely necessary.

The accuracy of solutions also depends on the condition of the matrix. A matrix is ill-conditioned if small changes in its entries or in the right-hand side produce large changes in the solution. The condition number of a matrix measures this sensitivity; large condition numbers indicate that even a stable algorithm may produce solutions with significant errors when data contain small uncertainties. Recognizing ill-conditioning is important in interpreting numerical results.

Special forms of LU decomposition exist for particular classes of matrices. For symmetric positive definite matrices, which arise frequently in engineering and statistics, the Cholesky decomposition expresses A as L multiplied by the transpose of L. It requires about half the computation of general LU decomposition, needs no pivoting for stability, and is widely used in finite element analysis and in fitting statistical models. Tridiagonal systems, in which non-zero entries occur only on the main diagonal and the diagonals immediately above and below it, arise in discretized differential equations and can be solved very efficiently with a specialized version of LU decomposition known as the Thomas algorithm, which requires only a number of operations proportional to n. For large sparse matrices, in which most entries are zero, sparse LU methods reorder equations to limit the creation of new non-zero entries, called fill-in, during factorization.

LU decomposition is implemented in standard numerical libraries, such as LAPACK, and in software environments including MATLAB and Python's scientific libraries, where solving a linear system typically calls an LU-based routine internally. Understanding the method helps users interpret numerical results, choose efficient approaches for repeated solutions, and recognize when special structure in a matrix can be exploited.<|im_end|>

source_text:
Classical mechanics describes how objects move in response to forces. Its foundation consists of three laws of motion published by Isaac Newton in 1687. These laws apply with great accuracy to everyday objects moving at speeds much lower than the speed of light and at scales much larger than atoms, and they underpin engineering design, vehicle dynamics, structural analysis, and orbital mechanics. Applying Newton's laws effectively depends on identifying all the forces acting on an object, which is done systematically using free-body diagrams.

Newton's first law, often called the law of inertia, states that an object remains at rest or continues to move in a straight line at constant speed unless acted on by a net external force. Inertia is the tendency of objects to resist changes in their state of motion, and mass is the quantitative measure of inertia. The first law challenged the older idea, associated with Aristotle, that a force is required to keep an object moving. In everyday experience, moving objects slow down because of friction and air resistance, not because motion naturally stops. The first law also defines inertial reference frames, frames in which it holds; a frame accelerating relative to an inertial frame, such as a braking bus, is not inertial, which is why passengers appear to be pushed forward.

Newton's second law relates net force to acceleration. It states that the net external force on an object equals the product of its mass and its acceleration, written F equals m times a. Force and acceleration are vector quantities, having both magnitude and direction, and the acceleration is in the direction of the net force. The SI unit of force, the newton, is defined as the force needed to give a mass of one kilogram an acceleration of one metre per second squared. The second law shows that, for a given force, a larger mass experiences a smaller acceleration. A more general form states that net force equals the rate of change of momentum, which is useful for systems in which mass changes, such as rockets.

Newton's third law states that when one object exerts a force on a second object, the second object exerts a force of equal magnitude and opposite direction on the first. These forces, often called an action-reaction pair, act on different objects and are of the same type. When a person pushes against a wall, the wall pushes back on the person with an equal force. When a rocket expels exhaust gases backwards, the gases push the rocket forwards. A common misconception is that action-reaction forces cancel out. They do not, because they act on different bodies; only forces acting on the same object can be combined to determine its motion. For a book resting on a table, the weight of the book and the normal force exerted by the table are equal and opposite, but they are not a third-law pair: both act on the book, and they balance because the book is in equilibrium. The third-law partner of the book's weight is the gravitational force that the book exerts on the Earth.

Several types of forces commonly appear in mechanics problems. Weight is the gravitational force on an object, equal to its mass multiplied by the gravitational field strength, about 9.8 newtons per kilogram near Earth's surface. The normal force is the perpendicular contact force exerted by a surface on an object resting on it. Tension is the pulling force transmitted through a string, rope, or cable. Friction acts parallel to contact surfaces and opposes relative motion or the tendency to move. Static friction can adjust up to a maximum value equal to the coefficient of static friction times the normal force, while kinetic friction, acting during sliding, is usually approximately equal to the coefficient of kinetic friction times the normal force. Applied forces, spring forces, and air resistance may also be present.

A free-body diagram is a simplified sketch that isolates a single object and shows all the external forces acting on it as arrows starting from the object, each labelled and drawn in the correct direction. Forces that the object exerts on other objects are not included, nor are internal forces within the object. The procedure for solving a problem typically involves several steps: identifying the object or system of interest, drawing its free-body diagram, choosing a convenient coordinate system, resolving forces into components along the axes, applying Newton's second law separately in each direction, and solving the resulting equations. For an object on an inclined plane, it is often convenient to choose axes parallel and perpendicular to the slope, so that the weight is resolved into a component of mg times the sine of the angle down the slope and a component of mg times the cosine of the angle into the slope.

When several objects are connected, as in two blocks joined by a string over a pulley, a separate free-body diagram is drawn for each object. If the string is light and does not stretch, the tension is the same throughout and the objects share the same magnitude of acceleration, which provides the equations needed to solve for the unknowns. In equilibrium problems, where the acceleration is zero, the vector sum of the forces in each direction equals zero. Engineers use the same principles in statics to determine forces in bridges, cranes, and structural members.

Newton's laws have limits. At speeds approaching the speed of light, special relativity is required, and at atomic and subatomic scales, quantum mechanics replaces classical descriptions. In accelerating reference frames, fictitious forces such as the centrifugal force must be introduced if Newton's laws are to be applied. Nevertheless, within their domain, Newton's laws combined with careful free-body analysis provide a powerful and reliable method for predicting motion.

Newtonian mechanics fails near light speed and at atomic scales and needs fictitious forces in accelerating frames, but remains powerful within its domain.

source_text:
The Laplace transform is a mathematical tool that converts a function of time into a function of a complex variable, usually denoted s. It is named after the French mathematician Pierre-Simon Laplace, and it is widely used in engineering and applied mathematics, particularly for solving linear ordinary differential equations with constant coefficients and for analysing electrical circuits, mechanical vibrations, and control systems. The central advantage of the Laplace transform is that it changes differentiation and integration in the time domain into algebraic operations in the s-domain, so that differential equations become algebraic equations that are much easier to solve.

For a function f of t defined for t greater than or equal to zero, the Laplace transform F of s is defined as the integral from zero to infinity of e to the power minus s t multiplied by f of t, with respect to t. The transform exists when this integral converges, which is the case for functions that are piecewise continuous and of exponential order, meaning that they do not grow faster than some exponential function as t increases. The variable s may be real or complex, and the set of values for which the integral converges is called the region of convergence. The inverse Laplace transform recovers the original function from F of s.

Several basic transforms are used repeatedly. The transform of the constant function one is one divided by s. The transform of t is one divided by s squared, and more generally the transform of t to the power n is n factorial divided by s to the power n plus one. The transform of the exponential function e to the power a t is one divided by s minus a, for s greater than a. The transforms of sine of omega t and cosine of omega t are omega divided by s squared plus omega squared and s divided by s squared plus omega squared, respectively. These results are collected in tables of Laplace transform pairs, which allow transforms and inverse transforms to be found without performing integration each time.

The Laplace transform has several properties that make it powerful. It is linear: the transform of a sum of functions multiplied by constants equals the same combination of their transforms. The most important property for solving differential equations concerns derivatives. The transform of the first derivative of f equals s times F of s minus f of zero, and the transform of the second derivative equals s squared times F of s minus s times f of zero minus the first derivative evaluated at zero. Thus, differentiation corresponds to multiplication by s, and initial conditions are incorporated automatically into the transformed equation. Similarly, integration in the time domain corresponds to division by s. The first shifting theorem states that multiplying a function by e to the power a t shifts its transform, replacing s with s minus a. The second shifting theorem deals with time delays: a function that is delayed by a time a and switched on at that time, represented using the unit step function, has a transform equal to e to the power minus a s multiplied by the transform of the original function. These properties allow engineers to handle discontinuous inputs, such as switches being closed or forces suddenly applied, in a systematic way.

The procedure for solving an initial value problem using the Laplace transform involves three steps. First, the transform is applied to both sides of the differential equation, using the derivative property to incorporate the initial conditions. Second, the resulting algebraic equation is solved for the transformed unknown function, Y of s. Third, the inverse transform is found to obtain the solution y of t. The third step often requires expressing Y of s as a sum of simpler fractions using partial fraction decomposition, so that each term can be matched with an entry in the table of transform pairs. For example, a first-order equation describing a circuit, such as the voltage across a charging capacitor, or a second-order equation describing a mass-spring-damper system, can be solved in this way, including the effects of initial displacement, initial velocity, and external forcing.

The convolution theorem is another important result. It states that the Laplace transform of the convolution of two functions equals the product of their transforms. In system analysis, the output of a linear time-invariant system is the convolution of the input with the system's impulse response. Taking Laplace transforms converts this convolution into a simple multiplication, leading to the concept of the transfer function. The transfer function of a system is the ratio of the Laplace transform of the output to the Laplace transform of the input, assuming zero initial conditions. It provides a compact description of the system's dynamic behaviour and is a fundamental tool in control engineering and circuit analysis.

The transfer function can be written as a ratio of polynomials in s. The roots of the denominator are called poles, and the roots of the numerator are called zeros. The locations of the poles in the complex s-plane determine the nature of the system's response. Poles with negative real parts correspond to responses that decay over time, indicating a stable system; poles with positive real parts correspond to responses that grow without bound, indicating instability; and poles on the imaginary axis correspond to sustained oscillations. Complex conjugate poles produce oscillatory responses, with the imaginary part determining the frequency and the real part determining the rate of decay. The initial value theorem and final value theorem allow the initial and steady-state values of a time function to be determined directly from its transform, provided certain conditions are met.

Although the Laplace transform is most effective for linear systems with constant coefficients, it remains one of the most widely used methods in engineering mathematics because it connects the time-domain behaviour of physical systems with algebraic and graphical methods of analysis in the s-domain.

source_text:
Bearings support rotating or sliding machine parts while allowing relative motion with minimal friction. They are found in electric motors, gearboxes, vehicle wheels, pumps, turbines, and almost every machine with a rotating shaft. Bearings fall into two broad families: plain or sliding bearings, in which surfaces slide over each other separated by a lubricant film, and rolling-element bearings, in which balls or rollers roll between an inner and an outer ring. Rolling-element bearings, often called antifriction bearings, have low starting friction, are standardized and easily replaced, and can carry both radial and axial loads, which makes them the most common choice for general machinery.

A rolling-element bearing consists of an inner ring mounted on the shaft, an outer ring fitted in the housing, rolling elements between them, and a cage or separator that keeps the elements evenly spaced. Seals or shields may be added to retain lubricant and exclude contaminants. Deep groove ball bearings are the most widely used type; they carry moderate radial loads and some axial load in both directions and operate at high speeds. Angular contact ball bearings have raceways arranged so that the load is transmitted at an angle, allowing them to carry larger axial loads in one direction, and they are often used in pairs. Cylindrical roller bearings carry heavy radial loads because line contact between rollers and raceways spreads the load over a larger area, but most designs carry little or no axial load. Tapered roller bearings carry combined heavy radial and axial loads and are common in vehicle wheel hubs. Spherical roller bearings tolerate shaft misalignment, and thrust bearings are designed mainly for axial loads.

Bearing selection is usually based on the required life under a specified load. Because rolling elements and raceways experience repeated contact stresses with every revolution, the dominant failure mode of a properly lubricated, clean bearing is rolling contact fatigue. Subsurface cracks initiate below the contact surface and eventually cause material to flake away, a process called spalling. Fatigue life varies widely even among identical bearings under identical conditions, so it is expressed statistically. The basic rating life, L10, is the number of revolutions, or operating hours at a given speed, that 90 percent of a group of identical bearings will complete or exceed before the first evidence of fatigue appears.

Manufacturers' catalogues list a basic dynamic load rating, C, for each bearing, defined as the constant load under which the bearing achieves an L10 life of one million revolutions. The basic life equation states that L10, in millions of revolutions, equals C divided by the equivalent dynamic load P, raised to the power p, where p equals three for ball bearings and ten-thirds for roller bearings. The equation shows that life is very sensitive to load: doubling the load on a ball bearing reduces its life to one eighth. When a bearing carries both radial and axial loads, an equivalent dynamic load is calculated by combining the components using factors given in catalogues. For a required life and known load, the equation is rearranged to find the minimum dynamic load rating, and a suitable bearing is selected.

Modern standards extend the basic equation with life modification factors. A reliability factor adjusts the life for reliabilities higher than 90 percent, such as 95 or 99 percent for critical applications. Another factor accounts for lubrication and contamination conditions, because a clean, well-lubricated bearing can last much longer than its basic rating life, while contamination or inadequate lubrication can shorten life dramatically. A static load rating, C0, is also specified to prevent permanent deformation of the raceways under heavy loads at very low speeds or when stationary.

Lubrication is essential for bearing performance. It reduces friction and wear, protects surfaces against corrosion, helps dissipate heat, and, in the case of grease, helps seal out contaminants. In rolling contact, the lubricant forms an extremely thin film between the rolling elements and raceways, described by elastohydrodynamic lubrication theory. Under the very high contact pressures, the lubricant's viscosity increases greatly and the contacting surfaces deform elastically, allowing a film of only a fraction of a micrometre to separate them. The ratio of this film thickness to the combined surface roughness, often called the lambda ratio, indicates whether full separation is achieved. If the film is too thin, metal-to-metal contact occurs, accelerating wear and surface distress.

Most rolling-element bearings are lubricated with grease, a lubricating oil thickened with a soap or other thickener. Grease is easy to retain in the bearing, requires simple seals, and provides protection against contamination, making it suitable for moderate speeds and temperatures. Relubrication intervals depend on speed, temperature, and bearing size, and both under-greasing and over-greasing are harmful; excessive grease causes churning and overheating. Oil lubrication is used for high speeds, high temperatures, or where heat must be removed, using methods such as oil bath, circulating oil, oil mist, or oil jet lubrication. Lubricant viscosity at operating temperature must be sufficient to form an adequate film.

Many bearings fail before reaching their expected fatigue life because of factors other than fatigue. Common causes include contamination by dirt or moisture, inadequate or incorrect lubrication, misalignment, improper mounting that damages raceways, excessive interference fits, electrical currents passing through the bearing, and overloading. Inspection of failed bearings, examining characteristic patterns of wear, indentation, discoloration, and spalling, helps identify the cause. Condition monitoring techniques, such as vibration analysis, temperature monitoring, and lubricant analysis, allow developing faults to be detected early so that bearings can be replaced before failure causes unplanned downtime.

Lecture material:
Bearings support rotating or sliding machine parts while allowing relative motion with minimal friction. They are found in electric motors, gearboxes, vehicle wheels, pumps, turbines, and almost every machine with a rotating shaft. Bearings fall into two broad families: plain or sliding bearings, in which surfaces slide over each other separated by a lubricant film, and rolling-element bearings, in which balls or rollers roll between an inner and an outer ring. Rolling-element bearings, often called antifriction bearings, have low starting friction, are standardized and easily replaced, and can carry both radial and axial loads, which makes them the most common choice for general machinery.

A rolling-element bearing consists of an inner ring mounted on the shaft, an outer ring fitted in the housing, rolling elements between them, and a cage or separator that keeps the elements evenly spaced. Seals or shields may be added to retain lubricant and exclude contaminants. Deep groove ball bearings are the most widely used type; they carry moderate radial loads and some axial load in both directions and operate at high speeds. Angular contact ball bearings have raceways arranged so that the load is transmitted at an angle, allowing them to carry larger axial loads in one direction, and they are often used in pairs. Cylindrical roller bearings carry heavy radial loads because line contact between rollers and raceways spreads the load over a larger area, but most designs carry little or no axial load. Tapered roller bearings carry combined heavy radial and axial loads and are common in vehicle wheel hubs. Spherical roller bearings tolerate shaft misalignment, and thrust bearings are designed mainly for axial loads.

Bearing selection is usually based on the required life under a specified load. Because rolling elements and raceways experience repeated contact stresses with every revolution, the dominant failure mode of a properly lubricated, clean bearing is rolling contact fatigue. Subsurface cracks initiate below the contact surface and eventually cause material to flake away, a process called spalling. Fatigue life varies widely even among identical bearings under identical conditions, so it is expressed statistically. The basic rating life, L10, is the number of revolutions, or operating hours at a given speed, that 90 percent of a group of identical bearings will complete or exceed before the first evidence of fatigue appears.

Manufacturers' catalogues list a basic dynamic load rating, C, for each bearing, defined as the constant load under which the bearing achieves an L10 life of one million revolutions. The basic life equation states that L10, in millions of revolutions, equals C divided by the equivalent dynamic load P, raised to the power p, where p equals three for ball bearings and ten-thirds for roller bearings. The equation shows that life is very sensitive to load: doubling the load on a ball bearing reduces its life to one eighth. When a bearing carries both radial and axial loads, an equivalent dynamic load is calculated by combining the components using factors given in catalogues. For a required life and known load, the equation is rearranged to find the minimum dynamic load rating, and a suitable bearing is selected.

Modern standards extend the basic equation with life modification factors. A reliability factor adjusts the life for reliabilities higher than 90 percent, such as 95 or 99 percent for critical applications. Another factor accounts for lubrication and contamination conditions, because a clean, well-lubricated bearing can last much longer than its basic rating life, while contamination or inadequate lubrication can shorten life dramatically. A static load rating, C0, is also specified to prevent permanent deformation of the raceways under heavy loads at very low speeds or when stationary.

Lubrication is essential for bearing performance. It reduces friction and wear, protects surfaces against corrosion, helps dissipate heat, and, in the case of grease, helps seal out contaminants. In rolling contact, the lubricant forms an extremely thin film between the rolling elements and raceways, described by elastohydrodynamic lubrication theory. Under the very high contact pressures, the lubricant's viscosity increases greatly and the contacting surfaces deform elastically, allowing a film of only a fraction of a micrometre to separate them. The ratio of this film thickness to the combined surface roughness, often called the lambda ratio, indicates whether full separation is achieved. If the film is too thin, metal-to-metal contact occurs, accelerating wear and surface distress.

Most rolling-element bearings are lubricated with grease, a lubricating oil thickened with a soap or other thickener. Grease is easy to retain in the bearing, requires simple seals, and provides protection against contamination, making it suitable for moderate speeds and temperatures. Relubrication intervals depend on speed, temperature, and bearing size, and both under-greasing and over-greasing are harmful; excessive grease causes churning and overheating. Oil lubrication is used for high speeds, high temperatures, or where heat must be removed, using methods such as oil bath, circulating oil, oil mist, or oil jet lubrication. Lubricant viscosity at operating temperature must be sufficient to form an adequate film.

Many bearings fail before reaching their expected fatigue life because of factors other than fatigue. Common causes include contamination by dirt or moisture, inadequate or incorrect lubrication, misalignment, improper mounting that damages raceways, excessive interference fits, electrical currents passing through the bearing, and overloading. Inspection of failed bearings, examining characteristic patterns of wear, indentation, discoloration, and spalling, helps identify the cause. Condition monitoring techniques, such as vibration analysis, temperature monitoring, and lubricant analysis, allow developing faults to be detected early so that bearings can be replaced before failure causes unplanned downtime.<|im_end|>

topic: Laboratory Shear Strength Tests for Soils
source_text:
The shear strength of a soil is its maximum resistance to shearing stresses before failure. It governs the bearing capacity of foundations, the stability of slopes and embankments, and the earth pressures acting on retaining walls. Because soil is a particulate material, its strength depends mainly on friction and interlocking between particles and, in fine-grained soils, on cohesive forces. Laboratory tests are used to measure shear strength parameters so that engineers can apply them in design.

Shear strength is usually described by the Mohr-Coulomb failure criterion, in which shear strength equals the cohesion intercept plus the effective normal stress multiplied by the tangent of the effective angle of shearing resistance. Because pore water pressure reduces the stress transmitted between particles, strength is governed by effective stress, the total stress minus the pore water pressure. Analyses may be carried out in terms of effective stress, using drained parameters, or in terms of total stress, using the undrained shear strength of saturated clays, which applies when loading is rapid enough that excess pore water pressures cannot dissipate. Selecting the appropriate test and drainage condition to represent field conditions is one of the most important decisions in geotechnical practice.

The direct shear test, or shear box test, is the simplest method. A soil specimen, typically square, is placed in a split box consisting of upper and lower halves. A vertical normal load is applied, and then the lower half is displaced horizontally relative to the upper half, forcing the specimen to shear along a predetermined horizontal plane. The horizontal shear force and the vertical and horizontal displacements are recorded. The test is repeated on several specimens under different normal stresses, and the peak shear stresses are plotted against the corresponding normal stresses. The slope of the best-fit line gives the friction angle, and its intercept gives the cohesion. Dense sands typically show a peak strength followed by a decrease to a lower residual or critical state value as they dilate, while loose sands compress and show gradually increasing resistance.

The direct shear test is quick and inexpensive and is well suited to sands and to measuring the residual strength of clays by repeated reversals of shearing. However, it has significant limitations. The failure plane is forced to be horizontal rather than forming along the weakest plane. Stress distribution across the specimen is non-uniform, especially near the edges. Drainage cannot be controlled precisely, and pore water pressures cannot be measured, so the test is normally conducted slowly enough to allow full drainage in sands or run very quickly to approximate undrained conditions, without confirming either.

The triaxial test is more versatile and is the standard method for determining shear strength parameters. A cylindrical specimen, typically with a height about twice its diameter, is enclosed in a thin rubber membrane and placed in a cell filled with water. The cell water is pressurized to apply an all-round confining pressure, representing the lateral stress in the ground. An additional axial load, the deviator stress, is applied through a loading ram until the specimen fails. Drainage lines connected to the ends of the specimen allow pore water to drain or be prevented from draining, and pore water pressure can be measured with a transducer. Volume change during drained tests is measured from the water flowing into or out of the specimen.

Three main types of triaxial test are distinguished by their drainage conditions. In the unconsolidated undrained, UU, test, drainage is not permitted during either the application of confining pressure or shearing. The test is rapid and gives the undrained shear strength of saturated clay, which, for a saturated specimen, is independent of the confining pressure, so the Mohr circles have the same diameter and the failure envelope is horizontal. In the consolidated undrained, CU, test, the specimen is first allowed to consolidate under the confining pressure, and drainage is then closed during shearing while pore pressures are measured. This allows both total and effective stress parameters to be obtained from fewer specimens and reveals how the soil generates pore pressure: normally consolidated clays develop positive pore pressures when sheared, while heavily overconsolidated clays tend to dilate and develop negative pore pressures. In the consolidated drained, CD, test, drainage is allowed throughout, and shearing is performed slowly enough that no excess pore pressure develops. The CD test directly gives effective stress parameters but can take a long time for clays because of their low permeability.

Results are interpreted by drawing Mohr circles for the stress state at failure of each specimen. The minor principal stress is the confining pressure, and the major principal stress is the confining pressure plus the deviator stress at failure. The common tangent to the circles defines the failure envelope, from which cohesion and friction angle are obtained. Plots of stress paths, which track the changing stress state during shearing, provide further insight into soil behaviour.

The unconfined compression test is a special case of the triaxial test in which the confining pressure is zero. It is used for saturated clays that can stand without lateral support, and the undrained shear strength is taken as half the unconfined compressive strength. Field tests, such as the vane shear test, are often used to supplement laboratory results in soft clays, because sampling can disturb soft soil and reduce its measured strength.

Choosing a test requires consideration of the soil type and the loading conditions in the field. Short-term stability of a foundation on saturated clay immediately after construction is commonly evaluated using undrained strength from UU or unconfined compression tests, while long-term stability of slopes and retaining structures is evaluated using effective stress parameters from CU tests with pore pressure measurement or CD tests. Sample quality, specimen preparation, and rates of loading all influence results, so laboratory values must be interpreted with engineering judgement.

topic: Symmetrical Components and Power System Faults
source_text:
A fault in an electrical power system is any abnormal condition that causes current to flow along an unintended path, most commonly a short circuit between conductors or between a conductor and ground. Faults may be caused by lightning strikes, insulation failure, falling trees, animals, equipment damage, or human error. They produce currents that may be many times larger than normal load currents, causing overheating, mechanical stress on equipment, voltage collapse, and danger to people. Protection systems must detect and isolate faults within fractions of a second. Calculating fault currents is therefore essential for selecting circuit breakers with adequate interrupting capacity, setting protective relays, and designing equipment to withstand fault stresses.

Faults are classified as symmetrical or unsymmetrical. A symmetrical, or balanced, fault is a three-phase fault in which all three phases are short-circuited together, with or without ground. Although it is the most severe type in terms of current magnitude in many cases, it is relatively rare, accounting for only around five percent of faults. Because the system remains balanced, it can be analysed using a single-phase equivalent circuit. Unsymmetrical faults are far more common and include the single line-to-ground fault, which accounts for roughly seventy to eighty percent of faults on overhead lines, the line-to-line fault, and the double line-to-ground fault. Open-conductor faults, in which one or two phases are broken, are also unsymmetrical. Unsymmetrical faults make the system unbalanced, so the simple per-phase method cannot be used directly.

The method of symmetrical components, introduced by Charles Fortescue in 1918, provides a systematic way to analyse unbalanced three-phase systems. Fortescue showed that any set of three unbalanced phasors can be expressed as the sum of three balanced sets of components. The positive-sequence components consist of three phasors of equal magnitude, displaced by 120 degrees, with the same phase sequence as the original system, conventionally a, b, c. The negative-sequence components consist of three equal phasors displaced by 120 degrees but with the opposite phase sequence, a, c, b. The zero-sequence components consist of three phasors of equal magnitude that are in phase with one another.

The transformation between phase quantities and sequence components uses a complex operator, usually written as a, which represents a rotation of 120 degrees and has a magnitude of one. Multiplying a phasor by a rotates it by 120 degrees, and multiplying by a squared rotates it by 240 degrees. The phase voltages can be written in terms of the sequence voltages using a three-by-three transformation matrix containing one, a, and a squared, and the sequence components can be obtained from the phase quantities using the inverse matrix. For example, the zero-sequence component equals one third of the sum of the three phase quantities. In a balanced system, only positive-sequence components are present. Negative-sequence components indicate unbalance, and zero-sequence components exist only when current can return through a neutral or ground path.

The value of the method lies in the fact that, for balanced, symmetrical equipment such as transmission lines, transformers, and machines, the sequence networks are independent of one another. A positive-sequence current produces only positive-sequence voltage drops, and similarly for the other sequences. Each component of the system can therefore be represented by a positive-sequence impedance, a negative-sequence impedance, and a zero-sequence impedance, and three separate sequence networks can be constructed. The positive-sequence network includes the internal voltages of generators, since generators produce balanced positive-sequence voltages, whereas the negative- and zero-sequence networks contain no sources. For static equipment such as transmission lines, positive- and negative-sequence impedances are equal, while the zero-sequence impedance is usually larger because zero-sequence currents return through the ground or ground wires. For rotating machines, the negative-sequence impedance differs from the positive-sequence value.

Zero-sequence networks require particular care because they depend on grounding and transformer connections. Zero-sequence current can flow only where there is a return path. A star-connected winding with a solidly grounded neutral provides such a path, while an ungrounded star connection blocks zero-sequence current. A delta winding allows zero-sequence currents to circulate within the delta but prevents them from passing to the external line. Grounding impedances in the neutral appear in the zero-sequence network as three times their value, because the neutral carries the sum of the three zero-sequence currents.

Each type of fault corresponds to a particular interconnection of the sequence networks at the fault point. For a single line-to-ground fault on phase a through a fault impedance, the positive-, negative-, and zero-sequence currents are equal, and the three sequence networks are connected in series. The fault current equals three times the zero-sequence current and depends on the sum of the three sequence impedances plus three times the fault impedance. For a line-to-line fault between phases b and c, the positive- and negative-sequence networks are connected in parallel, and the zero-sequence network is not involved because no ground path exists. For a double line-to-ground fault, all three networks are connected in parallel at the fault point. Once the sequence currents and voltages have been found from the connected networks, they are transformed back to obtain the actual phase currents and voltages.

Fault calculations are typically performed using the per-unit system, in which quantities are expressed as fractions of chosen base values, simplifying calculations across transformers with different voltage levels. In large networks, the bus impedance matrix, Zbus, allows fault currents at any bus to be calculated efficiently, and computer programs perform these studies routinely. Results are used to determine the required interrupting ratings of circuit breakers and fuses, to coordinate protective relays so that the device nearest a fault operates first, and to evaluate ground potential rise and touch voltages for safety. Symmetrical components are also used directly in protection: negative-sequence relays detect unbalanced conditions that can overheat generators, and zero-sequence relays detect ground faults sensitively.

Faults may be caused by lightning strikes, insulation failure, falling trees, animals, equipment damage, or human error. topic: Alternate Wetting and Drying in Rice Cultivation
source_text:
Rice is the staple food for more than half of the world's population and the most important crop in Bangladesh, where it occupies most of the cultivated land and supplies a large share of daily calorie intake. Traditional irrigated rice cultivation keeps fields continuously flooded with a layer of standing water throughout most of the growing season. Continuous flooding helps control weeds, provides a buffer against water stress, and is easy to manage, but it uses very large amounts of water. Producing one kilogram of rice under continuous flooding commonly requires between about 2,500 and 5,000 litres of water when losses through evaporation, seepage, and percolation are included. In Bangladesh, the dry-season boro rice crop depends heavily on irrigation from groundwater pumped by tube wells, and in many areas groundwater tables have declined, increasing pumping costs and raising concerns about sustainability. Alternate wetting and drying, AWD, is a water-saving irrigation technique developed to reduce water use in rice cultivation without significantly reducing yields.

In alternate wetting and drying, fields are not kept continuously flooded. Instead, irrigation water is applied to flood the field, after which the water is allowed to disappear gradually through evaporation, transpiration, and percolation until the soil surface becomes unsaturated. The field is then flooded again. This cycle of flooding and drying is repeated throughout much of the growing season. The approach is based on research showing that rice does not need continuous standing water to achieve good yields, provided that the roots continue to have access to adequate soil moisture.

A practical tool for implementing AWD is the field water tube, sometimes called the pani pipe, developed with farmers by the International Rice Research Institute and national research partners, including the Bangladesh Rice Research Institute. The tube is a perforated plastic pipe or bamboo tube about 25 to 30 centimetres long and around 10 to 15 centimetres in diameter, with holes drilled along its sides. It is inserted vertically into the soil so that about 15 to 20 centimetres remain below the soil surface and the rest protrudes above. The soil inside the tube is removed, allowing the farmer to see the water level beneath the surface. When the water level inside the tube drops to about 15 centimetres below the soil surface, the field is irrigated again to a depth of about five centimetres of standing water. This threshold, known as safe AWD, is designed to ensure that the water level does not fall so low that the rice plants experience water stress severe enough to reduce yields, because the roots can still access water in the soil.

Timing is important. AWD is generally not practised during the first one to two weeks after transplanting, when seedlings are establishing and standing water helps suppress weeds, and fields are usually kept flooded during the flowering stage, when rice is particularly sensitive to water stress and drought can cause spikelet sterility. AWD is commonly practised during the vegetative stages and the later grain-filling stage. Fertilizer management is coordinated with irrigation: nitrogen fertilizer is preferably applied to dry soil just before reflooding, so that it moves into the soil with the water rather than being lost.

Field studies in Bangladesh, the Philippines, Vietnam, and other countries have found that safe AWD can reduce irrigation water use by about fifteen to thirty percent compared with continuous flooding, without significant yield losses. Water savings reduce the hours of pumping required, lowering fuel or electricity costs for farmers who pay for irrigation, and can increase the area that can be irrigated with limited water supplies. In some cases, AWD has also been associated with stronger root systems, reduced lodging, and reduced incidence of some diseases favoured by continuously humid conditions.

AWD also offers environmental benefits, particularly in reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Continuously flooded rice fields are a major source of methane, a potent greenhouse gas, because the waterlogged soil becomes anaerobic, allowing methanogenic archaea to decompose organic matter and produce methane. Periodic drying introduces oxygen into the soil, suppressing methane production. Studies have reported reductions in methane emissions of roughly thirty to seventy percent under AWD. However, drying and rewetting can increase emissions of nitrous oxide, another greenhouse gas, because alternating aerobic and anaerobic conditions favour nitrification and denitrification. In most studies, the reduction in methane outweighs the increase in nitrous oxide, giving a net reduction in global warming potential. For these reasons, AWD is promoted as a climate-smart agricultural practice and has been included in some carbon credit and mitigation programmes.

Despite its benefits, adoption of AWD faces several constraints. Farmers may perceive risks of yield loss and be reluctant to change long-established practices. Weed pressure can increase when fields are not continuously flooded, requiring additional weed control. AWD is most suitable for fields with reliable control over irrigation timing; where farmers depend on canal water delivered on fixed schedules or share irrigation from a single tube well under group arrangements, individual farmers may not be able to irrigate exactly when needed. Payment systems also matter. When farmers pay a fixed seasonal fee for irrigation regardless of the amount of water used, they have little financial incentive to save water, whereas volumetric or hourly charges encourage water saving. AWD is less suitable for soils with very high percolation rates, where water drains too quickly, and for areas where rainfall keeps fields flooded. Extension services, farmer training, demonstrations, and institutional arrangements that align incentives are therefore essential for successful adoption.

Continuous flooding helps control weeds, provides a buffer against water stress, and is easy to manage, but it uses very large amounts of water. Producing one kilogram of rice under continuous flooding commonly requires between about 2,500 and 5,000 litres of water when losses through evaporation, seepage, and percolation are included. In Bangladesh, the dry-season boro rice crop depends heavily on irrigation from groundwater pumped by tube wells, and in many areas groundwater tables have declined, increasing pumping costs and raising concerns about sustainability. Alternate wetting and drying, AWD, is a water-saving irrigation technique developed to reduce water use in rice cultivation without significantly reducing yields.

In alternate wetting and drying, fields are not kept continuously flooded. Instead, irrigation water is applied to flood the field, after which the water is allowed to disappear gradually through evaporation, transpiration, and percolation until the soil surface becomes unsaturated. The field is then flooded again. This cycle of flooding and drying is repeated throughout much of the growing season. The approach is based on research showing that rice does not need continuous standing water to achieve good yields, provided that the roots continue to have access to adequate soil moisture.

A practical tool for implementing AWD is the field water tube, sometimes called the pani pipe, developed with farmers by the International Rice Research Institute and national research partners, including the Bangladesh Rice Research Institute. It is inserted vertically into the soil so that about 15 to 20 centimetres remain below the soil surface and the rest protrudes above. The soil inside the tube is removed, allowing the farmer to see the water level beneath the surface. When the water level inside the tube drops to about 15 centimetres below the soil surface, the field is irrigated again to a depth of about five centimetres of standing water. This threshold, known as safe AWD, is designed to ensure that the water level does not fall so low that the rice plants experience water stress severe enough to reduce yields, because the roots can still access water in the soil.

source_text:
Fiscal policy refers to the use of government spending and taxation to influence the level of economic activity, the distribution of income, and the provision of public goods. Together with monetary policy, it is one of the two main tools of macroeconomic management. Governments use fiscal policy to stabilize the economy over the business cycle, to finance infrastructure, education, health, and social protection, and to pursue long-term development goals. The effect of fiscal policy on total output depends heavily on the multiplier, the ratio of the change in output to the change in government spending or taxes that caused it.

The government budget consists of expenditures and revenues. Expenditures include government purchases of goods and services, such as salaries of teachers and doctors and spending on roads and power plants, and transfer payments, such as pensions, unemployment benefits, and subsidies, which redistribute income without directly purchasing output. Revenues come mainly from taxes, including income taxes, value added tax, customs duties, and corporate taxes. When spending exceeds revenue, the government runs a budget deficit, which is financed by borrowing, increasing public debt. When revenue exceeds spending, there is a budget surplus.

Fiscal policy is described as expansionary when the government increases spending or reduces taxes to raise aggregate demand, and contractionary when it reduces spending or increases taxes to slow demand. Expansionary policy is typically used during recessions, when output is below its potential level and unemployment is high, while contractionary policy may be used when the economy is overheating and inflation is rising. Discretionary fiscal policy involves deliberate changes in spending or tax laws. Automatic stabilizers, by contrast, are features of the budget that change automatically with economic conditions. In a recession, income tax revenues fall as incomes decline and spending on unemployment benefits rises, supporting household incomes and moderating the downturn without new legislation. In a boom, the opposite occurs.

The multiplier explains why a change in government spending can change total output by more than the initial amount. Suppose the government spends an additional 100 crore taka on building a bridge. The construction workers and firms that receive this money spend part of it on consumer goods, which raises the incomes of shopkeepers and producers, who in turn spend part of their additional income, and so on. Each round of spending is smaller than the one before, because some income is saved, paid in taxes, or spent on imports. The total increase in output is the sum of all these rounds.

In the simplest Keynesian model, which assumes a closed economy without taxes and with prices fixed, the size of each round depends on the marginal propensity to consume, MPC, the fraction of additional income that households spend. The spending multiplier equals one divided by one minus the MPC, or equivalently one divided by the marginal propensity to save. If the MPC is 0.8, the multiplier is five, so an increase of 100 crore taka in government spending would ultimately raise output by 500 crore taka. A tax cut has a smaller effect than an equal increase in government purchases, because households save part of the tax cut before spending the rest; the simple tax multiplier equals minus MPC divided by one minus MPC, which is minus four when the MPC is 0.8. A balanced budget increase, in which spending and taxes rise by the same amount, therefore still raises output, with a balanced budget multiplier of one in this simple model.

In practice, multipliers are much smaller than these simple calculations suggest. Taxes that rise with income reduce the amount available for spending in each round, and imports cause part of spending to leak abroad, which is especially important in small open economies. The marginal propensities to save, tax, and import together determine the size of the leakages. Monetary and financial conditions also matter. If the central bank raises interest rates in response to higher government spending, private investment may fall, an effect known as crowding out. Large deficits financed by borrowing may also raise interest rates in financial markets. Crowding out is weaker when the economy has substantial unused capacity and when interest rates are near zero, which is why many economists argue that fiscal multipliers are larger during deep recessions.

Expectations can further influence the effectiveness of fiscal policy. According to the Ricardian equivalence hypothesis, rational households that anticipate future tax increases to repay government debt may save the proceeds of a debt-financed tax cut, leaving demand unchanged. Empirical evidence suggests that strict Ricardian equivalence does not hold, partly because many households face borrowing constraints and spend additional income readily, but expectations about future policy still affect behaviour. Confidence effects may also work in both directions: credible plans to stabilize public debt can support confidence, while doubts about debt sustainability can raise borrowing costs.

Fiscal policy faces practical limitations. Recognition, decision, and implementation lags mean that discretionary measures may take effect after the economic situation has changed. Large infrastructure projects can take years to plan and execute. Political considerations may lead to spending increases that are difficult to reverse. High public debt can limit fiscal space, the room a government has to expand spending without endangering financial stability, and interest payments may absorb a large share of revenue. In developing economies, narrow tax bases and limited administrative capacity constrain both revenue and spending quality.

The composition of fiscal policy also matters for long-term growth. Spending on productive investment, such as transport, energy, education, and health, can raise future output, while poorly targeted subsidies may be costly and inefficient. Tax design affects incentives to work, save, and invest. For these reasons, fiscal policy is evaluated not only by its short-term effect on demand but also by its contribution to sustainable growth and equity.

In a recession, income tax revenues fall as incomes decline and spending on unemployment benefits rises, supporting household incomes and moderating the downturn without new legislation. In a boom, the opposite occurs.

The multiplier explains why a change in government spending can change total output by more than the initial amount. Suppose the government spends an additional 100 crore taka on building a bridge. The construction workers and firms that receive this money spend part of it on consumer goods, which raises the incomes of shopkeepers and producers, who in turn spend part of their additional income, and so on. Each round of spending is smaller than the one before, because some income is saved, paid in taxes, or spent on imports. The total increase in output is the sum of all these rounds.

In the simplest Keynesian model, which assumes a closed economy without taxes and with prices fixed, the size of each round depends on the marginal propensity to consume, MPC, the fraction of additional income that households spend. The spending multiplier equals one divided by one minus the MPC, or equivalently one divided by the marginal propensity to save. If the MPC is 0.8, the multiplier is five, so an increase of 100 crore taka in government spending would ultimately raise output by 500 crore taka. A tax cut has a smaller effect than an equal increase in government purchases, because households save part of the tax cut before spending the rest; the simple tax multiplier equals minus MPC divided by one minus MPC, which is minus four when the MPC is 0.8. A balanced budget increase, in which spending and taxes rise by the same amount, therefore still raises output, with a balanced budget multiplier of one in this simple model.

In practice, multipliers are much smaller than these simple calculations suggest. Taxes that rise with income reduce the amount available for spending in each round, and imports cause part of spending to leak abroad, which is especially important in small open economies. The marginal propensities to save, tax, and import together determine the size of the leakages. Monetary and financial conditions also matter. If the central bank raises interest rates in response to higher government spending, private investment may fall, an effect known as crowding out. Large deficits financed by borrowing may also raise interest rates in financial markets. Crowding out is weaker when the economy has substantial unused capacity and when interest rates are near zero, which is why many economists argue that fiscal multipliers are larger during deep recessions.

Expectations can further influence the effectiveness of fiscal policy. According to the Ricardian equivalence hypothesis, rational households that anticipate future tax increases to repay government debt may save the proceeds of a debt-financed tax cut, leaving demand unchanged. Empirical evidence suggests that strict Ricardian equivalence does not hold, partly because many households face borrowing constraints and spend additional income readily, but expectations about future policy still affect behaviour. Confidence effects may also work in both directions: credible plans to stabilize public debt can support confidence, while doubts about debt sustainability can raise borrowing costs.

Fiscal policy faces practical limitations. Recognition, decision, and implementation lags mean that discretionary measures may take effect after the economic situation has changed. Large infrastructure projects can take years to plan and execute. Political considerations may lead to spending increases that are difficult to reverse. High public debt can limit fiscal space, the room a government has to expand spending without endangering financial stability, and interest payments may absorb a large share of revenue. In developing economies, narrow tax bases and limited administrative capacity constrain both revenue and spending quality.

The composition of fiscal policy also matters for long-term growth. Spending on productive investment, such as transport, energy, education, and health, can raise future output, while poorly targeted subsidies may be costly and inefficient. Tax design affects incentives to work, save, and invest. For these reasons, fiscal policy is evaluated not only by its short-term effect on demand but also by its contribution to sustainable growth and equity.<|im_end|>
