source_text:
Tobacco use is the leading preventable cause of death worldwide. Smoking and other forms of tobacco use cause lung cancer and many other cancers, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, heart disease, stroke, and adverse pregnancy outcomes, and second-hand smoke harms non-smokers, including children. The World Health Organization estimates that tobacco kills more than eight million people each year, including over one million deaths from exposure to second-hand smoke. In South Asia, including Bangladesh, the burden includes not only cigarettes but also bidi, a cheap hand-rolled cigarette, and widespread use of smokeless tobacco products such as zarda, gul, and betel quid with tobacco, which cause oral cancers and other diseases.

Because tobacco is addictive and heavily marketed, individual education alone has limited effect. Public health experts emphasise comprehensive policy approaches that change the environment in which people decide whether to use tobacco. The WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control, FCTC, adopted in 2003 and entering into force in 2005, was the first international treaty negotiated under the auspices of WHO and has been ratified by most countries, including Bangladesh. It commits parties to evidence-based measures to reduce both the demand for and the supply of tobacco. To help countries implement the treaty, WHO introduced the MPOWER package, which summarizes six key measures.

The first measure, Monitor, involves tracking tobacco use and the effectiveness of prevention policies. Surveys such as the Global Adult Tobacco Survey and the Global Youth Tobacco Survey provide comparable data on prevalence, exposure to second-hand smoke, quit attempts, and exposure to marketing, allowing governments to set targets and evaluate progress.

The second measure, Protect, refers to protecting people from tobacco smoke through smoke-free laws covering indoor workplaces, public places, and public transport. There is no safe level of exposure to second-hand smoke, and designated smoking rooms and ventilation systems do not provide adequate protection, so comprehensive bans are recommended. Smoke-free laws reduce exposure among non-smokers, encourage smokers to cut down or quit, and contribute to changing social norms. Studies in several countries have found reductions in hospital admissions for heart attacks after the introduction of comprehensive smoke-free legislation.

The third measure, Offer, involves offering help to quit tobacco use. Most smokers want to stop, but nicotine dependence makes quitting difficult. Effective cessation support includes brief advice from health professionals, telephone quit lines, behavioural counselling, and pharmacotherapy such as nicotine replacement therapy, varenicline, and bupropion. Integrating cessation advice into primary health care allows large numbers of tobacco users to be reached.

The fourth measure, Warn, involves warning about the dangers of tobacco through health warnings on packages and mass media campaigns. Large graphic pictorial warnings, showing the health consequences of tobacco use, are more noticeable and effective than text-only warnings, particularly for people with low literacy. The FCTC guidelines recommend that warnings cover at least half of the principal display areas of packs. Plain or standardized packaging, which removes logos, colours, and promotional design and requires a uniform plain colour, has been introduced in a growing number of countries to reduce the appeal of packs and increase the effectiveness of warnings. Mass media campaigns can increase knowledge of risks and motivate quitting.

The fifth measure, Enforce, involves enforcing bans on tobacco advertising, promotion, and sponsorship. Tobacco marketing attracts new users, especially young people, and normalizes tobacco use. Partial bans are relatively ineffective because the industry shifts spending to permitted channels, so comprehensive bans covering direct and indirect advertising, point-of-sale displays, sponsorship of events, and online and social media promotion are recommended.

The sixth measure, Raise, refers to raising taxes on tobacco. Tobacco taxation is considered the single most effective and cost-effective tobacco control measure. Higher taxes increase prices, which reduces consumption, prevents initiation, and encourages quitting. Young people and low-income groups are particularly responsive to price increases, so taxes can reduce health inequalities. Evidence from many countries indicates that a ten percent increase in price reduces tobacco consumption by around four percent in high-income countries and by a larger amount in low- and middle-income countries. Taxes also generate revenue that can be used for health programmes. For maximum effectiveness, tax increases should exceed inflation and income growth so that tobacco becomes less affordable, and tax structures should minimize the price gap between cheap and expensive products, which otherwise allows users to switch to cheaper brands.

Additional supply-side measures include combating illicit trade through tracking and tracing systems, licensing retailers, prohibiting sales to minors, and supporting tobacco farmers in shifting to alternative livelihoods. The FCTC also requires parties to protect public health policies from the commercial interests of the tobacco industry, recognizing that the industry has historically opposed and delayed effective control measures.

Tobacco control faces continuing challenges. The industry adapts to regulations through new products and marketing strategies. Electronic nicotine delivery systems, including e-cigarettes, and heated tobacco products raise complex regulatory questions about their potential role in helping smokers quit versus the risk of attracting young people to nicotine use. In countries with large informal markets, enforcing regulations on loose cigarettes, bidi, and smokeless products is difficult. Nevertheless, comprehensive implementation of MPOWER measures has contributed to substantial declines in smoking prevalence in many countries, demonstrating that policy can significantly reduce the burden of tobacco-related disease.

source_text:
Organizations increasingly rely on teams to carry out work, from project teams and product development groups to cross-functional task forces, self-managed work teams, and virtual teams spread across countries. Teams can combine diverse skills and perspectives, solve complex problems, and respond flexibly to change. However, simply placing people together does not create an effective team. Groups typically go through a process of development in which members get to know one another, establish relationships, clarify goals and roles, and learn how to work together. Understanding this process helps team leaders and members anticipate common challenges and take appropriate action. The most widely known model of team development was proposed by the psychologist Bruce Tuckman in 1965 and later extended.

Tuckman reviewed research on small groups and identified four stages that groups commonly pass through, which he called forming, storming, norming, and performing. In 1977, together with Mary Ann Jensen, he added a fifth stage, adjourning. Each stage is characterized by particular patterns of interpersonal relationships and task-related activity.

The forming stage occurs when a team first comes together. Members are often polite, cautious, and uncertain. They try to understand the purpose of the team, what is expected of them, and how they fit in. They may be enthusiastic about the new task but anxious about whether they will be accepted and whether they have the necessary skills. Members tend to depend on the leader for direction and guidance, and discussions may focus on defining the task, setting ground rules, and getting acquainted. Relatively little substantive work may be accomplished. Effective leadership at this stage involves providing clear direction, explaining the team's purpose and goals, clarifying roles, and helping members become familiar with one another.

The storming stage follows as members begin to express their individual opinions, challenge ideas, and compete for influence and status. Conflict may arise over goals, priorities, approaches to the task, allocation of roles and responsibilities, and leadership. Members may resist the constraints that the team places on their individuality or question the authority of the leader. This stage can be uncomfortable, and some teams become stuck in it, experiencing persistent conflict that prevents progress. However, storming is a normal and potentially productive part of team development, because it brings differences into the open and allows them to be addressed. Effective leaders help the team manage conflict constructively, encourage open communication and active listening, focus disagreements on issues rather than personalities, and reaffirm shared goals.

In the norming stage, the team begins to resolve its differences and develop cohesion. Members accept the team and one another, agree on roles and working methods, and establish norms, shared expectations about how members should behave, such as how decisions are made, how meetings are conducted, and how members communicate and support one another. A sense of team identity and commitment develops, and members begin to trust and cooperate with one another. The leader may take a more facilitative role, encouraging participation and shared responsibility. A potential risk at this stage is that the desire for harmony may discourage disagreement, which can lead to groupthink, a tendency to reach consensus without critically evaluating alternatives.

The performing stage is reached when the team functions effectively as a cohesive unit focused on achieving its goals. Members understand their roles, work interdependently, and handle disagreements constructively. The team can make decisions and solve problems with relatively little supervision, adapt to changing circumstances, and achieve high levels of productivity. Leaders at this stage typically delegate and support the team, focusing on removing obstacles, providing resources, and developing members. Not every team reaches this stage; some remain at norming, achieving adequate but not outstanding performance.

The adjourning stage, sometimes called mourning, occurs when a team completes its task and disbands, as with project teams and temporary task forces. Members may feel a sense of accomplishment, but also sadness or uncertainty as relationships end and they move on to new roles. Recognizing the team's achievements, evaluating what was learned, and providing closure help members make the transition.

Tuckman's model has several practical implications. It reminds leaders that conflict and uncertainty are normal in new teams and should be managed rather than avoided. It suggests that leadership style should adapt to the team's stage of development, providing more direction early and more delegation later, an idea consistent with situational leadership models. It also highlights the importance of investing time in establishing goals, roles, and norms, which can accelerate a team's progress to effective performance. Team-building activities, clear charters, and regular reflection on how the team is working can support development.

The model has limitations. It suggests a linear sequence, whereas real teams may move back and forth between stages; for example, a team that has reached performing may return to storming when new members join, goals change, or a crisis occurs. Stages may overlap, and their duration varies widely. The model was based largely on studies of therapy groups, training groups, and laboratory groups, and may not apply equally to all work teams. Alternative models have been proposed. Connie Gersick's punctuated equilibrium model, based on studies of project teams with deadlines, found that teams did not develop gradually through stages; instead, they followed an initial pattern of behaviour until roughly the midpoint of their allotted time, when they experienced a transition, often triggered by awareness of the deadline, and adopted a new pattern of work. Virtual and globally distributed teams may face additional challenges, such as building trust without face-to-face interaction and managing cultural differences. Despite these limitations, Tuckman's model remains a widely used and intuitive framework for understanding and supporting team development.

Groups typically go through a process of development in which members get to know one another, establish relationships, clarify goals and roles, and learn how to work together. Understanding this process helps team leaders and members anticipate common challenges and take appropriate action. The most widely known model of team development was proposed by the psychologist Bruce Tuckman in 1965 and later extended.

Tuckman reviewed research on small groups and identified four stages that groups commonly pass through, which he called forming, storming, norming, and performing. In 1977, together with Mary Ann Jensen, he added a fifth stage, adjourning. Each stage is characterized by particular patterns of interpersonal relationships and task-related activity.

The forming stage occurs when a team first comes together. Members are often polite, cautious, and uncertain. They try to understand the purpose of the team, what is expected of them, and how they fit in. They may be enthusiastic about the new task but anxious about whether they will be accepted and whether they have the necessary skills. Members tend to depend on the leader for direction and guidance, and discussions may focus on defining the task, setting ground rules, and getting acquainted. Relatively little substantive work may be accomplished. Effective leadership at this stage involves providing clear direction, explaining the team's purpose and goals, clarifying roles, and helping members become familiar with one another.

The storming stage follows as members begin to express their individual opinions, challenge ideas, and compete for influence and status. Conflict may arise over goals, priorities, approaches to the task, allocation of roles and responsibilities, and leadership. Members may resist the constraints that the team places on their individuality or question the authority of the leader. This stage can be uncomfortable, and some teams become stuck in it, experiencing persistent conflict that prevents progress. Effective leaders help the team manage conflict constructively, encourage open communication and active listening, focus disagreements on issues rather than personalities, and reaffirm shared goals.

In the norming stage, the team begins to resolve its differences and develop cohesion. Members accept the team and one another, agree on roles and working methods, and establish norms, shared expectations about how members should behave, such as how decisions are made, how meetings are conducted, and how members communicate and support one another. A sense of team identity and commitment develops, and members begin to trust and cooperate with one another. Members understand their roles, work interdependently, and handle disagreements constructively. source_text:
Before a new medicine can be approved for general use, it must be shown to be both effective and acceptably safe for its intended purpose. Laboratory studies and animal experiments provide essential preliminary information, but they cannot predict with certainty how a drug will behave in humans. Clinical trials are research studies in human volunteers designed to answer specific questions about new treatments. Drug development proceeds through a sequence of trial phases, each with different objectives, sizes, and designs, and the overall process typically takes many years and involves substantial cost. Only a small proportion of compounds that enter clinical testing ultimately receive approval.

Drug development begins long before human testing, with the discovery and preclinical stages. Researchers identify a biological target involved in disease, screen or design compounds that act on it, and optimize promising candidates. Preclinical studies in cell cultures and animals investigate pharmacological activity, pharmacokinetics, and toxicity, including effects on major organs, reproductive toxicity, genotoxicity, and, for long-term medicines, carcinogenicity. These studies help determine whether a compound is reasonably safe to test in humans and suggest a starting dose. Before clinical trials begin, the sponsor submits an application to the regulatory authority, such as an Investigational New Drug application in the United States, together with the preclinical data and the proposed trial protocol.

Phase I trials are the first studies of a new drug in humans. Their primary purpose is to assess safety and tolerability, to determine how the drug is absorbed, distributed, metabolized, and excreted, and to establish a safe dose range for further studies. Phase I trials usually involve a small number of participants, often twenty to around one hundred, and are frequently conducted in healthy volunteers. However, for drugs with significant expected toxicity, such as many cancer treatments, phase I trials are conducted in patients with the disease. Dose escalation designs are common: small groups of participants receive increasing doses, with careful monitoring, until the maximum tolerated dose is identified or adverse effects appear. Some development programmes include phase 0 or microdosing studies, in which very small doses are given to obtain early pharmacokinetic information.

Phase II trials evaluate whether the drug has the intended effect in patients with the target condition and continue to assess safety. They typically involve from about one hundred to several hundred patients. Phase II studies are often divided into phase IIa, which explores whether the drug shows biological activity and helps define the appropriate dose, and phase IIb, which investigates efficacy at selected doses in more detail. These trials may compare the drug with a placebo or with standard treatment and often use surrogate endpoints, such as reduction in blood pressure or tumour size, that can be measured relatively quickly. Many drugs fail at this stage because they do not show sufficient efficacy or because unexpected safety problems appear.

Phase III trials are large studies designed to confirm efficacy, monitor adverse effects, compare the new treatment with existing standard treatments or placebo, and collect the information needed to support regulatory approval and safe use. They often involve hundreds to several thousand patients, frequently at many centres in different countries, and may last several years. Phase III trials are usually randomized controlled trials, in which participants are allocated by chance to receive the investigational treatment or the comparator. Randomization helps ensure that the groups are similar in both known and unknown characteristics, so that differences in outcome can be attributed to the treatment. Blinding, in which participants and often investigators do not know which treatment each participant receives, reduces bias in the reporting and assessment of outcomes; a double-blind trial conceals the allocation from both. Phase III trials typically measure clinically important outcomes, such as survival, prevention of heart attacks, or symptom relief, and are designed with sufficient statistical power to detect meaningful differences. Usually, regulators require at least one, and often two, adequate and well-controlled phase III trials.

Following successful phase III trials, the sponsor submits a marketing authorization application, such as a New Drug Application in the United States or an application to the European Medicines Agency. In Bangladesh, the Directorate General of Drug Administration regulates the approval of medicines. Regulators review data on efficacy, safety, manufacturing quality, and labelling before deciding whether to approve the drug and under what conditions.

Phase IV studies, also called post-marketing studies or post-marketing surveillance, take place after approval. Clinical trials before approval involve limited numbers of patients for limited durations, and they often exclude certain groups, such as pregnant women, children, older people with multiple conditions, and patients taking many other medicines. Rare adverse effects, those occurring in perhaps one in ten thousand patients, and effects that appear only after long-term use may not be detected. Phase IV activities include pharmacovigilance systems that collect reports of suspected adverse drug reactions, observational studies of large populations, and additional trials to investigate new indications, long-term effects, or use in specific groups. Several drugs have been withdrawn from the market or restricted after post-marketing surveillance revealed serious risks.

Clinical trials must be conducted according to strict ethical and scientific standards. The Declaration of Helsinki, developed by the World Medical Association, sets out ethical principles for medical research involving humans, and Good Clinical Practice guidelines, harmonized internationally, specify standards for designing, conducting, recording, and reporting trials. Each trial must be reviewed and approved by an independent research ethics committee or institutional review board, which assesses whether the risks to participants are justified by the potential benefits and whether participants' rights are protected. Participants must give informed consent, voluntarily agreeing to take part after receiving clear information about the purpose, procedures, risks, and benefits of the study, and they may withdraw at any time. Independent data monitoring committees may review accumulating results and recommend stopping a trial early if clear benefit or harm emerges. Registration of trials in public registries before they begin and publication of results, whether positive or negative, help prevent selective reporting and improve transparency.

source_text:
Urbanization is the process by which an increasing proportion of a population comes to live in towns and cities. It is one of the most significant social transformations of the modern era. In 1950, less than one third of the world's population lived in urban areas; by the late 2000s, more than half did, and the United Nations projects that about two thirds of humanity will be urban by the middle of the twenty-first century. Urbanization involves not only the physical growth of cities but also profound changes in economic activity, family life, social relationships, and culture. Sociologists study how cities develop, how urban life differs from rural life, and what social problems and opportunities urbanization brings.

Urban growth results from three main processes: natural increase, when births exceed deaths among urban residents; rural-to-urban migration; and the reclassification of rural areas as urban as settlements expand. In many developing countries, migration is driven by push factors in rural areas, such as limited land, low agricultural incomes, unemployment, natural disasters, and river erosion, and by pull factors in cities, including employment opportunities, higher wages, education, health care, and the perceived attractions of urban life. In Bangladesh, the rapid growth of Dhaka has been closely linked to migration associated with the expansion of the garment industry and other urban employment, as well as displacement from areas affected by flooding and erosion.

Historically, urbanization in Europe and North America accompanied industrialization in the nineteenth century, as factories concentrated workers in cities. Many countries in Asia, Africa, and Latin America are now urbanizing more rapidly, and at lower levels of income, than Western countries did. This has produced megacities, urban areas with more than ten million inhabitants, such as Dhaka, Delhi, Lagos, and São Paulo. Rapid urban growth often outpaces the capacity of governments to provide housing, infrastructure, and services, resulting in informal settlements, sometimes called slums, where residents face insecure tenure, overcrowding, poor sanitation, and exposure to environmental hazards. At the same time, many urban residents earn their living in the informal economy, working as street vendors, rickshaw pullers, domestic workers, and casual labourers without formal contracts or social protection.

Early sociologists were deeply interested in how city life changed social relationships. Ferdinand Tönnies contrasted Gemeinschaft, or community, characterized by close personal ties, shared values, and kinship, typical of rural villages, with Gesellschaft, or society, characterized by impersonal, contractual, and instrumental relationships, typical of modern cities. Émile Durkheim distinguished mechanical solidarity, based on similarity in small traditional societies, from organic solidarity, based on interdependence among people performing specialized roles in complex urban societies. Georg Simmel, in his essay The Metropolis and Mental Life, argued that the constant stimulation of city life leads urban residents to develop a blasé attitude, a protective reserve and indifference that allows them to cope with crowds and rapid change, along with a calculating, money-oriented outlook but also greater individual freedom.

The Chicago School of sociology, which flourished in the early twentieth century, studied the city as a social laboratory. Louis Wirth's influential essay Urbanism as a Way of Life argued that the size, density, and heterogeneity of urban populations produce distinctive social patterns, including superficial and segmented relationships, weakened kinship ties, greater reliance on formal institutions, and higher tolerance of diversity. Ernest Burgess proposed the concentric zone model, in which cities grow outward in rings, with a central business district surrounded by a zone in transition containing poorer housing and immigrants, followed by working-class, middle-class, and commuter zones. Robert Park and others developed the human ecology approach, comparing processes in cities, such as competition for space, invasion, and succession of neighbourhoods by different groups, to processes in natural ecosystems.

Later research challenged the idea that cities inevitably destroy community. Herbert Gans, studying Italian-American residents of a Boston neighbourhood, described them as urban villagers who maintained strong family and neighbourhood ties within the city. Other researchers have shown that urban residents often maintain personal networks based on friendship, kinship, work, and shared interests, even if these networks are spread across the city rather than concentrated in a single neighbourhood. Migrants frequently rely on networks of relatives and people from their home districts to find housing and jobs, creating forms of community within cities.

Contemporary urban sociology also emphasises inequality and power. Political economy approaches, associated with scholars such as David Harvey and Manuel Castells, argue that urban development is shaped by capital investment, property markets, and state policies, which can produce segregation, displacement, and unequal access to resources. Gentrification, the process by which wealthier residents and investment move into lower-income neighbourhoods, can improve housing and services but also raise rents and displace existing residents. Residential segregation by income, ethnicity, or religion affects access to schools, jobs, and services. Studies of the global city examine how cities such as London, New York, and Tokyo function as command centres of the global economy, while also containing large low-wage service workforces.

Urbanization brings both opportunities and challenges. Cities concentrate economic activity, innovation, education, and cultural life, and urban residents generally have better access to health care, schooling, and employment than rural residents. Urbanization has been associated with declining fertility and expanding opportunities for women's employment. At the same time, cities face problems such as traffic congestion, air pollution, inadequate housing, crime, and vulnerability to climate-related hazards such as flooding and heat waves. Sustainable urban development seeks to address these issues through inclusive planning, affordable housing, public transport, environmental management, and the participation of residents in decisions that shape their cities.

source_text:
Room acoustics is the study of how sound behaves within enclosed spaces and how the design of those spaces affects what people hear. It is important for a wide range of buildings, including classrooms, lecture halls, concert halls, theatres, places of worship, offices, hospitals, and homes. Good acoustics allow speech to be understood clearly and music to sound rich and balanced, while poor acoustics can cause fatigue, reduced learning, communication errors, and discomfort. Architects and acoustic consultants therefore consider sound from the earliest stages of design, because changing the shape or materials of a completed room can be difficult and costly.

When a sound is produced in a room, it reaches the listener first by the direct path. Shortly afterwards, reflections from walls, ceiling, floor, and furniture arrive. Early reflections, which arrive within roughly fifty milliseconds for speech and eighty milliseconds for music, are perceived as reinforcing the direct sound and can improve loudness and clarity. Later reflections merge into reverberation, the persistence of sound in a room after the source has stopped, as sound energy continues to reflect between surfaces and gradually decays. A certain amount of reverberation gives a sense of fullness and spaciousness, particularly for music, but excessive reverberation causes successive sounds to overlap and blur, reducing speech intelligibility.

The most important single measure of a room's acoustics is reverberation time, commonly denoted RT60. It is defined as the time required for the sound pressure level to decay by sixty decibels after the sound source stops, which corresponds to a reduction in sound energy to one millionth of its original value. The appropriate reverberation time depends on the intended use of the room and its volume. Spaces for speech, such as classrooms and lecture rooms, require relatively short reverberation times, often around 0.4 to 0.8 seconds depending on size, so that syllables remain distinct. Concert halls for orchestral music typically aim for about 1.8 to 2.2 seconds, which gives warmth and blending of sound. Large churches may have reverberation times of several seconds, which suits certain choral and organ music but makes speech difficult to understand without careful design or electronic reinforcement.

Reverberation time can be estimated using the Sabine formula, developed by Wallace Clement Sabine around 1900 during his work on the acoustics of a lecture hall at Harvard University. The formula states that reverberation time is proportional to the volume of the room divided by its total sound absorption. In metric units, RT60 is approximately 0.161 times the room volume in cubic metres divided by the total absorption in square metre sabins. The total absorption is calculated by multiplying the area of each surface by its absorption coefficient and adding the results. The absorption coefficient is a number between zero and one representing the fraction of incident sound energy absorbed rather than reflected; a value of zero indicates perfect reflection and one indicates complete absorption. Absorption coefficients vary with frequency, so calculations are usually performed for several octave bands. The Sabine formula works well for rooms with moderate absorption that is evenly distributed; for highly absorptive rooms, alternative formulas such as the Eyring formula are more accurate.

Materials differ greatly in how they absorb sound. Hard, smooth, dense surfaces such as concrete, glass, ceramic tile, and plaster reflect most sound and have low absorption coefficients. Porous absorbers, such as mineral wool, acoustic foam, fibrous ceiling tiles, carpets, and heavy curtains, absorb sound by converting acoustic energy into heat through friction as air moves within their pores; they are most effective at middle and high frequencies, and their low-frequency absorption increases with thickness or with an air gap behind them. Panel or membrane absorbers, consisting of a thin panel mounted over an enclosed air space, absorb mainly low frequencies through vibration. Resonant absorbers, such as perforated panels backed by cavities, can be tuned to absorb particular frequency ranges. People and upholstered seats also contribute significant absorption, which is why the acoustics of an empty hall differ from those of a full one.

Room shape strongly influences the distribution of sound. Parallel hard surfaces can produce flutter echoes, rapid repeated reflections heard as a ringing or buzzing sound. Concave surfaces, such as domes and curved rear walls, can focus reflections into particular areas, creating hot spots of loud sound and dead spots elsewhere. Distinct echoes occur when a strong reflection arrives more than about fifty to one hundred milliseconds after the direct sound, which can happen in large rooms with highly reflective rear walls. Designers use techniques such as angling or splaying walls, adding diffusers that scatter sound in many directions, and placing absorbent materials on surfaces that produce problematic reflections. Reflectors above a stage or lecturer's position can direct useful early reflections towards the audience.

Background noise is another important consideration. Noise from ventilation systems, traffic, adjacent rooms, and equipment can mask speech. The signal-to-noise ratio, the difference between the level of the desired sound and the background noise, is a key factor in speech intelligibility, and recommendations for classrooms often call for speech to be at least fifteen decibels louder than background noise. Background noise is controlled through sound insulation of the building envelope and partitions, quiet mechanical systems, and careful siting of noisy spaces.

In practice, acoustic design balances the needs of different users and activities. Multipurpose halls may use adjustable elements, such as movable panels or retractable curtains, to vary reverberation time. Open-plan offices require absorption and screening to limit the spread of conversation, while hospitals require quiet environments to support patient rest. Field measurements of reverberation time and speech intelligibility indices are used to verify that completed rooms meet their design objectives.

Lecture material:
Room acoustics is the study of how sound behaves within enclosed spaces and how the design of those spaces affects what people hear. It is important for a wide range of buildings, including classrooms, lecture halls, concert halls, theatres, places of worship, offices, hospitals, and homes. Good acoustics allow speech to be understood clearly and music to sound rich and balanced, while poor acoustics can cause fatigue, reduced learning, communication errors, and discomfort. Architects and acoustic consultants therefore consider sound from the earliest stages of design, because changing the shape or materials of a completed room can be difficult and costly.

When a sound is produced in a room, it reaches the listener first by the direct path. Shortly afterwards, reflections from walls, ceiling, floor, and furniture arrive. Early reflections, which arrive within roughly fifty milliseconds for speech and eighty milliseconds for music, are perceived as reinforcing the direct sound and can improve loudness and clarity. Later reflections merge into reverberation, the persistence of sound in a room after the source has stopped, as sound energy continues to reflect between surfaces and gradually decays. A certain amount of reverberation gives a sense of fullness and spaciousness, particularly for music, but excessive reverberation causes successive sounds to overlap and blur, reducing speech intelligibility.

The most important single measure of a room's acoustics is reverberation time, commonly denoted RT60. It is defined as the time required for the sound pressure level to decay by sixty decibels after the sound source stops, which corresponds to a reduction in sound energy to one millionth of its original value. The appropriate reverberation time depends on the intended use of the room and its volume. Spaces for speech, such as classrooms and lecture rooms, require relatively short reverberation times, often around 0.4 to 0.8 seconds depending on size, so that syllables remain distinct. Concert halls for orchestral music typically aim for about 1.8 to 2.2 seconds, which gives warmth and blending of sound. Large churches may have reverberation times of several seconds, which suits certain choral and organ music but makes speech difficult to understand without careful design or electronic reinforcement.

Reverberation time can be estimated using the Sabine formula, developed by Wallace Clement Sabine around 1900 during his work on the acoustics of a lecture hall at Harvard University. The formula states that reverberation time is proportional to the volume of the room divided by its total sound absorption. In metric units, RT60 is approximately 0.161 times the room volume in cubic metres divided by the total absorption in square metre sabins. The total absorption is calculated by multiplying the area of each surface by its absorption coefficient and adding the results. The absorption coefficient is a number between zero and one representing the fraction of incident sound energy absorbed rather than reflected; a value of zero indicates perfect reflection and one indicates complete absorption. Absorption coefficients vary with frequency, so calculations are usually performed for several octave bands. The Sabine formula works well for rooms with moderate absorption that is evenly distributed; for highly absorptive rooms, alternative formulas such as the Eyring formula are more accurate.

Materials differ greatly in how they absorb sound. Hard, smooth, dense surfaces such as concrete, glass, ceramic tile, and plaster reflect most sound and have low absorption coefficients. Porous absorbers, such as mineral wool, acoustic foam, fibrous ceiling tiles, carpets, and heavy curtains, absorb sound by converting acoustic energy into heat through friction as air moves within their pores; they are most effective at middle and high frequencies, and their low-frequency absorption increases with thickness or with an air gap behind them. Panel or membrane absorbers, consisting of a thin panel mounted over an enclosed air space, absorb mainly low frequencies through vibration. Resonant absorbers, such as perforated panels backed by cavities, can be tuned to absorb particular frequency ranges. People and upholstered seats also contribute significant absorption, which is why the acoustics of an empty hall differ from those of a full one.

Room shape strongly influences the distribution of sound. Parallel hard surfaces can produce flutter echoes, rapid repeated reflections heard as a ringing or buzzing sound. Concave surfaces, such as domes and curved rear walls, can focus reflections into particular areas, creating hot spots of loud sound and dead spots elsewhere. Distinct echoes occur when a strong reflection arrives more than about fifty to one hundred milliseconds after the direct sound, which can happen in large rooms with highly reflective rear walls. Designers use techniques such as angling or splaying walls, adding diffusers that scatter sound in many directions, and placing absorbent materials on surfaces that produce problematic reflections. Reflectors above a stage or lecturer's position can direct useful early reflections towards the audience.

Background noise is another important consideration. Noise from ventilation systems, traffic, adjacent rooms, and equipment can mask speech. The signal-to-noise ratio, the difference between the level of the desired sound and the background noise, is a key factor in speech intelligibility, and recommendations for classrooms often call for speech to be at least fifteen decibels louder than background noise. Background noise is controlled through sound insulation of the building envelope and partitions, quiet mechanical systems, and careful siting of noisy spaces.

In practice, acoustic design balances the needs of different users and activities. Multipurpose halls may use adjustable elements, such as movable panels or retractable curtains, to vary reverberation time. Open-plan offices require absorption and screening to limit the spread of conversation, while hospitals require quiet environments to support patient rest. Field measurements of reverberation time and speech intelligibility indices are used to verify that completed rooms meet their design objectives.<|im_end|>

source_text:
When people look for information, products, or services online, they usually begin with a search engine. Search engines answer billions of queries each day by ranking web pages according to how relevant and useful they appear to be. Because users rarely look beyond the first page of results, and most clicks go to the first few listings, appearing prominently in search results can bring substantial traffic to a website. Search engine optimization, SEO, is the practice of improving a website and its content so that it ranks higher in the unpaid, or organic, search results. It differs from search engine advertising, in which businesses pay to display sponsored listings; SEO and paid search are often combined under the broader term search engine marketing.

To understand SEO, it is useful to know how search engines work. First, automated programs called crawlers or spiders discover web pages by following links from page to page and reading sitemaps submitted by website owners. Second, the search engine indexes the pages it finds, analysing their content, structure, and other signals and storing information about them in a large database. Third, when a user enters a query, ranking algorithms evaluate indexed pages and order them according to hundreds of factors intended to identify the most relevant and trustworthy results. Search engines keep the exact details of their algorithms confidential and update them frequently, partly to improve results and partly to prevent manipulation.

SEO activities are commonly divided into technical SEO, on-page SEO, and off-page SEO. Technical SEO ensures that search engines can crawl and index a website efficiently and that the site provides a good user experience. It includes creating a clear site structure and internal linking, submitting an XML sitemap, using a robots.txt file to guide crawlers, avoiding broken links and duplicate content, and using canonical tags to indicate the preferred version of similar pages. Page loading speed is important, because slow pages frustrate users; search engines have incorporated measures of loading performance, interactivity, and visual stability into their assessments. Mobile-friendliness is essential, since a large share of searches occur on smartphones, and search engines increasingly evaluate the mobile version of a site first. Secure connections using HTTPS are also considered a positive signal. Structured data, written in standardized formats, helps search engines understand content such as products, events, reviews, and recipes and may enable enhanced displays called rich results.

On-page SEO concerns the content and elements of individual pages. It begins with keyword research, the process of identifying the words and phrases that potential customers use when searching. Marketers analyse search volume, competition, and the intent behind queries. Search intent can be informational, when users seek knowledge; navigational, when they want a specific website; commercial, when they compare options; or transactional, when they intend to buy. Content should match the intent behind the target keywords. Short, general keywords often have high search volume but intense competition, while longer, more specific phrases, called long-tail keywords, typically have lower volume but clearer intent and higher conversion rates.

Important on-page elements include the title tag, which appears as the clickable headline in search results and should accurately describe the page and include relevant keywords; the meta description, a short summary that may appear below the title and influences whether users click; headings that structure content logically; descriptive URLs; and alternative text for images, which helps both search engines and visually impaired users understand image content. Above all, content quality is central. Search engines aim to reward content that is original, comprehensive, accurate, and useful to readers. Search engine guidelines emphasise experience, expertise, authoritativeness, and trustworthiness, particularly for topics that may affect health, finances, or safety. Practices such as keyword stuffing, the excessive and unnatural repetition of keywords, are penalized rather than rewarded.

Off-page SEO refers to signals outside the website itself, most importantly backlinks, links from other websites to the site. Search engines have long treated backlinks as indications that other sites consider the content valuable, an idea central to Google's original PageRank algorithm, which evaluated pages partly according to the number and quality of links pointing to them. Links from reputable, relevant websites carry more weight than many links from low-quality sources. Marketers earn backlinks through creating valuable content that others want to reference, digital public relations, partnerships, and guest contributions. Attempting to manipulate rankings by buying links or participating in link schemes violates search engine guidelines and can lead to penalties. Brand mentions, social media activity, and online reviews may also influence visibility indirectly.

For businesses serving specific geographic areas, local SEO is important. It involves creating and maintaining business profiles on search engines' local listing services with accurate names, addresses, phone numbers, and opening hours, encouraging customer reviews, and ensuring consistent information across online directories. Local SEO helps businesses appear in map results and local searches such as those including near me.

SEO practices are often described as white-hat, which follow search engine guidelines and focus on providing value to users, or black-hat, which attempt to deceive search engines through tactics such as hidden text, cloaking, in which different content is shown to search engines and users, and automated spam. Black-hat techniques may produce short-term gains but risk severe penalties, including removal from search results.

Measuring SEO performance requires analytics. Common metrics include organic traffic, keyword rankings, click-through rates from search results, bounce rates, time on page, conversions, and the number and quality of backlinks. Tools provided by search engines show how pages appear in search, which queries bring visitors, and whether technical problems exist. SEO is a long-term investment; results often take months to appear, and rankings can change as competitors improve their sites and algorithms evolve. The growth of voice search and search engines that generate direct answers using artificial intelligence is further changing how users interact with search results, encouraging marketers to focus on clear, authoritative content that answers users' questions directly.

source_text:
Gears are toothed wheels that transmit motion and power between rotating shafts. They are found in vehicle gearboxes, wind turbines, machine tools, clocks, and countless other machines. Compared with belts and chains, gears provide a positive drive without slip, can transmit large torques in a compact space, and maintain an exact speed ratio. Their design requires an understanding of tooth geometry, the kinematics of meshing gears, and the arrangement of gears in trains.

Gears are classified according to the relative position of their shafts. Spur gears have straight teeth parallel to the axis of rotation and connect parallel shafts; they are simple and efficient but can be noisy at high speeds because each tooth engages suddenly across its full width. Helical gears also connect parallel shafts, but their teeth are cut at an angle to the axis, so engagement begins at one end of the tooth and spreads gradually, producing smoother and quieter operation. The inclined teeth, however, generate an axial thrust that must be carried by the bearings; double helical or herringbone gears cancel this thrust. Bevel gears connect intersecting shafts, usually at right angles, and worm gears connect non-intersecting perpendicular shafts, providing large speed reductions in a single stage, though with lower efficiency because of sliding between the worm and wheel.

Several geometric terms describe gear teeth. The pitch circle is an imaginary circle on which two meshing gears roll without slipping, and its diameter is the pitch diameter. The circular pitch is the distance between corresponding points on adjacent teeth measured along the pitch circle. In metric practice, tooth size is expressed by the module, equal to the pitch diameter divided by the number of teeth, while in the inch system the diametral pitch, the number of teeth per inch of pitch diameter, is used. Two gears can mesh correctly only if they have the same module. The addendum is the radial height of a tooth above the pitch circle, and the dedendum is the depth below it; the dedendum is slightly larger than the addendum to provide clearance at the root.

Correct meshing requires that the gears maintain a constant angular velocity ratio throughout engagement. This requirement is expressed by the fundamental law of gearing, which states that the common normal to the tooth profiles at the point of contact must always pass through a fixed point on the line joining the centres, called the pitch point. Profiles that satisfy this law are called conjugate. The involute curve, traced by the end of a taut string unwound from a circle called the base circle, is used for almost all modern gears. Involute teeth have the important advantage that small changes in centre distance, caused by manufacturing tolerances or bearing wear, do not affect the velocity ratio. The angle between the line of action and the tangent to the pitch circles is the pressure angle, commonly 20 degrees in modern standards.

For a pair of gears, the speed ratio is inversely proportional to the numbers of teeth. If a driving pinion with 20 teeth meshes with a driven gear with 60 teeth, the gear rotates at one third of the pinion speed, and, neglecting losses, the torque on the output shaft is three times the input torque, since power is the product of torque and angular speed. The two gears rotate in opposite directions. The contact ratio, the average number of tooth pairs in contact, should exceed one, typically 1.4 to 1.8, so that a new pair of teeth begins to engage before the previous pair separates, ensuring smooth transmission.

Interference is a geometric problem that occurs when the tip of a tooth on one gear contacts the non-involute portion of the mating tooth below the base circle. It can cause undercutting during manufacture, which weakens the tooth root. Interference is more likely when a pinion has very few teeth. For standard 20-degree full-depth teeth, the minimum number of teeth on a pinion to avoid undercutting when meshing with a rack is about 17. Profile shifting, in which the cutting tool is displaced during manufacture, can allow fewer teeth.

Gear trains combine several gears to achieve large speed ratios, change direction, or connect distant shafts. In a simple gear train, each shaft carries one gear, and the overall ratio depends only on the first and last gears; intermediate idler gears change the direction of rotation without changing the ratio. In a compound gear train, some shafts carry two gears rigidly connected, so the overall ratio equals the product of the ratios of each meshing pair, allowing large reductions in a compact arrangement. A reverted gear train is a compound train in which the input and output shafts are coaxial, as in some vehicle gearboxes.

Epicyclic or planetary gear trains contain gears whose axes move. A typical arrangement includes a central sun gear, several planet gears that mesh with the sun and rotate on a carrier, and an outer ring gear with internal teeth. By holding one of the three members stationary and driving another, different speed ratios are obtained. Planetary trains offer high torque capacity, compact size, and coaxial shafts, which is why they are used in automatic transmissions, hybrid vehicle drives, and wind turbine gearboxes. Their speed ratios are analysed using relative motion, for example with the tabular method or the Willis equation.

Gear design must also consider strength and durability. Teeth may fail by bending fatigue at the root, by surface fatigue such as pitting caused by repeated contact stresses, or by wear and scoring when lubrication is inadequate. The Lewis equation provides a basic estimate of bending stress, and contact stress is evaluated using Hertzian contact theory, both modified by factors for dynamic loading, misalignment, and material properties in standards such as those of the American Gear Manufacturers Association and ISO.

Compared with belts and chains, gears provide a positive drive without slip, can transmit large torques in a compact space, and maintain an exact speed ratio. Their design requires an understanding of tooth geometry, the kinematics of meshing gears, and the arrangement of gears in trains.

Gears are classified according to the relative position of their shafts. Spur gears have straight teeth parallel to the axis of rotation and connect parallel shafts; they are simple and efficient but can be noisy at high speeds because each tooth engages suddenly across its full width. source_text:
A text is more than a sequence of grammatical sentences. When we read a well-written paragraph or listen to a clear explanation, we experience it as a unified whole in which ideas connect logically and each sentence builds on what came before. Linguists use two related concepts to describe what makes a stretch of language function as a text: cohesion and coherence. Understanding these concepts is important in discourse analysis, writing instruction, translation, second language teaching, and the evaluation of student writing.

Cohesion refers to the explicit linguistic links that connect sentences and parts of a text. It is visible in the surface form of the language, through words and grammatical structures that point to other parts of the text. The most influential account of cohesion was presented by Michael Halliday and Ruqaiya Hasan in their 1976 book Cohesion in English. They identified five main types of cohesive devices: reference, substitution, ellipsis, conjunction, and lexical cohesion. The first four are grammatical forms of cohesion, while the fifth is lexical.

Reference occurs when an item in the text cannot be interpreted on its own but refers to something else for its meaning. Personal pronouns such as he, she, it, and they, demonstratives such as this, that, these, and those, and comparatives such as same, similar, and other are common reference items. In the sentences The committee reviewed the proposal. It was approved unanimously, the pronoun it refers back to the proposal. Reference that points back to something mentioned earlier is called anaphoric, while reference that points forward to something mentioned later is cataphoric, as in Here is the news: the election has been postponed. Reference to something outside the text, in the immediate situation, is called exophoric, as when a speaker points and says Look at that.

Substitution replaces one item with another word that functions as a placeholder, such as one, do, or so. In My laptop is old; I need a new one, the word one substitutes for laptop. In Did she finish the report? I think so, so substitutes for the clause that she finished the report. Ellipsis is the omission of an item that can be recovered from the context, sometimes described as substitution by zero. In Some students prefer morning classes; others, afternoon classes, the verb prefer is omitted in the second clause but understood. Ellipsis is common in conversation, as in answers such as Yes, I have, meaning Yes, I have finished.

Conjunction uses connecting words and phrases to signal logical relationships between sentences or clauses. Halliday and Hasan grouped these into additive relations, using items such as and, also, furthermore, and in addition; adversative relations, expressing contrast or concession, using but, however, although, and nevertheless; causal relations, using because, so, therefore, and as a result; and temporal relations, expressing sequence in time, using then, next, finally, and meanwhile. These connectives guide readers through the logical structure of an argument or narrative.

Lexical cohesion is achieved through the choice of vocabulary. Reiteration includes repeating the same word, using a synonym or near-synonym, using a superordinate term, or using a general word. A text might mention a dog, later refer to the animal, and later to the creature. Collocation refers to the tendency of words that are associated in meaning to occur in the same text, creating a network of related vocabulary; a text about a hospital might contain doctor, nurse, patient, ward, and surgery. These lexical chains help readers recognize that sentences are about the same topic.

Coherence, by contrast, refers to the underlying logical and conceptual connectedness that makes a text meaningful and sensible to readers. It concerns the relationships among ideas, the overall structure of the text, and whether the text makes sense in relation to the reader's background knowledge and the communicative situation. A text can contain many cohesive devices yet still be incoherent, as in a series of sentences linked by repeated words and connectives but jumping between unrelated ideas. Conversely, a text may have few explicit cohesive markers but still be coherent because readers can infer the connections. In the exchange A: The phone is ringing. B: I'm in the shower, there is no explicit cohesive link, but listeners understand that B is explaining why they cannot answer the phone, drawing on shared knowledge and pragmatic inference.

Several factors contribute to coherence. A clear overall organization, such as an introduction, development, and conclusion, or a problem-solution pattern, helps readers follow the text. Information structure also matters: English texts typically present given information, already known to the reader, before new information, and the theme of a sentence, its starting point, often links to what came before. Topic sentences in paragraphs help indicate the main idea, and the logical sequencing of ideas, whether chronological, spatial, or argumentative, supports understanding. Schema theory explains that readers interpret texts by drawing on organized knowledge structures about the world; a text about a visit to a restaurant can omit many details because readers know the typical sequence of events.

Cohesion and coherence have practical importance in language teaching. Second language learners may overuse some connectives, such as moreover, use them incorrectly, or rely heavily on repetition, producing writing that feels mechanical. Teaching students to use a range of cohesive devices appropriately, to organize paragraphs around clear main ideas, and to consider the reader's knowledge can improve the quality of their writing. Writing assessment rubrics, including those used in international English tests, often include criteria for coherence and cohesion. In translation, preserving cohesion can be challenging because languages differ in how they use reference, ellipsis, and connectives; for example, languages such as Bengali may omit subject pronouns where English requires them, so translators must make different choices to maintain clarity in the target language.

source_text:
A digital filter is a system that processes a sequence of discrete-time samples to modify the signal in some desired way, typically by passing certain frequency components and attenuating others. Digital filters are used to remove noise from biomedical signals, separate frequency bands in communication receivers, shape audio in music systems, and smooth sensor measurements in control systems. Compared with analogue filters built from resistors, capacitors, and inductors, digital filters offer precise and repeatable behaviour, are not affected by component tolerances or temperature drift, and can be reprogrammed easily in software or on digital hardware.

A linear time-invariant digital filter is described by a difference equation that relates the current output sample to current and past input samples and, in some cases, to past output samples. Its behaviour can also be characterized by its impulse response, the output produced when the input is a single unit impulse, and by its transfer function in the z-domain, H of z, obtained using the z-transform. Evaluating the transfer function on the unit circle gives the frequency response, which describes how the filter changes the amplitude and phase of sinusoidal components at each frequency.

Filters are classified by the shape of their frequency response. Low-pass filters pass low frequencies and attenuate high frequencies, high-pass filters do the reverse, band-pass filters pass a range of frequencies, and band-stop or notch filters reject a particular band, for example 50-hertz power-line interference in an electrocardiogram. A practical specification defines a passband, in which the gain should remain within a tolerance of one, a stopband, in which the gain should be below a specified attenuation, and a transition band between them. Narrower transition bands and greater stopband attenuation require more complex filters.

The two fundamental classes of digital filters are finite impulse response, FIR, and infinite impulse response, IIR, filters. An FIR filter computes each output as a weighted sum of the current and a finite number of past input samples. Its difference equation contains no feedback from previous outputs, so its impulse response lasts for only a finite number of samples, equal to the number of coefficients, or taps. In the z-domain, the transfer function of an FIR filter is a polynomial, which means it has zeros but no poles other than at the origin.

FIR filters have several important advantages. Because there is no feedback, they are always stable. They can be designed to have exactly linear phase by making their coefficients symmetric or antisymmetric about the centre. Linear phase means that all frequency components are delayed by the same amount of time, so the shape of the signal within the passband is preserved; this property is valuable in applications such as data communications, image processing, and biomedical signal analysis, where waveform distortion must be avoided. FIR filters are also relatively robust to the effects of finite-precision arithmetic. Common design methods include the window method, in which the ideal infinite impulse response is truncated and multiplied by a window function such as the Hamming or Kaiser window to control ripple; frequency sampling; and optimal equiripple design using the Parks-McClellan algorithm, which minimizes the maximum error in the passband and stopband.

The main disadvantage of FIR filters is that achieving a sharp transition between passband and stopband may require a large number of taps, which increases the computational load and introduces a larger delay. For a symmetric FIR filter with N taps, the delay is about half of N samples.

An IIR filter uses feedback: each output depends on current and past inputs and on past outputs. Because of this recursion, its impulse response can, in principle, continue indefinitely. Its transfer function is a ratio of polynomials, giving it both poles and zeros. The poles allow an IIR filter to achieve a sharp frequency response with far fewer coefficients than an FIR filter meeting the same magnitude specification, so IIR filters require less computation and memory and have shorter delays.

IIR filters are commonly designed by transforming well-established analogue filter prototypes into the digital domain. Butterworth filters have a maximally flat passband with no ripple, Chebyshev filters provide a sharper transition at the cost of ripple in the passband or stopband, and elliptic filters give the sharpest transition for a given order, with ripple in both bands. The bilinear transform is widely used to map an analogue prototype into a digital filter; it avoids aliasing but compresses the frequency axis nonlinearly, so critical frequencies are pre-warped before the transformation. Another method, impulse invariance, preserves the shape of the impulse response but can suffer from aliasing and is unsuitable for high-pass designs.

IIR filters have important limitations. They can become unstable: a causal IIR filter is stable only if all its poles lie strictly inside the unit circle in the z-plane, and rounding of coefficients in fixed-point implementations can move poles outward. Their phase response is generally nonlinear, which distorts waveforms, although this matters less in applications such as audio equalization, where the ear is relatively insensitive to phase. Feedback also makes them more sensitive to quantization effects, including limit cycles, small sustained oscillations caused by rounding. To reduce these problems, high-order IIR filters are usually implemented as cascades of second-order sections, often called biquads.

The choice between FIR and IIR filters therefore involves trade-offs. FIR filters are preferred when linear phase, guaranteed stability, and robustness are essential and sufficient computational resources are available. IIR filters are preferred when efficiency, low delay, and sharp selectivity are priorities and phase distortion is acceptable. Software tools such as MATLAB and Python's signal processing libraries support both design approaches and allow engineers to verify frequency responses, stability, and quantization effects before implementation.

Digital filters are used to remove noise from biomedical signals, separate frequency bands in communication receivers, shape audio in music systems, and smooth sensor measurements in control systems. Compared with analogue filters built from resistors, capacitors, and inductors, digital filters offer precise and repeatable behaviour, are not affected by component tolerances or temperature drift, and can be reprogrammed easily in software or on digital hardware.

A linear time-invariant digital filter is described by a difference equation that relates the current output sample to current and past input samples and, in some cases, to past output samples. Its behaviour can also be characterized by its impulse response, the output produced when the input is a single unit impulse, and by its transfer function in the z-domain, H of z, obtained using the z-transform. Evaluating the transfer function on the unit circle gives the frequency response, which describes how the filter changes the amplitude and phase of sinusoidal components at each frequency.

Filters are classified by the shape of their frequency response. Low-pass filters pass low frequencies and attenuate high frequencies, high-pass filters do the reverse, band-pass filters pass a range of frequencies, and band-stop or notch filters reject a particular band, for example 50-hertz power-line interference in an electrocardiogram. A practical specification defines a passband, in which the gain should remain within a tolerance of one, a stopband, in which the gain should be below a specified attenuation, and a transition band between them. Narrower transition bands and greater stopband attenuation require more complex filters.

The two fundamental classes of digital filters are finite impulse response, FIR, and infinite impulse response, IIR, filters. An FIR filter computes each output as a weighted sum of the current and a finite number of past input samples. Its difference equation contains no feedback from previous outputs, so its impulse response lasts for only a finite number of samples, equal to the number of coefficients, or taps. In the z-domain, the transfer function of an FIR filter is a polynomial, which means it has zeros but no poles other than at the origin.

FIR filters have several important advantages. Because there is no feedback, they are always stable. They can be designed to have exactly linear phase by making their coefficients symmetric or antisymmetric about the centre. Linear phase means that all frequency components are delayed by the same amount of time, so the shape of the signal within the passband is preserved; this property is valuable in applications such as data communications, image processing, and biomedical signal analysis, where waveform distortion must be avoided. FIR filters are also relatively robust to the effects of finite-precision arithmetic. Common design methods include the window method, in which the ideal infinite impulse response is truncated and multiplied by a window function such as the Hamming or Kaiser window to control ripple; frequency sampling; and optimal equiripple design using the Parks-McClellan algorithm, which minimizes the maximum error in the passband and stopband.

The main disadvantage of FIR filters is that achieving a sharp transition between passband and stopband may require a large number of taps, which increases the computational load and introduces a larger delay. For a symmetric FIR filter with N taps, the delay is about half of N samples.

An IIR filter uses feedback: each output depends on current and past inputs and on past outputs. Because of this recursion, its impulse response can, in principle, continue indefinitely. Its transfer function is a ratio of polynomials, giving it both poles and zeros. The poles allow an IIR filter to achieve a sharp frequency response with far fewer coefficients than an FIR filter meeting the same magnitude specification, so IIR filters require less computation and memory and have shorter delays.

IIR filters are commonly designed by transforming well-established analogue filter prototypes into the digital domain. Butterworth filters have a maximally flat passband with no ripple, Chebyshev filters provide a sharper transition at the cost of ripple in the passband or stopband, and elliptic filters give the sharpest transition for a given order, with ripple in both bands. The bilinear transform is widely used to map an analogue prototype into a digital filter; it avoids aliasing but compresses the frequency axis nonlinearly, so critical frequencies are pre-warped before the transformation. Another method, impulse invariance, preserves the shape of the impulse response but can suffer from aliasing and is unsuitable for high-pass designs.

IIR filters have important limitations. They can become unstable: a causal IIR filter is stable only if all its poles lie strictly inside the unit circle in the z-plane, and rounding of coefficients in fixed-point implementations can move poles outward. Their phase response is generally nonlinear, which distorts waveforms, although this matters less in applications such as audio equalization, where the ear is relatively insensitive to phase. Feedback also makes them more sensitive to quantization effects, including limit cycles, small sustained oscillations caused by rounding. To reduce these problems, high-order IIR filters are usually implemented as cascades of second-order sections, often called biquads.

The choice between FIR and IIR filters therefore involves trade-offs. FIR filters are preferred when linear phase, guaranteed stability, and robustness are essential and sufficient computational resources are available. IIR filters are preferred when efficiency, low delay, and sharp selectivity are priorities and phase distortion is acceptable. Software tools such as MATLAB and Python's signal processing libraries support both design approaches and allow engineers to verify frequency responses, stability, and quantization effects before implementation.<|im_end|>

Oscillations are repetitive motions about an equilibrium position, and they occur throughout nature and technology. Examples include a mass bouncing on a spring, a pendulum swinging, the vibration of a guitar string, the motion of atoms in a crystal lattice, the alternating current in an electrical circuit, and the swaying of tall buildings in the wind. The simplest and most important type of oscillation is simple harmonic motion, SHM. Many more complex vibrations can be understood as combinations of simple harmonic motions, and many oscillating systems behave approximately harmonically when the oscillations are small.

Simple harmonic motion occurs when a body experiences a restoring force that is directly proportional to its displacement from equilibrium and directed towards the equilibrium position. For a mass attached to an ideal spring on a frictionless surface, Hooke's law states that the spring force equals minus k times x, where x is the displacement and k is the spring constant, a measure of stiffness. The minus sign indicates that the force always acts opposite to the displacement, pulling the mass back towards equilibrium. Applying Newton's second law gives the equation of motion: mass times acceleration equals minus k times x, so the acceleration is proportional to the displacement and opposite in direction. Any system whose acceleration satisfies this relationship, with acceleration equal to minus omega squared times displacement, undergoes simple harmonic motion, where omega is a constant called the angular frequency.

The solution of this equation shows that the displacement varies sinusoidally with time. It can be written as x of t equals A times the cosine of omega t plus phi. The amplitude, A, is the maximum displacement from equilibrium. The angular frequency, omega, is measured in radians per second and is related to the frequency, f, by omega equals two pi f, and to the period, T, the time for one complete oscillation, by T equals two pi divided by omega. The phase constant, phi, depends on the initial position and velocity of the body and determines where in the cycle the motion begins. For the mass-spring system, the angular frequency equals the square root of k divided by m, so the period equals two pi times the square root of m divided by k. A stiffer spring produces faster oscillations, while a larger mass produces slower ones. An important feature of simple harmonic motion is that the period does not depend on the amplitude: small and large oscillations take the same time, provided the restoring force remains proportional to displacement. Such oscillations are called isochronous.

Velocity and acceleration in SHM also vary sinusoidally. The velocity is greatest when the body passes through the equilibrium position and zero at the extreme positions, where the body momentarily stops and reverses direction. The maximum speed equals omega times A. The acceleration is zero at equilibrium, where the net force is zero, and greatest in magnitude at the extreme positions, where the restoring force is largest; its maximum magnitude is omega squared times A. Velocity leads displacement by a quarter of a cycle, and acceleration is exactly opposite in phase to displacement.

Energy is continually exchanged between kinetic and potential forms during simple harmonic motion. For a mass-spring system, the elastic potential energy stored in the spring is one half k x squared, and the kinetic energy of the mass is one half m v squared. At the extreme positions, all the energy is potential; at the equilibrium position, all of it is kinetic. In the absence of friction, the total mechanical energy remains constant and equals one half k A squared, so it is proportional to the square of the amplitude. Doubling the amplitude therefore quadruples the energy of oscillation.

The simple pendulum provides another important example. It consists of a small mass, or bob, suspended from a fixed point by a light, inextensible string of length L. When displaced and released, the bob swings under the influence of gravity. The restoring force is the component of the weight along the arc, which equals minus m g times the sine of the angular displacement. This force is not exactly proportional to displacement, so the motion is not exactly simple harmonic. However, for small angles, typically less than about ten to fifteen degrees, the sine of the angle is approximately equal to the angle in radians, and the motion becomes approximately simple harmonic. The period is then two pi times the square root of L divided by g, independent of the mass of the bob and approximately independent of amplitude. This relationship has been used to measure the acceleration due to gravity and formed the basis of pendulum clocks. For larger amplitudes, the period increases slightly.

Real oscillating systems lose energy because of friction, air resistance, and internal damping, so their amplitude gradually decreases. This is called damped harmonic motion. In light damping, the system oscillates with an amplitude that decays exponentially over time. In critical damping, the system returns to equilibrium in the shortest possible time without oscillating; this is desirable in devices such as car suspension systems and the needles of measuring instruments. In heavy damping, or overdamping, the system returns to equilibrium slowly without oscillating.

When a periodic external force drives an oscillating system, the system undergoes forced oscillations at the frequency of the driving force. If the driving frequency approaches the natural frequency of the system, the amplitude can become very large, a phenomenon called resonance. The sharpness and height of the resonance peak depend on damping; lightly damped systems show high, narrow peaks. Resonance is exploited in musical instruments, radio tuning circuits, and magnetic resonance imaging, but it can also be destructive, as when vibrations from machinery, wind, or earthquakes match the natural frequencies of structures. Engineers therefore design structures and machines to avoid dangerous resonances or to provide sufficient damping.

At the extreme positions, all the energy is potential; at the equilibrium position, all of it is kinetic. This force is not exactly proportional to displacement, so the motion is not exactly simple harmonic.
