Raw cotton fabric coming from the loom or knitting machine, often called greige or grey fabric, is not ready for use. It contains natural impurities such as waxes, pectins, and coloured matter, as well as sizing agents added to strengthen warp yarns during weaving. The fabric also has properties that may not suit its intended end use, such as limited lustre, a tendency to shrink and wrinkle, and harsh handle. Chemical processing converts greige fabric into a finished product through preparatory treatments, colouration, and finishing. Among these processes, mercerization is one of the most important for cotton because it improves lustre, strength, dye uptake, and dimensional stability.

Preparatory processes come first. Desizing removes the size, usually starch or synthetic polymers such as polyvinyl alcohol, applied to warp yarns before weaving. Starch sizes are commonly removed by enzymatic desizing using amylase enzymes, which break starch into soluble sugars, or by oxidative treatments. Scouring removes natural waxes, fats, pectins, and other impurities, typically by treating the fabric with hot sodium hydroxide solution and wetting agents, which makes the fabric absorbent so that it can take up water, dyes, and chemicals evenly. Bleaching removes the natural yellowish colour of cotton to produce a white base for dyeing or for white goods, most commonly using hydrogen peroxide under alkaline conditions with stabilizers. Optical brightening agents, which absorb ultraviolet light and emit blue light, may be applied to give a brilliant white appearance.

Mercerization is named after John Mercer, who discovered in 1844 that treating cotton with concentrated sodium hydroxide caused it to swell and shrink and increased its affinity for dyes. In 1889, Horace Lowe found that if cotton was held under tension during treatment, preventing shrinkage, it developed a silk-like lustre. Modern mercerization therefore treats cotton yarn or fabric with cold, concentrated sodium hydroxide solution, typically around eighteen to twenty-four percent, while it is held under tension, followed by thorough washing to remove the alkali and neutralization with dilute acid. Fabric mercerization is carried out on chainless or clip-type mercerizing ranges that stretch the fabric in both width and length while it passes through the caustic bath and stabilization zones.

The changes produced by mercerization result from modifications of cotton's structure. A raw cotton fibre has a flattened, twisted ribbon shape with a central hollow called the lumen and a kidney-shaped cross-section. During treatment with concentrated alkali, the fibre swells considerably, the lumen nearly disappears, and the cross-section becomes more circular. The fibre untwists, and its surface becomes smoother, so that it reflects light more regularly, producing increased lustre. At the molecular level, the crystalline structure of cellulose changes from cellulose I, the natural form, to cellulose II, and the proportion of amorphous, less ordered regions increases. Because dyes and chemicals penetrate mainly the amorphous regions, this change increases dye absorption.

The benefits of mercerization are significant. Lustre improves markedly when the treatment is carried out under tension. Tensile strength typically increases, by roughly fifteen to thirty percent, because the fibrils become better aligned and stresses are distributed more evenly. Dye affinity increases, so mercerized cotton requires less dye to achieve a given depth of shade, can be dyed more uniformly, and covers immature or dead cotton fibres that would otherwise appear as light specks. Dimensional stability improves, because the fabric has been preshrunk during processing, reducing later shrinkage. Absorbency and reactivity also increase. For these reasons, mercerization is widely used for high-quality shirtings, sewing threads, knitted fabrics, and denim-related applications. A related process, ammonia mercerization, uses liquid ammonia instead of sodium hydroxide and produces softer handle and improved easy-care performance. Causticization, using lower alkali concentrations without tension, improves dye uptake with less effect on lustre.

After dyeing or printing, finishing processes give the fabric its final properties. Mechanical finishes include calendering, which passes fabric between heated rollers under pressure to smooth it and increase lustre; sanforizing, a compressive shrinkage process that mechanically shortens the fabric so that it shrinks little during washing; raising or napping, which lifts fibres from the surface to create a soft, fuzzy texture; and sueding. Chemical finishes modify fabric performance using applied chemicals, usually applied by padding, in which the fabric is immersed in a finishing bath and squeezed between rollers to a controlled pickup, followed by drying and curing.

Several chemical finishes are important for cotton. Easy-care or wrinkle-resistant finishes reduce creasing and the need for ironing. Cotton wrinkles easily because hydrogen bonds between cellulose chains break and reform in new positions when the fabric is bent, especially when damp. Crosslinking agents, such as dimethyloldihydroxyethyleneurea, DMDHEU, form covalent bonds between cellulose chains, holding them in position and helping the fabric recover from creasing. These finishes reduce abrasion resistance and tensile strength, so they are carefully controlled, and concerns about formaldehyde release from some crosslinking agents have led to the development of low-formaldehyde and formaldehyde-free alternatives, such as polycarboxylic acids. Softeners, commonly cationic or silicone-based compounds, improve handle and drape. Water-repellent finishes, using silicones, waxes, or fluorochemicals, cause water to bead on the surface; fluorochemical finishes also provide oil and stain repellency but face increasing regulation because some per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances persist in the environment. Flame-retardant finishes reduce the flammability of cotton for workwear, children's sleepwear, and furnishings. Antimicrobial finishes inhibit the growth of bacteria and odour.

Chemical processing consumes large quantities of water, energy, and chemicals and generates effluents containing alkalis, salts, surfactants, and residual chemicals. Recovery of caustic soda from mercerizing wash liquors by evaporation is common in large mills, both to reduce costs and to limit effluent alkalinity. Enzymatic preparation, combined processes that merge several steps, low-liquor application techniques, and environmentally safer finishing chemicals are being adopted to reduce the environmental footprint of textile wet processing.
summary:
Greige cotton contains waxes, pectins, colour, and size and needs chemical processing to become usable fabric. Preparation includes desizing, often with amylase for starch, scouring with hot sodium hydroxide to make fabric absorbent, bleaching with alkaline hydrogen peroxide, and optional optical brighteners. Mercerization, from Mercer's 1844 discovery and Lowe's 1889 finding that tension gives silk-like lustre, treats cotton under tension with cold 18–24% sodium hydroxide, followed by washing and neutralization, using chainless or clip ranges for fabric.

Treatment swells fibres, nearly closes the lumen, rounds and untwists them, and converts cellulose I to cellulose II with more amorphous regions, increasing lustre, strength by about 15–30%, dye affinity and coverage of dead cotton, dimensional stability, and absorbency; liquid ammonia mercerization softens fabric, and causticization improves dye uptake without tension. Mechanical finishes include calendering, sanforizing, raising, and sueding, while chemical finishes are padded, dried, and cured. Easy-care finishes crosslink cellulose with agents like DMDHEU, reducing wrinkling but also strength and abrasion resistance, prompting low-formaldehyde polycarboxylic alternatives; other finishes provide softness, water and stain repellency (with regulatory concerns over persistent fluorochemicals), flame retardancy, and antimicrobial protection. Processing uses much water, energy, and chemicals, so mills recover caustic soda and adopt enzymatic, combined, low-liquor, and safer finishing methods.

source_text:
A tort is a civil wrong, other than a breach of contract, for which the law provides a remedy, usually compensation in the form of damages. Torts protect a range of interests, including physical safety, property, reputation, and economic interests. Negligence is the most important and most frequently litigated tort. It covers situations in which a person suffers harm because someone else failed to take reasonable care, such as road accidents, injuries caused by defective premises, medical errors, and harm from careless professional advice. Unlike intentional torts such as battery or trespass, negligence does not require that the defendant intended to cause harm.

To succeed in a negligence claim, the claimant must generally establish four elements: that the defendant owed the claimant a duty of care, that the defendant breached that duty, that the breach caused the claimant's harm, and that the harm was of a kind recognized by the law and not too remote. The burden of proving these elements lies on the claimant, on the balance of probabilities.

The modern law of duty of care traces back to the English case of Donoghue v Stevenson, decided by the House of Lords in 1932. Mrs Donoghue allegedly became ill after drinking ginger beer from an opaque bottle that contained the decomposed remains of a snail. Because she had not bought the drink herself, she had no contract with the manufacturer. Lord Atkin nevertheless held that the manufacturer owed her a duty of care, stating the neighbour principle: a person must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions that they can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure their neighbour, meaning persons so closely and directly affected that they ought reasonably to have been in contemplation. Later cases refined the test. In Caparo Industries v Dickman, the courts considered whether harm was reasonably foreseeable, whether there was sufficient proximity between the parties, and whether it was fair, just, and reasonable to impose a duty. Courts also develop duties incrementally by analogy with established categories, such as those between road users, doctors and patients, employers and employees, and occupiers and visitors.

Breach of duty is assessed against the standard of the reasonable person, an objective standard that asks what a reasonably careful person would have done in the defendant's position. The defendant's own inexperience does not usually lower the standard; a learner driver is judged by the standard of a reasonably competent driver. Professionals are judged by the standard of a reasonably competent member of their profession. Under the Bolam test, derived from a 1957 English case, a doctor is not negligent if the conduct was in accordance with a practice accepted as proper by a responsible body of medical opinion, although later decisions require that such opinion be capable of withstanding logical analysis. In deciding whether reasonable care was taken, courts weigh factors such as the likelihood of harm, the seriousness of potential injury, the cost and practicality of precautions, and the social value of the defendant's activity.

Causation has two components. Factual causation is usually tested by the but-for test: would the harm have occurred but for the defendant's breach? If the harm would have happened anyway, the breach did not cause it. In a well-known case, a hospital doctor negligently failed to examine a patient who later died of arsenic poisoning, but the claim failed because the evidence showed he would have died even with proper treatment. Legal causation concerns whether the chain of causation was broken by an intervening act, such as the free and deliberate act of a third party or the claimant's own unreasonable conduct.

Remoteness of damage limits liability to harm that is not too far removed from the breach. Under the Wagon Mound principle, the defendant is liable only for damage of a kind that was reasonably foreseeable, even if the precise manner in which it occurred or its extent was not foreseen. The eggshell skull rule, however, means that once some physical harm of a foreseeable kind is established, the defendant must take the claimant as they find them, and is liable for the full extent of the injury even if a pre-existing condition made it unusually severe.

Courts have been cautious about extending negligence to certain types of harm. Pure economic loss, financial loss not resulting from physical damage to the claimant or their property, is generally not recoverable unless there is a special relationship, such as where a professional assumes responsibility for advice on which the claimant reasonably relies. Psychiatric harm suffered by people who witness accidents to others is subject to restrictive conditions concerning the closeness of the relationship and proximity to the event.

Defendants may raise defences. Contributory negligence applies when the claimant's own lack of care contributed to the harm, such as failing to wear a seat belt, and damages are reduced in proportion to the claimant's share of responsibility. Voluntary assumption of risk, expressed in the maxim volenti non fit injuria, may defeat a claim where the claimant freely and knowingly accepted the risk. Illegality may also bar recovery in some circumstances. Negligence law in common law jurisdictions, including Bangladesh and India, has developed largely through judicial decisions, often drawing on English authorities, alongside statutes governing areas such as motor vehicle accidents and consumer protection.

source_text:
Classrooms contain students with diverse abilities, backgrounds, interests, languages, and ways of learning. Traditional curricula are often designed for an imagined average learner and then adapted for individuals who do not fit, through accommodations added after the fact, such as extra time on examinations or alternative materials for a student with a disability. Universal Design for Learning, or UDL, takes a different approach. It is a framework for designing curricula, instruction, and assessment that are flexible from the beginning, so that a wide range of learners can access and engage with learning without the need for extensive later modification.

UDL draws its name and inspiration from universal design in architecture, a movement associated with architect Ronald Mace. Universal design aims to create buildings and products usable by as many people as possible without special adaptation. Curb cuts in pavements, for example, were introduced to help wheelchair users but also benefit people pushing prams, travellers with luggage, and cyclists. Similarly, UDL proposes that instructional features designed to support learners with particular needs often benefit many other students. The framework was developed in the 1990s by the Center for Applied Special Technology, known as CAST, in the United States, and it draws on research in neuroscience, cognitive psychology, and education.

The UDL framework is organized around three core principles, each associated with a broad network of brain functions involved in learning. The first principle is to provide multiple means of engagement, addressing the why of learning. Learners differ in what motivates them, what captures their interest, and how they respond to challenge. Some students thrive on spontaneity and novelty, while others prefer routine; some prefer working alone, others in groups. Teachers can support engagement by offering choices of topics or tasks, connecting learning to students' interests and real-world relevance, minimizing threats and distractions, varying the level of challenge, fostering collaboration, and helping students develop self-regulation strategies, such as setting goals and reflecting on progress.

The second principle is to provide multiple means of representation, addressing the what of learning. Students differ in how they perceive and comprehend information. A student with a visual impairment, a student with dyslexia, a student learning in a second language, and a student who lacks background knowledge each face different barriers when information is presented only as printed text. Teachers can present content in several formats, such as text, audio, video, images, diagrams, and physical models; offer options for customizing displays, such as adjustable text size or captions; clarify vocabulary, symbols, and notation; activate or supply relevant background knowledge; and highlight patterns, critical features, and relationships. These options help all learners build understanding, not only those with identified needs.

The third principle is to provide multiple means of action and expression, addressing the how of learning. Learners differ in how they navigate learning environments and demonstrate what they know. Some students express understanding effectively through writing, while others do better through speaking, drawing, constructing models, or using digital media. A student with motor difficulties may find handwriting slow but use voice recognition software effectively. Teachers can offer varied ways for students to respond and demonstrate learning, provide tools and assistive technologies, and support executive functions, such as planning, organizing information, and monitoring progress, through checklists, templates, and scaffolded steps.

A central idea in UDL is that barriers to learning often lie in the design of the curriculum rather than in the learner. A history lesson that requires students to read a dense textbook chapter creates barriers for many students, not because they cannot understand history but because the method of access is limited. If the learning goal is to understand the causes of a historical event, students could achieve it through reading, listening to an audio version, watching a documentary, or examining primary sources with guidance. Distinguishing the essential learning goal from the means of reaching it is therefore crucial. If the goal is specifically to develop reading comprehension, then reading remains necessary, but supports such as vocabulary assistance can be provided.

UDL also applies to assessment. Traditional assessments may measure abilities unrelated to the intended learning, such as speed of handwriting or reading fluency, rather than understanding of the subject. Designing assessments with flexible formats, clear criteria, and appropriate supports increases their validity, ensuring that they measure what they are intended to measure. Formative assessment and feedback help teachers adjust instruction to learners' progress.

Implementing UDL involves several practical steps. Teachers begin by setting clear learning goals, anticipate the variability of learners and potential barriers, design flexible methods and materials, and select assessments aligned with goals. Digital technologies, such as text-to-speech, captioning, interactive simulations, and learning management systems, make flexible design easier, although UDL does not depend on technology and can be implemented with low-cost strategies.

UDL has gained widespread support and has been incorporated into education policies in several countries. It aligns with goals of inclusive education, which seek to educate students with disabilities alongside their peers. Critics and researchers note, however, that the evidence base, while growing, includes many studies that are small or focus on specific components rather than the framework as a whole. Curb cuts in pavements, for example, were introduced to help wheelchair users but also benefit people pushing prams, travellers with luggage, and cyclists. Similarly, UDL proposes that instructional features designed to support learners with particular needs often benefit many other students. The framework was developed in the 1990s by the Center for Applied Special Technology, known as CAST, in the United States, and it draws on research in neuroscience, cognitive psychology, and education.

Teachers can support engagement by offering choices of topics or tasks, connecting learning to students' interests and real-world relevance, minimizing threats and distractions, varying the level of challenge, fostering collaboration, and helping students develop self-regulation strategies, such as setting goals and reflecting on progress.

The second principle is to provide multiple means of representation, addressing the what of learning. Students differ in how they perceive and comprehend information. A student with a visual impairment, a student with dyslexia, a student learning in a second language, and a student who lacks background knowledge each face different barriers when information is presented only as printed text. Teachers can present content in several formats, such as text, audio, video, images, diagrams, and physical models; offer options for customizing displays, such as adjustable text size or captions; clarify vocabulary, symbols, and notation; activate or supply relevant background knowledge; and highlight patterns, critical features, and relationships. These options help all learners build understanding, not only those with identified needs.

The third principle is to provide multiple means of action and expression, addressing the how of learning. Learners differ in how they navigate learning environments and demonstrate what they know. Some students express understanding effectively through writing, while others do better through speaking, drawing, constructing models, or using digital media. A student with motor difficulties may find handwriting slow but use voice recognition software effectively. source_text:
A differential equation is an equation that relates a function to one or more of its derivatives. Differential equations describe how quantities change and are therefore central to modelling in physics, engineering, biology, economics, and many other fields. An ordinary differential equation, or ODE, involves a function of a single independent variable and its ordinary derivatives, in contrast to partial differential equations, which involve several independent variables. The order of an ODE is the order of the highest derivative it contains. First-order ODEs, which involve only the first derivative, are the simplest class and model many important processes, such as population growth, radioactive decay, cooling, mixing in tanks, and the charging of capacitors.

A solution of a differential equation is a function that satisfies the equation identically over some interval. A first-order ODE usually has a general solution containing one arbitrary constant, representing a family of solution curves. To select a particular solution, an initial condition is specified, such as the value of the function at a given time. A differential equation together with an initial condition is called an initial value problem. Under suitable conditions, described by existence and uniqueness theorems, an initial value problem has exactly one solution in a neighbourhood of the initial point. Specifically, if the right-hand side function and its partial derivative with respect to the dependent variable are continuous near the initial point, a unique solution exists locally.

Separable equations are among the easiest to solve. An equation is separable if it can be written so that all terms involving the dependent variable y appear on one side with dy, and all terms involving the independent variable x appear on the other side with dx. Both sides can then be integrated. For example, the equation describing exponential growth or decay, dy/dt equals k times y, can be separated to give dy over y equals k dt. Integrating gives the natural logarithm of the absolute value of y equals kt plus a constant, so y equals C times e to the power kt. If k is positive, the solution grows exponentially, as in unrestricted population growth or compound interest; if k is negative, it decays exponentially, as in radioactive decay, where the half-life equals the natural logarithm of two divided by the absolute value of k.

Linear first-order equations have the standard form dy/dx plus P of x times y equals Q of x. They are solved using an integrating factor, mu of x, equal to e raised to the integral of P of x dx. Multiplying both sides of the equation by the integrating factor makes the left-hand side the derivative of the product mu times y. Integrating both sides then gives mu times y equals the integral of mu times Q dx plus a constant, from which y can be found. A classic application is Newton's law of cooling, which states that the rate of change of an object's temperature is proportional to the difference between its temperature and the ambient temperature. The equation dT/dt equals minus k times T minus T ambient is both linear and separable, and its solution shows that the temperature difference decays exponentially over time. Similarly, the current in a circuit containing a resistor and an inductor connected to a constant voltage source satisfies a linear first-order equation whose solution approaches a steady value exponentially.

Exact equations form another class. An equation of the form M of x and y dx plus N of x and y dy equals zero is exact if there exists a function F of x and y whose partial derivative with respect to x is M and whose partial derivative with respect to y is N. A test for exactness is that the partial derivative of M with respect to y equals the partial derivative of N with respect to x. When the equation is exact, its solution is given implicitly by F of x and y equals a constant. Equations that are not exact can sometimes be made exact by multiplying by a suitable integrating factor.

Some nonlinear equations can be transformed into solvable forms by substitution. Homogeneous equations, in which the right-hand side depends only on the ratio y over x, become separable after the substitution v equals y over x. Bernoulli equations, which have the form dy/dx plus P y equals Q y to the power n, become linear through the substitution v equals y to the power one minus n.

The logistic equation is an important nonlinear first-order model. It modifies exponential growth by assuming that the growth rate decreases as the population approaches a maximum sustainable size, the carrying capacity K. The equation dP/dt equals r times P times one minus P over K is separable and can be solved using partial fractions. Its solution has an S-shaped curve: population grows nearly exponentially when small, growth slows as the population increases, and the population approaches K asymptotically. The logistic model is used in ecology, epidemiology, and the study of the adoption of new technologies.

Not all first-order equations can be solved analytically. In such cases, qualitative and numerical methods are used. A direction field, or slope field, displays short line segments indicating the slope of solution curves at points in the plane, allowing the behaviour of solutions to be visualized without solving the equation. Equilibrium solutions, where the derivative is zero, can be classified as stable or unstable depending on whether nearby solutions approach or move away from them. Numerical methods such as Euler's method and the more accurate Runge-Kutta methods approximate solutions by advancing step by step from the initial condition, and they are widely used in scientific computing.

source_text:
Magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, produces detailed images of the body's internal structures without using ionizing radiation. It is particularly valuable for imaging soft tissues such as the brain, spinal cord, muscles, ligaments, and abdominal organs, where it provides much better contrast than X-ray-based methods. MRI is based on the behaviour of hydrogen nuclei, which are abundant in the water and fat that make up most of the body, when they are placed in a strong magnetic field and exposed to radio waves.

The hydrogen nucleus consists of a single proton, which possesses a property called spin and behaves like a tiny magnet. In the absence of an external field, these magnetic moments point in random directions and cancel out. When the patient is placed in the strong static magnetic field of the scanner, called B0, typically 1.5 or 3 tesla, the protons align either parallel or antiparallel to the field. A slight excess aligns parallel, the lower-energy state, producing a small net magnetization along the direction of B0. The protons also precess, wobbling around the field direction like spinning tops, at a characteristic frequency called the Larmor frequency, which is proportional to the field strength. For hydrogen, it is about 42.6 megahertz per tesla, or roughly 64 megahertz at 1.5 tesla.

To generate a signal, the scanner transmits a radiofrequency pulse at the Larmor frequency through a coil. This pulse causes resonance: protons absorb energy, and the net magnetization is tipped away from the direction of B0, for example by 90 degrees into the transverse plane. The precessing transverse magnetization induces a small voltage in a receiver coil, which is the MR signal. After the pulse is switched off, the magnetization returns towards equilibrium through two independent relaxation processes.

Longitudinal relaxation, also called T1 or spin-lattice relaxation, describes the recovery of magnetization along the direction of B0 as protons release energy to their surroundings. The time constant T1 is the time needed for about 63 percent of the longitudinal magnetization to recover. Transverse relaxation, called T2 or spin-spin relaxation, describes the loss of transverse magnetization as protons fall out of phase with one another because of interactions between them. T2 is the time for the transverse magnetization to decay to about 37 percent of its initial value. In practice, the signal decays even faster, with a time constant called T2 star, because of small inhomogeneities in the magnetic field. Different tissues have different T1 and T2 values. Fat has a short T1 and appears bright on T1-weighted images, while water and cerebrospinal fluid have long T1 and long T2 values, appearing dark on T1-weighted images and bright on T2-weighted images. These differences are the main source of contrast in MRI.

Image contrast is controlled by the timing parameters of the pulse sequence. The repetition time, TR, is the interval between successive excitation pulses, and the echo time, TE, is the time between excitation and signal measurement. A short TR and short TE produce T1-weighted images, which show anatomy clearly. A long TR and long TE produce T2-weighted images, which are sensitive to oedema, inflammation, and many pathological changes that increase tissue water. A long TR and short TE produce proton density-weighted images, which reflect the number of hydrogen nuclei. Common sequences include spin echo, which uses a 180-degree refocusing pulse to cancel the effects of field inhomogeneity, and gradient echo, which is faster and sensitive to T2 star effects. Specialized techniques include fluid-attenuated inversion recovery, which suppresses the signal from cerebrospinal fluid, and diffusion-weighted imaging, which detects restricted water movement and is highly sensitive to acute stroke.

To form an image, the scanner must determine where each signal originates. This is achieved with gradient coils that superimpose small, linearly varying magnetic fields on B0 along the three spatial directions. Because the Larmor frequency depends on field strength, a gradient makes the precession frequency vary with position. A slice-selection gradient applied during the radiofrequency pulse ensures that only protons within a chosen slice are excited. Phase-encoding and frequency-encoding gradients then make the phase and frequency of the signal depend on position within the slice. The acquired data fill a frequency-domain dataset called k-space, and a two-dimensional Fourier transform converts k-space into the final image. The rapid switching of gradients produces the loud knocking noise characteristic of MRI scans.

MRI has important safety considerations. The strong static field attracts ferromagnetic objects, which can become dangerous projectiles, so access to the scanner room is controlled and patients are screened carefully. Some implanted devices, including certain older pacemakers, cochlear implants, and aneurysm clips, may malfunction, move, or heat, although many modern devices are designed to be MR-conditional. Radiofrequency energy deposited in tissue can cause heating, limited by the specific absorption rate. Gadolinium-based contrast agents, which shorten T1 and enhance vascular and abnormal tissues, are generally safe, but they require caution in patients with severe kidney disease. Compared with CT, MRI scans take longer, are more expensive, and are more sensitive to patient movement, but they provide superior soft-tissue contrast without radiation.

topic: Criteria Air Pollutants and the Air Quality Index
source_text:
Air pollution is the presence in the atmosphere of substances at concentrations high enough to harm human health, ecosystems, or materials. It is among the largest environmental risks to health worldwide, contributing to heart disease, stroke, chronic respiratory disease, lung cancer, and acute respiratory infections. To manage air quality, regulatory agencies identify a set of common pollutants for which they set legally enforceable standards. In many systems these are called criteria pollutants, because their standards are based on scientific criteria documenting their effects on health and the environment.

Particulate matter is a complex mixture of solid particles and liquid droplets suspended in air. It is classified by aerodynamic diameter. PM10 refers to particles with diameters of ten micrometres or less, which can be inhaled into the upper airways. PM2.5, or fine particulate matter, consists of particles of 2.5 micrometres or less, which penetrate deep into the lungs and can enter the bloodstream. Fine particles are produced mainly by combustion in vehicles, power plants, industries, brick kilns, and household cooking with solid fuels, and they also form in the atmosphere from gases such as sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and ammonia. Coarse particles come from road dust, construction, and natural sources such as soil and sea spray. PM2.5 is generally considered the pollutant with the greatest health impact.

Ground-level ozone is a secondary pollutant, meaning that it is not emitted directly but forms in the atmosphere. It is produced when nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds react in the presence of sunlight, so concentrations tend to peak on hot, sunny afternoons and may be high downwind of cities. Ozone irritates the airways, reduces lung function, and worsens asthma, and it also damages crops and forests. It should be distinguished from stratospheric ozone, which protects the Earth from ultraviolet radiation.

Nitrogen dioxide is produced mainly by high-temperature combustion in vehicle engines and power plants. It inflames the airways and contributes to the formation of ozone and fine particles. Sulphur dioxide is emitted largely from burning sulphur-containing fuels such as coal and heavy oil and from some industrial processes; it irritates the respiratory system and contributes to acid deposition and secondary sulphate particles. Carbon monoxide is a colourless, odourless gas produced by incomplete combustion. It binds to haemoglobin much more strongly than oxygen does, reducing the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity, and is especially dangerous in enclosed spaces and for people with heart disease. Lead, historically emitted from leaded petrol, damages the nervous system, particularly in children; its atmospheric levels fell sharply in countries that phased out leaded fuel, though emissions from battery recycling and smelting remain concerns in some areas.

Air quality standards specify a maximum concentration and an averaging time, such as a 24-hour average for PM2.5 or an eight-hour average for ozone, because health effects depend on both the level and the duration of exposure. The World Health Organization publishes air quality guidelines based on health evidence, and national governments set their own standards, which may be less stringent because of economic and technical considerations. Monitoring networks measure pollutant concentrations continuously using instruments such as beta attenuation monitors for particles and chemiluminescence analysers for nitrogen oxides, while satellite observations and low-cost sensors provide additional spatial coverage.

Concentrations of several different pollutants are difficult for the public to interpret, so many countries report an air quality index, AQI. The AQI converts the measured concentration of each pollutant into a number on a common scale using breakpoints defined by health-based standards. The index for each pollutant is calculated by linear interpolation between breakpoint concentrations and their corresponding index values. The overall AQI reported for a location is the highest of the individual pollutant indices, and the pollutant responsible is identified as the dominant pollutant. Index values are grouped into categories with colours and descriptions, ranging from good, through moderate and unhealthy for sensitive groups, to unhealthy, very unhealthy, and hazardous in some systems.

The value of the AQI lies in communication. Each category is linked to health messages, such as advising children, older adults, and people with asthma or heart disease to reduce prolonged outdoor exertion when air quality is unhealthy for sensitive groups, and advising everyone to limit outdoor activity at higher levels. Forecasts of the AQI allow schools and individuals to plan activities. However, the index has limitations. Because it reports only the highest single pollutant, it may understate the combined effects of several pollutants at moderate levels, and because it is based on outdoor monitoring stations, it may not reflect exposure indoors or in locations far from monitors.

Improving air quality requires controlling emissions at their sources. Measures include stricter vehicle emission standards and cleaner fuels, expansion of public transport, modernization of brick kilns and industrial processes, flue gas desulphurization and particulate controls at power plants, dust control at construction sites, and replacement of solid household fuels with cleaner cooking technologies. Because pollutants travel long distances, regional cooperation is often needed in addition to local action.

topic: Recombinant DNA Technology and Cloning Vectors
source_text:
Recombinant DNA technology is the set of methods used to combine DNA from different sources into a single molecule and introduce it into a host organism where it can be copied and, if desired, expressed. Developed in the 1970s, these methods made it possible to isolate individual genes, study their functions, and produce proteins such as human insulin, growth hormone, clotting factors, and vaccine antigens in microorganisms or cultured cells. Gene cloning, the production of many identical copies of a particular DNA fragment, is the foundation of the technology.

A basic cloning procedure involves several steps. First, the DNA fragment of interest, often called the insert, is obtained, for example by cutting genomic DNA with restriction enzymes, by amplifying a gene with the polymerase chain reaction, or by synthesizing complementary DNA from messenger RNA using reverse transcriptase. Complementary DNA is particularly useful for expressing eukaryotic genes in bacteria, because it lacks introns, which bacteria cannot remove. Second, the insert is joined to a vector, a DNA molecule capable of replicating in a host cell. Third, the recombinant molecule is introduced into host cells. Fourth, cells that contain the desired recombinant DNA are identified and grown.

Restriction endonucleases, enzymes that recognize specific short DNA sequences and cut both strands, are central tools. Many recognize palindromic sequences of four to eight base pairs, which read the same on both strands in the 5' to 3' direction. EcoRI, for instance, recognizes GAATTC and cuts between G and A on each strand. Some enzymes produce staggered cuts that leave short single-stranded overhangs called sticky ends, while others cut straight across to give blunt ends. If the insert and the vector are cut with the same enzyme, their complementary sticky ends can base-pair with each other. DNA ligase then forms phosphodiester bonds that seal the sugar-phosphate backbones, creating a stable recombinant molecule.

Vectors must have several features. They need an origin of replication, which allows them to be copied in the host independently of the host chromosome. They need one or more selectable markers, typically genes conferring resistance to an antibiotic, so that only cells that have taken up the vector survive on media containing that antibiotic. They need a multiple cloning site, a short region containing several unique restriction sites into which inserts can be placed. Expression vectors additionally contain a promoter that drives transcription of the inserted gene, a ribosome-binding site, and transcription termination signals, and sometimes sequences encoding tags that simplify protein purification.

Plasmids are the most commonly used vectors. They are small, circular, double-stranded DNA molecules that replicate independently in bacteria and can carry inserts up to roughly ten kilobases. Bacteriophage lambda vectors accept larger inserts, around 20 kilobases, and cosmids, which combine plasmid features with lambda packaging sequences, carry up to about 45 kilobases. For very large fragments, such as those used in genome sequencing projects, bacterial artificial chromosomes can carry 100 to 300 kilobases and yeast artificial chromosomes even more. Viral vectors derived from retroviruses, lentiviruses, or adenoviruses are used to deliver genes into animal cells, and the Ti plasmid of Agrobacterium tumefaciens is used to transfer genes into plants.

Introducing recombinant DNA into bacteria is called transformation. Bacterial cells such as Escherichia coli can be made competent to take up DNA by treatment with calcium chloride followed by a brief heat shock, or by electroporation, in which a short electrical pulse creates temporary pores in the cell membrane. Transformation efficiency is low, so selection is essential. Colonies growing on antibiotic-containing medium contain the vector, but not all vectors contain the insert, since some vectors reclose without it. Blue-white screening helps distinguish them. Many plasmids carry the lacZ alpha gene, which encodes part of the enzyme beta-galactosidase, with the multiple cloning site located inside it. When an insert is ligated into this site, the gene is disrupted. On media containing the substrate X-gal, colonies with an intact lacZ gene produce a blue product, while colonies carrying recombinant plasmids with disrupted lacZ remain white and can be selected for further analysis.

Selected clones are verified by methods such as colony PCR, restriction digestion followed by gel electrophoresis to check insert size and orientation, and DNA sequencing to confirm that the insert is correct and free of mutations. When the goal is protein production, the recombinant cells are grown under conditions that induce expression, and the protein is extracted and purified.

The choice of host depends on the protein. Bacterial hosts such as E. coli are inexpensive and grow rapidly, but they cannot perform many post-translational modifications, such as glycosylation, that some eukaryotic proteins require for proper function. Yeast, insect cells, and mammalian cell lines are used when such modifications are necessary, although they are more expensive and slower to culture. Because recombinant DNA technology involves creating organisms with new genetic combinations, laboratories follow biosafety guidelines that specify containment levels according to the potential risks of the organisms and genes involved.

source_text:
Spinning is the process of converting fibres into yarn, a continuous strand strong enough to be woven, knitted, or sewn. Staple fibres, such as cotton, wool, and cut synthetic fibres, have limited length, so they must be aligned, drawn into a fine strand, and twisted together to create cohesion. Ring spinning, developed in the nineteenth century, remains the most widely used method for producing staple yarns, particularly fine and high-quality cotton yarns, because it can spin a very wide range of counts and gives yarns with excellent strength and structure.

Before ring spinning, fibres pass through a sequence of preparatory processes. In blowroom operations, compressed bales are opened into small tufts, mixed for uniformity, and cleaned of trash such as seeds and leaf fragments. Carding further opens the tufts into individual fibres, removes remaining impurities and very short fibres, and forms a soft rope-like strand called a card sliver, although the fibres in it are not well aligned. Drawing combines several slivers and stretches them between rollers moving at different speeds, which straightens and parallelizes the fibres and improves evenness by averaging irregularities. For fine, high-quality yarns, combing is added to remove short fibres and neps, small tangled knots of fibre. Finally, the roving frame, or speed frame, draws the sliver into a thinner strand called roving and inserts a small amount of twist to give it enough strength to be wound onto a bobbin and fed to the ring frame.

On the ring spinning frame, the roving is fed into a drafting system, usually consisting of three pairs of rollers. Each successive pair rotates faster than the one before, so the strand is stretched, or drafted, reducing its linear density to that of the final yarn. Total drafts on modern ring frames are commonly in the range of about 20 to 50. Aprons, thin belts running around the middle rollers, control the movement of short fibres during drafting, which would otherwise float uncontrolled between roller pairs and create irregularities.

After drafting, the thin ribbon of fibres emerges from the front rollers and is immediately twisted. The yarn passes through a guide, then through a small C-shaped metal clip called a traveller, which runs freely around a steel ring surrounding a rotating spindle. The spindle carries a bobbin on which the yarn is wound. As the spindle rotates at high speed, often 15,000 to 25,000 revolutions per minute, the yarn drags the traveller around the ring. Because of friction and air resistance, the traveller lags slightly behind the spindle, and this difference in speed winds the yarn onto the bobbin. At the same time, each rotation of the traveller inserts one turn of twist into the yarn. The ring rail moves up and down to build the yarn package in a regular shape.

Twist is a key factor in yarn properties. Twist binds the fibres together by creating radial pressure that increases friction between them, so up to a certain level, more twist increases strength. Beyond an optimum, further twist reduces strength because fibres become increasingly inclined to the yarn axis and are subjected to additional stresses. The amount of twist is described by turns per metre or turns per inch and is often expressed through the twist multiplier, which relates twist to yarn count so that yarns of different fineness can be compared. Twist also affects handle, softness, lustre, and appearance: low-twist yarns are soft and bulky, suitable for knitted fabrics, while higher-twist yarns are stronger and used for warp yarns in weaving. Twist direction is designated as S or Z, depending on whether the fibre spirals match the central part of the letter.

During twisting, the fibre strand emerging from the front rollers forms a small triangular region called the spinning triangle. Fibres at the edges of this triangle are not fully integrated into the yarn and can form protruding ends, contributing to hairiness. Compact spinning modifies the ring frame by using suction or mechanical condensing devices to narrow the fibre strand before twisting, nearly eliminating the spinning triangle. Compact yarns are less hairy, stronger, and more even, and they are used for premium fabrics.

The main limitation of ring spinning is productivity. Because the spindle must rotate once for each turn of twist and the traveller speed is limited by frictional heating and wear, production speed per spindle is relatively low, and frequent doffing, the removal of full bobbins, is required. Energy consumption is also significant. Higher-productivity methods such as rotor and air-jet spinning have therefore replaced ring spinning for some coarser counts. Nevertheless, ring spinning remains dominant for fine and medium counts and for applications requiring the best combination of strength, evenness, and fabric quality.

Quality control in ring spinning involves monitoring yarn count, twist, strength, elongation, evenness, imperfections such as thin places, thick places, and neps, and hairiness. Instruments measure unevenness using capacitance sensors and report the coefficient of variation of mass along the yarn. Electronic yarn clearers on winding machines remove objectionable faults and splice the yarn ends together.

Ring spinning is the most widely used method for producing staple yarns, especially fine, strong cotton yarns. Preparation includes blowroom opening, mixing, and cleaning; carding to separate fibres and form sliver; drawing to parallelize fibres and improve evenness; optional combing to remove short fibres and neps for fine yarns; and the roving frame, which produces a lightly twisted roving. On the ring frame, a three-roller drafting system with aprons reduces the roving to yarn fineness, typically with drafts of about 20–50.

The yarn passes through a traveller that circulates on a ring around a spindle rotating at about 15,000–25,000 rpm; the traveller's lag winds yarn onto the bobbin while each rotation inserts one turn of twist, and the moving ring rail builds the package. Twist increases strength up to an optimum, is expressed as turns per metre or a twist multiplier, influences softness and appearance, and has S or Z direction. Fibres at the edges of the spinning triangle cause hairiness, which compact spinning reduces to give stronger, more even yarn. Ring spinning's low productivity, frequent doffing, and energy use have led to rotor and air-jet spinning for coarser counts, though ring yarns dominate fine and medium counts. Quality control measures count, twist, strength, elongation, evenness, imperfections, and hairiness, with electronic clearers removing faults.

Twist is a key factor in yarn properties. Twist binds the fibres together by creating radial pressure that increases friction between them, so up to a certain level, more twist increases strength. Plant breeding is the deliberate improvement of crop plants to increase yield, quality, resistance to pests and diseases, and tolerance of environmental stresses. One of the most successful breeding strategies of the twentieth century has been the development of hybrid varieties. Hybrid maize transformed agriculture in the United States from the 1930s onwards, and hybrids are now widely used in maize, sorghum, sunflower, many vegetables, and increasingly rice. The success of hybrids is based on the phenomenon of heterosis, or hybrid vigour.

Heterosis refers to the superior performance of a hybrid offspring compared with its parents for traits such as yield, growth rate, biomass, and stress tolerance. It is usually measured as mid-parent heterosis, the superiority of the hybrid over the average of its two parents, or as better-parent heterosis, the superiority over the better parent. For commercial purposes, the most relevant comparison is with the best existing variety, sometimes called standard heterosis. The genetic basis of heterosis is still being researched. The dominance hypothesis proposes that each parent carries different harmful recessive alleles, and in the hybrid these are masked by favourable dominant alleles from the other parent. The overdominance hypothesis proposes that heterozygosity at certain loci is itself advantageous, so the heterozygote performs better than either homozygote. Epistasis, interactions between genes at different loci, is also thought to contribute.

The opposite phenomenon, inbreeding depression, helps explain hybrid breeding methods. In naturally cross-pollinated crops such as maize, repeated self-pollination over several generations exposes harmful recessive alleles and causes a decline in vigour and yield. Hybrid breeding exploits both processes. Breeders first develop inbred lines by repeated self-pollination, typically for six or more generations, until the lines are nearly homozygous and breed true. Many inbred lines are weak and low yielding, but when two genetically different inbred lines are crossed, the resulting single-cross hybrid can show strong heterosis and is highly uniform, because all plants receive the same combination of alleles from the two parents.

Not all crosses produce useful heterosis, so breeders evaluate combining ability. General combining ability refers to the average performance of an inbred line in crosses with many other lines, mainly reflecting additive genetic effects. Specific combining ability refers to the performance of a particular cross relative to what would be expected from the general combining ability of its parents, reflecting non-additive effects. Test crosses and diallel crosses are used to estimate these values. Breeders also organize germplasm into heterotic groups, sets of genetically related lines that produce strong heterosis when crossed with lines from a different group but not when crossed within the group. In maize, distinct heterotic groups developed from different source populations are maintained to maximize hybrid performance.

Several types of hybrids exist. Single-cross hybrids, produced from two inbred lines, are the most uniform and generally the highest yielding, but seed production can be expensive because the female parent is an inbred line with relatively low seed yield. Three-way crosses use a single-cross hybrid as the female parent and an inbred as the male, and double-cross hybrids are produced by crossing two single-cross hybrids. These alternatives produce seed more cheaply, though with less uniformity.

Producing hybrid seed on a commercial scale requires preventing self-pollination of the female parent. In maize, which has separate male flowers in the tassel and female flowers in the ear, this was originally achieved by manual or mechanical detasselling of the female rows in seed production fields. In crops with perfect flowers containing both male and female parts, such as rice, emasculation by hand is impractical at large scale, so male sterility systems are used. Cytoplasmic male sterility, CMS, is caused by mitochondrial genes that prevent the production of functional pollen. A three-line system uses a male-sterile A line, a maintainer B line that is genetically identical except for normal cytoplasm and is used to multiply the A line, and a restorer R line carrying nuclear genes that restore fertility in the hybrid so that the farmer's crop produces grain. Hybrid rice, first developed on a large scale in China in the 1970s, relies on this approach or on a two-line system using environment-sensitive genic male sterility, in which sterility depends on temperature or day length. Some crops use self-incompatibility systems or chemical hybridizing agents.

Hybrids offer several advantages to farmers: higher yield potential, greater uniformity in maturity and plant height, which helps mechanical harvesting, and sometimes improved stress tolerance. However, they also have disadvantages. The heterosis and uniformity of hybrids are lost in the next generation, because seeds saved from a hybrid crop produce a segregating population with variable and usually lower yields. Farmers must therefore purchase new seed each season, which increases costs and creates dependence on seed companies. Hybrid seed production is technically demanding and requires isolation, synchronized flowering of the parents, and quality control. For smallholder farmers with limited capital, the benefits of hybrids depend on reliable seed supply, affordable prices, and appropriate inputs such as fertilizer and irrigation.

Hybrid breeding continues to evolve. Molecular markers are used to assign lines to heterotic groups, accelerate the development of inbred lines, and select for specific genes. Doubled haploid technology allows completely homozygous lines to be produced in one or two generations rather than six or more. Genomic selection, which predicts breeding values from genome-wide marker data, helps breeders identify promising combinations before extensive field testing. These tools aim to increase the rate of genetic gain while maintaining the genetic diversity needed for future breeding.

source_text:
Max Weber, one of the founders of sociology, argued that the discipline should seek to understand the meanings that people attach to their actions. Whereas some early sociologists emphasised social facts and structures that exist independently of individuals, Weber defined sociology as the science that attempts the interpretive understanding of social action in order to arrive at a causal explanation of its course and effects. His approach, often called interpretive or verstehen sociology, from the German word for understanding, remains central to the study of social behaviour.

For Weber, social action is behaviour to which the actor attaches a subjective meaning and which takes account of the behaviour of others. A cyclist accidentally colliding with another is not social action in this sense, but the subsequent attempt to avoid an argument, to apologize, or to demand compensation is, because each response is meaningfully oriented towards the other person. Understanding social action requires grasping the motives and meanings that lie behind it. Weber distinguished between direct observational understanding, such as recognizing that a person is angry from their facial expression, and explanatory understanding, which places the action within a broader context of motives, for example understanding that a person is chopping wood to earn money or to prepare fuel.

Weber identified four ideal types of social action. Ideal types are analytical constructs that emphasise certain features of social phenomena to aid comparison; they are not descriptions of any particular real case, and actual actions usually combine several types. Instrumentally rational action, sometimes called goal-rational or purposive-rational action, is determined by calculation of the most efficient means to achieve a chosen end, taking into account possible consequences. A business person comparing suppliers to minimize costs or a student planning study time to maximize examination performance acts in this way. Value-rational action is determined by a conscious belief in the intrinsic value of a certain type of behaviour, whether ethical, religious, or aesthetic, regardless of its consequences. A person who refuses to lie even when lying would bring benefits, or who fulfils a religious obligation at personal cost, acts in a value-rational manner. Affectual action is determined by emotions and feelings, such as acting out of anger, love, or fear. Traditional action is determined by ingrained habit and custom, performed because things have always been done that way, often with little conscious reflection.

Weber used this typology to analyse broad historical changes, particularly the process he called rationalization. He argued that modern Western societies had been increasingly characterized by the spread of instrumentally rational action into more and more spheres of life. Rationalization involves the replacement of traditional, emotional, and value-based ways of thinking and acting by calculation, efficiency, predictability, and control. It is evident in the growth of modern capitalism, with its systematic accounting and pursuit of profit; in modern science and technology, which seek to master the world through calculation and experiment; in law, which becomes codified and systematic; and in bureaucratic administration, which organizes activity through impersonal rules.

Weber's famous study The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism, published in 1904 and 1905, examined the cultural origins of modern capitalism. Weber argued that certain forms of Protestantism, especially Calvinism, encouraged a distinctive ethic. The doctrine of predestination held that God had already determined who would be saved, creating anxiety among believers. Hard work in a worldly calling, disciplined living, and the avoidance of luxury came to be seen as signs of being among the elect. This ethic encouraged the systematic accumulation of wealth and its reinvestment rather than consumption, contributing to the spirit of capitalism. Weber did not argue that religion alone caused capitalism, and he acknowledged material factors, but he showed that ideas and values could have significant and unintended economic consequences. His argument was also a response to purely economic explanations of history.

Rationalization also brings what Weber called disenchantment of the world. As scientific and technical explanations replace magical and religious interpretations, the world comes to be seen as governed by calculable forces rather than mysterious powers. Although rationalization increases efficiency and technical control, Weber was ambivalent about its consequences. He warned that modern people could become trapped in an iron cage of rationality, in which bureaucratic and economic systems, originally created to serve human purposes, come to dominate individuals and narrow the scope for meaning, freedom, and spontaneity. He also observed a tension between formal rationality, which concerns calculable efficiency and rule-following, and substantive rationality, which concerns whether outcomes are consistent with particular values such as justice or human welfare. An organization can be highly efficient formally while producing outcomes that are substantively irrational.

Weber's ideas have shaped later sociology in many ways. His emphasis on meaning and interpretation influenced symbolic interactionism and phenomenological sociology. His analysis of rationalization inspired later work, such as George Ritzer's concept of McDonaldization, which describes how the principles of efficiency, calculability, predictability, and control, exemplified by fast-food restaurants, have spread to other sectors of society. Critics have argued that Weber's account of the Protestant ethic is historically contestable and that his ideal types can be difficult to apply, but his insistence that sociologists must understand both social structures and the meanings individuals give to their actions remains fundamental to the discipline.

topic: The Extended Marketing Mix for Services
source_text:
The marketing mix is the set of controllable tools that an organization combines to produce the response it wants in a target market. For physical goods, the traditional mix is summarized as the four Ps: product, price, place, and promotion. Services, however, differ from goods in important ways, and marketers of services such as banking, education, healthcare, hotels, airlines, and telecommunications found that the four Ps did not capture all the elements that shape customer experience. In 1981, Bernard Booms and Mary Jo Bitner proposed an extended marketing mix for services that adds three further elements: people, process, and physical evidence, creating the seven Ps.

The need for an extended mix arises from the distinctive characteristics of services. Intangibility means that services cannot be seen, touched, or tried before purchase in the way physical products can, which makes it difficult for customers to evaluate quality in advance and increases perceived risk. Inseparability means that services are usually produced and consumed at the same time, often with the customer present, so the provider and the customer interact during delivery. Variability, or heterogeneity, means that service quality depends on who provides it, when, where, and how, making consistency difficult to achieve. Perishability means that services cannot be stored; an unsold hotel room or an empty airline seat on a particular night represents revenue lost forever, which makes matching supply and demand especially important.

The original four elements are adapted to services. The service product includes the core service, such as transportation for an airline, and supplementary services that add value, such as reservations, baggage handling, meals, and loyalty programmes. Designing a service involves specifying not only what is delivered but also the level of quality and the range of options. Pricing services is often complex because costs are difficult to allocate and value perceptions vary. Service firms frequently use demand-based pricing, such as higher fares during peak periods and discounts during off-peak times, to manage perishable capacity, a practice known as revenue or yield management. Place, or distribution, concerns how and where customers access the service, which may involve physical branches, intermediaries, home delivery, or electronic channels such as mobile applications and online platforms. Promotion communicates the value of intangible services, often by using tangible cues, testimonials, and guarantees to reduce perceived risk.

The first additional element is people. Because services are produced in interaction with customers, the employees who deliver them are part of the service itself. Frontline staff such as bank tellers, nurses, waiters, and call centre agents strongly influence customer perceptions through their competence, courtesy, responsiveness, and appearance. Service firms therefore emphasise recruiting employees with appropriate skills and attitudes, training them, empowering them to resolve problems, and motivating them through internal marketing, which treats employees as internal customers. The concept of the service-profit chain links employee satisfaction and loyalty to service quality, customer satisfaction, customer loyalty, and ultimately profitability. The people element also includes other customers present during service delivery, whose behaviour can enhance or detract from the experience, as in a cinema or a classroom.

The second additional element is process, the procedures, mechanisms, and flow of activities by which the service is delivered. Customers experience the process directly, so waiting times, the number of steps required, ease of use, and reliability shape satisfaction. A process can be designed using service blueprinting, a visual tool that maps the customer's actions, frontstage employee actions visible to the customer, backstage actions, and support processes, separated by a line of visibility. Blueprinting helps identify fail points where errors may occur and opportunities for improvement. Process decisions include the degree of standardization versus customization, the use of self-service technologies such as automated teller machines and online check-in, and approaches to managing queues. Well-designed processes improve efficiency and consistency, reducing the variability characteristic of services.

The third additional element is physical evidence, the tangible elements that help customers evaluate an intangible service. It includes the servicescape, the physical environment in which the service takes place, such as the layout, décor, cleanliness, lighting, music, and signage of a hotel, restaurant, or hospital. It also includes tangible items such as uniforms, brochures, websites, tickets, invoices, and business cards. Because customers cannot inspect a service before purchase, they often use physical evidence as cues to judge quality. A clean, well-organized clinic signals professionalism, while a disorganized reception area may suggest poor care, regardless of the actual medical expertise available.

The extended marketing mix encourages service organizations to manage all aspects of the customer experience in an integrated way. The elements are interdependent: an attractive servicescape cannot compensate for rude staff, and skilled staff are hampered by inefficient processes. Critics have noted that some of the additional elements could be incorporated within the original four Ps and that the framework is primarily a checklist rather than a theory. Others have proposed alternative frameworks focused on customer value and relationships. Nevertheless, the seven Ps remain widely used in teaching and practice because they highlight the human, procedural, and tangible dimensions that distinguish service marketing from the marketing of goods.

Intangibility means that services cannot be seen, touched, or tried before purchase in the way physical products can, which makes it difficult for customers to evaluate quality in advance and increases perceived risk. Inseparability means that services are usually produced and consumed at the same time, often with the customer present, so the provider and the customer interact during delivery. Variability, or heterogeneity, means that service quality depends on who provides it, when, where, and how, making consistency difficult to achieve. Perishability means that services cannot be stored; an unsold hotel room or an empty airline seat on a particular night represents revenue lost forever, which makes matching supply and demand especially important.

The original four elements are adapted to services. The service product includes the core service, such as transportation for an airline, and supplementary services that add value, such as reservations, baggage handling, meals, and loyalty programmes. Designing a service involves specifying not only what is delivered but also the level of quality and the range of options. Pricing services is often complex because costs are difficult to allocate and value perceptions vary. Service firms frequently use demand-based pricing, such as higher fares during peak periods and discounts during off-peak times, to manage perishable capacity, a practice known as revenue or yield management. Place, or distribution, concerns how and where customers access the service, which may involve physical branches, intermediaries, home delivery, or electronic channels such as mobile applications and online platforms. Promotion communicates the value of intangible services, often by using tangible cues, testimonials, and guarantees to reduce perceived risk.

The first additional element is people. Because services are produced in interaction with customers, the employees who deliver them are part of the service itself. Frontline staff such as bank tellers, nurses, waiters, and call centre agents strongly influence customer perceptions through their competence, courtesy, responsiveness, and appearance. Service firms therefore emphasise recruiting employees with appropriate skills and attitudes, training them, empowering them to resolve problems, and motivating them through internal marketing, which treats employees as internal customers. The concept of the service-profit chain links employee satisfaction and loyalty to service quality, customer satisfaction, customer loyalty, and ultimately profitability. The people element also includes other customers present during service delivery, whose behaviour can enhance or detract from the experience, as in a cinema or a classroom.

The second additional element is process, the procedures, mechanisms, and flow of activities by which the service is delivered. Customers experience the process directly, so waiting times, the number of steps required, ease of use, and reliability shape satisfaction. A process can be designed using service blueprinting, a visual tool that maps the customer's actions, frontstage employee actions visible to the customer, backstage actions, and support processes, separated by a line of visibility. Blueprinting helps identify fail points where errors may occur and opportunities for improvement. Process decisions include the degree of standardization versus customization, the use of self-service technologies such as automated teller machines and online check-in, and approaches to managing queues. Well-designed processes improve efficiency and consistency, reducing the variability characteristic of services.

The third additional element is physical evidence, the tangible elements that help customers evaluate an intangible service. It includes the servicescape, the physical environment in which the service takes place, such as the layout, décor, cleanliness, lighting, music, and signage of a hotel, restaurant, or hospital. It also includes tangible items such as uniforms, brochures, websites, tickets, invoices, and business cards. Because customers cannot inspect a service before purchase, they often use physical evidence as cues to judge quality. A clean, well-organized clinic signals professionalism, while a disorganized reception area may suggest poor care, regardless of the actual medical expertise available.

The extended marketing mix encourages service organizations to manage all aspects of the customer experience in an integrated way. The elements are interdependent: an attractive servicescape cannot compensate for rude staff, and skilled staff are hampered by inefficient processes. Critics have noted that some of the additional elements could be incorporated within the original four Ps and that the framework is primarily a checklist rather than a theory. Others have proposed alternative frameworks focused on customer value and relationships. Nevertheless, the seven Ps remain widely used in teaching and practice because they highlight the human, procedural, and tangible dimensions that distinguish service marketing from the marketing of goods.
