topic: Bacterial Cell Walls and Gram Staining
source_text:
The cell wall is one of the most important structures of bacterial cells. It lies outside the cytoplasmic membrane and gives the cell its characteristic shape, whether spherical cocci, rod-shaped bacilli, or spiral forms. More importantly, it protects the cell from osmotic lysis. Bacterial cytoplasm contains a high concentration of dissolved solutes, so water tends to flow into the cell. Without a rigid wall, most bacteria living in dilute environments would swell and burst. Differences in wall structure also determine how bacteria react to stains, how they interact with the immune system, and which antibiotics can affect them.

The main structural component of most bacterial cell walls is peptidoglycan, also called murein. Peptidoglycan is a mesh-like polymer made of long glycan chains composed of alternating sugar derivatives, N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetylmuramic acid, joined by beta-1,4 glycosidic bonds. A short peptide chain is attached to each N-acetylmuramic acid residue, and peptides on adjacent glycan strands are cross-linked to one another. This cross-linking produces a strong, continuous network surrounding the cell, sometimes described as a single giant molecule. Because peptidoglycan is found in bacteria but not in human cells, the enzymes that build it are excellent targets for antibiotics.

Bacteria are divided into two major groups according to their wall architecture. Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan layer, often making up most of the dry weight of the wall, that may be twenty to eighty nanometres thick. Embedded in this layer are teichoic acids, negatively charged polymers of glycerol phosphate or ribitol phosphate. Some teichoic acids are linked to peptidoglycan, while lipoteichoic acids are anchored to the cytoplasmic membrane. These molecules contribute to the negative surface charge of the cell and help regulate cell growth and ion movement. Gram-positive bacteria do not have an outer membrane.

Gram-negative bacteria have a more complex envelope. Their peptidoglycan layer is thin, only a few nanometres, and lies within the periplasmic space between the cytoplasmic membrane and a second lipid bilayer, the outer membrane. The inner leaflet of the outer membrane contains phospholipids, while the outer leaflet contains lipopolysaccharide, abbreviated LPS. LPS consists of lipid A, a core polysaccharide, and an O-specific polysaccharide chain. Lipid A is an endotoxin: when released from bacteria, it can trigger strong inflammatory responses, fever, and in severe infections septic shock. The O-polysaccharide varies between strains and is used to classify them serologically. The outer membrane is a permeability barrier against many hydrophobic compounds and large molecules, although small hydrophilic molecules can pass through protein channels called porins. Lipoproteins link the outer membrane to the peptidoglycan layer.

The Gram stain, developed by Hans Christian Gram in 1884, distinguishes these two groups and remains one of the most widely used procedures in microbiology. A heat-fixed smear of bacteria is first flooded with crystal violet, the primary stain, which colours all cells purple. Iodine is then applied as a mordant; it combines with crystal violet to form a large crystal violet-iodine complex within the cells. The smear is next treated with a decolourizer, usually ethanol or an acetone-alcohol mixture. This is the critical step. In Gram-positive cells, the decolourizer dehydrates the thick peptidoglycan layer, shrinking its pores and trapping the dye complex, so the cells remain purple. In Gram-negative cells, the decolourizer dissolves lipids of the outer membrane and the thin peptidoglycan cannot retain the complex, so the cells lose the purple colour. Finally, a counterstain, typically safranin, is applied, which colours the decolourized Gram-negative cells pink or red.

Correct technique is necessary for reliable results. Excessive decolourization can make Gram-positive cells appear Gram-negative, while insufficient decolourization can make Gram-negative cells appear Gram-positive. Old cultures can also give misleading results, because ageing Gram-positive cells may lose wall integrity and stain variably. Smears that are too thick may not decolourize evenly. For these reasons, laboratories use fresh cultures and include known positive and negative control organisms.

Some bacteria do not fit the Gram classification well. Mycobacteria, including the agent of tuberculosis, have walls rich in mycolic acids, long-chain waxy lipids that make them resistant to the Gram procedure. They are identified using the acid-fast stain, in which carbol fuchsin is driven into the cells by heat and resists decolourization by acid alcohol. Mycoplasmas lack a cell wall entirely and therefore do not stain by the Gram method and are naturally resistant to antibiotics that target wall synthesis.

The structure of the wall has direct clinical significance. Beta-lactam antibiotics such as penicillins and cephalosporins bind to penicillin-binding proteins and block the cross-linking of peptidoglycan, weakening the wall so that growing cells lyse. Vancomycin binds to peptidoglycan precursors and also prevents wall assembly, but it is too large to cross the outer membrane, so it is mainly effective against Gram-positive bacteria. The enzyme lysozyme, present in tears and saliva, breaks the bonds between the sugars of peptidoglycan and acts more readily on Gram-positive bacteria, whose peptidoglycan is exposed. A Gram stain of a clinical specimen can therefore give clinicians rapid preliminary information that guides early antibiotic choice while culture results are awaited.
summary:
The bacterial cell wall lies outside the cytoplasmic membrane, determines cell shape, and prevents osmotic lysis. Its main component is peptidoglycan, a cross-linked mesh of N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetylmuramic acid chains with peptide bridges, which is absent from human cells and therefore a key antibiotic target. Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan layer containing teichoic and lipoteichoic acids and lack an outer membrane. Gram-negative bacteria have a thin peptidoglycan layer in the periplasm and an outer membrane containing lipopolysaccharide, whose lipid A is an endotoxin and whose O-polysaccharide varies serologically; the outer membrane restricts many molecules, while porins admit small hydrophilic ones.

The Gram stain applies crystal violet, an iodine mordant forming a dye complex, a decolourizer, and a safranin counterstain. Thick Gram-positive walls retain the complex and stay purple, while Gram-negative cells lose it and appear pink. Over- or under-decolourization, old cultures, and thick smears can cause errors, so fresh cultures and controls are used. Mycobacteria with mycolic acids require acid-fast staining, and wall-less mycoplasmas do not Gram stain. Wall structure explains the action of beta-lactams on peptidoglycan cross-linking, vancomycin's limited effect on Gram-negative bacteria, and lysozyme's action, and Gram stains guide early antibiotic choices.

It lies outside the cytoplasmic membrane and gives the cell its characteristic shape, whether spherical cocci, rod-shaped bacilli, or spiral forms. More importantly, it protects the cell from osmotic lysis. Bacterial cytoplasm contains a high concentration of dissolved solutes, so water tends to flow into the cell. Without a rigid wall, most bacteria living in dilute environments would swell and burst. Differences in wall structure also determine how bacteria react to stains, how they interact with the immune system, and which antibiotics can affect them.

The main structural component of most bacterial cell walls is peptidoglycan, also called murein. Peptidoglycan is a mesh-like polymer made of long glycan chains composed of alternating sugar derivatives, N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetylmuramic acid, joined by beta-1,4 glycosidic bonds. A short peptide chain is attached to each N-acetylmuramic acid residue, and peptides on adjacent glycan strands are cross-linked to one another. This cross-linking produces a strong, continuous network surrounding the cell, sometimes described as a single giant molecule. Because peptidoglycan is found in bacteria but not in human cells, the enzymes that build it are excellent targets for antibiotics.

Bacteria are divided into two major groups according to their wall architecture. Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan layer, often making up most of the dry weight of the wall, that may be twenty to eighty nanometres thick. Embedded in this layer are teichoic acids, negatively charged polymers of glycerol phosphate or ribitol phosphate. Some teichoic acids are linked to peptidoglycan, while lipoteichoic acids are anchored to the cytoplasmic membrane. These molecules contribute to the negative surface charge of the cell and help regulate cell growth and ion movement. Gram-positive bacteria do not have an outer membrane.

Gram-negative bacteria have a more complex envelope. Their peptidoglycan layer is thin, only a few nanometres, and lies within the periplasmic space between the cytoplasmic membrane and a second lipid bilayer, the outer membrane. The inner leaflet of the outer membrane contains phospholipids, while the outer leaflet contains lipopolysaccharide, abbreviated LPS. LPS consists of lipid A, a core polysaccharide, and an O-specific polysaccharide chain. Lipid A is an endotoxin: when released from bacteria, it can trigger strong inflammatory responses, fever, and in severe infections septic shock. The O-polysaccharide varies between strains and is used to classify them serologically. The outer membrane is a permeability barrier against many hydrophobic compounds and large molecules, although small hydrophilic molecules can pass through protein channels called porins. Lipoproteins link the outer membrane to the peptidoglycan layer.

The Gram stain, developed by Hans Christian Gram in 1884, distinguishes these two groups and remains one of the most widely used procedures in microbiology. A heat-fixed smear of bacteria is first flooded with crystal violet, the primary stain, which colours all cells purple. Iodine is then applied as a mordant; it combines with crystal violet to form a large crystal violet-iodine complex within the cells. The smear is next treated with a decolourizer, usually ethanol or an acetone-alcohol mixture. This is the critical step. In Gram-positive cells, the decolourizer dehydrates the thick peptidoglycan layer, shrinking its pores and trapping the dye complex, so the cells remain purple. In Gram-negative cells, the decolourizer dissolves lipids of the outer membrane and the thin peptidoglycan cannot retain the complex, so the cells lose the purple colour. Finally, a counterstain, typically safranin, is applied, which colours the decolourized Gram-negative cells pink or red.

Correct technique is necessary for reliable results. Excessive decolourization can make Gram-positive cells appear Gram-negative, while insufficient decolourization can make Gram-negative cells appear Gram-positive. Old cultures can also give misleading results, because ageing Gram-positive cells may lose wall integrity and stain variably. Smears that are too thick may not decolourize evenly. For these reasons, laboratories use fresh cultures and include known positive and negative control organisms.

Some bacteria do not fit the Gram classification well. Mycobacteria, including the agent of tuberculosis, have walls rich in mycolic acids, long-chain waxy lipids that make them resistant to the Gram procedure. They are identified using the acid-fast stain, in which carbol fuchsin is driven into the cells by heat and resists decolourization by acid alcohol. Mycoplasmas lack a cell wall entirely and therefore do not stain by the Gram method and are naturally resistant to antibiotics that target wall synthesis.

The structure of the wall has direct clinical significance. Beta-lactam antibiotics such as penicillins and cephalosporins bind to penicillin-binding proteins and block the cross-linking of peptidoglycan, weakening the wall so that growing cells lyse. Vancomycin binds to peptidoglycan precursors and also prevents wall assembly, but it is too large to cross the outer membrane, so it is mainly effective against Gram-positive bacteria. The enzyme lysozyme, present in tears and saliva, breaks the bonds between the sugars of peptidoglycan and acts more readily on Gram-positive bacteria, whose peptidoglycan is exposed. A Gram stain of a clinical specimen can therefore give clinicians rapid preliminary information that guides early antibiotic choice while culture results are awaited.

Its main component is peptidoglycan, a cross-linked mesh of N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetylmuramic acid chains with peptide bridges, which is absent from human cells and therefore a key antibiotic target. source_text:
Max Weber, the German sociologist and political economist who lived from 1864 to 1920, developed one of the most influential theories of organization. Writing during a period of rapid industrialization and expansion of the modern state, Weber sought to explain how large organizations could coordinate the work of many people efficiently and predictably. He described bureaucracy as an ideal type of organization based on rational-legal authority and argued that it was technically superior to other forms of administration. Although the word bureaucracy is often used today to mean inefficiency and excessive paperwork, Weber used it in a neutral, analytical sense.

Weber's theory of bureaucracy is rooted in his classification of authority, which he defined as legitimate power that people accept as rightful. He identified three pure types of legitimate authority. Traditional authority rests on established customs and the sanctity of long-standing traditions, as in hereditary monarchies or patriarchal family enterprises, where people obey because things have always been done that way. Charismatic authority rests on devotion to the exceptional qualities of an individual leader, such as a religious prophet, a revolutionary hero, or a visionary founder; it is powerful but unstable, because it depends on the leader's continued success and may not survive the leader's departure. Rational-legal authority rests on belief in the legality of formally enacted rules and the right of those appointed under such rules to issue commands. People obey the office and the rules, not the person. Weber argued that rational-legal authority was increasingly dominant in modern societies and that bureaucracy was its purest administrative expression.

Weber identified several characteristics of the ideal-type bureaucracy. First, there is a clear division of labour, with official duties fixed and distributed among positions according to rules, so that each office has a defined sphere of competence. Second, offices are arranged in a hierarchy of authority, in which each lower office is under the control and supervision of a higher one, creating a clear chain of command and a system of appeals. Third, the organization operates according to a consistent system of abstract rules and procedures that govern decisions and ensure uniformity regardless of who occupies a position. Fourth, administration is based on written documents, or files, which provide a record of decisions and ensure continuity. Fifth, officials conduct their work impersonally, treating cases according to rules without hatred, passion, affection, or personal favouritism. Sixth, employment is based on technical qualifications, typically demonstrated through education, examinations, or certificates, rather than on family connections or political loyalty. Seventh, officials are full-time, salaried employees who follow a career with promotion based on seniority, achievement, or both, and who enjoy security of tenure. Finally, there is a separation between the official position and personal ownership; officials do not own the means of administration or their offices, and organizational property is separate from personal property.

Weber argued that these characteristics made bureaucracy the most efficient form of administration for large-scale tasks. Its advantages included precision, speed, unambiguity, knowledge of the files, continuity, discretion, unity, strict subordination, and reduction of friction and of material and personal costs. Bureaucracy also promoted fairness and equality before the rules, since decisions were supposed to be based on objective criteria rather than personal relationships. The recruitment of officials based on merit replaced patronage and nepotism, which had characterized many earlier administrations. These principles continue to underpin modern civil services, courts, universities, hospitals, and large corporations.

At the same time, Weber was deeply concerned about the consequences of bureaucratization. He used the image of an iron cage to describe how the rational, rule-bound organization of modern life could constrain human freedom and creativity, subordinating individuals to impersonal systems. He also worried about the concentration of power in the hands of bureaucratic officials, who possess expert knowledge and control information, potentially escaping political control.

Later scholars identified practical problems in bureaucracies, often called bureaucratic dysfunctions. Robert Merton described goal displacement, in which officials become so focused on following rules that conformity becomes an end in itself rather than a means to achieve organizational goals, leading to rigidity and trained incapacity to respond to unusual cases. Excessive formalization can produce red tape, delays, and resistance to change. Strict specialization can create narrow perspectives and poor coordination between departments. Impersonality, intended to ensure fairness, can make organizations seem cold and unresponsive to clients. Hierarchical communication can be slow and distort information as it passes through many levels. In addition, bureaucracies may grow in size and complexity beyond what their tasks require.

Weber's theory remains relevant in contemporary management. Many organizations still rely on formal rules, hierarchical structures, merit-based recruitment, and documented procedures to ensure accountability and consistency, particularly in public administration and regulated industries. At the same time, environments characterized by rapid change, innovation, and complex customer demands have encouraged flatter, more flexible, and team-based structures that reduce some bureaucratic features. Researchers such as Burns and Stalker showed that mechanistic, bureaucratic structures suit stable environments, while organic structures suit dynamic ones. Modern management thus often seeks a balance, retaining the strengths of bureaucracy, such as fairness, predictability, and accountability, while avoiding excessive rigidity.
summary:
Max Weber analysed bureaucracy as an ideal type of organization based on rational-legal authority, viewing it neutrally as technically superior for large-scale administration. He distinguished traditional authority based on custom, unstable charismatic authority based on a leader's exceptional qualities, and rational-legal authority based on formally enacted rules and offices, which dominates modern societies.

Ideal-type bureaucracy has a rule-based division of labour, a hierarchy of offices, consistent abstract rules, written files, impersonal conduct, selection by technical qualifications, full-time salaried careers with promotion and tenure, and separation of office from personal ownership. Weber argued these features provide precision, speed, continuity, discretion, reduced friction and costs, and fairness, replacing patronage with merit, and they underpin civil services, courts, universities, hospitals, and corporations. He also feared an "iron cage" constraining freedom and the power of expert officials. Later critics such as Merton identified dysfunctions including goal displacement, rigidity, red tape, narrow specialization, coldness toward clients, slow distorted communication, and excessive growth. Bureaucratic principles remain important for accountability and consistency, especially in public and regulated sectors, but dynamic environments favour flatter, team-based organic structures, as Burns and Stalker showed, so modern management balances bureaucratic strengths against rigidity.

source_text:
Irrigation supplies water to crops when rainfall is insufficient or poorly timed. Traditional surface methods, such as flood, basin, and furrow irrigation, distribute water across the field by gravity. They require little equipment but often have low efficiency, because water is lost through deep percolation below the root zone, surface runoff, and evaporation, and because uneven application leaves some parts of the field over-watered and others under-watered. As water becomes scarcer and more expensive, pressurized methods, mainly sprinkler and drip irrigation, are increasingly used to deliver water more precisely.

Sprinkler irrigation applies water as a spray that falls on the crop and soil surface somewhat like natural rain. A pump supplies water under pressure to a network of main and lateral pipes, and sprinkler heads or nozzles break the flow into droplets and distribute them over a circular or rectangular area. System types include portable or hand-move systems, solid-set systems with permanently placed laterals, travelling guns, and mechanized systems such as centre pivots, in which a long lateral line mounted on wheeled towers rotates around a central point and can irrigate large circular fields with little labour.

Sprinkler systems have several advantages. They can be used on sloping or uneven land without levelling, on soils too sandy for surface irrigation, and for light, frequent applications that help seedlings establish. They can also be used to apply fertilizers dissolved in water and, in some cases, to protect crops from frost. However, their performance depends strongly on design and operating conditions. Wind distorts the spray pattern and causes drift, reducing uniformity. Evaporation from droplets and wet foliage can be significant in hot, dry weather. Wetting of leaves may encourage some foliar diseases. Energy is needed to maintain pressure, and if the application rate exceeds the soil's infiltration rate, water ponds and runs off.

Drip irrigation, also called trickle or micro-irrigation, delivers water slowly and directly to the root zone through emitters placed along small-diameter polyethylene laterals laid on the soil surface or buried below it. Emitters typically discharge from one to several litres per hour. Water spreads from each emitter through the soil by capillary action and gravity, forming a wetted bulb whose shape depends on soil texture: sandy soils produce narrow, deep bulbs, while clay soils produce wider, shallower ones. A complete system includes a water source and pump, a head unit with filters, pressure regulators, and often a fertilizer injector, followed by main lines, sub-main lines, laterals, and emitters. Pressure-compensating emitters maintain nearly constant discharge across a range of pressures, which improves uniformity on long laterals and slopes.

The main advantage of drip irrigation is high water use efficiency. Because water is applied only near plants and at low rates, losses to runoff, deep percolation, and evaporation from wet soil surfaces are small, and weeds between rows receive less water. Application efficiencies of about 85 to 95 percent are commonly reported for well-managed drip systems, compared with roughly 70 to 80 percent for sprinklers and often much less for surface methods. Frequent small applications maintain soil moisture close to optimal levels, which can increase yields and improve quality, especially for high-value horticultural crops, orchards, and vegetables. Fertigation, the application of fertilizers through the drip system, delivers nutrients directly to the root zone in small doses, improving nutrient uptake and reducing leaching. Drip systems also keep foliage dry and can use slightly saline water more safely, because continuous moisture near the emitter keeps salts at the edge of the wetted zone.

Drip irrigation also has limitations. Its initial cost is relatively high, which can be a barrier for smallholder farmers. Emitters can clog because of suspended particles, chemical precipitation of calcium carbonate or iron, or biological growth such as algae and bacterial slime. Clogging is prevented by appropriate filtration with screen, disc, or sand media filters, regular flushing of laterals, and periodic chemical treatment such as acid injection or chlorination. Salts can accumulate at the margins of wetted zones and may need to be leached by rainfall or occasional heavier irrigation. Rodents and farm operations can damage lateral pipes, and the system requires careful management and maintenance.

Choosing between sprinkler and drip irrigation depends on the crop, soil, topography, water quality, labour availability, energy cost, and capital available. Closely spaced field crops such as wheat or forage are often irrigated by sprinklers, while widely spaced row crops, vegetables, and orchards are well suited to drip. In both systems, irrigation scheduling determines how much water to apply and when. Scheduling can be based on estimates of crop evapotranspiration calculated from weather data and crop coefficients, on soil moisture measurements using tensiometers or capacitance sensors, or on plant-based indicators. Good scheduling ensures that the potential efficiency of pressurized irrigation is actually realized in the field.

source_text:
Morphology is the branch of linguistics that studies the internal structure of words and the rules by which words are formed. Speakers of a language know, usually without being aware of it, that the word unhappiness can be divided into the parts un-, happy, and -ness, and that each part contributes to the meaning of the whole. They can also understand and create new words they have never heard before, such as un-Googleable, by applying the word formation processes of their language. Morphology describes this knowledge.

The basic unit of morphology is the morpheme, the smallest unit of language that carries meaning or grammatical function. The word cats contains two morphemes, cat and the plural marker -s. Morphemes are classified as free or bound. Free morphemes can stand alone as words, such as book, run, and quick. Bound morphemes cannot occur on their own and must be attached to other morphemes; examples include the prefix re-, the suffix -ful, and the plural -s. Some bound morphemes are bound roots, which carry the main meaning of a word but cannot stand alone, such as -ceive in receive and perceive.

Bound morphemes that attach to other forms are called affixes. Prefixes are attached before a base, as in un-, pre-, and dis-, while suffixes are attached after it, as in -ment, -ly, and -er. Some languages also use infixes, inserted within a word, and circumfixes, which surround a base. The base to which affixes are attached is called the stem, and the core morpheme carrying the principal meaning is the root.

Affixes are further divided into derivational and inflectional morphemes, a fundamental distinction in morphology. Derivational morphemes create new words, often by changing the meaning or the grammatical category of the base. Adding -ness to the adjective kind creates the noun kindness, adding -ize to the noun modern creates the verb modernize, and adding un- to happy creates the opposite meaning, unhappy. Derivational affixes in English can be prefixes or suffixes, and a word can contain several, as in nationalization. Inflectional morphemes, by contrast, do not create new words or change grammatical category; instead, they mark grammatical information such as number, tense, aspect, person, comparison, or possession. English has only eight inflectional suffixes: plural -s, possessive -'s, third-person singular present -s, past tense -ed, past participle -en or -ed, present participle -ing, comparative -er, and superlative -est. Inflectional suffixes typically appear at the end of a word, after any derivational suffixes, so the order modernizes is acceptable while modernsize is not.

Morphemes can have different forms in different contexts, called allomorphs. The English plural morpheme, for instance, is pronounced as s in cats, z in dogs, and iz in buses, depending on the final sound of the stem. The past tense morpheme similarly has the pronunciations t, d, and id, as in walked, played, and wanted. Some forms are irregular, such as the plural children or the past tense went, which must be learned individually.

Beyond affixation, languages use several other word formation processes. Compounding combines two or more free morphemes to form a new word, such as blackboard, toothbrush, and laptop. The meaning of a compound is often not fully predictable from its parts; a blackboard need not be black. In English compounds, the rightmost element usually determines the category and core meaning, so a houseboat is a kind of boat while a boathouse is a kind of house. Conversion, or zero derivation, changes the grammatical category of a word without adding an affix, as when the noun email becomes the verb to email, or the verb run becomes the noun a run.

Other processes create words by shortening or combining existing forms. Clipping shortens a longer word, as in lab from laboratory, exam from examination, and phone from telephone. Blending combines parts of two words, as in brunch from breakfast and lunch, smog from smoke and fog, and motel from motor and hotel. Acronyms are formed from the initial letters of a phrase and pronounced as words, such as NASA and UNESCO, while initialisms, such as BBC, are pronounced as individual letters. Back-formation creates a new word by removing what appears to be an affix, as when the verb edit was formed from editor. Borrowing introduces words from other languages; English has borrowed extensively from Latin, French, Greek, and many other languages, including words such as bungalow and jungle from languages of the Indian subcontinent. Coinage creates entirely new words, sometimes from brand names, such as xerox, and eponyms derive words from names, as with sandwich.

Languages differ in how they use morphology. Isolating languages, such as Mandarin Chinese, use few affixes, with most words consisting of single morphemes and grammatical relations expressed by word order and separate words. Agglutinative languages, such as Turkish and Swahili, build words by stringing together many affixes, each with a clear meaning. Fusional languages, such as Latin and Russian, use affixes that combine several grammatical meanings in a single form. Bengali shows extensive inflection for case and verb forms. These differences make morphology central to the comparison of languages, to language learning, and to computational applications such as spell checking and machine translation.

Lecture material:
Morphology is the branch of linguistics that studies the internal structure of words and the rules by which words are formed. Speakers of a language know, usually without being aware of it, that the word unhappiness can be divided into the parts un-, happy, and -ness, and that each part contributes to the meaning of the whole. They can also understand and create new words they have never heard before, such as un-Googleable, by applying the word formation processes of their language. Morphology describes this knowledge.

The basic unit of morphology is the morpheme, the smallest unit of language that carries meaning or grammatical function. The word cats contains two morphemes, cat and the plural marker -s. Morphemes are classified as free or bound. Free morphemes can stand alone as words, such as book, run, and quick. Bound morphemes cannot occur on their own and must be attached to other morphemes; examples include the prefix re-, the suffix -ful, and the plural -s. Some bound morphemes are bound roots, which carry the main meaning of a word but cannot stand alone, such as -ceive in receive and perceive.

Bound morphemes that attach to other forms are called affixes. Prefixes are attached before a base, as in un-, pre-, and dis-, while suffixes are attached after it, as in -ment, -ly, and -er. Some languages also use infixes, inserted within a word, and circumfixes, which surround a base. The base to which affixes are attached is called the stem, and the core morpheme carrying the principal meaning is the root.

Affixes are further divided into derivational and inflectional morphemes, a fundamental distinction in morphology. Derivational morphemes create new words, often by changing the meaning or the grammatical category of the base. Adding -ness to the adjective kind creates the noun kindness, adding -ize to the noun modern creates the verb modernize, and adding un- to happy creates the opposite meaning, unhappy. Derivational affixes in English can be prefixes or suffixes, and a word can contain several, as in nationalization. Inflectional morphemes, by contrast, do not create new words or change grammatical category; instead, they mark grammatical information such as number, tense, aspect, person, comparison, or possession. English has only eight inflectional suffixes: plural -s, possessive -'s, third-person singular present -s, past tense -ed, past participle -en or -ed, present participle -ing, comparative -er, and superlative -est. Inflectional suffixes typically appear at the end of a word, after any derivational suffixes, so the order modernizes is acceptable while modernsize is not.

Morphemes can have different forms in different contexts, called allomorphs. The English plural morpheme, for instance, is pronounced as s in cats, z in dogs, and iz in buses, depending on the final sound of the stem. The past tense morpheme similarly has the pronunciations t, d, and id, as in walked, played, and wanted. Some forms are irregular, such as the plural children or the past tense went, which must be learned individually.

Beyond affixation, languages use several other word formation processes. Compounding combines two or more free morphemes to form a new word, such as blackboard, toothbrush, and laptop. The meaning of a compound is often not fully predictable from its parts; a blackboard need not be black. In English compounds, the rightmost element usually determines the category and core meaning, so a houseboat is a kind of boat while a boathouse is a kind of house. Conversion, or zero derivation, changes the grammatical category of a word without adding an affix, as when the noun email becomes the verb to email, or the verb run becomes the noun a run.

Other processes create words by shortening or combining existing forms. Clipping shortens a longer word, as in lab from laboratory, exam from examination, and phone from telephone. Blending combines parts of two words, as in brunch from breakfast and lunch, smog from smoke and fog, and motel from motor and hotel. Acronyms are formed from the initial letters of a phrase and pronounced as words, such as NASA and UNESCO, while initialisms, such as BBC, are pronounced as individual letters. Back-formation creates a new word by removing what appears to be an affix, as when the verb edit was formed from editor. Borrowing introduces words from other languages; English has borrowed extensively from Latin, French, Greek, and many other languages, including words such as bungalow and jungle from languages of the Indian subcontinent. Coinage creates entirely new words, sometimes from brand names, such as xerox, and eponyms derive words from names, as with sandwich.

Languages differ in how they use morphology. Isolating languages, such as Mandarin Chinese, use few affixes, with most words consisting of single morphemes and grammatical relations expressed by word order and separate words. Agglutinative languages, such as Turkish and Swahili, build words by stringing together many affixes, each with a clear meaning. Fusional languages, such as Latin and Russian, use affixes that combine several grammatical meanings in a single form. Bengali shows extensive inflection for case and verb forms. source_text:
Most of the electrical energy used in the world is produced by synchronous generators, also called alternators, driven by steam turbines, gas turbines, hydraulic turbines, or diesel engines. A synchronous generator converts mechanical power into alternating-current electrical power at a frequency that is fixed by the speed of rotation. Understanding how these machines produce voltage and how their terminal voltage changes with load is basic to the operation of power stations and electrical grids.

A synchronous generator has two main parts. The stator, which is stationary, carries a three-phase armature winding distributed in slots around its inner surface; the generated power is taken from this winding. The rotor carries a field winding supplied with direct current through slip rings or, in brushless designs, from a small exciter mounted on the same shaft. The direct current creates a magnetic field that rotates with the rotor. As this field sweeps past the stator conductors, it induces alternating voltages in the three phases, displaced from one another by 120 electrical degrees.

The electrical frequency is linked to mechanical speed by the relation f equals P times n divided by 120, where f is frequency in hertz, P is the number of magnetic poles on the rotor, and n is speed in revolutions per minute. A two-pole generator must therefore run at 3,000 rpm to supply 50 hertz, while a hydroelectric generator with many poles can produce the same frequency at a much lower speed. This fixed relationship is why the machine is called synchronous. Rotor construction reflects these speeds: high-speed turbine generators use cylindrical, or round, rotors with two or four poles to withstand large centrifugal forces, whereas slow-speed hydro generators use salient-pole rotors with many projecting poles.

The internally generated voltage, often written as E, is proportional to the speed and to the magnetic flux produced by the field current. At constant speed, increasing the field current raises E until the iron begins to saturate. The relationship between field current and generated voltage at no load is described by the open-circuit characteristic, which is linear at first and then bends as saturation sets in.

When the generator supplies a load, current flows in the stator winding and the terminal voltage V differs from E. Part of the difference arises from the small resistance of the winding, but the dominant effect is the synchronous reactance. Stator current produces its own magnetic field, a phenomenon called armature reaction, which combines with the field of the rotor and alters the net flux. Together with the leakage reactance of the winding, armature reaction is represented in the simple per-phase equivalent circuit by a synchronous reactance in series with E. The phasor relation is that E equals V plus the voltage drops across the armature resistance and the synchronous reactance.

The effect of load on terminal voltage depends strongly on power factor. With a lagging power factor, typical of loads containing induction motors, the reactive voltage drop is oriented so that the terminal voltage falls considerably below the internal voltage. With a unity power factor load the fall is smaller, and with a leading power factor load, such as one dominated by capacitors, the terminal voltage can actually rise above E. Voltage regulation quantifies this behaviour. It is defined as the no-load voltage minus the full-load voltage, divided by the full-load voltage, usually expressed as a percentage, with the field current and speed held constant. Lagging loads therefore produce positive and relatively large regulation, while leading loads can produce negative regulation.

Because synchronous reactance cannot be measured directly under operating conditions, it is often estimated from an open-circuit test and a short-circuit test. In the short-circuit test, the stator terminals are short-circuited and the field current is increased until rated armature current flows. Dividing the open-circuit voltage by the short-circuit current at the same field current gives an approximate synchronous impedance. Methods such as the electromotive force method, the magnetomotive force method, and the zero power factor method use these test results to predict regulation, with differing accuracy because of saturation.

In practice, generators must deliver a nearly constant voltage despite changing loads. An automatic voltage regulator continuously measures the terminal voltage and adjusts the field current: when voltage falls under a heavy lagging load, the regulator increases excitation, and when voltage rises, it reduces excitation. In a large interconnected system, where many generators run in parallel and the grid voltage and frequency are largely fixed, changing the field current of one machine mainly alters the reactive power it supplies. An over-excited generator delivers reactive power and operates at a lagging power factor, while an under-excited generator absorbs reactive power. The real power delivered, by contrast, is controlled by the mechanical input from the prime mover through the turbine governor.

Lecture material:
Most of the electrical energy used in the world is produced by synchronous generators, also called alternators, driven by steam turbines, gas turbines, hydraulic turbines, or diesel engines. A synchronous generator converts mechanical power into alternating-current electrical power at a frequency that is fixed by the speed of rotation. Understanding how these machines produce voltage and how their terminal voltage changes with load is basic to the operation of power stations and electrical grids.

A synchronous generator has two main parts. The stator, which is stationary, carries a three-phase armature winding distributed in slots around its inner surface; the generated power is taken from this winding. The rotor carries a field winding supplied with direct current through slip rings or, in brushless designs, from a small exciter mounted on the same shaft. The direct current creates a magnetic field that rotates with the rotor. As this field sweeps past the stator conductors, it induces alternating voltages in the three phases, displaced from one another by 120 electrical degrees.

The electrical frequency is linked to mechanical speed by the relation f equals P times n divided by 120, where f is frequency in hertz, P is the number of magnetic poles on the rotor, and n is speed in revolutions per minute. A two-pole generator must therefore run at 3,000 rpm to supply 50 hertz, while a hydroelectric generator with many poles can produce the same frequency at a much lower speed. This fixed relationship is why the machine is called synchronous. Rotor construction reflects these speeds: high-speed turbine generators use cylindrical, or round, rotors with two or four poles to withstand large centrifugal forces, whereas slow-speed hydro generators use salient-pole rotors with many projecting poles.

The internally generated voltage, often written as E, is proportional to the speed and to the magnetic flux produced by the field current. At constant speed, increasing the field current raises E until the iron begins to saturate. The relationship between field current and generated voltage at no load is described by the open-circuit characteristic, which is linear at first and then bends as saturation sets in.

When the generator supplies a load, current flows in the stator winding and the terminal voltage V differs from E. Part of the difference arises from the small resistance of the winding, but the dominant effect is the synchronous reactance. Stator current produces its own magnetic field, a phenomenon called armature reaction, which combines with the field of the rotor and alters the net flux. Together with the leakage reactance of the winding, armature reaction is represented in the simple per-phase equivalent circuit by a synchronous reactance in series with E. The phasor relation is that E equals V plus the voltage drops across the armature resistance and the synchronous reactance.

The effect of load on terminal voltage depends strongly on power factor. With a lagging power factor, typical of loads containing induction motors, the reactive voltage drop is oriented so that the terminal voltage falls considerably below the internal voltage. With a unity power factor load the fall is smaller, and with a leading power factor load, such as one dominated by capacitors, the terminal voltage can actually rise above E. Voltage regulation quantifies this behaviour. It is defined as the no-load voltage minus the full-load voltage, divided by the full-load voltage, usually expressed as a percentage, with the field current and speed held constant. Lagging loads therefore produce positive and relatively large regulation, while leading loads can produce negative regulation.

source_text:
Why are some industries consistently more profitable than others? Airlines have often struggled to earn their cost of capital, while industries such as branded soft drinks or certain software segments have generated high returns for long periods. Michael Porter's five forces framework, introduced in 1979, explains these differences by analysing the structure of an industry. Porter argued that profitability is not determined only by how fiercely existing firms compete, but by five competitive forces that together determine how much of the value created in an industry the firms can capture as profit.

The first force is rivalry among existing competitors. Rivalry is intense when there are many competitors of similar size, when industry growth is slow so that firms can grow only by taking share from rivals, when products are undifferentiated so that customers switch easily, and when fixed costs are high, which pushes firms to cut prices to fill capacity. High exit barriers, such as specialized assets or long-term labour obligations, also keep struggling firms in the industry and sustain rivalry. Rivalry that takes the form of price competition is particularly damaging to profitability, because it transfers value directly to customers, whereas competition on product features or service may expand demand.

The second force is the threat of new entrants. Even if an industry currently has few competitors, the possibility that new firms may enter limits the prices incumbents can charge. The strength of this threat depends on barriers to entry. These include economies of scale, which force newcomers to enter at large scale or accept a cost disadvantage; large capital requirements; strong brand loyalty and product differentiation; access to distribution channels; government licensing and regulation; network effects, where a product becomes more valuable as more people use it; and switching costs faced by customers. Expected retaliation by incumbents can also deter entry.

The third force is the bargaining power of suppliers. Powerful suppliers can capture value by charging higher prices, limiting quality, or shifting costs to industry participants. Suppliers are powerful when they are more concentrated than the industry they sell to, when their product is differentiated or essential, when buyers face high costs in switching suppliers, when there are no good substitutes for what they provide, and when they could credibly integrate forward into the industry themselves. A small number of firms supplying critical components or specialized labour may therefore earn a large share of an industry's value.

The fourth force is the bargaining power of buyers. Buyers, whether consumers or business customers, can force down prices or demand better quality and service. Their power is greater when they are few in number or purchase in large volumes, when the industry's products are standardized, when switching costs are low, when buyers could integrate backward and produce the product themselves, and when they are price-sensitive because the product represents a large share of their costs. Large retail chains, for instance, often exercise considerable power over manufacturers of packaged goods.

The fifth force is the threat of substitute products or services. Substitutes perform the same or a similar function through a different means, such as video conferencing as a substitute for business travel or mobile banking as a substitute for visits to bank branches. Substitutes place a ceiling on the prices an industry can charge, because if prices rise too high, customers move to the alternative. The threat is strongest when the substitute offers an attractive price-performance trade-off and when customers' switching costs are low. Substitutes are often overlooked because they come from outside the industry's traditional boundaries.

Analysing the five forces involves assessing each force as weak, moderate, or strong and explaining the underlying drivers. Industries in which all five forces are weak tend to be attractive, while industries in which several forces are strong tend to have low average profitability. The analysis can guide strategy in several ways. A firm may position itself where the forces are weakest, for example by serving customer segments that are less price-sensitive. It may seek to influence the forces, for instance by building switching costs, developing proprietary technology that raises entry barriers, or diversifying its supplier base. It may also anticipate how changes in technology, regulation, or consumer behaviour will shift the forces over time and act early.

The framework has limitations. It provides a largely static snapshot, whereas many industries change rapidly. Defining the boundaries of an industry can be difficult, and the result depends on that definition. The model emphasises competition and may underplay cooperation, such as alliances and the role of complementors, firms whose products increase the value of an industry's offerings, which some scholars have proposed as an additional force. It also focuses on industry-level conditions and says relatively little about the internal resources and capabilities that allow one firm to outperform others within the same industry. For these reasons, five forces analysis is usually combined with other tools, such as analysis of the macro-environment and of firm resources.

topic: Krashen's Hypotheses of Second Language Acquisition
source_text:
Second language acquisition is the field that studies how people learn a language other than their first. Among the many theories proposed in the late twentieth century, Stephen Krashen's Monitor Model became one of the most influential, particularly in language teaching. Krashen presented his ideas as five related hypotheses. Although several of them have been strongly criticized, they shaped communicative approaches to language teaching and continue to inform debates about how classroom instruction should be designed.

The first is the acquisition-learning hypothesis. Krashen distinguished between two independent ways of developing ability in a second language. Acquisition is a subconscious process similar to the way children pick up their first language; it occurs when learners use language for meaningful communication, and the resulting knowledge is implicit, so speakers may use structures correctly without being able to state the rules. Learning, in contrast, is a conscious process of studying the forms of the language, such as grammar rules and vocabulary lists, and produces explicit knowledge about the language. Krashen argued that acquisition, not learning, is responsible for fluent, spontaneous language use, and that learned knowledge does not turn into acquired knowledge.

The second is the monitor hypothesis, which describes the limited role of learned knowledge. According to Krashen, utterances are initiated by the acquired system, while conscious learning functions only as a monitor or editor that can check and correct output. The monitor can operate only when three conditions are met: the learner has enough time, is focused on form rather than meaning, and knows the relevant rule. These conditions are rarely satisfied together in ordinary conversation, though they may be met in written work or grammar tests. source_text:
Thermochemistry is the study of the heat absorbed or released during chemical reactions and physical changes. Most reactions involve a change in energy, because bonds are broken and new bonds are formed. These energy changes determine whether a fuel releases useful heat, how much cooling an industrial reactor requires, and how biological organisms obtain energy from food. Thermochemistry provides methods for measuring and calculating such changes even when they cannot be measured directly.

At constant pressure, the heat exchanged between a reacting system and its surroundings equals the change in enthalpy, written delta H. Enthalpy is a state function, which means that its value depends only on the current state of the system, defined by temperature, pressure, composition, and physical state, and not on the path by which that state was reached. A reaction that releases heat to the surroundings is exothermic and has a negative delta H; combustion of methane and the neutralization of acids by bases are examples. A reaction that absorbs heat is endothermic and has a positive delta H, as in the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate or the dissolution of ammonium nitrate in water.

Enthalpy changes are reported under standard conditions so that values from different sources can be compared. The standard state of a substance is its pure form at a pressure of one bar, and data are usually tabulated at 298 kelvin. The standard enthalpy of reaction, delta H degree, refers to the reaction occurring with all reactants and products in their standard states. Because enthalpy is an extensive property, its value depends on the amount of substance reacting. A thermochemical equation therefore shows the balanced chemical equation together with delta H for the amounts indicated, and the physical states of all species must be specified, because, for example, forming liquid water releases more heat than forming water vapour.

Thermochemical equations can be manipulated algebraically. If an equation is reversed, the sign of delta H is reversed. If the coefficients are multiplied by a factor, delta H is multiplied by the same factor. These rules follow directly from enthalpy being a state function and an extensive property.

Hess's law, formulated by Germain Hess in 1840, states that the total enthalpy change for a reaction is the same whether the reaction occurs in one step or in several steps. It is a consequence of enthalpy being a state function. Hess's law is extremely useful because many enthalpy changes cannot be measured directly. For example, the formation of carbon monoxide from carbon and oxygen cannot be carried out cleanly, because some carbon dioxide always forms as well. However, the enthalpies of combustion of carbon to carbon dioxide and of carbon monoxide to carbon dioxide can both be measured. By writing the combustion of carbon, then subtracting the combustion of carbon monoxide, which means reversing that equation, the target reaction is obtained, and its enthalpy change is found by the same combination of enthalpy values.

A particularly important application uses standard enthalpies of formation. The standard enthalpy of formation, delta Hf degree, of a compound is the enthalpy change when one mole of the compound is formed from its elements in their standard states. By definition, the standard enthalpy of formation of an element in its most stable form, such as oxygen gas or graphite, is zero. Using Hess's law, the standard enthalpy of any reaction can be calculated as the sum of the standard enthalpies of formation of the products, each multiplied by its stoichiometric coefficient, minus the corresponding sum for the reactants. Extensive tables of formation enthalpies therefore allow the enthalpy changes of thousands of reactions to be calculated without separate experiments.

Bond enthalpies provide another approach. The bond enthalpy is the energy required to break one mole of a particular type of bond in gaseous molecules. The enthalpy of a gas-phase reaction can be estimated as the total energy of bonds broken minus the total energy of bonds formed. Because tabulated bond enthalpies are averages over many different molecules, these estimates are approximate and less accurate than calculations based on formation enthalpies.

Experimental measurement of heat changes is carried out by calorimetry. In a simple coffee-cup calorimeter, a reaction in solution occurs at constant pressure, and the temperature change of the solution is measured. The heat absorbed or released is calculated from the mass of the solution, its specific heat capacity, and the temperature change, with corrections for heat absorbed by the container. A bomb calorimeter, used for combustion reactions, operates at constant volume and measures the change in internal energy, which can be converted to enthalpy. Combining calorimetric data with Hess's law forms the basis of the thermochemical tables used throughout chemistry and engineering.

source_text:
Slopes occur naturally in hillsides and riverbanks and are created artificially in road cuttings, embankments, earth dams, and excavations. Gravity continually tends to move soil downslope, and the soil resists this movement through its shear strength. Slope stability analysis evaluates whether the resisting forces are sufficiently larger than the driving forces to prevent failure. Landslides and embankment failures can destroy infrastructure and endanger lives, so stability assessment is a central task in geotechnical engineering.

The degree of safety is usually expressed by a factor of safety, defined as the ratio of the available shear strength of the soil to the shear stress required for equilibrium along a potential failure surface. A factor of safety of one indicates that the slope is on the verge of failure. Design values are higher to allow for uncertainty in soil properties, loading, and groundwater; values around 1.3 to 1.5 are commonly specified for permanent slopes, with the exact requirement depending on the consequences of failure and the quality of the site investigation.

The shear strength of soil is normally described by the Mohr-Coulomb criterion, in which strength equals cohesion plus the effective normal stress multiplied by the tangent of the angle of internal friction. The word effective is essential. Pore water pressure within the soil reduces the effective stress between particles and therefore reduces frictional strength. This is why many slope failures occur during or after heavy rainfall, rapid snowmelt, or a sudden drop in the water level of a reservoir or river: rising pore pressures lower effective stress, while the weight of saturated soil increases the driving force.

Slope failures take several forms. Rotational slides move along a curved, roughly circular surface and are typical of fairly uniform cohesive soils. Translational slides move along a planar surface parallel to the ground, often where a weak layer or the interface between soil and bedrock lies at a shallow depth. Flows involve soil behaving like a viscous fluid, as in mudflows in saturated fine-grained material, while falls and topples occur mainly in rock and very steep cuts. The appropriate method of analysis depends on which mechanism is plausible at a given site.

For a long slope with a shallow failure plane parallel to the surface, the infinite slope method provides a simple expression. In a dry cohesionless soil, the factor of safety equals the tangent of the friction angle divided by the tangent of the slope angle, so such a slope is stable only if it is flatter than the friction angle. When seepage occurs parallel to the slope, pore pressure reduces the effective stress and the factor of safety for a cohesionless soil is roughly halved, illustrating the strong influence of groundwater.

For rotational failures, engineers commonly use limit equilibrium methods based on slices. A trial circular failure surface is drawn, and the soil mass above it is divided into vertical slices. For each slice, the weight, the normal force on its base, the pore water pressure, and the available shear resistance are evaluated, and the factor of safety is obtained by comparing resisting and driving moments about the centre of the circle. The ordinary method of slices, also called the Fellenius method, neglects the forces between slices and tends to give conservative results. Bishop's simplified method includes horizontal interslice forces and usually gives more accurate values for circular surfaces, although it must be solved iteratively because the factor of safety appears on both sides of the equation. More rigorous methods, such as those of Spencer or Morgenstern and Price, satisfy both force and moment equilibrium and can analyse non-circular surfaces.

Because the critical failure surface is not known in advance, many trial surfaces must be examined, and the one with the lowest factor of safety governs the design. Computer programs search systematically over possible centres and radii or over non-circular shapes. Numerical methods such as finite element analysis offer an alternative by modelling stress and deformation directly; the strength reduction technique progressively lowers the soil strength until the model fails, giving a factor of safety without assuming a failure surface.

When analysis indicates inadequate stability, several remedial measures are available. Flattening the slope or removing material from the crest reduces the driving force, while placing a berm or counterweight at the toe increases resistance. Drainage measures, including surface ditches, horizontal drains, and relief wells, lower pore water pressures and are often the most cost-effective solution. Retaining walls, soil nailing, ground anchors, and piles provide structural support, and vegetation can reduce surface erosion and shallow instability. Monitoring with inclinometers and piezometers allows engineers to detect movement and rising groundwater before failure occurs.

Slopes occur naturally in hillsides and riverbanks and are created artificially in road cuttings, embankments, earth dams, and excavations. The shear strength of soil is normally described by the Mohr-Coulomb criterion, in which strength equals cohesion plus the effective normal stress multiplied by the tangent of the angle of internal friction. The word effective is essential. Pore water pressure within the soil reduces the effective stress between particles and therefore reduces frictional strength. Flows involve soil behaving like a viscous fluid, as in mudflows in saturated fine-grained material, while falls and topples occur mainly in rock and very steep cuts. The appropriate method of analysis depends on which mechanism is plausible at a given site.

For a long slope with a shallow failure plane parallel to the surface, the infinite slope method provides a simple expression. source_text:
Ophthalmic dosage forms are pharmaceutical preparations intended for application to the eye or its surrounding tissues. They are used to treat conditions such as glaucoma, bacterial and viral infections, allergic conjunctivitis, inflammation after surgery, and dry eye disease. Formulating medicines for the eye is challenging, because the eye is a sensitive organ with efficient protective mechanisms that rapidly remove applied drugs, and because any preparation must be sterile, comfortable, and non-irritating.

The anatomy and physiology of the eye strongly influence drug delivery. When a drop is instilled into the lower conjunctival sac, it mixes with the tear film, but the sac can hold only about 7 to 10 microlitres in addition to the normal tear volume, whereas a typical eye drop is 30 to 50 microlitres. Much of the instilled volume therefore overflows onto the cheek or drains through the nasolacrimal duct into the nasal cavity, from which it may be absorbed into the systemic circulation. Reflex tearing and blinking further dilute and wash away the drug. As a result, only a small fraction of a topically applied dose, often less than five percent, reaches the internal tissues of the eye.

The cornea is the main barrier to drug penetration into the anterior chamber. It consists of three principal layers with contrasting properties. The outer epithelium is lipophilic and has tight junctions, the middle stroma is hydrophilic and makes up most of the corneal thickness, and the inner endothelium is a single cell layer. A drug must therefore have a balance of lipophilic and hydrophilic properties to cross all layers efficiently. Many ophthalmic drugs are weak bases or acids whose degree of ionization, and therefore penetration, depends on pH.

Eye drops, or ophthalmic solutions, are the most common dosage form because they are easy to administer and do not interfere with vision. Formulation requires attention to several properties. Sterility is essential, since contaminated eye products can cause serious infections; solutions are sterilized by filtration or by heat when the drug is stable. Multi-dose containers contain antimicrobial preservatives, such as benzalkonium chloride, to prevent contamination after opening. Benzalkonium chloride is effective but can damage the corneal epithelium with long-term use, which has led to preservative-free single-dose units and specialized multi-dose bottles for patients who use drops frequently.

Tonicity and pH also affect comfort and stability. Tears are approximately isotonic with 0.9 percent sodium chloride, and solutions with tonicity roughly equivalent to 0.6 to 2.0 percent sodium chloride are generally tolerated. Tonicity agents such as sodium chloride or mannitol are added when needed. Tear fluid has a pH of about 7.4 and some buffering capacity. Although a pH close to that of tears is most comfortable, the pH chosen is often a compromise between comfort, drug solubility, and chemical stability, so many products use a weak buffer that tears can quickly neutralize. Viscosity-enhancing agents, such as hydroxypropyl methylcellulose or polyvinyl alcohol, increase the residence time of the solution on the eye surface and are also used alone as artificial tears.

Ophthalmic suspensions are used for drugs that are poorly soluble in water, such as some corticosteroids. Particle size must be very small, typically below about ten micrometres, to avoid irritation and to ensure uniform dosing, and patients must shake the container before use. Ophthalmic ointments, usually based on white petrolatum and mineral oil, provide prolonged contact time and protect the eye surface, and they are often used at night because they blur vision. Gels offer a compromise between solutions and ointments.

Several approaches have been developed to overcome rapid precorneal elimination. In situ gelling systems are liquids that turn into gels on contact with the eye in response to temperature, pH, or ions present in tears; gellan gum, for instance, gels in the presence of tear cations. Mucoadhesive polymers interact with the mucin layer of the tear film and prolong residence. Ocular inserts are solid or semi-solid devices placed in the conjunctival sac that release drug at a controlled rate. Nanoparticles, liposomes, and nanoemulsions can improve the penetration and retention of poorly soluble drugs. For diseases of the retina and other posterior segment tissues, which topical drops rarely reach in therapeutic concentrations, drugs are delivered by intravitreal injections or biodegradable implants.

Patients also influence the effectiveness of ophthalmic therapy. Correct technique involves washing hands, pulling down the lower eyelid to form a pocket, instilling one drop without touching the eye or lashes with the dropper tip, and closing the eye gently for about one to two minutes. Pressing on the inner corner of the eye, called nasolacrimal occlusion, reduces drainage into the nose, increasing ocular absorption and decreasing systemic side effects. When several eye medicines are prescribed, an interval of about five minutes between drops prevents the first from being washed out by the second.

The anatomy and physiology of the eye strongly influence drug delivery. When a drop is instilled into the lower conjunctival sac, it mixes with the tear film, but the sac can hold only about 7 to 10 microlitres in addition to the normal tear volume, whereas a typical eye drop is 30 to 50 microlitres. Much of the instilled volume therefore overflows onto the cheek or drains through the nasolacrimal duct into the nasal cavity, from which it may be absorbed into the systemic circulation. Reflex tearing and blinking further dilute and wash away the drug. As a result, only a small fraction of a topically applied dose, often less than five percent, reaches the internal tissues of the eye.

The cornea is the main barrier to drug penetration into the anterior chamber. It consists of three principal layers with contrasting properties. The outer epithelium is lipophilic and has tight junctions, the middle stroma is hydrophilic and makes up most of the corneal thickness, and the inner endothelium is a single cell layer. A drug must therefore have a balance of lipophilic and hydrophilic properties to cross all layers efficiently. Many ophthalmic drugs are weak bases or acids whose degree of ionization, and therefore penetration, depends on pH.

Eye drops, or ophthalmic solutions, are the most common dosage form because they are easy to administer and do not interfere with vision. Formulation requires attention to several properties. Sterility is essential, since contaminated eye products can cause serious infections; solutions are sterilized by filtration or by heat when the drug is stable. Multi-dose containers contain antimicrobial preservatives, such as benzalkonium chloride, to prevent contamination after opening. Benzalkonium chloride is effective but can damage the corneal epithelium with long-term use, which has led to preservative-free single-dose units and specialized multi-dose bottles for patients who use drops frequently.

Tonicity and pH also affect comfort and stability. Tears are approximately isotonic with 0.9 percent sodium chloride, and solutions with tonicity roughly equivalent to 0.6 to 2.0 percent sodium chloride are generally tolerated. Tonicity agents such as sodium chloride or mannitol are added when needed. Tear fluid has a pH of about 7.4 and some buffering capacity. Although a pH close to that of tears is most comfortable, the pH chosen is often a compromise between comfort, drug solubility, and chemical stability, so many products use a weak buffer that tears can quickly neutralize. Viscosity-enhancing agents, such as hydroxypropyl methylcellulose or polyvinyl alcohol, increase the residence time of the solution on the eye surface and are also used alone as artificial tears.

Ophthalmic suspensions are used for drugs that are poorly soluble in water, such as some corticosteroids. Particle size must be very small, typically below about ten micrometres, to avoid irritation and to ensure uniform dosing, and patients must shake the container before use. Ophthalmic ointments, usually based on white petrolatum and mineral oil, provide prolonged contact time and protect the eye surface, and they are often used at night because they blur vision. Gels offer a compromise between solutions and ointments.

Several approaches have been developed to overcome rapid precorneal elimination. In situ gelling systems are liquids that turn into gels on contact with the eye in response to temperature, pH, or ions present in tears; gellan gum, for instance, gels in the presence of tear cations. Mucoadhesive polymers interact with the mucin layer of the tear film and prolong residence. Ocular inserts are solid or semi-solid devices placed in the conjunctival sac that release drug at a controlled rate. Nanoparticles, liposomes, and nanoemulsions can improve the penetration and retention of poorly soluble drugs. For diseases of the retina and other posterior segment tissues, which topical drops rarely reach in therapeutic concentrations, drugs are delivered by intravitreal injections or biodegradable implants.

Patients also influence the effectiveness of ophthalmic therapy. Correct technique involves washing hands, pulling down the lower eyelid to form a pocket, instilling one drop without touching the eye or lashes with the dropper tip, and closing the eye gently for about one to two minutes. Pressing on the inner corner of the eye, called nasolacrimal occlusion, reduces drainage into the nose, increasing ocular absorption and decreasing systemic side effects. When several eye medicines are prescribed, an interval of about five minutes between drops prevents the first from being washed out by the second.<|im_end|>

topic: Linear Programming and the Simplex Method
source_text:
Linear programming is a mathematical method for choosing the best value of several decision variables when the objective and the restrictions on those variables can all be expressed as linear relationships. It is widely used to plan production, allocate budgets, design diets, schedule staff, and route goods, because many practical decisions involve maximizing profit or minimizing cost while respecting limited resources.

A linear programming model has three components. Decision variables represent the quantities to be chosen, such as the number of units of each product to manufacture. The objective function is a linear expression in these variables that is to be maximized or minimized, for example total profit equal to forty times the units of product A plus thirty times the units of product B. Constraints are linear inequalities or equations that limit the variables, such as the total machine hours used not exceeding the hours available. Non-negativity conditions are normally added because physical quantities cannot be negative.

The set of all points that satisfy every constraint is called the feasible region. In a problem with two decision variables, this region can be drawn on a graph as a polygon bounded by the constraint lines. The graphical method illustrates a fundamental property of linear programming: if an optimal solution exists, at least one optimal solution lies at a corner point, also called an extreme point or vertex, of the feasible region. This happens because the objective function is linear, so its value changes steadily in one direction across the region; moving parallel lines of equal objective value outward, the last point touched before leaving the region is a vertex. When the objective line is parallel to a boundary edge, every point along that edge may be optimal, giving multiple optimal solutions.

Not every model has a single finite optimum. A model is infeasible when the constraints contradict one another so that no point satisfies them all, as when one constraint requires x to be at least ten and another requires it to be at most five. A model is unbounded when the feasible region extends indefinitely in a direction that keeps improving the objective, which usually indicates that a real-world restriction has been omitted. Recognizing these cases is an important part of model validation.

The graphical method is impractical beyond two or three variables, so larger problems are solved with the simplex method developed by George Dantzig. The simplex method exploits the corner-point property: rather than examining every vertex, it moves from one vertex to an adjacent vertex that improves the objective, stopping when no adjacent move gives further improvement. To apply the algorithm, inequality constraints are first converted into equations. A slack variable is added to each less-than-or-equal constraint to represent unused resource, while a surplus variable is subtracted from each greater-than-or-equal constraint to represent the amount by which a requirement is exceeded.

The method is commonly organized in a tableau. At each stage, some variables are basic and take values determined by the constraint equations, while the remaining nonbasic variables are set to zero; each such combination corresponds to a vertex. In a maximization problem, the entering variable is chosen as a nonbasic variable whose coefficient in the objective row indicates that increasing it will raise the objective. The leaving variable is selected by the minimum ratio test, which divides the right-hand-side values by the positive coefficients in the entering column and chooses the smallest ratio. This test ensures that the next solution remains feasible. A pivot operation then updates the tableau, and the process repeats until no entering variable can improve the objective, at which point the current solution is optimal.

Starting the simplex method requires an initial feasible vertex. For constraints of the less-than-or-equal type with non-negative right-hand sides, the origin with all slack variables basic provides one. Other constraint types require artificial variables and techniques such as the two-phase method or the big-M method, which first drive the artificial variables to zero and then optimize the real objective.

Every linear program has an associated dual problem. If the original, or primal, problem maximizes profit subject to resource limits, the dual minimizes the total imputed value of those resources. The optimal dual variables, known as shadow prices, indicate how much the objective would improve if one more unit of a resource were available, provided the change stays within a certain range. Sensitivity analysis uses this information to determine how far objective coefficients or resource quantities can change before the optimal basis changes, which helps managers judge how robust a recommended plan is.

Linear programming relies on assumptions that must be checked. Proportionality and additivity require that contributions and resource use scale linearly and combine without interaction. Divisibility assumes variables may take fractional values; when only whole units make sense, integer programming is needed. Certainty assumes all coefficients are known exactly, which is rarely true, so results are best interpreted together with sensitivity analysis.
